One deck, seven boxes, 86 games

Kanasu's Adventure Game System

Fifty-four cards, a handful of dice and six pawns. Every card is a real child in the guise of an explorer, so the same deck can hold a 5-year-old’s first game, a family evening and a grown-up bluffing night. The games grow with the players: every one has three levels, from age 5 to adult.

Recommended games · All 86 games · How it came about

What is on a card

Every explorer has one face and appears on two cards, the twins. Everything printed on a card is there so that some game can use it.

  • 1Number, 1 to 9. Twins add to 9 (1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5). The nines pair with nines.
  • 2Nine-frame. The same number as dots out of nine.
  • 3Two border colours with a letter chip each: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.
  • 4Two suit medals: compass, hook and rope, binoculars, torch, tent, boots.
  • 5Face and name. A real child, drawn as an explorer.
  • 6Team. Tigers, Elephants, Bears, Monkeys, Peacocks or Cobras.
  • 7Letter tile. One letter, used for word games.
  • 8Serial, 1 to 54. Every card has its own.
  • 9Picture clues. A mood on the face and a place behind it.

Two sides, two jobs

The fronts hold the people. The backs hold a pattern: six cells in two columns and three rows, read left to right and top to bottom. Each back shows three suits, twice each, and no two backs are the same.

Backs are public and fronts are private. Opponents see the backs of the cards you hold, so a back is shared information. Turn a card half way round and the slot order reverses.

Most games use the fronts. Several use the backs, among them: Pack the Rucksack, Map the Island, Stock Take and Trail Run.

Dice and pawns

Four plain dice, with no colours or symbols on them, and six pawns. A die means whatever a game says: roll it and read it on a key card, the Colour key (Ref 3), the Team key or the Suit key (both Ref 4). Pawns serve as flags, ropes, beacons and votes. Many games need no dice at all, and none needs more than three.

Levels

L1 · age 5

The whole rule and nothing else. A helper is welcome.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

One new twist. Counting and spelling start to count.

L3 · age 8 and up

How to use this rulebook

Not sure where to begin? Open Recommended games, or use the filters on All games,: twenty-five games picked for teaching speed and fairness, with a list by occasion.

Every game page has the whole game in one line, what you need, set-up, how to play, a worked example with the real cards from your deck, three levels, solo and two-player rules where they exist, and what testing showed.

Every element earns a job. Colours, suits, teams, numbers, letters, the serial from 1 to 54, names, expressions, places and the backs each do real work in at least one game. The System page shows which.

Tested before printed. Bots played the games thousands of times to check length, luck against skill and ties. Where a game could not be simulated, its page says so.

About this deck: it was made as a keepsake for Kanasu’s fifth birthday on 25 October 2026 in Bangalore, with every child at the party on a card.

Why this exists

How the game system came about

Kanasu turns five on 25 October 2026 in Bangalore. Her birthday gift to the children who come is a deck of cards with every one of them on it. This page is the story of how a deck became a game system.

The idea

A return gift is usually forgotten by the next morning. A deck of cards with a child’s own face on it is not. So the plan was: 27 children, drawn as explorers, two cards each, 54 cards in all. The guests run from a baby to about 13, so the deck could not be one game for one age. It had to grow with Kanasu: playable at 5, still worth taking out at 8, and fair enough that a 5-year-old can beat a grown-up.

Cards first, games second

The cards were designed as a small database that you can hold. Every card carries a number from 1 to 9, two colours, two gear suits, a face, a name, a team, a letter, a serial from 1 to 54, an expression and a Bangalore place. They were balanced on purpose so that any game could lean on them: six of each number, every colour and suit exactly twice at each number, twins that always add to 9. The System page shows how these elements fit together and what the balance gives you.

Then the cards were fixed. Once the first set was printed, a game could never ask for a card to change, which turned out to be a useful discipline: every game had to find its fun inside the deck as it is.

Seven rules the games had to follow

  • Every game has levels. L1 for age 5, L2 for ages 6 and 7, L3 for 8 and up. The same cards, with a rule added at each step.

  • Faces are not decoration. Names, teams, twins, expressions and places have to do real work in at least one game.

  • Maths hides inside the mechanic. Number bonds to 9, adding to a target, subtraction as distance. No game says it is a maths game.

  • Dice choose what to look for. Two random cards share a colour 59% of the time, so a die decides which attribute counts and the card supplies the decision.

  • Nothing extra in the box. The 54 cards, up to four plain dice, up to six pawns and one small reference card.

  • Test before printing. Bots played each game that could be simulated, thousands of times, to measure length, luck against skill and ties. The numbers are on every page under “Stats for nerds”.

  • Take a position. One rule set per game, with a reason, not a list of options.

From eleven games to 86

The base box began with eleven games that were printed on rule cards: one push-your-luck game, one deduction game, one bidding game, word and clue games, and two that use the backs of the cards. From there the list grew in rounds. Ideas were drafted, run through bots, and sorted into keep, merge or cut. Games that overlapped were folded into the stronger one, and games that were weak were cut. What survived is the 86 on All games, grouped into seven boxes by who is playing.

The base box11 gamesGrown-ups13 gamesKids only12 gamesFamily table20 gamesFast and loud6 gamesParty nights9 gamesMind games15 games

What is not finished

Bots can measure length and fairness but not fun. Every game here has been played by a program, and most have not yet been played by a full table of people. The times on the pages therefore carry a 20% allowance for learning the rules and for thinking, and no game is listed under ten minutes. If a game plays differently in your home, trust your table.

How these were chosen

Easy to teach. A new group can play after one reading of the card, and the first level asks for nothing else.

Fair. No seat has an edge, and the game does not end in a tie. Where simulations were possible, the picks are the ones where a better player wins more often, and where a weaker player still has a chance.

Different from each other. The list covers push your luck, deduction, bidding, bluffing, co-op, trick-taking, shedding and both sides of the card.

Every other game is still worth a night. The full list links to all of them.

Also in the base box: the party sheets, Shared Expedition (Avalanche Pass for a crowd) and Fox in the Camp on a big-print A4 sheet.

The first eleven

The base box

Nine games play on the fronts and two on the backs. This is the box with printed rule cards. Each uses a different mechanism and gives the dice and pawns a different job. Every game has levels, a worked example with real cards and a printed rule card.

How the eleven were chosen

Every element has a rule in at least one game: the serial in Summit Bid and Twin Tracker, letters in Signal Fire and Avalanche Pass, expressions and places in Postcard Home, Cave Crawl and Twin Tracker, suits and the back pattern in Treasure Ring and both back games, colours in Twin Tracker, Treasure Ring and Summit Bid.

The two back games are Pack the Rucksack, the easiest and shortest, and Map the Island, the deepest. They were the best performers of nine back-side ideas.

Kids games

Kids only

The kids only box is the kids’ box: short games from age 5 where a child can win. Most take under ten minutes, the first level uses at most one die, and every game has solo or two-player rules where it makes sense. Three of them, Jungle Totem, Cave Crawl and Campfire Tales, are here from the original set.

About the testing

Bots played each game that can be simulated on the real card list. Acting (Charades Camp) and counting by sight (Stock Take) cannot be played by a bot, so those pages use probability checks and say so. Children play differently from bots: expect shorter attention and more laughing, and treat the times as a guide.

Mixed ages

Family table

Twenty card games for a mixed table. Turns are short, the first level asks for one rule, and a 6-year-old and a grown-up can sit down together. Most take 10 to 25 minutes with learning.

Avalanche Pass

A rope line climbs the pass. Any step could shake the snow loose.

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasy
Game code
BB-01
Players
1 to 6
Time
10 min
Age
5+
Dice
1 die
Pawns
Flag (L2+)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Flip cards to climb. Same animal as the die? Avalanche: you lose the climb. Otherwise bank it, or climb on.

What you need

All 54 cards
one face-down pile
1 die
read on the Team key, Ref 4
1 pawn each
L2 and up: your flag

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards into one face-down pile.
  • Each player gets 4 climbs (L1), 6 (L2) or 8 (L3). One turn is one climb.
  • The youngest player starts. Play goes clockwise (to the left).

How to play

Your turn is one climb. Make a row of cards in front of you:

  1. Roll a die. Read it on the Team key: that animal is the danger.

  2. Flip the top card onto your row. Say the child’s name. Find its animal in the band at the bottom.

  3. Same animal as the die? Avalanche! Throw away this climb’s cards. Your turn ends.

  4. Different animal? Say the number on the card. Keep a running total.

  5. Roll again (back to 1), or bank: keep your row face up as your score and pass the die.

How it ends

When everyone has had all their climbs, add up the numbers on your banked cards. Highest total wins. If the pile runs out, shuffle the thrown-away cards.

Words in this game

  • Number the big numeral, top-left of a card.
  • Animal (team) the emblem and name in the bottom band. See Ref 2.

Common questions

  • The teams are not equal in size. Is that unfair? No. The die is rolled fresh before every flip, and nobody chooses it. Averaged over the die, each flip is an avalanche exactly 1 time in 6, however many cards each team has.

  • Can I bank before I flip anything? No. Bank only after at least one safe flip.

  • What if I roll my own team? Teams do not belong to players. Only the animal on the card and the animal on the die matter.

  • Do banked cards stay in the game? They stay in front of you as your score. Thrown-away cards are reshuffled when the pile is empty.

  • Can a big group play together? Yes. There is a shared Expedition mode for a whole table. Scan the QR card to find it online.

Tips

  • Every flip is an avalanche exactly 1 time in 6 whatever the team sizes, so stop chasing a 'safe' team. Decide your stopping total before you roll and stick to it.

  • At L1, bank near 20 to 25. At L2 and L3 the echoes pull the best stopping point down to about 15, so bank sooner once a vowel tile has shown twice.

  • At L2, plant the flag early, on a card at about 8 to 10. The simulation found the flag worth about 3 points a climb (11.4 against 8.5), and the player who planted at 8 to 10 and stopped at 25 won 72% of L2 games.

  • Count your echoes out loud. The 3rd vowel tile in one climb is also an avalanche, so after two echoes treat the next safe flip as a bank-now moment.

  • With a 5-year-old, play the first climbs with the child choosing when to bank and you saying the total aloud. Ask 'Do you want to keep this, or go again?' before every roll, and never tell them the answer.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. Roll 4 (Monkeys). Flip Nakul, a Tiger, number 4, tile A. Safe. Total 4. A is a vowel, so that is echo 1.

  2. Roll 2 (Elephants). Flip Rihansh, a Peacock, number 9, tile T. Safe. Total 13. The player plants the flag on Rihansh, so 13 is now safe.

  3. Roll 6 (Cobras). Flip Amay, a Monkey, number 8, tile E. Safe. Total 21. E is a vowel: echo 2.

  4. Roll 2 (Elephants). Flip Archana, an Elephant. Avalanche. The 8 above the flag is lost, and the player keeps 13. Had the player banked at 21, the score would have been 21.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

4 climbs. Just the rule above. A good plan: bank near 20 to 25.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

6 climbs. Echo: a card whose letter tile is a vowel (A E I O U). The 3rd echo in one climb is also an avalanche. Flag: once per climb, after a safe flip, stand your pawn on that card. If an avalanche comes later, you keep the cards up to your flag.

L3 · age 8 and up

8 climbs. Bond skip: if a card and the card before it add to 9 (a 9 bonds with a 9), your next flip needs no die roll.

Solo

Climb alone against the medals. L1, 4 climbs: Bronze 25, Silver 40, Gold 55. L2, 6 climbs: 50, 70, 90. L3, 8 climbs: 75, 95, 115.

Two players

Two players work as written. Each player also watches the other's stopping habit.

Maths in this game

Running totals up to about 25 and beyond. Reading odds as 1 in 6. At L3, bonds to 9.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Not used
Letter tileRule vowel tiles are echoes (L2)
People and namesFlavour say the name
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour say the place when you plant the flag
TeamRule the die

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Every flip is an avalanche 1 time in 6, whichever team the card is on, because the die is fair.
  • With no echoes the best stopping point is about 25. With echoes it falls to about 15.
  • The flag is worth about 3 points a climb to a player who uses it well (11.4 against 8.5).
  • Skill: a player who plants the flag at 8 to 10 and stops at 25 wins 72% of L2 games against three cautious players (25% is even) and 80% at L3. Against three players who stop at 15 with no flag the share is 50%.
  • Luck: four equal players each win 25%.
  • A climb takes about 3.6 flips, so a four-player L2 game runs about 10 minutes.

Twin Tracker

A scout has wandered off. Their twin is somewhere in camp.

RecommendedKidsFamilyMedium
Game code
BB-02
Players
2 to 6
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
5+
Dice
2–3 dice
Pawns
Accusation pawn

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

One player hides a child’s twin among a camp of cards. The others ask yes or no questions, then point to it.

What you need

All 54 cards
the Keeper hides one child
2 dice
a third at L2 and up · Refs 3, 4
1 pawn per Seeker
to accuse
Pencil and paper
to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • The Keeper (youngest first) hides any card face down: the mystery card.
  • Find its twin (same child, same name). Add 8 more cards (L1), 11 (L2) or 15 (L3), every one a different child. Lay all face up: 3×3, 3×4 or 4×4. Remember where the twin is.
  • Everyone else is a Seeker and takes a pawn.

How to play

Seekers take turns, starting left of the Keeper:

  1. Roll two dice. Read one on the Colour key (Ref 3) and the other on the Team key (Ref 4). Your choice which is which.

  2. Ask one question: “Does the twin have [colour rolled]?” (either border colour) or “Is the twin on [team rolled]?” Keeper says only yes or no.

  3. Yes: turn sideways every card that does not match. No: turn sideways every card that does.

  4. Or, instead of asking, accuse: put your pawn on a card. Right: you win the hunt. Wrong: you are out until the next hunt.

How it ends

The hunt ends when the twin is found or every Seeker is out. Next player is Keeper. After everyone has been Keeper, most points wins. A find scores 3 (L1), or the camp size minus all questions asked that hunt (L2 up: 12 or 16, at least 1 point). All Seekers out: Keeper scores 3.

Words in this game

  • Twin the other card of the same child. Same face and name, numbers add to 9.
  • Colour one of the two border colours. Team the animal in the bottom band.

Common questions

  • Why must every camp card be a different child? If both cards of a child were visible, neither could be the hidden card’s twin. You would rule them out for free.

  • Does the Keeper have to answer truthfully? Yes, always. The Keeper may not point, hint or pull faces.

  • Can I ask twice in a row? No. One question or one accusation per turn.

  • The last two cards look the same on colour and team. Now what? At L1 that happens in about 1 hunt in 20. Just accuse one of them. From L2 the number and serial questions always separate them.

  • How many questions count for the score? All questions anyone asked in that hunt, not only yours.

Tips

  • Ask the colour question first when you roll one. In the simulation team questions alone found the twin only 29% of the time, because a team covers too many of the nine cards.

  • Pick the die that splits the camp most evenly. A question that turns about half the cards sideways teaches you more than one that clears two or three.

  • Do not accuse while three or more cards are still standing unless the score is close. A wrong accusation puts you out until the next hunt, and every extra question lowers the L2 score for everybody.

  • Watch the questions already asked. The score is the camp size minus all questions in that hunt, so a fourth question from you costs you and the other Seekers too.

  • As Keeper with a 5-year-old, answer slowly and clearly, and never point or hint. Let the child turn the cards sideways themselves, which makes the 'yes means keep matching, no means flip the matches' rule physical.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. The Keeper draws Kanasu as the mystery (face down) and finds her twin, Kanasu with the 6. The camp is Kanasu , Adhiraa , Arvind , Smaya , Avika , Ammlu , Archana , Pinku and Anayka . The mystery card is shown first, then the nine camp cards.

  2. Seeker 1 rolls a 2 (Orange on the Colour key) and asks 'Does the twin have orange?' No. Arvind, Ammlu and Anayka all have orange, so they turn sideways.

  3. Seeker 2 rolls a 1 (Tigers on the Team key) and asks 'Is the twin a Tiger?' Yes. Only Kanasu and Adhiraa are Tigers.

  4. Seeker 3 rolls a 5 (Blue on the Colour key) and asks 'Does the twin have blue?' Yes. Adhiraa is red and purple, Kanasu is yellow and blue. Seeker 3 puts the pawn on Kanasu. Right.

  5. Three questions were asked: 3 points at L1, 12 minus 3 = 9 points at L2, with a 12-card camp.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

9-card camp (3×3). Colour and team questions only. A find scores 3.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

12-card camp (3×4). Roll a third die for new questions: “Is its number higher than the die?” and “Is its serial above ___?” (name any number, 1 to 54: try halving at 27). Score 12 minus questions.

L3 · age 8 and up

16-card camp (4×4). Also ask: vowel or consonant letter tile? Name longer than 5 letters? Which expression? Which place? Which suit (Suit key, Ref 4)? Mirror: pay 2 questions to hear the mystery card’s number. The twin’s number is 9 minus it. Score 16 minus questions.

Solo

Not a natural fit, because the Keeper has to know the answer. Cave Crawl is the solo twin game.

Two players

One Keeper and one Seeker, swapping each hunt. The fewer questions, the better.

Maths in this game

L2 and L3: subtracting the questions from 9, inverse bonds (n and 9 minus n) with the Mirror, and halving the serials 1 to 54.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Rule halving questions (L2)
Letter tileRule vowel question (L3)
People and namesRule the Keeper finds the twin by name
ExpressionRule expression question (L3)
PlaceRule place question (L3)
TeamRule question and clue

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • With team questions alone the twin was found only 29% of the time, because a team has too many cards in nine. That is why L1 also has a colour question.
  • L1: 6.4 questions on average (median 4, 9 or fewer in 90% of hunts). L2: about 3.6. L3: about 3.4 before the Mirror.
  • The Mirror gives the twin's number outright and cut a hunt to under 1 more question, so it costs 2 questions to keep it a trade.
  • Every question type is answerable from the cards alone, except expression and place, which the Keeper judges.

Treasure Ring

Twelve relics lie round a ring of old stones. Each night the sky names the kind of find worth keeping.

KidsFamilyEasy
Game code
BB-03
Players
1 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
2 dice
Pawns
Explorer

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Walk round a ring of cards, taking one each turn. Each round a die names a set you may turn in for points.

What you need

All 54 cards
12 in a ring, the rest a pile
2 dice
rule key on the back
1 pawn each
your explorer
Pencil and paper
to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Lay 12 cards face up in a ring. Keep the rest as a face-down pile.
  • Stand the pawns on cards, spread out evenly round the ring.
  • Everyone starts with an empty pack (the cards you collect). Youngest starts.

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Roll two dice.

  2. Move your pawn clockwise that many cards: one die, both added, or one minus the other (not 0). Never stop on a pawn.

  3. Take the card you landed on into your pack. Fill the gap from the pile. Packs hold 5: throw one away if you have 6.

  4. When everyone has moved, re-roll one die. It is the rule die. Find it on the key (back of this card). Everyone may turn in one set shown there: lay the cards down and score the points for that set.

Round 1 is a gathering round: move and take a card, skip step 4.

How it ends

First to 15 points at the end of a round wins (12 at L1). Tie: fewer cards in your pack. Turned-in cards are discarded. Reshuffle the discards if the pile runs out.

Words in this game

  • Colour trio 3 cards that share a border colour.
  • Suit trio 3 cards that share a medal.
  • Run of three 3 numbers in a row, like 4 5 6.
  • Bond pair 2 numbers that add to 9.
  • Team trio 3 cards of the same animal.
  • Twin pair 2 cards of the same child.

Common questions

  • Why can I not turn in a set in round 1? Everyone holds only one card, and every set needs at least two.

  • Can I turn in two sets? Not at L1 or L2. At L3 you may, if you hold enough cards.

  • Do I have to turn in a set? No. You may keep cards for a better set. Remember the pack limit.

  • Does a card count towards two sets? A card can only be turned in once. Keep cards that fit two different rules.

Tips

  • Hold your cards for the rule die, not for a plan. The chances of banking each rule are about colour trio 39%, suit trio 41%, run 22%, bond 51%, team trio 14% and twin pair 14%, so aim for the bond or a colour or suit trio.

  • Remember the points are set the other way round (3, 3, 5, 2, 6, 6). A rare team trio or twin pair pays 6, so keep a partial one only if your pack has room.

  • Look one move ahead when you roll: use the sum, a single die or the difference to land on the card that helps your pack. A player who thinks one move ahead won 62% against two random movers.

  • Mind the pack limit of 5. Throw away the card that fits the fewest sets, not the oldest one.

  • With a 5-year-old, play at L1 (first to 12) and help them count moves with a finger on each card. Let them say which set the rule die names before anybody turns anything in.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. Move: a pawn stands on space 4 and the dice show 3 and 5. The pawn can move 3, 5, 8 (the sum) or 2 (the difference).

  2. Rule die 1, colour trio, 3 points. The pack holds Amyra (red and green), Guhan (red and green) and Ajay (red and purple). All three share red. Bank them for 3.

  3. Rule die 3, run of three numbers, 5 points. The pack holds Avika (4), Nakul (5) and Naresh (6). Bank the run for 5.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Rule die: 1–2 colour trio, 3–4 suit trio, 5–6 bond pair. First to 12.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The full rule die. First to 15. Say the place of every card you take.

L3 · age 8 and up

Turn in two sets at once if you can spare the cards. First to 21.

Solo

Play 15 rounds alone and bank what the die allows. L2 and L3: Explorer 14, Ranger 16, Legend 20. L1, 12 rounds: Bronze 9, Silver 10, Gold 11.

Two players

Two players share the ring and work as written.

Maths in this game

Adding and subtracting two dice for distance. Seeing runs of three. Bonds to 9. Counting points to 15.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Not used
Letter tileNot used
People and namesRule twin pair (die 6)
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour say the place of each card you take
TeamRule team trio (die 5)

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • How often a good player could bank each rule: colour trio 39%, suit trio 41%, run 22%, bond 51%, team trio 14%, twin pair 14%. The points are set the other way round (3, 3, 5, 2, 6, 6) so no rule face is worth chasing alone.
  • Skill: a player who thinks one move ahead wins 62% against two random movers (33% is even). Three players of equal skill each win about a third.
  • Length: about 13 rounds to reach 15, so about 11 minutes with 3 players.
  • Solo scores, 15 rounds: 14 at the quarter mark, 16 median, 18 at the three-quarter mark. Tested with 2 to 4 players. Five or six players are not simulated.
  • The simulation reshuffled the whole deck when it ran out, a small distortion from the real rule that shuffles only the discards.

The base box · Game 4 of 11 · Sealed bidding

Summit Bid

Each ledge on the mountain holds supplies. Send your best climber.

KidsFamilyEasy
Game code
BB-04
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
1 die (L2+)
Pawns
Rope

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round a prize card is turned over. Everyone plays one card face down. The highest serial wins the prize.

What you need

All 54 cards
deal 6 each (4 at L1)
1 die
L2 and up · Colour key, Ref 3
1 rope each
L2 and up
Pencil and paper
to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal 6 cards to each player (4 at L1). These are your climbers. Keep them secret.
  • Lay a row of prize cards face down: as many as each player holds (6, or 4 at L1).
  • Everyone plays at the same time. There are no turns.

How to play

Each round:

  1. Flip the next prize card.

  2. L2 and up: roll a die and read it on the Colour key. That is the lucky colour. If the prize’s border has that colour, the prize is worth double its number.

  3. L2 and up: once per game you may put your pawn (your rope) on the prize now.

  4. Everyone picks one climber and puts it face down. Turn them over together.

  5. The highest serial wins the prize. Rope: win and it scores twice. Lose and you drop 2.

How it ends

After the last prize, add up your prizes. Most points wins. L2 and up: shuffle the used cards, deal again, play a second ascent and add both.

Words in this game

  • Serial the small number from 1 to 54 in the pill under the letter tile. Not the big number.
  • Lucky colour the colour rolled each round. A prize wearing it is worth double.

Common questions

  • What is the lucky colour for? It makes some prizes worth more than others. Save your strongest climbers for a prize in the lucky colour.

  • Can two climbers tie? No. Every serial is different.

  • Do the lucky colour and the rope both apply? Yes. The prize value is its number, doubled if it wears the lucky colour. A rope win scores that value twice.

  • Do I get my climber back? No. Played cards are used up.

  • What if there are not enough cards for a second ascent? Shuffle everything used in the first ascent and deal from that.

Tips

  • Match your climber to the prize. Play big serials on big prizes and throw a low serial at a small one. The sim player doing this won 61% against two random players.

  • Roll the lucky colour before you choose. A prize in the lucky colour is worth double, so it is the one to spend your 40s and 50s on.

  • Plant the rope on a prize worth 9 or more, and only when you hold a high serial. A rope win scores twice, but a loss drops 2, and the rope was worth about 6 points of win share in the simulation.

  • Count the high serials gone. Every serial is different, so once the 50s have been played your 40s are safe, and a sealed bid never ties.

  • With a 5-year-old at L1, keep the hand to 4 climbers and have them say which card is 'biggest' before they put it down. Do not steer them, because losing a prize to a higher serial is how they learn.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. L3. The prize is Anayka, number 8, orange and blue. Lucky colour 5 is blue. The prize is worth 16.

  2. A plays Gopi, serial 13. B plays Smaya, serial 54. C plays Avika, serial 3.

  3. B wins with the highest serial, 54, and scores 16. Bond bonus (L3): Smaya's number 1 plus the prize's 8 makes 9, so +3 for 19 in all.

  4. Had A planted the rope on this prize, A would have lost 2 points.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

4 climbers, 4 rounds. No lucky colour, no rope. Biggest serial wins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

6 climbers. Lucky colour, the rope and two ascents. Say the prize child’s name.

L3 · age 8 and up

Bond bonus: if the winning climber’s number and the prize’s number add to 9, +3 points.

Solo

Bid against the Ghost. Each round the Ghost plays the top card of the deck. Bronze: beat the Ghost. Silver: beat it by 18. Gold: beat it by 33. A good bot won 76% of games.

Two players

Add a Ghost as a third bidder. Flip the Ghost's climber from the top of the deck each round.

Maths in this game

Comparing two-digit numbers (serials up to 54), doubling, adding, and at L3 bonds to 9.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Rule the whole game
Letter tileNot used
People and namesFlavour say the prize child's name (L2)
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used
TeamNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The prize is doubled 1 time in 3.
  • Skill: a player who plays big serials on big prizes wins 61% against two random players (33% is even) and 59% against three who always play their highest. Four equal players each win 25%.
  • Without the rope the same player won 55%, so the rope is worth about 6 points of win share. A rope penalty from 0 to 6 changed nothing in the simulation, since the bot only used it on prizes worth 9 or more.
  • Serials are all different, so a sealed bid never ties.
  • Length: 6 rounds about 5 minutes, two ascents about 10 minutes.

Signal Fire

Smoke over the ridge. Spell the word before the rescue party turns back.

KidsFamilyMedium
Game code
BB-05
Players
1 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
1 die
Pawns
Beacon

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Spell a real word, using the beacon card’s letter. The first to shout one takes the cards.

What you need

All 54 cards
9 face up, the rest a pile
1 die
word length, key on the back
1 beacon pawn
shared by all

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Lay 9 cards face up in a 3×3. Put the rest face down as a pile. The letter is the letter tile, bottom right of each card.
  • The beacon is the pawn. The youngest player is the first beacon keeper.

How to play

Each round:

  1. Roll a die. The key on the back says how many letters the word needs.

  2. The beacon keeper stands the pawn on any card.

  3. Everyone races. Shout a real word of exactly that length, using the beacon card’s letter and letters from other face-up cards. Each card once. The first to shout takes those cards. Fill the gaps from the pile.

  4. Nobody finds one after about a minute? The keeper throws away 3 cards (consonants first), fills the gaps and a new round starts.

  5. The player with the fewest cards is the next beacon keeper (youngest if tied).

How it ends

First to hold 15 cards wins (12 at L2, 6 at L1).

Words in this game

  • Letter tile the letter at the bottom right of a card. Vowels: A E I O U.
  • Beacon the one card every word must use.

Common questions

  • Can I use a card twice in one word? No. Each card once, and so each letter once.

  • Do names count as words? Only at L3. Then spelling a name takes 2 bonus cards.

  • Can I shout a word with fewer letters? No. It must match the die exactly (L1 ignores the die).

  • Who decides if it is a real word? Everyone together. If unsure, ask a grown-up.

Tips

  • Beacon keeper: look before you place the pawn. A well-chosen beacon gave a word of the rolled length 97% of the time, against 83% for a random one.

  • Hunt for the vowels first. 20 of the 54 tiles are vowels and E appears 7 times, so a spread with only one vowel is a good moment to shout 'No signal' and clear 3 consonants.

  • Do not hoard consonants. Leftover consonants clog the spread, which is why the No signal rule exists.

  • Say a word out loud as soon as you see one. A five-letter roll is the hardest (a word existed 91% of the time) and three-letter rolls the easiest (100%), so spend your thinking time on the long words.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1 (first to 6 cards, ignoring the die). Point at the beacon letter and ask 'What starts with that?' before you let anyone shout.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. L3. The spread letters: J, A, E, R, V, E, T, F, O.

  2. The die shows 6, a five-letter word. The keeper puts the beacon on the T (Bn Sharada).

  3. A shouts 'AFTER': A from Nakul, F from Idhayan, T under the beacon, E from Ammlu, R from Bharati. A takes those 5 cards.

  4. Other words were there too. OVERT also works, from O, V, E, R, T.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Two-letter words only, ignore the die: am an as at be by do go he hi if in is it me my no of oh on or so to up us we. First to 6 cards.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The die: 1–3 is a 2-letter word, 4–6 a 3-letter word. First to 12.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full die. Names count as words: spell a name and take 2 bonus cards. First to 15.

Solo

Roll the die and find a word each time, taking the cards. Roll 8 times at L1 and L2, 10 times at L3, find a word each time and take the cards. If you cannot, clear the fog (discard 3 consonants). Cards after the rolls. L1: Bronze 8, Silver 10, Gold 12. L2: Bronze 12, Silver 15, Gold 18. L3: Bronze 15, Silver 21, Gold 27. A bot that never misses a word scored 13, 19 and 29.

Two players

Two players work as written.

Maths in this game

Counting letters, adding the cards you hold, and spelling. This is mainly a reading game.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Not used
Letter tileRule the whole game
People and namesRule names as words (L3)
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used
TeamNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • A real word exists most of the time with 9 cards and a well-chosen beacon. With the beacon chosen well, a word of the rolled length existed 97% of the time (96% for 2 letters, 100% for 3, 99% for 4, 91% for 5).
  • With 8 cards the chance falls to 92% overall, and 73% for five letters. That is why the spread is 9.
  • A random beacon is worse (83% overall), so the beacon keeper should look first. The word list was 40,000 common English words, filtered to 932 three-letter, 2,109 four-letter and 2,704 five-letter words, plus 28 two-letter words.
  • Leftover consonants clog the spread. In the first simulation, most games never finished, because vowels get used up and consonants pile up. The fix is the No signal rule: discard 3 consonants and refill. With it, 3 players finish L1 in about 8 rounds, L2 in about 11 and L3 in about 12, and 4 players finish L3 in about 14. Each round takes about a minute.
  • The letter tiles follow English frequency: E appears 7 times, 20 of the 54 tiles are vowels.

Postcard Home

Every explorer sends a postcard home. Can your family find yours?

FamilyMedium
Game code
BB-06
Players
3 to 6
Time
20 min
Age
5+
Dice
None
Pawns
The vote

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Give a clue for a secret card. Friends add decoys. Everyone votes with a pawn.

What you need

All 54 cards
deal 5 each
1 pawn each
your vote
Pencil and paper
to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal 5 cards to each player. Keep them secret.
  • Everyone takes a pawn.
  • The youngest is the first storyteller. The role passes clockwise.

How to play

Each round:

  1. The storyteller secretly picks a card from their hand.

  2. Give one clue aloud: a word, a sound or a short act. No letters, numbers or names.

  3. Everyone else picks a card from their hand that also fits. Put it face down. Shuffle in the storyteller’s card. Lay all face up in a row.

  4. Everyone except the storyteller puts a pawn on the card they think is the storyteller’s (not your own).

  5. Reveal the storyteller’s card. Some but not all found it: storyteller and finders score 3. All or none found it: storyteller 0, everyone else 2. Decoy owners: 1 per pawn on their card (max 3). Draw back to 5.

Clue ideas

How it feels (the face) · where it is (the picture behind) · a sound · something the child might say · what they are wearing · a colour · what happens next.

How it ends

Everyone is storyteller twice (3 or 4 players) or once (5 or 6 players). Most points wins.

Words in this game

  • Finder a player whose pawn sat on the storyteller’s card.
  • Decoy a card played to fool the others.

Common questions

  • What is a good clue? Not too easy and not too hard. If everyone or nobody finds your card, you score 0.

  • Can I vote for my own card? No.

  • Does a clue have to be a word? No. A sound, a gesture or a tiny act works. The only ban is on letters, numbers and names.

  • How do decoys score? 1 point for each pawn that lands on your card, up to 3.

Tips

  • Aim for a clue that about half the table can follow. The storyteller scores whenever some but not all find the card, and that is most likely at p = 0.5, which is 75% with 3 guessers and 88% with 4.

  • Clue the feeling or the picture, not the obvious detail. 'Just saw a magic trick' worked in the example because it fits more than one card.

  • Pick decoys that fit the clue as well as your card does. You earn 1 point per pawn on a decoy (up to 3), so a decoy that truly fits is worth more than a joke card.

  • Vote for the card that feels like it was chosen to match, not the one that matches best. The storyteller picked their card first and had to make a clue.

  • With a 5-year-old, let them be the first storyteller and accept a sound or a gesture as the clue. The only ban is on letters, numbers and names.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. The storyteller holds Dhruv, mind blown, hands on his head. The clue is 'Just saw a magic trick.'

  2. The three decoys are Amyra (a gleeful gasp), Sharada (suddenly wide awake) and Shreya (caught red-handed).

  3. Two guessers vote for Dhruv. One votes for Amyra. Some found it, but not all: the storyteller scores 3 and each of the two finders scores 3. Amyra's owner scores 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Six cards in the open, no hands. A right guess scores 1. The storyteller scores 1 if anyone finds it.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Hands of 5, decoys and full scoring.

L3 · age 8 and up

The clue must also fit the card’s twin, and may not use the child’s name.

Solo

This is a social game. It has no solo mode.

Two players

One storyteller and one guesser. Lay out 6 cards (the secret card and 5 decoys from the deck). The guesser picks one, and if it is right, both score 1.

Maths in this game

Little arithmetic. This game builds language and inference: describing a picture, and listening for a clue.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Not used
Letter tileNot used
People and namesRule the child is the subject
ExpressionRule mood clues
PlaceRule place clues
TeamRule team clue (die 5)

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • No bot can test this one. The scoring can be checked with probability: if each guesser finds the card with chance p, the storyteller scores whenever some but not all find it, which has probability 1 minus p to the power g minus (1 minus p) to the power g.
  • That peaks at p = 0.5. The chance is 50% with 2 guessers, 75% with 3, 88% with 4 and 94% with 5.
  • A good clue is neither obvious nor hopeless. A clue so easy that everyone finds the card scores 0.
  • Length: 8 rounds is about 15 minutes with 4 players.

Fox in the Camp

One of the scouts is not what they seem. Can the camp find the Fox?

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasy
Game code
BB-07
Players
5 to 11
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone holds a card. All but one share a secret thing. The odd one out is the Fox: find them without saying what you share.

What you need

All 54 cards
one card each, face down
A Keeper
a grown-up works well
Pencil and paper
to count points
REF
4
Ref 3 / 4
keys for L2 and L3

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • One person is the Keeper (sits out this round, then passes the job on).
  • The Keeper picks the shared thing (L1: a team animal) and deals each player one card face down. Every card shows it except one: the Fox’s. Players peek at their own card and never show it.

How to play

Each round:

  1. Starting left of the Keeper, everyone says one clue about their card: a word or a sound. Do not say the shared thing itself.

  2. Talk for a minute. Who sounds odd? On “three”, everyone points at the Fox.

  3. The Keeper reveals the Fox’s card and the shared thing. Score the round.

Scoring. Pointing at the Fox: 1 each. If most pointed at it, it is caught and gets one guess at the shared thing (right: 2). A Fox that is not caught scores 2.

The shared thing

L1 a team animal (Ref 4). L2 a colour (Ref 3). L3 a suit medal (Ref 4, other side).

How it ends

Play until everyone has been Keeper once. Most points wins. Nobody is ever out.

Words in this game

  • Shared thing what all the Scouts’ cards have in common.
  • Fox the one card that does not have it.
  • Scouts everyone else.

Common questions

  • Does the Fox know they are the Fox? Only when they hear clues that do not fit their own card, or the Keeper says so. At L1 most Foxes work it out after two clues. That is part of the fun.

  • Can I say the animal? No. Say what the animal does, eats, sounds like or says. “Up, up and away!” is a clue.

  • What if the Keeper deals the wrong card? Start the round again. The Keeper shuffles and deals again.

  • How many can play? 5 to 11 at a table: one Keeper and 4 to 10 players. At a party, use one grown-up Keeper per table.

  • At L2 a card has two colours. Which one is shared? Only one of them. Say a clue for the colour you think it is. That is the clue game.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

The shared thing is a team animal. Clues are words or sounds.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The shared thing is a colour. Every card shows two colours, so only one is shared. Clues must fit the colour.

L3 · age 8 and up

The shared thing is a suit medal, or play with two Foxes (8 or more players). With two Foxes, everyone points at two players.

Solo

Not a solo game. It needs at least five people.

Maths and thinking in this game

Listening for a word that does not fit, bluffing, and noticing which clues copy others. L2 and L3 ask children to sort cards by two colours or two suits.

What the testing showed

  • Not simulated, because the game depends on how people talk. It is new in this version and has not been played with children yet.
  • The count is safe: a team has 8 or 10 cards, enough for a table of up to 10 players, and every colour and suit is on 18 cards.
  • Test it once on a small table before the party. Watch whether L1 Foxes work out what they are, and shorten the clue round if the children lose interest.

The base box · Game 8 of 11 · Trick-taking · uses the card fronts

Trail Tricks

Follow the animal. Beat it with a trump. Count what is left.

FamilyMedium
Game code
BB-08
Players
3 to 6
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
8+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Win tricks. Follow the animal that was led. The trump animal beats everything. The trump changes every hand.

What you need

All 54 cards
deal 9 each
Pencil and paper
to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal 9 cards each (3 to 6 players). Set the rest aside unseen.
  • Play 6 hands (3 at L1). The trump animal is on the back: hand 1 Tigers, 2 Elephants, 3 Bears, 4 Monkeys, 5 Peacocks, 6 Cobras. Youngest leads.

How to play

A hand is 9 tricks. For each trick:

  1. The leader plays any card face up. Everyone else plays one: you must follow the animal led if you can, else play any card.

  2. Winner: the highest trump played. No trump? The highest number of the animal led. Same number: higher serial.

  3. The winner keeps the trick face down and leads next.

L2: before each hand, say how many tricks you will win. Exactly right: +5. L3: a trick holding two cards that add to 9 scores 2.

How it ends

Score 1 per trick won plus bonuses. Most points wins.

Words in this game

  • Follow play a card of the animal that was led.
  • Trump the animal for this hand. It beats every other animal.
  • Serial the small number 1 to 54, used only to break a tie.

Common questions

  • What if I cannot follow? Play any card. A trump card will win the trick unless someone plays a higher trump.

  • Does the lead card have to be a trump? No. Lead any card. Leading a trump is allowed.

  • How do I know what is left? Counting is the game. Each animal has 8 or 10 cards, and each number appears 6 times.

  • Why do I leave 9 cards from 54? With fewer than 6 players some cards are not dealt. Nobody knows which, so keep counting.

Level ladder

L1 · age 8

3 hands (Tigers, Elephants, Bears). Most tricks wins. No predictions.

L2 · age 10 and up

6 hands. Predict your tricks before each hand. Exactly right earns +5.

L3 · 12+

As L2, plus the bond bonus: a trick with two cards that add to 9 is worth 2.

Solo

Not a solo game. Three players is the minimum.

Maths and thinking in this game

Counting cards, predicting how many tricks you will win, and spotting two numbers that add to 9 (L3 bond bonus).

What the testing showed

  • Simulated with four players over 3,000 hands. One player who played sensibly (following, winning cheaply, saving trumps) took 2.69 of 9 tricks a hand against an even share of 2.25, so skill helps but luck still matters.
  • About 12.5 of the 27 follow-on plays in a hand could not follow the animal led, and about 6 trump cards were played a hand, so trumps matter every hand.
  • The L2 prediction and L3 bond bonus were not simulated. Counting is the intended strategy: each animal has 8 or 10 cards and each number appears 6 times.

Rule card

The printed card for this game. Front and back, 63.5 x 88.9 mm.

Pack the Rucksack

Every call packs one more thing. Who fills their rucksack first?

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasy

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone has nine cards face down. Each call names a symbol. Flip a card that shows it.

What you need

All 54 cards
deal 9 each, back up
1 die
L2: two dice
REF
4
Ref 4
the Suit key (other side)
1 wild pawn
L3 only

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal 9 cards to each player. Lay them back up in a 3×3. Do not peek at the fronts.
  • Pick a caller. The caller passes to the left after every call.
  • Put the Suit key (back of this card, or Ref 4) where everyone can see it.

How to play

Each call:

  1. The caller rolls a die and reads the suit on the Suit key.

  2. Everyone at once: look at the backs of your unturned cards. If one shows that suit anywhere, flip one of them face up. Say the child’s name.

  3. No card matches? Nothing happens. Next call.

  4. Turn your ninth card and shout “Packed!”

How it ends

First to turn all nine wins. Two on the same call: first to shout wins. Tie: higher total of the nine front numbers.

Words in this game

  • Back the navy side with six icons in 2 columns and 3 rows.
  • Slot a place on the back, numbered 1 to 6 (see the picture).
  • Suit one of six icons: compass, hook and rope, binoculars, torch, tent, boots.

Common questions

  • Can I flip more than one card per call? No. One card per call, even if several match.

  • I flipped a card by mistake. What now? It stays flipped. Look at the whole back before you flip.

  • Can I look at my fronts? Not until you flip. Fronts stay secret, backs are public.

  • What does a back look like upside down? The slots run in the opposite order, so check which way your card faces.

  • Is there any strategy? Very little, on purpose. We tested letting the caller choose the call and choosing which matching card to flip. Neither changed who wins. It is a game of quick eyes, built for the youngest players.

Tips

  • Look at every back before you flip. A call matches a suit anywhere on the back, so check all six cells, in both directions if the card is half way round.

  • Once you have a choice of cards, flip the one that shows the suit most often on its back. That is the only choice that matters, from L2 on.

  • At L2, read the slot number on the die as a position and not just the suit. Half the calls match nothing, so do not panic when you cannot flip.

  • If two players shout 'Packed!' together, the first to shout wins. Tie: higher total of the nine front numbers. Add up your fronts as you flip so you know where you stand.

  • With a 5-year-old, help them keep the three-by-three neat so the backs stay visible. This is a game of quick eyes with very little strategy, so celebrate flips rather than wins.

Worked example

A real nine from the deck, played at L1. Backs are shown as they lie on the table.

  1. Call 1: the die shows 1 (Compass). Sharada (K16) has that suit on the back, so it turns over.

  2. Call 2: the die shows 5 (Tent). Kanasu (K35) has that suit on the back, so it turns over.

  3. Call 3: the die shows 1 (Compass). Pinku (K38) has that suit on the back, so it turns over.

  4. Call 4: the die shows 4 (Torch). No card in this layout shows that suit that is still face down, so nothing happens.

  5. Call 5: the die shows 3 (Binoculars). Pinku (K09) has that suit on the back, so it turns over.

  6. Call 6: the die shows 5 (Tent). Archana (K24) has that suit on the back, so it turns over.

The game went on for 11 calls in total. A call that matches nothing is normal, and it happened 2 times here.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

One die, the suit. About 10 calls.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Two dice: the first is the suit, the second is the slot (1 to 6). Flip a card that shows that suit in that slot. About 14 calls.

L3 · age 8 and up

As L2, plus a wild pawn: once per game, put it on a card. It flips on any call that shows that suit anywhere on it.

Solo

Beat the caller. Count the calls to flip all nine alone. Fewer is better. Roll the die yourself and flip one card per call.

Two players

As written, both flip on every call.

Maths in this game

Spotting a shape in a pattern and matching it. Counting calls. At L2, reading a position (slot 1 to 6) as a place on the card.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • A line of three was broken: in the simulation it ended in a median of 3 calls, and 74% of four-player games were tied. That is why the goal is all nine cards.
  • L1, suit call only: all nine flipped in a median of 10 calls alone (middle half 9 to 12, nine in ten games within 14). With four players, 49% of games tie for first, so the tie-break is the higher total of the nine front numbers.
  • L2, suit and slot: a median of about 19 calls alone (middle half 16 to 24) and about 14 with four players, where ties fall to 12%.
  • L3, wild pawn once per game: a median of 13 calls and 12% ties.
  • Solo medals count calls, and fewer is better: L1 14, 11, 9 and L2 24, 19, 16.
  • No skill is tested except choosing which matching card to flip first, which matters from L2 on. This is a game of luck with small choices, built for the youngest players.

Map the Island

Draw your island one card at a time. The biggest patch wins.

RecommendedFamilyMedium
Game code
BB-10
Players
1 to 4
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
6+
Dice
None
Pawns
Landmark (L3)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Build an island from card backs, each new card overlapping the last. Score the biggest patch of your two suits.

What you need

All 54 cards
deal 2 each, plus a market
REF
4
Ref 4
the Suit key (other side)
1 landmark pawn
L3 only

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal each player 2 cards. Lay one back up: it is your island. Lay the other face up beside it: your contract card. The two suit medals on its front are your two suits. (L1: use the left medal only.)
  • Lay players + 1 cards back up in a row. This is the market.
  • Youngest starts.

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Take one card from the market.

  2. Place it on your island so it overlaps at least one cell and lines up with the grid. You may turn it half way round.

  3. It may cover cells, but never a whole card.

  4. Fill the market from the pile.

How it ends

Everyone stops at 6 cards (L1), 9 (L2) or 12 (L3). For each of your suits, find the biggest group of cells touching side by side, visible cells only. Add your two groups. Highest wins. Tie: more visible cells of your suits, then higher front numbers.

Words in this game

  • Cell one icon on a back. A card has 6 cells.
  • Patch cells of one suit that touch side by side.
  • Contract card your card, front up: its two medals are your suits. Everyone can see it.

Common questions

  • Why is my contract card face up? So everyone can check your suits. They are public. Watch what others need and take those cards first.

  • Can I turn a card upside down? Yes, half way round, before you place it. Never flip it over.

  • Do hidden cells score? No. Only cells you can see at the end.

  • Does a diagonal touch count? No. Cells must share a side.

  • Can both medals be the same suit? No. Every card shows two different suits.

Tips

  • Plan which cells stay visible. Each placement covers cells below it, and the best patch comes from deciding which cells to bury, not which to show.

  • Take the card your rival needs. Contract cards are public, so check their two suits before you take from the market.

  • Turn the card half way round before you place it. That is the only way to change which cells line up, and it often joins two groups.

  • Score the biggest group of cells touching side by side, so diagonals are worth nothing. Aim for one big patch, not scattered spots.

  • With a 6-year-old, start at L1 (6 cards, left medal only). Count the patch together after each placement so the idea of 'touching side by side' sinks in.

Worked example

An L1 game with six real cards and one suit from the contract card: Tent (a left medal on a card kept face up). Numbers on the cards show the order they were placed. The gold frame is the biggest patch.

  1. Amyra (K19) is the start card, placed back-up.

  2. Take Anayka (K06). Turn it 180 degrees. Place it so it overlaps the island and covers some cells. Your biggest patch of tent is now 3 cells.

  3. Take Arvind (K01). Place it so it overlaps the island and covers some cells. Your biggest patch of tent is now 3 cells.

  4. Take Archana (K28). Place it so it overlaps the island and covers some cells. Your biggest patch of tent is now 4 cells.

  5. Take Gopi (K20). Turn it 180 degrees. Place it so it overlaps the island and covers some cells. Your biggest patch of tent is now 7 cells.

  6. Take Idhayan (K48). Place it so it overlaps the island and covers some cells. Your biggest patch of tent is now 7 cells.

Score: 7. The outlined patch has 7 cells touching edge to edge. Each placement covered the cells beneath it, so the best patch comes from planning which cells stay visible.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5+

6 cards and one suit (the left medal). Ask a helper for the first game.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

9 cards, two suits.

L3 · age 8 and up

12 cards, two suits, and a landmark: at the end, stand your pawn on one visible cell. It counts as both your suits.

Solo

Be the Cartographer: a market of 3, same rules, score against the medals. The Cartographer plays the same rules with a market of 3.

Two players

Market of 3 cards. Works as written.

Maths in this game

Counting connected cells, spatial planning, and adding two patch scores at L2 and L3.

Which card elements do the work

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Four greedy bots building an island: 6 cards and 1 suit scored a median of 10, 9 cards and 2 suits a median of 19 (about 32 placements in a game), and 12 cards a median of 26.
  • Skill: the greedy bot beat three random players 98% of the time at 6 cards and 100% at 9 cards (25% is even). Choosing placements matters a lot.
  • Four equal bots tied for first about 22% of the time. That is why ties go to more visible cells of your suits, then to higher front numbers.
  • Solo with a market of 3: 6 cards and 1 suit median 6 (nine in ten games up to 9); 9 cards and 2 suits median 16 (middle half to 18, nine in ten to 19); 12 cards median 21 (nine in ten to 25). The medals sit on those numbers.
  • The L3 landmark pawn has not been simulated.

Boundary Stones

Five stones mark the border. Each has its own law. Take three to win.

FamilyGrown-upsMedium
Game code
BB-11
Players
2
Time
20 min
Age
6+
Dice
None
Pawns
5 stones

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Play cards onto five stones. Each stone has its own law. First to win three stones wins.

What you need

All 54 cards
5 each, the rest a pile
5 pawns
the five stones

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Stand the 5 pawns in a row between you, a hand apart. They are stones 1 to 5.
  • Deal 5 cards each (L1: 4). This is your hand: keep the fronts secret. The rest is the draw pile.
  • Your cards go in a line towards you from each pawn. Overlap them a little so every number and animal still shows. The youngest starts.

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Play one card from your hand, face up, on your side of any stone. A stone holds 3 of your cards (stone 5 holds 2).

  2. Draw one card from the pile.

  3. When both sides of a stone are full, its law decides it (see the back). The winner lies the pawn down on their side.

  4. Stuck? If every stone on your side is full, pass.

Ties: the higher total wins. Still level? Whoever filled their stone first wins.

How it ends

First to win 3 stones wins. There can be no draw: there are five stones.

Words in this game

  • Stone a pawn with a line of cards on each side of it.
  • Law the rule that says who wins one stone. Each stone has its own.
  • Run numbers one after another, like 4 5 6.

Common questions

  • Why does each stone have a different law? So the same card is good in one place and wasted in another. Choosing where to put it is the game.

  • Do covered cards count? Yes. They are public. You may lift a card to look at it.

  • The Colour law: which colours count? Every card has two border colours. A colour counts for any card that shows it. Take the best colour.

  • Can I play on a stone my rival has filled? Yes, on your own side. Stones are only decided when both sides are full.

  • Can I play alone? No. It needs two players. At a party, play as two teams of two.

Level ladder

L1 · age 6

3 stones (Total, Animals, Colour) with 2 cards each. Hands of 4. First to 2 stones.

L2 · age 8 and up

The full game: 5 stones and all five laws. First to 3.

L3 · age 10 and up

Early claim: if your cards on a stone are full and you can show, from the cards you can see, that nothing left can beat them, claim it now. A right claim never changes the result, it only ends the stone sooner.

Solo

Not a solo game. It needs two players.

Maths and thinking in this game

Comparing sums, runs and sets of colours, matching animals, finding the pair nearest 9, and planning which stone each card is best spent on.

What the testing showed

  • Simulated with a Monte Carlo bot (it samples the cards that could still arrive). Over 300 games it beat a random player 97% of the time, so skill matters. Two such bots were even, and going first gave no edge (51%). A game ran a median of 29 turns, about 15 cards each.
  • The first design failed. With a normal ladder of formations (animal trio, run, shared colour, bond pair, total), careful players all reached the top formation, which won 62 to 82% of stones. The deck shares too many colours, suits and animals for a ladder to work, so each stone has its own law instead.
  • The fifth law first counted bond pairs among 3 cards, which is awkward (a pair plus a stray card). It became a 2-card stone where the total nearest 9 wins. Over 300 games it kept balance: going first won 47%, the median game was 27 turns, and about 1 stone in 9 tied on distance and went to the tie-break.
  • L1 (3 stones of 2 cards) was simulated: the bot beat a random player 88%. L3 early claims were not simulated, but a correct claim cannot change who wins a stone.

Nine Hunt

The campfire burns low and the explorers swap stories. Whose number finishes yours?

Inspired by Go Fish

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasy
Game code
KO-01
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
None at L1 · 1 die at L2 and up (Colour key)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Ask another player for the number that goes with a card in your hand to make 9. Lay down every pair you make. Most pairs wins.

What you need

All 54 cardshand of 5 each (7 with two players), the rest a stock pile
1 dieL2 and up · Colour key, Ref 3
Pencil and paperL3 only, to count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle. Deal 5 cards to each player (7 each if only two play). Keep your hand secret.

  • Put the rest face down as the stock.

  • If you hold two cards that add to 9, lay them in front of you now as a pair. Each pair is 1 point.

  • Youngest player starts.

How to play

On your turn, ask and ask again until you miss:

  1. L2 and up: roll the die and read it on the Colour key (Ref 3). Do this before every ask.

  2. Pick a card in your hand. Ask any player with cards: “Do you have a 5?” (the number that adds to 9 with your card: 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5, and a 9 with another 9). L2: your card must show the colour you rolled on one of its borders. If you have no card with that colour, use any card.

  3. They have it: they hand you one such card. Lay the pair down. Score 1 and ask again.

  4. They do not: they say “Go hunt!” You draw the top of the stock. If it is the number you asked for, lay the pair and ask again. Otherwise keep it (lay a pair if it makes one) and your turn ends.

  5. L3: after rolling the Colour die you may ask for a number in that colour: “Do you have a green 7?” The card must show green on one of its borders. A pair made that way scores 3, not 1. The drawn card must match the colour too.

  6. If your hand is ever empty, draw 3 from the stock at once (also when someone takes your last card).

How it ends

The game ends when the stock is empty and a whole round passes with no pair, or when every hand is empty. Most pairs wins (L3: most points). Tie: the player with fewer cards left in hand wins; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Pair Two cards whose numbers add to 9. Lay them face up in front of you.
  • Stock The face-down pile you draw from when you miss.
  • Nine A 9 only pairs with another 9. There are six of them. There is no 5 and 5, because 5 and 5 is 10.
  • Colour ask L3. Asking for a number in the colour you rolled. It scores 3 points if it lands.

Common questions

  • What if the player I ask has no cards? You cannot ask them. Ask someone else. A player whose hand is empty draws 3 at once, so it does not last.

  • Do I have to say the truth? Yes. If you have the number you must hand it over. If you have two, you choose which.

  • I hold a 9. What do I ask for? Ask for a 9. Only another 9 pairs with it, so 9s are the hardest cards to place.

  • Can I ask for a number I cannot use? No. You must hold a card that adds to 9 with it. Everyone then knows you hold that card, so choose with care.

  • What if I ask for a 5 and the stock card is a 5 but I asked for a 4? Only the number you asked for counts as a hit. Any other card goes in your hand, and your turn ends.

Tips

  • Ask for the number that matches a card you hold, but remember asking tells everyone you hold that card. Ask with a card you are happy to be known for, and keep a single card back if you can.

  • Nines are the hardest cards: a 9 pairs only with another 9, and there are six of them. When you hold a 9, ask for a 9 early.

  • Keep track of who asked for what. A bot that remembers it wins 58% against random bots at 2 players, and about 1 ask in 4 lands, so listening is the edge.

  • With a 5-year-old, say the partner number out loud first (the helper may do this at L1): 'You have a 3, so you need a 6.' Then let the child ask. Counting on to nine is the whole point of the game.

  • At L3 a coloured pair scores 3 and a plain pair 1, so after the die roll check whether you can ask for the rolled colour before you ask a plain question.

Worked example

L3, three players. A holds the cards shown, B holds an 8, 9, 2, 2 and 2, and C holds a 6, 1, 1, 4 and 6. A already checked: no pairs in the hand.

  1. A holds Arvind (1), Bharati (4), Guhan (3), Ajay (7) and Gowri (9). A asks B: “Do you have an 8?” (the Arvind (1) is a 1). B holds Smaya (8), an 8. B hands it over. 1 plus 8 is 9. A lays Arvind (1) and Smaya (8): 1 point. A asks again.

  2. A holds Bharati (4), a 4, and asks C for a 5. C has none: “Go hunt!” A draws Nakul (5), a 5. 4 plus 5 is 9, so the drawn card is a hit: A lays Bharati (4) and Nakul (5), 1 point. A asks again.

  3. A rolls a 2 (Orange on the Colour key) and asks C for an orange 6, for the Guhan (3) (a 3). C holds two 6s, Guhan (6) and Dhruv (6). Only Guhan (6) shows orange (orange and purple). C hands over Guhan (6). 3 plus 6 is 9, and it scores 3.

  4. A rolls again and asks B for a 9, using Gowri (9). B holds Adheesh (9), also a 9. 9 and 9 is the only pair a 9 can make. A lays both: 1 point. A has only Ajay (7) left and asks again.

  5. A has 6 points (1, 1, 3 and 1) and still holds Ajay (7), a 7. A asks again for a 2. The turn only ends at a miss.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5. The whole rule: ask for the number that makes 9, lay pairs, 1 point each. No dice. A helper may say the partner number.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Roll the Colour die before each ask. The card you ask with must show the colour you rolled (any card if you have none). Say the name of each explorer you hand over.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. Ask for a number in the rolled colour. A coloured pair scores 3, a plain pair 1. Count points, not pairs.

Solo

Hunt against two Ghost hands. Deal yourself 5 cards and two Ghost hands of 5. The Ghosts never ask. On your turn ask either Ghost, and draw from the stock when you miss. Play 12 turns (a turn ends on your first miss). L1 and L2: Bronze 6 pairs, Silver 7, Gold 8. L3: Bronze 6 points, Silver 8, Gold 10.

Two players

Deal 7 cards each so a hand never runs dry. You ask each other every time. Everything else is as written. About 19 rounds, 9 to 10 minutes.

Maths and skills in this game

Bonds to 9 (n and 9 minus n), the inverse of subtraction. L2: matching colours. L3: counting up to 12 or so, with 3 points a time.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule every ask and every pair is a bond to 9
ColoursRule L2 limits your asking card; L3 colour ask scores 3
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour L2: say the name of the explorer you hand over
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random 53% at 3p L1 (33% even); about 50 asks, 8 to 9 min; no stalls

SettingResult
2p L119 rounds median; memory bot 58% (50 even); 6% ties; median 12 pairs
3p L113 rounds; memory bot 53% (33 even); equal-skill 34%; 3% ties
4p L19 rounds; memory bot 52% (25 even); equal-skill 26%
5p L17 rounds; memory bot 50% (20 even); equal-skill 19%; 6% ties
3p L213 rounds; memory bot 47%; equal-skill 36%
3p L313 rounds; memory bot 50%; median 8 points (6 to 11)
Solo 12 turnspairs 6 / 7 / 8 at the 25th / 50th / 75th percent

  • No stalls in any setting: 1,500 games each at 2, 3, 4 and 5 players, L1, L2 and L3, three bot mixes (about 36,000 games).

  • Length is about 50 asks in total whatever the number of players: 19 rounds with 2 players, 13 with 3, 9 with 4, 7 with 5. At about 10 seconds an ask that is 8 to 9 minutes (a little more at L2 and L3 with the die).

  • About 1 ask in 4 lands (22% with 2 players to 35% for skilled players with 5). A turn is short: you ask until you miss.

  • A bot that remembers who asked for what wins 58% (2 players), 53% (3), 52% (4) and 50% (5) against random bots at L1, where a fair share is 50, 33, 25 and 20. At L2 the edge is 53, 47, 43, 45; at L3 63, 50, 47, 47. It is mostly luck, which is right for an age-5 game, and the memory edge grows a little with the colour ask.

  • Equal-skill bots win close to a fair share (34 / 26 / 19 for 3, 4, 5 players at L1), so no seat is favoured. Median score with 3 players: 7 pairs at L1 (quartiles 6 and 9), 7 at L2, 8 points at L3 (quartiles 6 to 11).

  • Testing changed the tie-break: with only 'most pairs' 12 to 21% of L1 games tied; with 'fewer cards left in hand' ties fell to 3 to 6% (3 players 3%, 5 players 6%).

  • Solo, 12 turns, a bot that asks the likeliest number: 6, 7, 8 pairs at the quarter marks (25th, 50th, 75th). A random bot gets the same 6, 7, 9, so solo is mostly luck of the stock; the medals are set to those numbers.

  • A bot that also counted laid pairs to improve guesses did worse (40% against 52% for the simple memory bot at 3 players), probably because of an error in its counting; the simple bot is the one reported.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: hand sizes other than 5 and 7, or a refill other than draw 3.

  • Not tested: optimal play of the L3 colour ask (the bot uses a simple threshold).

  • Not tested: real children's mistakes, such as asking for numbers they cannot use.

  • Not tested: stacked or unusual deals. Only the real 54 cards were used.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

NINE HUNT. The campfire burns low and the explorers swap stories. Whose number finishes yours? NEED: all the cards (5 each, 7 with two players), the rest a face-down stock. At L2 and up, a die (Colour key, Ref 3). SET UP: lay any pair you hold that adds to 9. HOW TO PLAY: on your turn ask any player for the number that makes 9 with a card in your hand: “Do you have a 5?” They hand it over: lay the pair, 1 point, ask again. They do not: draw from the stock. A hit lets you go on, a miss ends your turn. A 9 only pairs with a 9. Empty hand: draw 3. Ends when the stock is empty and nobody can pair. Most pairs wins; tie: fewer cards in hand.

Back

NINE HUNT: LEVELS. L1 (age 5): the whole rule. L2 (ages 6 to 7): roll the Colour die before each ask. The card you ask with must show that colour. Say the explorer's name. L3 (age 8 and up): ask for a number in the rolled colour, a coloured pair scores 3. BONDS: 1+8 2+7 3+6 4+5 9+9. SOLO: two Ghost hands, 12 turns. L1 and L2: Bronze 6 pairs, Silver 7, Gold 8. L3: Bronze 6, Silver 8, Gold 10 points. TWO PLAYERS: 7 cards each.

Kids only · Game 2 of 12 · Reflex grab

Jungle Totem

The temple totem wakes when two explorers look alike. Grab it first.

KidsFamilyEasy
Game code
KO-02
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Dice
1 spirit die (L2 and up)
Pawns
The totem

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole rule

Flip cards in turn. When your card matches an opponent's top card by the spirit rule, race to grab the totem. The winner gives their pile to the loser. First to empty their stack wins.

Set up

  • Deal 12 cards each, face down (10 each with 5 or 6 players).
  • Each player makes a face-up pile beside their stack.
  • Stand the totem pawn in the middle, within reach of everyone.
  • Roll the spirit die (L2 and L3).

On your turn

  1. Flip your top card onto your face-up pile.

  2. If it matches the top card of any opponent's pile by the spirit rule, those two players race for the totem.

  3. The first to grab wins the duel and gives their whole face-up pile to the loser, who puts it under their stack.

  4. Roll the spirit die again after every duel.

  5. A false grab (no match) costs you the top card of every opponent's pile.

How it ends

The first player whose face-down stack is empty wins.

Tips

  • Look at the emblems first and the numbers second. At L1 only the same animal matters, so train your eye on team emblems before you flip.

  • Never grab on a guess. A false grab costs you the top card of every opponent's pile, which is worse than missing one duel.

  • Roll the die before each duel and say the rule out loud. At L3 the faces include vowels and letters, and a table that shares the rule does not waste a grab.

  • Same number matches about 9% of the time and same team about 15%, so expect long gaps between duels. Do not stare at the totem; watch every pile.

  • With a 5-year-old, play at L1 and let the child grab first when it is close. A grown-up who loses a duel hands over their pile, which is a gentle penalty and keeps the game going.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. Spirit die 2 (bond). A flips Guhan, a 3. B's top card is Naresh, a 6. 3 + 6 = 9. Both race. B grabs first and gives A her pile.

  2. Spirit die 4 (same first letter of the name). A flips Amyra. C's top card is Amay. Both names start with A. A grabs first.

  3. Spirit die 3 (both tiles are vowels). A flips Nakul (tile A). B's top card is Ammlu (tile E). Both vowels. Race.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

No die. The only rule is the same team (same animal). Look for matching emblems.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The spirit die: faces 1 to 3 are same team, faces 4 to 6 are bond (two numbers that add to 9).

L3 · age 8 and up

The full spirit die: 1 same team, 2 bond, 3 both tiles are vowels, 4 names start with the same letter, 5 same number, 6 share a colour and a suit.

Solo

Flip the deck one card at a time onto one pile. Roll the spirit die at the start and after each slap. When a card matches the one before it, slap the totem. A false slap loses 1. Score = slaps minus false slaps. L1 Bronze 4, Silver 6, Gold 8. L2 4, 6, 7. L3 5, 7, 9.

Two players

Two players work as written. Use 12 cards each.

Maths in this game

Spotting 3 + 6 = 9 at speed. L3 adds same number and combined rules.

  • Length with 12 cards each: 2 players about 50 flips (4 minutes), 3 players about 65, 4 players about 85, 5 or 6 players about 85. Play best of three.
  • Skill here is reflex and attention. The simulation can only count flips, because every duel in it is a coin toss. The cards add no luck beyond the deal.
  • Dealing all 54 cards to two players ran past 400 flips each, so the deal is 12 each.
