Stock Take

Before the expedition leaves, the camp cook needs the supplies counted. Count fast and count right.

Inspired by includes the Sum Hunt mode at L3

KidsEasy
Game code
KO-10
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
1 die (L1) · 2 dice (L2, L3)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Lay a few cards back up. Roll for a suit. Everyone counts how many times that suit shows on the backs, then shows the answer on their fingers at the same time.

What you need

All 54 cards4 to 6 laid back up in a row
1 die2 dice at L2 and L3
REF 4the Suit key (other side)
Pencil and paperto count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle the cards. Lay 4 (L1), 5 (L2) or 6 (L3) cards back up in a row. This is the camp. Keep the rest as the supply.

  • Put the Suit key (Ref 4) where everyone can see it.

  • Pick a roller. After every roll the roller passes to the left.

  • Look at a back: it is a grid of 2 columns and 3 rows, six slots. Three suits show, each twice. A card shows a suit twice or not at all.

How to play

Each roll:

  1. The roller rolls the die and reads the suit on the Suit key. L1: count how many times that suit shows on all the backs in the camp.

  2. L2: roll two dice. The first is the suit. The second says which column of each back to count: odd means the left column (slots 1, 3 and 5), even means the right column (slots 2, 4 and 6). Count only that column on every card.

  3. L3: roll two suit dice (roll again if they match). Count the first suit and the second suit on all the backs, and find the difference (how many more of one than the other). If they are equal the difference is 0.

  4. Everyone counts quietly and puts a hand behind their back. The roller counts out slowly: to 8 (L1), 10 (L2) or 13 (L3), then says "Show!"

  5. On "Show!" everyone holds out fingers at the same time for their answer. A closed fist is 0. Everyone who is right scores 1 point.

  6. The roller takes any card from the camp and puts it aside, then fills the gap from the supply. Roll again, with the next roller.

  7. Sum Hunt (L3 mode): lay 4 cards back up in a 2 by 2 block. Roll two plain dice and add them. Find two touching cells (sharing a side) whose suit numbers on the Suit key add to the total. First to point to both with two fingers scores 1 (the roller checks). A wrong point means you miss the next roll. Nobody finds one by the time the roller counts to 20? Roll again.

How it ends

After 16 rolls (12 for Sum Hunt) the most points wins. Tied? Play extra rolls with only the tied players showing, until one is right and the rest are wrong (up to 3 extra rolls, then share the win).

Words in this game

  • Camp the row of cards laid back up that you count.
  • Column left column is slots 1, 3 and 5. Right column is slots 2, 4 and 6.
  • Difference how many more of one suit than another.
  • Roller the player who rolls, counts out the time and checks the answers.
  • Touching two cells that share a side, on the same card or on cards that lie next to each other.

Common questions

  • Why are all the answers even at L1? Every back shows three suits twice each. So a card shows your suit two times or none. Count the cards that have it, then double. That is a good trick to learn.

  • What if I did not finish counting? Show your best guess. A guess can be right, but only a lucky one.

  • Why does everyone show at once? So that it is a counting game, not a shouting game. Being fastest does not help, being right does.

  • What if the answer is more than 10? It almost never happens. If it does, show 10 and say the number.

  • A younger and an older player together, is that fair? Older players are quicker. Give each younger player a head start of 1 point (2 at L3) for every 2 years of age difference, or let the youngest be the helper-roller who counts out the time.

Tips

  • At L1 count the cards that show your suit and double it. Every back shows each of its three suits twice, so the answer is always even, and that trick saves time.

  • Show a considered answer, not an instant guess. When everyone shows fingers at once, an instant-guess player wins 0% to 2% of four-player games, so being right beats being fast.

  • At L2 check the die for odd or even before counting: odd means the left column (slots 1, 3 and 5) and even the right (2, 4 and 6). Point at that column on each card as you count.

  • At L3 count both suits and subtract. A difference of 2 is the commonest answer (37% of the time), so when you are unsure show 2 rather than 0.

  • With a 5-year-old, take the helper-roller job and give a point head start when ages are far apart (the page suggests 1 point for every 2 years). Count the cards with the suit together, then double.

Worked example

Real cards, all verified. Backs are read as 2 columns by 3 rows, slots 1 to 6.

  1. L1: the camp is Bn Sharada (2), Gopi (5), Amay (8), Ammlu (7). The die shows suit 4 on the Suit key. Bn Sharada (2) shows suit 4 twice and Gopi (5) shows it twice. Amay (8) and Ammlu (7) do not show it. 2 + 2 = 4. Everyone shows 4 fingers.

  2. L2: the camp now has a fifth card, Amyra (4). The roller rolls suit 2, and the second die is odd, so count the left column. Amay (8) shows suit 2 once in that column, Ammlu (7) shows it twice, and the others not at all. 1 + 2 = 3. Everyone shows 3 fingers.

  3. L3: the camp has six cards, the fifth plus Guhan (3). The two suit dice show suits 4 and 5. Suit 4 shows 6 times. Suit 5 shows 8 times. The difference is 2. Everyone shows 2 fingers: suit 5 has two more.

  4. Sum Hunt: four cards in a block, Gopi (4) and Sharada (6) on top, Amyra (4) and Ammlu (2) below. The dice total 9. Gopi (4) has suit number 5 in its slot 4, and Sharada (6) has suit number 4 in its slot 3. These two cells touch across the gap between the cards. 5 + 4 = 9. A second answer: slots 1 and 2 of Ammlu (2) show suit numbers 4 and 5, and they touch too. Either scores.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5. Four cards. Count one suit on all the backs. Show fingers at the count of 8. A helper may help with counting the cards that have the suit and doubling.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Five cards, two dice. The second die picks the left or the right column, odd or even. Count to 10.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. Six cards. Two suits: show the difference. Count to 13. Sum Hunt: the touching-cells game, played point-and-score.

Solo

Beat the Cook. Roll, count quietly, and say your answer aloud before you finish counting slowly to 8 (L1), 10 (L2) or 13 (L3). Then check by counting the cells with a finger. Right: 1 point. Play 16 rolls (12 Sum Hunt). Medals are your points out of 16: L1 Gold 14, Silver 13, Bronze 12. L2 Gold 13, Silver 11, Bronze 10. L3 Gold 10, Silver 9, Bronze 8. These come from an assumed model of counting speed, not from children.

Two players

As written. Both show on "Show!", and both score if both are right. The older player will win most games, so use the head start rule for mixed ages.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting up to 16, counting in twos (each card shows a suit twice), subtracting at L3 (difference) and adding two numbers up to 12 in Sum Hunt. Left and right, rows and columns.

Variants and options

  • The main game is a suit count on the backs (levels from all cards to one row to a difference), and its "one row" becomes one column of the back at L2.

  • Sum Hunt (touching cells that add to the roll) is the L3 mode.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used the suit number 1 to 6 is used as a number only in Sum Hunt
ColoursNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Probability only. Instant-guess player wins 0 to 2% once everyone shows together (was 55% with shouting); 25% faster counter wins 44% to 63% at 4p; 16 rolls, 5 to 8 min

SettingResult
L1 answer chances (4 cards)0: 6%, 2: 25%, 4: 39%, 6: 25%, 8: 6%
L2 answer chances (5 cards, one column)0: 8%, 1: 19%, 2: 26%, 3: 23%, 4: 15%, 5+: 9%
L3 difference (6 cards)0: 21%, 2: 37%, 4: 25%, 6: 12%, 8+: 5%
Ties after 16 rolls (L1, 2 to 5p)15% / 23% / 28% / 32%
Typical score of 16L1 13, L2 11, L3 9
Sum Hunt roll answerable92.5%, 4.2 pairs on average

  • Status: probability only. There is no bot play, because counting is a human act. Exact answer distributions were worked out on the real 54 backs, and a model of players with assumed counting speeds was used; the model is an assumption, not measured on children. Length assumes 20 to 30 seconds a roll in total with the countdown, so 16 rolls take 5 to 8 minutes whatever the number of players (not timed with children).

  • Backs: every card shows three suits twice each, so one suit is on a back 0 or 2 times. With 4 cards the L1 answer is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 with chances 6%, 25%, 39%, 25% and 6%. The most common answer is right 39% of the time, so you cannot win by guessing the same number every time.

  • The cards per level were tuned by these numbers. L1, 4 cards: answers 0 to 8, 6% zeros. A 3 card camp had only 4 outcomes with the most common one 38%. L2 counts one column: with 5 cards the answers are 0 to 8 with the most common (2) at 26%; 5 cards spread the answers wider than 4 (2.56 bits against 2.40, and a most common answer of 26% against 28%). L3 difference with 6 cards: 0 in 21%, 2 in 37%, 4 in 25%, 6 in 12%, 8 or more in 5%. More than 10 comes up 0.07% of the time, so fingers are enough for all three levels.

  • A first rule (first to shout the right number wins the roll, and a wrong shout sits you out for that roll) let a player who simply shouts the commonest answer at once win 55% of four-player L1 games (25% is even) and 53% at L3. Testing changed it to everyone showing fingers at once, after which the instant-guess player wins 0% (L1), 0% (L2) and 2% (L3) of four-player games.

  • The shouting rule also let a quicker counter win nearly everything: a player 25% faster than three equals won 85% of L1 games (25% is even). With simultaneous fingers and a countdown of 8, 10 and 13 seconds, a 25% faster player wins 44%, 55% and 63% at four players, but a countdown of 5 at L1 brings it back to 78%, so the countdowns are generous: a tight countdown turns it into a speed game again. A head start of 1 point for the slower players cuts that edge from 44% to 21% at L1, 56% to 37% at L2 and 64% to 48% at L3 (2 points: 8%, 20% and 32%), which is the mixed-ages rule.

  • Equal players share wins evenly at every seat (25%/25%/25%/25% at four players). Ties after 16 rolls: 15% / 23% / 28% / 32% at L1 for 2 to 5 players, 11% / 16% / 21% / 24% at L2, and 11% / 15% / 19% / 20% at L3, which is why tied players play up to 3 extra rolls.

  • Scores over 16 rolls for a typical counter: L1 median 13 right out of 16 (middle half 12 to 14), L2 median 11 (9 to 13), L3 median 9 (7 to 11). At 12 to 14 right the L1 game is easy by design; the first game should be a win for every 5-year-old with a helper. Solo medals come from the same model for a typical, a quick and a slow counter: a typical counter scores 12 / 13 / 14 (L1), 10 / 11 / 13 (L2) and 8 / 9 / 10 (L3) at the 25th / 50th / 75th percentile.

  • Sum Hunt on the 2 by 2 block: a roll of two dice has a touching pair that adds to it in 92.5% of rolls, with 4.2 pairs on average, so a hunt is almost always answerable (re-roll the other 7.5%). In the reflex model, a player 25% faster wins 83% of two-player games and 76% of four-player games (25% is even), so Sum Hunt is a speed race and best for players of the same age. No rule was changed because of that.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real children counting. Every speed and error rate is an assumption.

  • Not tested: whether 5-year-olds can show fingers while counting from 0 and keep a fist for zero.

  • Not tested: the 8, 10 and 13 second countdowns when read by a child roller.

  • Not tested: Sum Hunt with real children, especially reading suit numbers off the Suit key.

  • Not tested: whether the one-card refill keeps rolls fresh enough (the same cards repeat for several rolls).

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

STOCK TAKE. The camp cook must count the supplies. Lay 4 cards back up in a row. The roller rolls the die and reads the suit on the Suit key (Ref 4). Count how many times that suit shows on all the backs. Everyone counts quietly. The roller counts slowly to 8 and says "Show!" Everyone holds out fingers together. A fist is 0. Right answers score 1. Swap one card and pass the roller to the left. After 16 rolls the most points wins. A card shows a suit twice or not at all.

Back

LEVELS. L1: 4 cards, count all. L2: 5 cards, second die odd = left column (slots 1, 3, 5), even = right column (slots 2, 4, 6). Count to 10. L3: 6 cards, two suit dice, show the difference. Count to 13. SUM HUNT: 4 cards in a 2 by 2 block, two plain dice, find two touching cells whose suit numbers add to the total. SOLO: points out of 16. L1 Gold 14, Silver 13, Bronze 12. L2 Gold 13, Silver 11, Bronze 10. L3 Gold 10, Silver 9, Bronze 8.

Charades Camp

Around the campfire, nobody may speak. Show us how the explorer feels.

KidsFamilyEasy
Game code
KO-11
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
1 die (Team key)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Act out the feeling on your card without words. The team die names who gets first guess.

What you need

All 54 cardsa pile of feelings, face down
1 dieread on the Team key
REF 4the Team key and animals (other side)
Pencil and paperto count points

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards into a pile, face down.

  • Everyone picks an animal team from the Team key (Ref 4): Tigers 1, Elephants 2, Bears 3, Monkeys 4, Peacocks 5, Cobras 6. Each player has a different animal. Say it out loud.

  • The youngest is the first Actor. The turn then goes left.

  • Each card has a feeling written on its front, under the name. Read it quietly. Keep it secret.

How to play

Each round:

  1. The Actor takes the top card and reads the feeling to themselves. Cannot act it? Put the card at the bottom and take the next one. You may do this once in a round.

  2. Roll the die and read it on the Team key. If it shows the animal of a player who is not the Actor, that player is the Spotlight. If it shows an animal nobody has, or the Actor's own, nobody is the Spotlight.

  3. The Actor acts the feeling with no words (at L1, funny noises are allowed; from L2, silence). Faces, hands and bodies are allowed.

  4. The Spotlight has 3 guesses. A guess is right if it names the feeling or action in words that fit it. The Actor nods or shakes the head. Right: Spotlight scores 2 and the Actor scores 1.

  5. If the Spotlight uses up three guesses, everyone else (not the Actor) may guess once each, going round. The first right guess scores 1 and the Actor scores 1.

  6. No Spotlight? Then everyone but the Actor guesses once each in turn. The first right guess scores 2 and the Actor 1.

  7. L2: after the first feeling, find its twin in the pile (the other card with the same child) and act that feeling too. Score each feeling. L3: act both feelings as one story, first one, then the other. Say the place name from the first card out loud (the only words you may say). If the same player guesses both, in order, they score 2 more.

How it ends

Everyone is the Actor 3 times (L1) or 2 times (L2 and L3). The most points wins. Ties share the win. Two players play together as one team and count the feelings guessed.

Words in this game

  • Actor the player acting the card. No words.
  • Spotlight the player named by the team die. First turn to guess, three guesses.
  • Twin the other card of the same child. Same face, same name, a different feeling.
  • Story L3: acting two feelings in a row as one tale, in the place named on the first card.

Common questions

  • What if I cannot act the feeling on my card? Put it at the bottom of the pile and take the next card. You may do this once in a round. After that, act what you have.

  • How exact must a guess be? Close is good. "Scared" counts for jumping in fright. "Sleepy" counts for a yawn. The Actor decides, but should be kind.

  • What if the team die shows an animal nobody picked? Nobody is the Spotlight, and everyone guesses once. This is a free-for-all round.

  • Is the die fair if some teams have more cards? Yes. The die picks who guesses, never which card is used. Every other player has the same 1 in 6 chance.

  • Can the Actor speak? No words at all. At L3 the Actor says the place name once. Nothing else.

Tips

  • Use your face first and your hands second. Subtle feelings like 'bored' or 'sheepish' are the hard cards, so make one big clear face before you add any body movement.

  • If you cannot act the card, swap it once. The swap rule cuts the chance of a Hard card from 18.5% to 3.1%, so use it rather than freezing.

  • As Spotlight, name the feeling in simple words and guess the strongest cue first. The Actor decides what counts, and a close word like 'scared' for a fright is accepted.

  • At L2 and L3 use the place on the card to plan the twin. Acting the second feeling as a continuation of the first makes the story bonus (2 points) much easier to earn.

  • With a 5-year-old, let them use funny noises at L1 and whisper the feeling if they cannot read. Be a generous guesser, and nod quickly when they are close.

Worked example

L3, three players. A (Tigers) is the Actor. B picked Monkeys. C picked Bears. Real cards.

  1. A turns over Nakul (4) and reads the feeling quietly: tiptoe sneaking with a finger on the lips. The twin of Nakul (4) is Nakul (5): a roaring pounce.

  2. The die shows 4. That is the Monkeys on the Team key, so B is the Spotlight.

  3. A says "Bannerghatta safari" (the place on Nakul (4)) and tiptoes forward with a finger on the lips. B guesses "hiding" (no) then "sneaking" (yes, guess 2). B scores 2 and A scores 1.

  4. Then A jumps up with claws curled and roars, the feeling on Nakul (5). B guesses "a lion roar" on the first go. A nods: right. B scores 2 and A scores 1.

  5. B guessed both feelings in order, so B also scores the story bonus of 2. Round total: A 2, B 6, C 0.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5. One card a round. Noises allowed. A helper may whisper the feeling to a child who cannot read it yet. Each player acts 3 times.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. No noises. After the first feeling, find its twin and act that too. Each player acts 2 times (4 feelings guessed in two rounds).

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. Act both feelings as one story, say the place, and score the story bonus of 2.

Solo

This game is not really a solo game, because it needs someone to guess. If you are alone, use a mirror and a toy or a pet as the audience. Draw 6 cards. For each one act the feeling, then check the card. Score 1 for the face, 1 for the hands or body. Medals: Bronze 6, Silver 8, Gold 10. These medals are only a guess.

Two players

Play as one team. One acts, the other is the Spotlight every round (no die). Swap each round. L1: 6 cards; count the feelings guessed out of 6. Bronze 4, Silver 5, Gold 6. L2 and L3: 4 rounds of two feelings: count out of 8. Bronze 5, Silver 6, Gold 7. These medals come from assumed guess rates, not from real children.

Maths and skills in this game

Mostly language, expression and turn-taking. Scoring 2 and 1 and adding up, and at L3 the story bonus. Reading is helpful but not needed with a helper.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule the team die names the Spotlight (players use animals from the Team key)
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesRule L2 the twin is found by the child's face and name
ExpressionRule the feeling you act is the expression written on the card
PlaceRule L3: the place is the setting of the story and is said aloud

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Probability only. Not simulable: 36 Easy / 8 Medium / 10 Hard expressions by rubric; swap rule cuts Hard rounds from 18.5% to 3.1%

CheckResult
Expressions by rubric36 Easy, 8 Medium, 10 Hard
Hard card chance, no swap / one swap18.5% / 3.1%
Twin pair has a Hard card, no swap / swap33% / 10%
Team die, chance a given other player is Spotlight1 in 6 (any team size)
Ties (assumed guess rates)3 to 5 players: 11% to 17%; 2 players 40% so played as a team
Length (assumed)L1 5 to 11 min, L2 6 to 14, L3 6 to 16

  • Not simulable with bots: acting and guessing is hand-judged. What was done instead is a feasibility check on the 54 real expressions plus a probability model of the scoring. Status: Probability only.

  • Easy to act? A transparent rubric: +1 for each subtle face detail (eyebrow, nostrils, "slightly", "tiny", up to 2), +1 for an abstract mood word (smirk, innocence, bored, determined), and minus 1 for each big body cue (roar, yawn, fist, jumping, hands on head, up to 2). Score 0 or below = Easy, 1 = Medium, 2 or more = Hard. Result: 36 Easy, 8 Medium, 10 Hard.

  • The 10 Hard cards (candidates to re-draw): K12 plotting smirk, K13 bored, K17 puzzled at a map, K18 proud with a flag, K24 suspicious side-eye, K29 gentle kind smile, K34 laser-focused stare, K37 sheepish grin, K44 brave small smile, K48 innocence. The rubric is blunt and has not been checked with children.

  • The re-draw rule (swap once per round) cuts the chance that an Actor ends up with a Hard card from 18.5% to 3.1%. For the 27 twin pairs: 18 have no Hard card, 9 do; a pair re-draw cuts a Hard pair from 33% to 10%.

  • The team die gives each other player exactly 1 in 6 to be the Spotlight, whatever the number of cards in each team (8, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10). Using the die to pick which team's cards come up would make a card from an 8-card team 25% more likely than one from a 10-card team (1/48 against 1/60), so the die picks the guesser, not the card. With 2 players the die never matters, so it is dropped. A specific Spotlight comes up in 33% of rounds with 3 players, 50% with 4 and 67% with 5; the rest are free-for-alls.

  • Cards and length: 3 acts a player at L1 means 6 to 15 cards plus swaps; L2 and L3 use 8 to 20 cards (4 to 10 twin pairs). At about 45 seconds a round at L1 and 85 to 95 at L2 and L3 (assumed, not timed), games last about 5 to 11 minutes at L1, 6 to 14 at L2 and 6 to 16 at L3 for 2 to 5 players.

  • Scoring model with assumed per-guess success of 45% (Easy), 30% (Medium), 15% (Hard): equal players win a fair share at every seat (3 players 34/33/33%). Ties are 15 to 17% at L1 with 3 to 5 players and 11% to 12% at L2. Two-player scores tied 40% of the time, so 2 players now play as one team with medals. The median personal score is 6 to 8 points at L1 and 8 to 10 at L2.

  • Sensitivity: if the true guess rates are 30% lower or 30% higher, a two-player team total moves from 12 to 15 (L1) and 15 to 21 (L2). Medals could easily be off by one.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real children acting and guessing. Every success rate is assumed.

  • Not tested: whether 5-year-olds can act the Medium and Hard feelings at all.

  • Not tested: how long a round really takes.

  • Not tested: guess judging. The Actor decides if a guess is close enough, and disputes are not modelled.

  • Not tested: a child-tested difficulty rating. The rubric is simple keywords.

Front

The animal it shows is the Spotlight. The Actor acts, no words. Spotlight has 3 guesses: right scores 2, the Actor 1. If wrong, everyone else guesses once: 1 point each. Cannot act it? Swap once. L2: also act its twin. L3: act both as a story and say the place. Most points wins.

Kids only · Game 12 of 12 · Bluff and challenge

Campfire Tales

Everyone swears their story is true. Only the fire knows.

KidsFamilyEasy
Game code
KO-12
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Dice
1 team die
Pawns
Challenge marker (L3)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole rule

Roll the team die, play a card face down and say it is that team. Call 'Tall tale!' on anyone you doubt. The liar, or the wrong doubter, takes the card back plus one more.

Set up

  • Deal 5 cards to each player.
  • The rest is a face-down stock.
  • Each player stands a pawn in front of them.

On your turn

  1. Roll the team die.

  2. Play one card from your hand face down and say: 'This explorer is a [team].' The team is the one on the die. At L2 add a name of a child on that team.

  3. Anyone may shout 'Tall tale!' The first to shout, starting at your left, challenges.

  4. Flip the card. If its team is not the die's team, you lied: take the card back and draw 1 from the stock. If it is the die's team, the challenger takes the card and draws 1.

  5. With no challenge the card stays face down and is out of the game.

  6. Play your last card without being caught and you win.

How it ends

The first player with an empty hand wins, once the challenge window on their last card has passed.

Tips

  • Count the cards that have been shown in challenges. A player who counts revealed cards wins 72% against random challengers, because teams have 8, 8, 8, 10, 10 and 10 cards and you can work out what is left.

  • Lie when the die team is rare in your hand and the last few cards are known. A claim for a team that looks used up is hard to challenge with confidence.

  • Do not challenge on a hunch. A wrong doubter takes the card plus one, so only call when your count says the team is nearly gone.

  • At L3 remember your pawn lies down when you challenge, so you cannot challenge again until your next turn. Save the call for the claim that matters most.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1 with the team reference card on the table, and ask 'which animal is this child?' before they say it. In 2-player games the first player wins 58%, so let the younger player start.

Worked example

The cards below are the real cards from your deck.

  1. Die 3 (Bears). A holds Dhruv, a Bear. A plays it and says 'a Bear' (at L2: 'Smaya'). Nobody shouts.

  2. Die 6 (Cobras). B has no Cobra. B plays Bn Sharada and says 'a Cobra: Gowri.' C shouts 'Tall tale!' The card is flipped. Bn Sharada is a Monkey. B lied and takes the card back plus 1 from the stock.

  3. Die 6 again. D plays Ajay and says 'a Cobra.' C shouts 'Tall tale!' Ajay is a Cobra, so the claim was true. C takes Ajay and draws 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Say the team only. The reference card shows all six teams and their children.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Say the team and also a name from that team. The names come from the reference card, so you learn who is on which team.

L3 · age 8 and up

Pawn rule: when you call 'Tall tale!', lay your pawn down. You cannot call again until your own turn begins, when you stand it up.

Solo

Play against Echo. Echo plays the top card of its hand face down each turn and claims the die's team. Echo calls 'Tall tale!' on you whenever its own die roll shows 1 to 3. This solo mode has not been simulated.

Two players

Two players work as written. The first player wins 58% of games, so let the younger player start.

Maths in this game

Counting cards by team (8, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10) and probability sense. There is little arithmetic here; this game teaches the roster.

Which card elements do the work

Serial 1 to 54Not used
Letter tileNot used
People and namesRule names from the team (L2)
ExpressionNot used

TeamRule the whole game

Take Six Rows

Everyone picks a card in secret and all are played at once into four growing rows. The unlucky player who adds the sixth card to a row has to pick the whole row up, and every card in it costs points.

Inspired by Take 5! (6 nimmt!) by Wolfgang Kramer

FamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-01
Players
2 to 6
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
L1 from 7
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Pick one card from your hand in secret, reveal together, and place cards lowest serial first onto the four rows. Whoever would play a sixth card, or a card lower than every row, picks up a row. Fewest penalty points wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsthe serial (small number in the pill) says where a card goes, the big number is what it costs if you pick it up
Pencil and paperto add up the penalty points after each hand

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 10 cards to each player (8 each at 6 players). Keep your hand secret.

  • Turn up 4 cards in a column. Each is the first card of a row. Put the rest of the deck back in the box; it is not used this hand.

  • Nobody has any penalty points yet. Write each player's name on the score sheet.

  • At 5 players the deal uses exactly 54 cards (50 in hands and 4 in rows). At 6 players it uses 52.

How to play

  1. Choose. Everyone picks one card from their hand and puts it face down in front of them. Nobody may change their mind once it is down.

  2. Reveal. Turn all the chosen cards over together.

  3. Place the cards one at a time, lowest serial first. A card goes at the end of the row whose last card has the highest serial that is still lower than the new card's serial.

  4. Sixth card. If the row you must join already has 5 cards, you pick up those 5 cards instead. Your new card becomes the first card of that row.

  5. Too low. If your serial is lower than the last card of every row, you may not join any row. You pick up a row of your choice, and your card becomes the first card of that row.

  6. Cards you pick up go face down in a penalty pile. Their printed numbers are penalty points. Play 10 turns (8 at 6 players) until every hand is empty; that is one hand of the game.

How it ends

After each hand, add up the numbers on the cards in your penalty pile (each card costs its printed number) and add that to your running total. Deal a new hand from the full 54 cards. The game ends at the end of the first hand in which any player reaches 150 or more. The player with the lowest total wins. A tie goes to the player who picked up the fewest cards over the whole game; still tied, share the win. Short game: play exactly 2 hands and compare totals.

Words in this game

  • Row a line of face-up cards. A row holds at most 5 cards.
  • Serial the small number in the pill on the front, 1 to 54. It decides where a card goes and who goes first when cards are placed.
  • Penalty pile the cards you were forced to pick up. They are worth their big printed numbers.
  • Hand one deal of 10 cards, ten turns long. A game is several hands.

Common questions

  • Which number decides the order? The serial. The big number is only the cost if you pick the card up. A card with a small serial is 'low' even if its big number is 9.

  • Can I choose which row to join? No, never. Your card always goes on the row whose last card has the highest serial below yours. The only choice you get is which row to pick up when your card is lower than every row.

  • What if two players choose cards that would both go on the same row? Place them in order of serial. The lower one goes on first, so the higher one may become the sixth card.

  • Do I have to pick up the cheapest row? No, you choose, but the cheapest in printed numbers is usually right. Remember the row you take starts again with your card, so a row you take with a tiny first card stays a trap for the next player.

  • What if I have no legal choice at all? There is always a legal card. Any card either joins a row or is lower than all rows and takes one.

Tips

  • Count the rows. A row with 4 cards is a trap: the next card that joins it makes 5, and the one after that picks it up. Avoid playing into a 4-card row unless you are sure someone lower will land first.

  • Low serials are not safe. A card with serial 5 is lower than almost every row end, so it forces you to pick up a row. Play your low serials early, while the rows still start low, or when a cheap one-card row is waiting.

  • Aim for the cheap row. A single card of number 1 or 2 is a bargain row to take. Read the numbers at the start of each turn and note which row you would take if forced.

  • Keep a middle serial for late. In the last turns the rows are long and the safe landing spots are gone. A card with serial near 30 to 40 is usually flexible when you have nothing else.

  • Do not try to guess everyone. Think about the two or three players who could land just ahead of you. If your card is the highest of the group you land last and may be the sixth.

  • Remember that 60% of penalty points came from who played the fifth card of a row (Fence Line testing). Timing beats power: do not hold your safest card until it is the last one left.

Worked example

  1. Three players, 10 cards each. Four rows begin with Ajay (7) (serial 53), Adheesh (9) (serial 49), Kanasu (6) (serial 7) and Nysha (8) (serial 41). Call them rows A, B, C and D.

  2. Turn 1. P0 picks Naresh (6) (serial 16), P1 picks Ammlu (7) (serial 14), P2 picks Ajay (2) (serial 46). Lowest serial first: serial 14 is above row C's 7 and is the highest end below it, so it joins row C. Serial 16 also joins row C, now ending in 14. Serial 46 joins row D (ends in 41). Nobody picks anything up.

  3. Turn 2. P0 picks Sharada (6) (serial 12), P1 picks Nakul (4) (serial 4), P2 picks Dharsh (2) (serial 38). Lowest first: serial 4 is lower than every row end (53, 49, 16, 46), so P1 must pick up a row. The rows cost A: 7, B: 9, C: 6+7+6 = 19, D: 8+2 = 10. P1 takes row A (7 points) and Nakul (4) becomes row A. Serial 12 is above row A's 4 and below the other ends, so P0 joins row A. Serial 38 joins row C (ends in 16).

  4. Turn 3. P0 picks Anayka (1) (serial 42), P1 picks Idhayan (8) (serial 44), P2 picks Smaya (8) (serial 28). Row C now holds Kanasu (6), Ammlu (7), Naresh (6), Dharsh (2): four cards. Serial 28 joins row A. Serial 42 joins row C as its fifth card. Serial 44 would be the sixth card in row C, so P1 picks up all five: 6 + 7 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 22 points. Idhayan (8) becomes the new row C.

  5. P1 has 29 points after three turns from one forced pick-up and one bad landing, while P0 and P2 have none. The hand continues for 7 more turns. At the end of the hand everyone adds their pile to their running total; if nobody reaches 150, a new hand is dealt.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Play with 5 cards each and only 2 rows (turn up 2 cards). Count the number of cards you pick up, not their numbers. A helper may look at the hand and say which row each card would join. Play one hand and fewest cards wins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Four rows and 10 cards, but play one hand only. Penalty is the printed numbers. Fewest points wins.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: several hands until a player reaches 150, penalty equals the printed number.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is all about guessing what other people play at the same moment.

Two players

Works well with two. Each player has 10 cards and four rows are shared, so a single pick-up is common. The counting bot had its biggest edge here: 64% in Fence Line testing against a 50% baseline. At 2 players the 150 line takes about 5 hands, so play 3 hands instead.

Maths and skills in this game

Comparing numbers up to 54 and adding small numbers, counting how many cards a row holds, and judging risk: the chance that another player lands before you.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (source: simulation chunk 1, 400 to 1,500 games per setting): a 20-sample look-ahead bot beat random players 37% to 58% of the time across 3 to 5 players, against baselines of 33%, 25% and 20%. So skill exists, but it is a moderate edge.

  • Penalty rule (chunk 1): printed number, one third of it, and a flat 1 per card made no clear difference to skill, so the printed number stays because it is the simplest to read.

  • Length (chunk 1): ten turns a hand, and a 150-point loss line took a median of 3 hands, about 15 minutes.

  • Fence Line testing (Grown-Up Games doc, 2,000 games per cell, 8-card hands, 4 rounds): a counting bot beat simple players 64% at 2 players, 44% at 3, 38% at 4, 33% at 5 and 34% at 6, against baselines of 50, 33, 25, 20 and 17%.

  • About 60% of penalty points came from who played the fifth card of a row, which is mostly timing luck. Always playing the lowest card won only 6.5% of games and always playing the highest 11%, so no shortcut works. Seats were fair within a point or two.

  • Rejected: letting a card of the same team or colour pair as the row's last card cancel a penalty. It did not change skill and added a check on every placement.

  • New figure (my computation, 150 simulated hands per player count, look-ahead bots all round): mean penalty per player per hand is 28.7 at 2 players, 36.8 at 3, 41.1 at 4 and 42.6 at 5. At 2 players that makes the 150 line about 5 hands, which is long, so play 3 hands at 2 players instead.

  • Deck fit: at 5 players the deal uses exactly 54 cards (5 x 10 + 4 rows). At 6 players the 8-card hand uses 52.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots pick by formula and do not bluff or read opponents.

  • Not tested: the 150-point line at 6 players (hands of 8); the bots were tested over fixed numbers of rounds there.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written; they are shortened variants of the same rules.

  • Not tested: the tie-break (fewest cards picked up).

Variants and options

  • Fence Line (Grown-Up Games doc, game 12) the same 6 nimmt! idea played with 8 cards over 4 rounds. Its 8-card hand is kept for 6 players, and its skill figures are listed above. It is no longer a separate game.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TAKE SIX ROWS. Deal 10 cards each (8 at 6 players). Turn up 4 cards as four rows. Each turn: everyone picks a card in secret and reveals together. Place cards LOWEST SERIAL first. A card joins the row whose last card has the highest serial below it. A row holds 5. If your card would be the 6th, or is lower than every row, you pick up a row (the 5 cards, or any row you choose) and your card starts the row. 10 turns make a hand.

Back

SCORING. Cards you pick up cost their printed numbers. Add up after each hand. The game ends when any player reaches 150 or more at the end of a hand. Lowest total wins; tie: fewer cards picked up. Short game: 2 hands (3 at 2 players). LEVELS. L1 two rows, 5 cards, count cards not numbers. L2 one hand. L3 full game. No solo mode.

No Takers

A card is turned up and nobody wants it. Take it and the coins that have piled onto it, or pay a coin to pass it on. The longer it travels, the sweeter the pot, and the more your rivals' neighbours matter.

Inspired by No Thanks! by Thorsten Gimmler (also No Merci!, Cloud 9)

RecommendedFamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-02
Players
3 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Flip a card. On your turn take it with all the coins on it, or pay one coin card to pass. Cards cost their serial divided by 3, but a run of neighbouring serials only costs its lowest card. Lowest total, after coins, wins.

What you need

All 54 cardssome are lots (the cards you take), some are coins (face down, money only)
Pencil and paperto add up the scores at the end; optional

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal face down to each player a stack of coin cards: 9 each at 3 players, 6 each at 4 players, 5 each at 5 players. Coin cards are money only; their faces do not matter. Keep your stack face down but you may count it.

  • Take the next 3 cards and put them in the box without looking. They are removed so nobody can count the deck exactly.

  • The cards that remain are the lot deck: 24 lots at 3 players, 27 at 4 players, 26 at 5 players. Put it face down in the middle.

  • Pick a first player at random. Everybody makes a row space in front of them for the lots they take, face up.

How to play

  1. Flip a lot. Turn the top card of the lot deck face up in the middle. It has no coins on it yet.

  2. Your choice. The active player either takes or passes.

  3. Take: put the lot in your row (face up, in serial order so you can see runs). Also take every coin card on top of it and add them to your stack. Then flip the next lot yourself and act again.

  4. Pass: put one coin card from your stack onto the lot. Play moves to the player on your left, who faces the same choice.

  5. No coins? If your stack is empty you cannot pass, so you must take.

  6. Keep going until the last lot has been taken. If the final lot is unwanted, players keep passing it until someone takes it or runs out of coins.

How it ends

When the last lot is taken, score. Each lot costs its serial divided by 3, rounded up (serial 1 to 3 costs 1, serial 52 to 54 costs 18). But if you hold a run of consecutive serials (for example 21, 22, 23, 24), only the lowest card in the run costs anything; the others are free. Each coin card you still hold is worth -1. Add it up. Lowest total wins. A tie goes to the player with more coin cards left; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Lot a card turned up in the middle that you may take.
  • Coin card a face-down card used as money. It scores -1 at the end if you still hold it.
  • Pot the coin cards lying on the current lot. Whoever takes the lot takes the pot.
  • Run two or more lots in your row whose serials follow each other with no gap. Only the lowest card counts.

Common questions

  • Do the coin cards' faces matter? No. They are money. Deal them face down and never look at them. You may count your own stack.

  • Why are 3 cards removed? So nobody can work out which lots are still to come. With 27 lots in play you can still guess; with 3 missing you cannot be sure.

  • If I take a lot, do I pay anything? No. You gain the pot. The cost shows up only at the end, in your score.

  • Can I take a lot with coins on it if I have none? Yes, and when you have no coins you have to take. That is why you should never spend your last coins too early.

  • What if I take a lot that touches a lot I already hold? It joins the run. Put it in serial order beside its neighbour. If it fills a gap between two of your runs, they merge into one run, and only the lowest card of the whole run counts.

Tips

  • Look at your row before you decide. A lot next to one of yours (serial one higher or lower) is nearly free, so take it at once, even with no coins on it.

  • The expensive lots are the high serials. Serial 54 costs 18. Pass those until the pot is big enough to pay for them, but remember each pass costs you a coin that is worth a point.

  • Do not run out of coins. A player with no coins must take whatever comes, and cannot ever pass a bad card back.

  • Watch the neighbours in other players' rows. If the player to your left holds serial 30, they will gladly take 31 or 29 for free. A pass that lands on them is a gift to them.

  • Taking too boldly or too timidly both lose. The bot that wins takes a lot when its extra cost is about 4 coins more than the pot, and gets more careful as its coins run low.

  • With a big pot and a middling lot you can afford to take. A pot of 4 or 5 on a lot costing 8 is a fair deal; the same pot on a lot costing 16 is not.

Worked example

  1. Three players, 9 coin cards each, 3 cards removed unseen, 24 lots left. P0 starts. First lot: Dhruv (6) (serial 22, so cost 8).

  2. P0 passes (pays 1 coin card, 8 left). P1 takes Dhruv (6) and the 1 coin card on it: P1 now has 10 coins and a lot costing 8. P1 flips the next lot themselves: Shreya (2) (serial 23).

  3. Serial 23 follows serial 22, so it joins P1's run and costs nothing extra. P1 takes it with an empty pot. P1 holds a run of 22 and 23, which costs just 8.

  4. P1 flips Ammlu (2) (serial 40, cost 14). P1 passes (9 coins, pot 1). P2 passes (8 coins, pot 2). P0 passes (7 coins, pot 3). P1 passes again (8 coins, pot 4). P2 now takes Ammlu (2) and 4 coins: P2 has 12 coins and a lot costing 14, a net of 2.

  5. Scoring at the end of a different game: a player holds serials 21, 22, 23 and 24 and 5 coin cards. That is one run, so only serial 21 costs: 21 divided by 3 is 7, so 7 points. Minus 5 coins gives a score of 2. If they had held the same four cards without being a run, the cost would be 7 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 31.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

A helper plays alongside. A lot costs its printed number (1 to 9). Runs do not count. Count coin cards as -1. Use only 24 lots and give each player 6 coins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

A lot costs its serial divided by 3, rounded up, but runs do not yet cancel anything. Add the run rule at the next game.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: runs count only the lowest card, three cards removed, coin cards as written.

Solo

No solo mode: the decision to pass depends on what the next player will do.

Two players

Not designed for two players; with 2 the pot grows without limit and the neighbour effect disappears.

Maths and skills in this game

Estimating whether a price is fair against a growing reward, adding and dividing by 3, and spotting neighbouring numbers in a row of cards.

Which card elements do the work

NumberFlavour the printed number is the cost at L1 only
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule a lot's cost is the serial divided by 3, and neighbouring serials form a run
NamesFlavour the children whose cards you collect
ExpressionNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (chunk 1, 400 to 1,500 games per cell): a tuned bot won 87% to 95% against random players. Against a competent mixed field it won 45%, 32% and 25% at 3, 4 and 5 players (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%). So skill exists, but it is much smaller against good opponents.

  • The threshold matters: a bot that is too bold or too timid drops below baseline. The tuned bot takes a lot when the extra cost, minus the pot, is no more than about 4, and it gets a bit more eager to take when its coins are under 3.

  • Seats: the first seat won 37% at 3 players against a 33% baseline, a small edge from the opening choice.

  • Length: 24 to 27 lots and 19 to 36 decisions per player, about 10 minutes at 12 to 20 seconds a decision.

  • Coins are cards: 9, 6 and 5 at 3, 4 and 5 players, which uses (54 - 3 hidden - 24 lots) = 27, 24 and 25 cards as coins.

  • Why runs: the Pass the Parcel version first scored a card as free if you held the number one lower. With six copies of every number a whole deck cost only about 6 points, so taking everything was almost free; a take-most bot beat a passing bot 95% of the time and the seat decided the game (seat 4 won 47%, seat 1 won 4%). Serials are unique, so runs of serial neighbours do not have this problem.

  • Pass the Parcel's colour-pair version (24 cards, 11 chips on paper, pass cost 1; 1,500 to 2,000 games per cell) gave a counting bot 70%, 57% and 53% at 3, 4, 5 players against 33, 25, 20%, with fair seats within 3 points of an even share and games of 13 to 19 minutes. Pots stayed small (the largest averaged about 5 chips).

  • Exact figure (my computation): the average lot cost over all 54 serials is 9.5 points, and a run of two saves the cost of the upper card.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots pass by formula and do not bluff or sulk.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written.

  • Not tested: the colour-pair variant with coin cards (it was only tested with chips on paper).

  • Not tested: the 3 hidden cards at 3 players against the 4 and 5 player counts as separate settings.

Variants and options

  • Pass the Parcel (Grown-Up Games doc, game 13) the same take-or-pay-to-pass game with chips on paper and colour-pair scoring. Kept: its fairness numbers. Optional colour-pair house rule: a lot scores 0 if you hold another lot with the same two colour numbers. It was tested with chips only. No longer a separate game.

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

NO TAKERS. Coin cards face down: 9 each at 3 players, 6 at 4, 5 at 5. Remove 3 cards unseen. Flip a lot. On your turn TAKE it with all coin cards on it (then flip the next lot and go again) or PASS by paying one coin card onto it. No coins: you must take. Keep your lots in serial order.

Back

SCORING. A lot costs serial / 3 rounded up. In a run of consecutive serials only the lowest costs. Each coin card left is -1. Lowest total wins; tie: more coins. LEVELS. L1 cost = printed number, no runs. L2 serial / 3, no runs. L3 full. No solo mode.

Add-Up Shed

Empty your hand first. Play a card that matches the middle card by number, makes nine with it, or shares a colour and a suit, or play two cards that add up to it. Sums are the whole point.

Inspired by DOS, Uno and Elfer raus

KidsFamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-03
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Match the middle card, make nine with it, share a colour and a suit with it, or play two cards that add up to its number. The first player to empty their hand wins the round. First to win three rounds wins.

What you need

All 54 cardshand cards and a draw pile
Colour and suit keysto check a match (colour borders and suit medals are printed on every card)

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 7 cards to each player at 2 or 3 players, 6 at 4 or 5 players, 5 at 6 players.

  • Turn the top card of the rest face up as the centre card. The remaining cards are the face-down draw pile.

  • The player on the dealer's left goes first. Later rounds: the player on the winner's left starts.

How to play

  1. On your turn, play one of these, putting it on the centre card:

  2. Number: a card with the same number as the centre card.

  3. Bond: a card whose number plus the centre card's number makes 9.

  4. Colour and suit: a card that shares at least one colour and at least one suit with the centre card (both, not just one).

  5. Pair: two cards from your hand whose numbers add up to the centre card's number. Play both. The one with the higher number is the new centre card; the other goes to the discard pile. If equal, you choose.

  6. Cannot play? Draw one card at a time from the draw pile until you can play. If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile (keep the centre card) to make a new one.

How it ends

The round ends as soon as a player has no cards left. That player wins the round. The game is won by the first player to win 3 rounds. If a draw pile and a discard pile are both empty and nobody can play, the player with the fewest cards in hand wins the round.

Words in this game

  • Centre card the face-up card on top of the pile that you must match.
  • Bond two cards whose numbers add to 9, for example 4 and 5.
  • Pair play putting down two cards whose numbers add up to the centre card's number.
  • Colour and suit each card has two border colours and two suit medals. A match needs one colour in common and one suit in common.

Common questions

  • Can I play a pair of cards that match each other? Only if their numbers add up to the centre card's number. For example, on a centre card of 6 you may play 2 and 4, or 1 and 5, or 3 and 3.

  • What is the centre card after a pair? The card with the higher number. The other goes to the discard. This choice can matter: keep the number you can follow up.

  • Does a match need both colours? No. One shared colour and one shared suit is enough. They do not have to be on the same side of the card.

  • Do I have to draw if I can play? No. You only draw when you cannot play. You draw one at a time and stop as soon as you can.

  • What if the centre card is a 9? A single card cannot make nine with a 9, so only another 9 (number match) or a colour and suit match plays alone. But pair plays are very flexible: any two cards that are a bond (4 and 5, 3 and 6, 2 and 7, 1 and 8) add up to 9.

Tips

  • Play two cards when you can. A pair play gets rid of two cards in one turn, which is the fastest way to empty your hand.

  • Choose which card becomes the centre. After a pair, the higher number stays. Think about which number your remaining cards can follow.

  • Count the ways each card in your hand can be played. A card that shares a colour and a suit with many others is easy to play later, so spend the awkward cards first and keep the flexible ones for the end.

  • Bonds are more flexible than numbers. A number match needs the exact same number, but a bond works with a different number, so a pair like 4 and 5 gives you two ways to answer.

  • Look at what you leave for the next player. If the centre is a number the next player cannot follow, they must draw, and you gain a turn.

  • Plan your last three cards. Try to finish with a card that will fit the centre you leave behind.

Worked example

  1. Two players, 7 cards each. The centre card is Dharsh (2) (serial 38). P0 holds Archana (5), Naresh (6), Guhan (3), Archana (4), Kanasu (6), Ammlu (7) and Ammlu (2).

  2. P0 plays Naresh (6). It shares the colour red and suits 2 and 6 with Dharsh (2), so it is a colour and suit match. Centre card: Naresh 6.

  3. P1 plays a pair: Gopi (5) and Amay (1) add up to 6. The higher card, Gopi (5), becomes the centre; Amay (1) goes to the discard. P0 replies with a pair: Guhan (3) and Ammlu (2) make 5. Centre: Guhan 3.

  4. P1 plays Adhiraa (3) on Guhan 3, a number match. P0 plays Kanasu (6) on Adhiraa 3: 3 + 6 = 9, so it is a bond. P1 plays Gowri (9) on Kanasu 6, a colour and suit match (blue, suit 4).

  5. P0 plays the pair Archana (5) and Archana (4), which add to 9, the centre card's number. Centre: Archana 5. P1 plays Rihansh (9) on it (shares yellow and suit 5). P0 plays Ammlu (7), their last card: it shares both colours and suit 5 with Rihansh 9. P0 has no cards left, so P0 wins the round after 5 turns, with no draws.

  6. The first player to win 3 rounds wins the game. If P1 starts the next round (the winner's left), they deal 7 new cards each.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Singles only: a card matches by number, bond, or colour and suit. No pair plays. One round, first to empty their hand wins. A helper can keep the keys beside them.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add pair plays (two cards that add up to the centre card). Play first to 2 rounds.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: first to 3 rounds, with the high card of a pair as the new centre.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is a race, so it needs an opponent.

Two players

Works best here: the bot won 64% at 2 players (baseline 50%). Rounds are short: a median of 6 turns each.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding two numbers to match a target, making nine, and planning which cards to hold: it trains mental addition without a worksheet.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule matches the centre card, makes nine with it, or adds to it
ColoursRule a shared colour is half of the colour and suit match
Suit pairRule a shared suit is the other half of the colour and suit match
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used

ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (chunk 1, 400 to 1,500 games per setting): with the final rules a hand-built bot won 64% at 2 players (baseline 50%) and 34% at 4 players (baseline 25%).

  • The first version never finished: with number match and pair sum only, nobody emptied their hand in 100% of games, even when players drew until they could play. Adding bond (a card that makes 9 with the centre) fixed part of it, but 38% of games at 4 players still did not finish. Adding the shared colour and suit match made every game finish.

  • Length: with the final rules a round has a median of 6 turns a player at 2 players and 4 at 4 players, so a game is scored over several rounds (first to 3).

  • Hand sizes: 7 at 2 to 3 players, 6 at 4 to 5, 5 at 6 players, set so the draw pile lasts.

  • Exact figure (my computation, all 54 x 53 centre and card pairs): a random other card can be played singly on a given centre card 49.7% of the time. 9.4% is by number, 10.1% by bond and 30.2% by colour and suit (counted in that order, so each pair is counted once).

  • Exact figure (my computation, 40,000 random deals): a 7-card hand has a single-card play 99.4% of the time (99.7% counting pair plays), a 6-card hand 98.7% (99.4%) and a 5-card hand 97.3% (98.4%). So you rarely draw on your first turn; the game is won by chains of good plays, not by luck of the first draw.

  • Number-only stalls: the design needed colour and suit because numbers alone leave too few legal plays when the hand shrinks.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot plays the move that empties the most cards and keeps the most follow-up plays.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written; they are subsets of the full rules.

  • Not tested: 5 and 6 player counts as separate settings, and the 'fewest cards' tie rule for a stuck round (rare, since stalls were 0% with the final rules).

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

ADD-UP SHED. Deal 7 (6 at 4 to 5 players, 5 at 6). Flip a centre card. On your turn play ONE card that: has the same number; makes 9 with it; or shares a colour AND a suit. OR play TWO cards whose numbers add up to the centre number (higher card becomes the centre, other goes to discard). Cannot play? Draw until you can.

Back

Rat Row

A small face-down row of four cards, a few you have peeked at, and a race to the lowest total. Swap in better cards, hope for matching numbers to cancel out, and knock when you dare.

Inspired by Rat-a-Tat Cat, Skyjo and Play Nine

KidsFamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-04
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min (6 rounds)
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each player has four face-down cards. Draw or take the discard, swap it into your row or throw it away, and knock when you think you are lowest. Two cards of the same number cancel to zero. Lowest total wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsfour in each player's row, a draw pile and a discard pile
Pencil and paperfor the round totals

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player 4 cards face down in a row (or a 2 by 2 square). Do not look at them yet.

  • Each player looks at any two of their own cards, then puts them back face down. Remember what they are and where they are.

  • Put the rest of the cards face down as the draw pile. Turn the top card face up beside it as the start of the discard pile.

  • The youngest player goes first.

How to play

  1. Take a card. Either take the top card of the draw pile or take the top card of the discard pile.

  2. Swap or throw. If you took the discard, you must swap it with one of your four cards. If you drew from the deck, you may swap it with one of your cards, or throw it onto the discard pile.

  3. How a swap works. Put the new card face down in the place of the old one, and put the old card face up on the discard pile. You now know where the new card is, and everybody sees what you threw away.

  4. Knock. At the end of your turn you may say Knock! if nobody has knocked yet. Every other player takes one more turn, and then all rows are turned over.

  5. Play goes clockwise. When the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discards (except the top card) and carry on.

How it ends

Turn all rows face up and add up the numbers. Two cards with the same number cancel to zero (at L1 only two cards of the same face, the twins, cancel). If you have three cards of one number, only one pair cancels; the third counts. Four of one number cancel in two pairs. The lowest total wins the round. Play 6 to 8 rounds, adding your totals; the lowest grand total wins. Ties share the win.

Words in this game

  • Row your four face-down cards.
  • Swap put a new card face down in the place of an old one, which goes face up on the discard pile.
  • Knock say 'Knock!' to end the round after one more turn each.
  • Cancel two cards with the same number count zero together.

Common questions

  • Can I look at my cards again? No. You peek at two at the start and after that you only learn a card's value by swapping it in yourself. Remember what you swapped.

  • What if I take the discard and do not want it? You must swap it with one of your cards. That is why taking the discard is a decision: it commits you.

  • Do I have to knock? No. If nobody knocks, the round ends when the draw pile runs out for the second time. Then everyone turns over.

  • What if I knock and someone else has a lower total? They win the round and you add your own total as usual. Knocking does not cost extra points in this version.

  • How do three of the same number score? One pair cancels and the third card counts. For example 5, 5, 5 and 2 scores 5 + 2 = 7.

Tips

  • Count unknown cards as 5. The average card is a 5, so a row with two unknown cards is worth about 10 plus whatever you know. Knock when your best estimate is about 9 or less.

  • Swap in any low card for a card you know to be high. Keep the 1s and 2s. A high card that you have peeked at is the first one to replace.

  • Match numbers on purpose. Two cards of the same number are zero, so a 4 in your row makes another 4 worth taking even if 4 is not low.

  • Look at the discard pile. A card you want may be on top. But taking the discard commits you to a swap, so only take it if it improves a known card or makes a pair.

  • Watch the others' discards. When someone throws a 9 face up after a swap, they got a better card in its place.

  • Do not knock on a guess. The bot only knocks at an estimate of 9 or less, or 11 or less when it knows all four cards.

Worked example

  1. Round 1, three players, same-number cancel (L2 and up). Each row holds four cards. P0 peeks at their first and last cards (Dhruv (6), 6, and Smaya (1), 1). P1 peeks at Guhan (3) and Anayka (1). P2 peeks at Nysha (8) and Bn Sharada (2). The discard pile starts with Idhayan (1).

  2. P0 takes the discard Idhayan (1) and must swap. They put it in place of the 6, so the 6 goes onto the discard pile. P0 now knows two 1s (Idhayan (1) and Smaya (1)), which cancel to zero.

  3. P1 draws Pinku (2) and swaps it for their first card (a hidden 4, Archana (4), that goes on the discard). P2 draws Ammlu (2). P2 peeked at Bn Sharada (2), so the two 2s cancel. P2 swaps the new 2 for their last card, a 9 (Adheesh (9)), which goes on the discard.

  4. P0 draws Amay (1) and swaps it for their second card, a 9 (Gowri (9)). P0's row is now 1, 1, a hidden card and 1. P0 guesses the hidden card is about 5 and the three 1s: one pair cancels and one 1 counts, so about 6. P0 says Knock!

  5. Everyone else gets one more turn. P1 draws Naresh (3) and swaps it for their second card (a hidden 6 that goes on the discard). Now P1 holds a 3 in two places: Naresh (3) and Guhan (3). P2 draws Naresh (6) and swaps it for their third card, a hidden 7.

  6. Reveal. P0: Idhayan (1) 1, Amay (1) 1, Pinku (7) 7, Smaya (1) 1. A pair of 1s cancels; the third 1 and the 7 count: 8. P1: Pinku (2) 2, Naresh (3) 3, Guhan (3) 3, Anayka (1) 1. The two 3s cancel: 2 + 1 = 3. P2: Nysha (8) 8, Bn Sharada (2) 2, Naresh (6) 6, Ammlu (2) 2. The 2s cancel: 8 + 6 = 14. P1 wins the round with 3, and P0's knock did not win. Round totals: P0 8, P1 3, P2 14.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Only two cards of the same face (a twin pair) cancel. This is rare, so most rows just add up. Play 4 rounds. A helper may check the sum.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Two cards of the same number cancel. Play 6 rounds.

L3 · age 8 and up

Same number cancels. Play 8 rounds. Optional twist (untested): if you knock and do not have the lowest total, add 5 to your score for the round.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is a race against other players' totals.

Two players

Works very well with two: the bot won 93% against a random player (baseline 50%). Rounds are short.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding four numbers up to 9, estimating an average (the unknown card is about a 5), and remembering where a card is.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the score, and two of the same number cancel
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesRule at L1, two cards of the same face (twins) cancel
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (chunk 6, 1,500 games per cell): the bot won 93%, 82%, 75% and 64% against random players at 2, 3, 4 and 5 players (baselines 50%, 33%, 25% and 20%), and sat at baseline against itself.

  • Why same number cancels: with twins only, a twin pair is in a row in just 6% to 11% of rows, so the cancel is a rare bonus. Letting any two cards of the same number cancel made it the main engine: 53% to 79% of rows cancel.

  • Length: the knocking bot ends a round in 4 to 5 turns each, so a round is about 1 to 2 minutes and 6 to 8 rounds make a game.

  • Exact figure (my computation): in a random row of four cards, the chance that two of them are twins is 11.2%, and the chance that at least two have the same number is 48.4%.

  • Exact figure (my computation, 100,000 random rows): the mean row total is 20 without cancelling and 14.9 with same-number cancel, so a typical winning total is in the single digits.

  • The bot's rules: it counts unknown cards as 5, takes the discard if it is 3 or lower or clearly below its worst known card, completes a known pair when it can, and knocks when its estimated total is 9 or less, or 11 or less when all four cards are known.

  • The bot started knowing two of its four cards. The peek-and-swap action from the idea list was not simulated, so the page has no peek during play.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot uses fixed thresholds and does not bluff by knocking early.

  • Not tested: the L3 knock penalty, the 4-round L1 game, or a game to a fixed number of points instead of rounds.

  • Not tested: the end of a round with no knock (the bots always knock), or 6 players, or a 2 by 2 layout against a single row.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

RAT ROW. Deal 4 face-down cards each. Peek at any 2 of yours. Turn the top of the deck face up as the discard. Your turn: take the top DISCARD (you must swap it in) or DRAW (swap it in or throw it away). A swap puts the new card face down in place of an old card, which goes face up on the discard. End your turn with Knock! if you think you are lowest: everyone else gets one more turn.

Back

SCORING. Add the four cards. Two cards with the same number cancel to zero (L1: twins only). Three of a number: one pair cancels. Lowest total wins the round. Play 6 to 8 rounds. LEVELS. L1 twins cancel, 4 rounds. L2 same number cancels. L3 8 rounds. No solo mode.

Foxes' Feast

Every child on a card has a twin. Turn two cards at a time to find a matching pair, and keep going while you are lucky. But one miss and everything you found this turn goes back.

Inspired by Memory with press-your-luck: Fox's Party, Stone Soup and Cowabunga

KidsEasyComplexity 1.1 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-05
Players
1 to 5
Time
5 to 10 min a board; 3 boards (15 to 30 min)
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Lay out pairs face down. On your turn flip two cards: if they are twins, keep flipping for more pairs, or stop and bank them. Any miss turns the cards back and you lose the pairs you had not banked.

What you need

24 cards (12 twin pairs)pick 12 faces at random and use both cards of each; or 8 faces (16 cards) at L1
Pencil and paperto keep score

Set up

  • Pick 12 faces at random from the 27 (L1 uses 8). Find both cards of each face: the twins. For 12 faces that is 24 cards.

  • Shuffle those cards and lay them out face down in a grid, 6 across and 4 down (4 across and 4 down at L1). The rest of the cards go back in the box.

  • Nobody has any points yet. The youngest player starts.

How to play

  1. Flip two. On your turn flip one card face up, then another. A pair is two cards of the same face (the twins: same name, same person).

  2. A hit. If they match, leave the pair face up in front of you for now. This is a pending pair. You may then press on and flip two more cards, or stop and bank.

  3. Stop. If you stop, move all your pending pairs to your score pile. They are yours for good.

  4. A miss. If the two cards are not twins, turn both back face down. Your pending pairs this turn also go back face down. You score nothing this turn.

  5. Everybody has seen the cards. Remember where they are! Then the next player goes.

How it ends

A board is finished when every pair has been banked. Each banked pair scores 1 point. A pair of one of the three double-nine faces (Rihansh, Gowri, Adheesh, where both cards are 9s) scores 2 points. Play 3 boards with new faces, add up the points; the most points wins. A tie shares the win.

Words in this game

  • Twins the two cards of the same face, with the same name and picture.
  • Pending pair a pair you have found this turn but not yet banked. A miss loses it.
  • Bank stop and move your pending pairs to your score pile.
  • Double-nine face a face whose two cards are both 9: Rihansh, Gowri and Adheesh.

Common questions

  • Do the numbers matter? Only for the double-nine bonus. Every pair of twins adds up to 9 (or 18 for the double-nine faces), so adding the numbers would tell you nothing. That is why a pair simply scores 1.

  • What if I flip a card I already know? You may do that on purpose. It is a safe first flip if you know where its twin is: flip the known card first, then its twin, and take the pair.

  • Why would I stop when I have a pair? Because every extra flip risks losing the pairs you have not banked. Late in the board, when few cards remain, pressing on is much safer.

  • Can I flip a card that is part of my pending pair? No. Pending pairs are not flipped again this turn.

  • What if I forget where a card is? Then you flip and find out. That is the game. Saying the names aloud as you flip helps everybody remember.

Tips

  • If you know where a twin pair is, take it first. That gives you a pair with no risk at all, and then you can decide whether to gamble on more.

  • Memory is the whole game, so say the names aloud while you play. 'Nakul in the top corner' sticks better than a picture.

  • Stop early on a full board. Early in a board you know almost nothing, and a miss costs your pending pairs. Bank the first pair and let the next player take the risk.

  • Press on when it is safe. Near the end of a board, the chance that a random flip finds a twin gets high. The bot only gambles when its chance of a hit is better than about one in three.

  • Watch where others miss. A card another player flipped and put back is free information for you.

  • With children, use fewer pairs. 8 pairs (16 cards) takes under 5 minutes and is very friendly for a 5 year old.

Worked example

  1. Two players, 12 faces, 24 cards laid out face down in 4 rows of 6, numbered 1 to 24. Cards are hidden and the layout is only known to the reader. Position 1 is Nakul (4), position 2 is Dharsh (7), position 4 is Nakul (5), position 5 is Gowri (9), position 6 is Adhiraa (6), position 8 is Adhiraa (3), position 17 is Gowri (9).

  2. P0 flips position 1 (Nakul (4), Nakul 4) and position 2 (Dharsh (7), Dharsh 7). Not twins. A miss, so both go back face down. Everybody now knows positions 1 and 2.

  3. P1 flips position 3 (Shreya 2) and position 4 (Nakul (5), Nakul 5). Not twins, so both go back. But positions 1 and 4 are now both known: they are both Nakul.

  4. P0 flips position 1 and position 4: Nakul (4) and Nakul (5), both Nakul. A pair, and it was no risk at all. P0 could press on, but the board is full of unknown cards, so P0 stops. P0 banks the pair: 1 point.

  5. P1 flips position 5 (a new card, Gowri (9), Gowri 9) then position 6 (Adhiraa (6), Adhiraa 6). Not twins. Both go back, but now P0 knows position 5 is Gowri and position 6 is Adhiraa.

  6. P0 flips position 8, a new card: Adhiraa (3), Adhiraa 3. Position 6 is Adhiraa, so P0 flips 6 as the second card: a pair (1 point pending). P0 presses on: position 17 is new: Gowri (9), Gowri 9. Position 5 is Gowri, so P0 flips 5: a pair of a double-nine face (2 points pending). P0 now has 3 points at risk and stops to bank them.

  7. Score after the first rounds: P0 has 1 + 3 = 4 points, P1 has 0. P1 has to find pairs on a board that now has only 9 pairs left.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Use 8 faces (16 cards). Stop after one pair: you flip until you miss or find one pair, then your turn ends and the pair is yours. No pending pairs, no risk. Play one board.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

12 faces (24 cards). You may press on after a pair, and a miss loses pending pairs. One board.

L3 · age 8 and up

12 faces, double-nine bonus, 3 boards. In a game of mixed ages, grown-ups cannot start a flip on a card that was turned over in either of the last two turns (untested handicap).

Solo

Solo: lay out 12 faces and play both sides. Count the number of turns it takes to clear the board (a turn ends at a miss or when you bank). A perfect-memory bot averages 16.2 turns on 12 faces and 9.8 turns on 8 faces. Suggested medals for 12 faces: Gold 16 or fewer, Silver 22 or fewer, Bronze 30 or fewer (a guess: the medal lines are not tested with people).

Two players

The board has 12 pairs. With two players a board takes about 8 turns each.

Maths and skills in this game

Visual memory, remembering where things are, and judging risk: when a gamble is worth more than the points you could lose.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule only for the double-nine bonus: both cards of the face are 9
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesRule twins are the two cards with the same face and name
ExpressionFlavour the mood on a face is a memory hook
PlaceFlavour the place behind the face is another memory hook

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Memory decides the game (chunk 6, 1,500 games per cell): a bot with perfect memory beat a bot with none every time. A seat that remembered only the last 2, 4 or 6 flips won 0%, 1% and 3% against two perfect-memory players at 3 players (baseline 33%).

  • I re-ran the perfect-memory bot against a no-memory bot for this page (300 games per cell): it won 100% at 2, 3 and 4 players with 12 pairs, and at 4 players with 8 pairs.

  • Why a pair scores 1: every twin pair adds up to 9 (24 faces) or to 18 (the three double-nine faces). So scoring a pair by its numbers, or giving a bond bonus, adds nothing. A pair scores 1, with a bonus for the three double-nine faces.

  • Length (chunk 6, and my re-run of 300 games): a board of 12 pairs takes 8.0, 5.4 and 4.0 turns each at 2, 3 and 4 players, and about 38 flips in all. A board of 8 pairs takes 4.9, 3.3 and 2.4 turns each, and about 25 flips. That is 4 to 6 minutes a board.

  • Solo (my run of 300 games): the perfect-memory bot clears 12 pairs in 16.2 turns on average, and 8 pairs in 9.8 turns.

  • Exact figure: a board of 12 faces drawn from 27 contains on average 12 x 3 / 27 = 1.33 of the three double-nine faces, so the bonus fires in most boards but is not huge.

  • The bot only presses its luck when its chance of a hit on the next flip is above about one in three, which happens late in a board. Early on it banks after the first pair.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real children. The memory-limited bots are a rough guide to how a younger player does, not a measurement.

  • Not tested: the double-nine bonus value of 2, the adult handicap, the solo medal lines, or 5 players.

  • Not tested: L1 as written (one pair per turn, no pending pairs).

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

FOXES' FEAST. Lay 12 twin pairs (24 cards) face down in a grid (8 pairs at L1). On your turn flip one card, then another. Twins (same face) = a pending pair. Press on and flip two more, or STOP to bank all pending pairs. A miss turns both cards back and loses the pending pairs of this turn.

Back

SCORING. A banked pair scores 1; a double-nine pair (Rihansh, Gowri, Adheesh) scores 2. Play 3 boards; most points wins. LEVELS. L1 8 pairs, one pair a turn. L2 12 pairs, press your luck. L3 3 boards, adult handicap. SOLO: clear the board in few turns; gold is 16 or fewer.
