Cockroach Court

Pass a card face down and tell the next player what team it is. They can believe you or not. If they guess right, you are stuck with the card. Take four of one team and you lose the hand.

Inspired by Cockroach Poker (Kakerlakenpoker) by Jacques Zeimet

RecommendedFamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-06
Players
2 to 6
Time
5 to 10 min a hand, 15 to 20 min for best of three
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Hand a card face down to another player and name a team, truthfully or not. They call it TRUE or FALSE. A correct call makes you keep the card; a wrong call makes them keep it. Four of one team face up loses the hand.

What you need

All 54 cardsthe team of each card is printed on the front; the claims are team animals
Team key (Ref 4)to read teams by animal name
Pencil and paperto count loser marks over three hands

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal them out evenly: 27 each at 2 players, 18 at 3, 13 at 4 (2 cards left over), 10 at 5 (4 left over), 9 at 6. Put the leftover cards face down in the box.

  • Keep your hand secret. Leave a space in front of you for cards you will have to take. Those go face up, grouped by team.

  • The youngest player offers first.

How to play

  1. Offer. Pick a card from your hand and a player to give it to. Put it face down in front of that player and name a team: 'This is a Cobra.' The claim can be true or false.

  2. Call. The receiver may look at the card, but only they look. They then say TRUE (I believe it is that team) or FALSE (it is not).

  3. Reveal. Turn the card over. If the receiver was right, the offerer takes the card. If the receiver was wrong, the receiver takes it. The taker puts it face up in front of them, grouped by team.

  4. Next offer. The receiver is the next to offer, whether they took the card or not.

  5. If you have no cards in hand when it is your turn to offer, you lose the hand.

How it ends

The hand ends the moment a player has four cards of one team face up in front of them. That player loses the hand and takes a loser mark. Play three hands (collect all the cards and deal again). The player with the fewest marks wins; players tied on marks share the win.

Words in this game

  • Offer a card passed face down with a claimed team.
  • TRUE / FALSE the receiver's call. TRUE means 'I believe it is that team.'
  • Loser mark a point against you. You get one when you lose a hand.
  • Team one of the six groups: Tigers, Elephants, Bears, Monkeys, Peacocks, Cobras. Teams have 8, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10 cards.

Common questions

  • Is the receiver ever allowed to look at the card? Yes, they look at it face down before they call, which gives no information to anyone else. In this version they cannot pass it on. A peek-and-pass option was not tested.

  • Which side takes the card if the receiver is right? The offerer. If you say the truth and the receiver believes it, you keep the card. If you lie and the receiver says FALSE, you also keep it.

  • Why do we deal out all the cards? Because the more cards you hold, the more you know. Holding six of the 8 Bears means a Bear claim from another player is very likely a lie.

  • Must I claim a different team every time? No. You may claim the real team or any other. Mix it up, because players who always lie or always tell the truth are easy to read.

  • What if two players reach four of a team on the same turn? This cannot happen: only one card is taken per offer.

Tips

  • Count what you hold. If you hold 6 of the 8 Tigers, there are only 2 left to claim, and someone else saying 'Tiger' is likely lying. The bots work out odds from cards not yet seen.

  • Watch the face-up cards. Every card taken is on the table, so you can work out how many of each team are still hidden. If most of a team is already face up, a new claim for that team is probably a lie.

  • Know who is in danger. A player with three of a team will do almost anything not to take a fourth. Hand them a card of that team under another name and they may call TRUE and take it.

  • Tell the truth to the player who expects a lie. If a player with three Cobras gets a Cobra offered, they will often say FALSE, thinking nobody would give them a Cobra. Offer it truthfully.

  • Do not become predictable. If you always bluff when you hold a card of a big team, the table learns it. Mix truthful and false claims about equally.

  • Remember the odds of a random card: 8 of 54 (14.8%) for Tigers, Elephants and Bears, and 10 of 54 (18.5%) for Monkeys, Peacocks and Cobras. A claim for a big team is a little more likely to be true by luck.

Worked example

  1. Three players, 18 cards each. P0 offers Bharati (4) (a Cobra) to P1 and says 'Cobra' truthfully. P1 believes it and calls TRUE. P1 was right, so P0 takes the card.

  2. P1 offers Naresh (6) (a Bear) to P2 and says 'Monkey'. P2 calls FALSE. Right again, so P1 takes the Bear.

  3. Many offers later, P0 has three Cobras face up: Bharati (4), Pinku (2) and Ammlu (2). P2 offers P0 Bharati (5), a Cobra, and truthfully says 'Cobra'.

  4. P0 thinks no one would give a player with three Cobras a Cobra, so P0 calls FALSE. P0 is wrong, so P0 takes the card. It is P0's fourth Cobra, so P0 loses the hand and gets a loser mark.

  5. Deal again. After three hands, the player with the fewest loser marks wins. If P0 has 2 marks and the others 1 and 0, the player with 0 marks wins.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Lose a hand at five of a team, not four. The hand is longer (23 to 25 offers in total) but forgiving. A helper may whisper a hint about the odds.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Four of a team loses; play one hand only.

L3 · age 8 and up

Four of a team loses; play three hands and count loser marks.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is reading other players.

Two players

Works with two. Each player has 27 cards, and every offer goes to the same person. Bluffs are easier to read, so mix your claims.

Maths and skills in this game

Estimating chances from what you can see, keeping track of team counts, and thinking about what the other player thinks about you.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (chunk 3, bots that work out odds from cards not yet seen): the bot ended as the loser of the hand only 6% to 15% of games, against baselines of 17% to 33% (one in six to one in three players), so skill matters.

  • Length (chunk 3): 13 to 18 offers in total when four of a team loses, and 23 to 25 when five do. At about 20 seconds an offer that is about 5 minutes for a hand of four, and about 8 for five.

  • Exact bound (my reasoning): a player can avoid losing only while they hold at most 3 of each team, so at most 18 cards can be taken before the 19th take loses the hand. With five as the limit the bound is 25. The simulated lengths fit under these.

  • Uneven teams on purpose (idea list): Tigers, Elephants and Bears have 8 cards and Monkeys, Peacocks and Cobras have 10, so a random card is a Tiger 14.8% of the time and a Cobra 18.5%. The three 10-card teams are the likelier danger.

  • Not tested in the bots: peek-and-pass, where the receiver passes the card on with a new claim. This is why the page does not allow it.

  • The bots assumed a player tells the truth about half of the time (a prior of 0.5), then adjusted by the cards they could see.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots call by odds and do not read faces or tone of voice.

  • Not tested: the three-hand scoring, L1 (limit five) with real players, or the team-key help for children.

  • Not tested: 2 players as a separate setting; the chunk 3 figures cover 3 to 6 players.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

COCKROACH COURT. Deal all cards evenly. On your turn pass a card face down to another player and name a team. They look, then call TRUE or FALSE. Receiver right: the OFFERER keeps the card. Receiver wrong: the receiver keeps it. Taken cards go face up by team. The receiver offers next.

Back

LOSING. Four of one team face up loses the hand (five at L1). No cards to offer? You lose. Best of three hands: fewest loser marks wins. Teams have 8, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10 cards. No solo mode.

Passport

Fill a Bangalore passport with a stamp from every kind of place, before the trip is over.

Inspired by From memory: Ticket to Ride style set collection reduced to six pages, and picture-bingo style place hunts.

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Roll a die for a kind of place, take a card of that kind from the spread, and fill six passport pages while chasing team and twin bonuses.

What you need

All 54 cards8 face up as the spread, the rest a face down draw pile, and each player's six passport cards
1 diethe Place die
Place keywhich place type each die number means
1 reference cardturn steps and scoring

Key cards for this game

Place key

One card with six pictures and words. Die 1 = Heritage and Worship (palaces, forts, temples, old gates). Die 2 = Hills and Caves. Die 3 = Museums and Sports. Die 4 = Parks and Wildlife. Die 5 = Streets, Markets and Rides. Die 6 = Water (lakes, tanks, rivers, boats). Each place type also has a small picture so a five year old can match it.

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. Put them in a face down draw pile.

  • Turn 8 cards face up in a row: the spread.

  • Each player makes a passport: six empty places in a row in front of them, numbered 1 to 6 left to right the same way as the Place key.

  • Keep a discard pile beside the draw pile. The youngest player starts.

How to play

  1. Roll the die. Read the place type on the Place key. You may roll once more, but you must keep the second roll.

  2. Look at the spread. If a card shows that place type, take one and put it in your passport at the place of that number. If that place already has a card, you may swap: the old card goes to the discard pile. Or take nothing.

  3. If the spread has no card of that type, flip the top card of the draw pile. If it is the right type, put it in your passport (same swap rule). If it is the wrong type, or you do not want it, add it to the spread.

  4. Refill the spread to eight cards from the draw pile.

  5. Pass the die left.

How it ends

Each player has twelve turns (count out loud). If the draw pile runs out first, finish that round. Score your passport. Highest score wins. Equal scores: share the win.

Words in this game

  • Spread The row of face up cards everyone can take from.
  • Passport Your row of six places, one for each place type. A place holds one card.
  • Twins The two cards showing the same child. Hold both and you score a bonus.
  • Team pair Two of your passport cards on the same team.

Common questions

  • The spread has two cards of the right type. Which do I take? Any one. That is the choice in the game: look at team and twin bonuses before you pick.

  • May I take a card to stop another player? Yes, if it is the type you rolled. You can swap it for a card in your own passport and it goes out of play.

  • My place already has a card and the new one is no better. Take nothing, or take it just to keep it from others. Swapped cards go to the discard pile and are out of play.

  • The draw pile has run out. Finish the round so everyone has the same number of turns. Then score.

  • Do I need to read the bonuses on the first game? No. In level 1, one point for each full place is all you count. The goal is a full passport.

Tips

  • Check the spread for team and twin bonuses before you take a card. A team pair scores 2 and a repeat child scores 3, and the choice between two cards of the right type is the whole decision.

  • Fill all six places by turn 12. A full passport adds 3, and a careful player fills it about 63% of the time at L1 against 28% for random play.

  • Roll twice only when your first roll gives you nothing. You must keep the second roll, and re-rolling when the average roll is better helped the simulated bots.

  • Take a card to deny a rival if it is the type you rolled. It also goes out of play if you swap it into your own passport.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1: one point for each full place. Let them roll the Place die and say the place type aloud before they hunt the spread.

Worked example

Three players, real seeded run. Players are Player 1, 2 and 3. Place die numbers: 1 Heritage, 2 Hills, 3 Museums, 4 Parks, 5 Streets, 6 Water.

  1. Player 1 rolls 6 (Water). The spread has Adheesh (9; Bears), a Water card. Player 1 puts it in place 6.

  2. Player 2 rolls 3 (Museums and Sports). The spread has Dhruv (6; Bears). Player 2 takes it for place 3.

  3. Player 3 rolls 2 (Hills and Caves). No Hills card is in the spread, so Player 3 flips the draw pile: Naresh (6; Bears), a Streets card. It is the wrong type, so it joins the spread and Player 3 takes nothing.

  4. Player 1 rolls 5 (Streets, Markets and Rides) and takes Naresh (6; Bears) from the spread for place 5. Player 1 now holds two Bears cards: Adheesh and Naresh, a team pair for 2 points.

  5. Turn 7. Player 1 holds Gowri (9; Cobras) in place 1 and Naresh (6; Bears) in place 5. Player 1 rolls 5 again and sees Gowri (9; Cobras) in the spread. It is the twin of Gowri (same child) and on the same team, so Player 1 swaps: Naresh goes to the discard pile and Gowri goes in place 5.

  6. End of turn 12. Player 1's passport is Gowri (9; Cobras), Adheesh (9; Bears), Ammlu (2; Cobras), Bharati (5; Cobras), Gowri (9; Cobras), Adheesh (9; Bears). Score: 6 for six full places, 3 for a full passport, team 6 has four cards (6 pairs, 12 points), team 3 has two (2 points), two twin pairs (Gowri and Adheesh, 6 points). Total 29. Player 2 scored 26 and Player 3 scored 10, who never filled places 4 and 5.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Only count one point per full place and aim to fill all six. Ignore bonuses. A grown-up reads the Place key aloud.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add the full passport bonus and twin bonus (3 each).

L3 · age 8 and up

Add team pairs (2 points per pair) and plan which team to chase. Swap and deny on purpose.

Solo

Play 12 turns alone. Level 1 goal: fill all six places (about 63% for a careful player, 28% for random play). Levels 2 and 3 score: Bronze 14, Silver 18, Gold 21 (25th, 50th and 75th percentile of the sim).

Two players

The spread is the same, so taking a card also denies it. Twelve turns each; the draw pile does not run out.

Maths and skills in this game

Sorting places into groups, counting points, noticing teams and twins, planning a set.

Not simulated. Fun of the stamping, whether children enjoy team and twin hunting, and how long children take to scan the spread. The place tags are approved.

Bots: random picks any legal card half the time, greedy takes the biggest immediate score gain and re-rolls when nothing useful shows, smart adds a team and twin planning bonus and re-rolls when the average roll is better. Smart is not clearly better than greedy, so I did not claim skill. Rerun after the mood tags moved: the engine does not read mood, so no number changed.

Tuning log

  • round 1: game ends as soon as one player fills all six places. The player who filled first won 83% of the time at two players (a pure race), and the whole game was 10 turns. Rejected.

  • round 2: fixed length, 12 turns each (the rest of the numbers use this). Bonuses: team pairs, twins, a full passport, mood variety. A greedy player already beats random 91% at 2 players; the 'smart' bot added team planning and gained only 54% against greedy.

  • round 3: removed the mood bonus (needed a second key, and the bots never planned for it). The skill gap did not change, so the choice is real but shallow: the best card is nearly always the one that scores most right now. The game stays as a quiet kids' filler, not a game of skill.

  • tags approved; K11 and K12 mood tags moved; re-ran. Passport reads place type only (the mood bonus was removed in round 3) and place types did not change, so every figure is unchanged: the same seeded games give identical results under the old and the new mood tags. Tags are now approved.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Treasure Ring (walk a ring, set turn-in by die): different, this one is collection by place type

  • Camp Kitchen (take cards, add to a target): this one is set collection and bonus pairs

Ratings

From memory, about like Sushi Go: one die, one placement, three scoring rules; teach about three minutes.

Start 10, minus one for the Place key being read each turn, minus one for scoring bookkeeping at levels 2 and 3. Teach about 3 minutes, setup under a minute, no downtime above 20 seconds.

Quiet and kind for a five year old, with a real but easy choice (which card, whether to swap). The weakest part: a greedy player is nearly as good as a smart one, and the tension is low. A filler, not a headline game.

Going Going Twin

Which of the two Arvinds is on the table? Only the child's other card knows, and it is hidden in somebody's hand.

Inspired by Dutch (descending) auction and Going Going Gone style shouting games; the private twin signal is new; from memory

FamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-08
Players
3 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
None (1 die in solo mode)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

A face-down card is shown by its name only while a count falls from nine to zero; shout Mine! to buy it at the current count and score its number minus the count, and if you hold the other card with the same name you know the number.

What you need

All 54 cardsEach player holds a hand (the twin signal); the rest is the lot deck. Each card is a possible lot.
Pencil and paper (Levels 2 and 3)A running score for each player. Level 1 needs no paper.
One thumbThe caller covers the number of the lot card with a thumb while the others see the child's name and face.
One die (solo mode only)Rolled for the ghost bidder.

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player a hand: 8 cards at 3 players, 6 at 4 players, 5 at 5 players, 4 at 6 players. Look at your hand and keep it hidden.

  • Put the rest face down as the lot deck. Leave room beside it for the sold row (Levels 1 and 2) or give each player room for a face-down pile (Level 3).

  • At Levels 2 and 3, write each player's name on the paper. The youngest player is the first caller. Callers go clockwise.

How to play

  1. Show the lot. The caller takes the top card of the lot deck without looking at its front. The caller holds it up with the front toward the other players and a thumb over the number. Everyone can see the child's name and face, nobody can see the number, and the caller cannot see the front at all. If anyone catches sight of the number, put that card on the bottom of the deck and take the next.

  2. Check your hand. Every child has two cards with the same name. If your hand holds the other card with that name, you are the twin holder: the lot's number is 9 minus the number on your card (if your card is a 9, the lot is a 9). You never have to say so. You also know the number if the other card of that child was sold earlier in this game: look in the sold row (Levels 1 and 2) or remember it (Level 3).

  3. Count down. The caller says the numbers aloud, nine, eight, seven and so on down to zero, at the pace of a slow clap, one number per clap.

  4. Shout. Any player, including the caller, may shout Mine! at any number. The count stops at the number being said. That number is your price. If two or more players shout at the same number, the one sitting first clockwise after the caller wins, and the caller is last in that order.

  5. Reveal and score. The caller shows the number. The winner scores the number minus the price, which can be below zero (Levels 2 and 3). Write it down. Level 1: you score the number only if the price is at or below it; if the price is higher you score nothing and the card is set aside.

  6. Put the lot away. Levels 1 and 2: the lot goes face up into the sold row, so everyone can see which children are gone. Level 3: show it to everyone, then the winner puts it face down in their own pile. Nobody may look through the piles.

  7. Zero is a price. If the count reaches zero and nobody has shouted, shouting at zero costs nothing and still wins. If nobody shouts at zero either, the caller turns the card up and sets it aside. That is called an unsold lot.

  8. Next caller. The next player clockwise takes the next lot.

How it ends

The game ends when every player has been caller the same number of times: 9 times each at 3 players (27 lots), 7 at 4 players (28 lots), 5 at 5 players (25 lots), 4 at 6 players (24 lots). The highest total wins. A tie goes to the player who won more lots; if still tied, they share the win. If the lot deck runs out early, the game ends at once and the last full round counts.

Words in this game

  • lot The face-down card up for sale, shown by its name only.
  • caller The player who shows the lot and counts down. The caller also shouts like anyone else.
  • price The number being said when someone shouts Mine!
  • twin holder A player whose hand holds the other card with the lot's name. That player knows the lot's number.
  • sold row The face-up row of sold lots (Levels 1 and 2). It helps everyone remember which children are gone.
  • unsold lot A lot nobody shouted for, even at zero.

Common questions

  • Two of us shout at the same number. Who wins? The shouter nearest clockwise after the caller. The caller is last. The caller changes every lot, so the order stays fair over the game.

  • Can I shout Mine! when I know the lot is a low number? Yes, but you pay the price and score number minus price, which is below zero if the price is higher. Usually you stay quiet and let someone else overpay.

  • What does a 9 tell me? Three children have two 9s: Rihansh, Gowri and Adheesh. If you hold a 9 with the lot's name, the lot is a 9 as well.

  • May I talk, bluff or say what I hold? You may say anything you like, but you never have to tell the truth and a promise is not binding. The sim says bluffing shouts does not pay, but it is allowed.

  • What if the lot's name matches a card in my hand? Then you are the twin holder: the lot is the child's other card, and its number is 9 minus yours.

  • The caller peeked at the number. Put the card on the bottom of the deck and take the next one. The caller keeps the turn.

  • Nobody wants the lot until zero. What then? Anyone may shout Mine! at zero for a price of nothing. Most of the time someone does.

Tips

  • If you hold the other card with the lot's name, you know the number: it is 9 minus yours (a 9 means 9). Shout when the count has fallen to a price below that number, and keep quiet when the lot is low.

  • Remember the sold row. About 22 to 25% of lots have a twin already sold, so you know those numbers too, and at L3 the row is face down, so you must remember.

  • Let others overpay when you know a lot is low. A twin-using bot won 74% at four players against three bots that ignored twins (even 25%).

  • Bluffing a shout does not pay in simulation, but it costs nothing to try once with children, as long as you do not mind paying the price.

  • The count is a slow clap. With a 5-year-old, play L1 (no minus scores) and let them shout at any count, and help them see that a lower count means a better price.

Worked example

Four players, A to D, 4 players, six cards each. A holds Idhayan (1), Pinku (2), Naresh (3), Shreya (7), Gowri (9) and Adheesh (9). B holds Ajay (2), Nakul (5), Avika (5), Naresh (6), Sharada (6) and Bn Sharada (7). C holds Amay (1), Dharsh (2), Adhiraa (3), Archana (5), Smaya (8) and Arvind (8). D holds Arvind (1), Dhruv (3), Kanasu (3), Kanasu (6), Ammlu (7) and Anayka (8). Level 3.

  1. Lot one: A is the caller. The card is Bn Sharada. B holds Bn Sharada (7), so B knows the lot is 9 minus 7, which is 2. B stays silent. A knows nothing, counts down and shouts Mine! at 5. The card turns out to be Bn Sharada (2). A scores 2 minus 5, which is minus 3.

  2. Lot two: B is the caller. The card is Dhruv. D holds Dhruv (3), so D knows the lot is 9 minus 3, which is 6. D and B both shout at 5. C did not shout. Order is C, D, A, B, so D wins. The card is Dhruv (6). D scores 6 minus 5, which is plus 1.

  3. Lot three: C is the caller and holds Amay (1), so C knows the lot named Amay is 9 minus 1, which is 8. C waits until 6 and shouts. The card is Amay (8). C scores 8 minus 6, which is plus 2.

  4. Lot four: D is the caller. The card is Rihansh. Nobody holds the other card of that name, so nobody knows. D shouts at 5. The card is Rihansh (9), a 9. D scores 9 minus 5, which is plus 4, and is lucky.

  5. Lot five: A is the caller. The card is Avika. B holds Avika (5), so B knows the lot is 4. B, D and A all shout at 3. Order is B, C, D, A, so B wins. The card is Avika (4). B scores 4 minus 3, which is plus 1.

  6. Lot six: B is the caller. The card is Adhiraa. C holds Adhiraa (3), so C knows the lot is 6. C, D and A all shout at 5, and C is first clockwise after B. The card is Adhiraa (6). C scores plus 1. After six lots: A is on minus 3, B on plus 1, C on plus 3, D on plus 5.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5: no paper and no minus scores. You win the card's number only if the price is at or below it, so the lesson is 'call when the count is as low as the card'. A grown-up covers the number and counts slowly. Lots go face up in the sold row, and each player keeps won cards in a pile to add up at the end.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 and 7: score the number minus the price on paper, including minus scores. Sold lots stay face up in the sold row.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: sold lots go face down into the winner's pile after everyone has seen the number, so you must remember which children were sold to work out their twins.

Solo

Take 8 cards as your hand and play 20 lots from the rest. Look at the lot's name only. Decide your price from 0 to 9 and write it down. Roll one die and add one; that is the ghost bidder's price (2 to 7). If your price is higher than the ghost's, you win the lot and score the number minus your price. If it is equal or lower, the ghost wins and you score nothing. The lot goes face up in the sold row either way. If you hold the twin, or the twin is already in the sold row, you know the number. Score after 20 lots: Bronze 4, Silver 8, Gold 12, Master 16 (these are the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles of a bot that uses its twins and the sold row).

Two players

Two players work: each holds 12 cards, the game is 10 calls each (20 lots), and the other player is the only one who can beat your shout. A twin-using bot beat a bot that ignored twins 86 percent of the time. It is more of a duel and has less noise than the 4 player game.

Maths and skills in this game

Subtraction as distance (number minus price), remembering what has been shown, and keeping a poker face. At Level 1: comparing a spoken count to a number.

Reference card

Going Going Twin

The caller shows a card with the number covered and counts down from nine. Shout Mine! to buy it at the current count. You score the number minus the count. Hold the other card with the lot's name and you know the number.

  • Twin: number = 9 minus yours (a 9 means 9)
  • Same count: nearest clockwise after the caller wins
  • Zero is a legal price

Not simulated. Human shouting speed, the count pace, whether the thumb hides the number reliably, how often two people really shout at the same number, humour, and how a child of 5 handles the count. Bots hold ideal memory of the sold row, which a person will not.

The Going Going Gone problems are fixed in three ways: ties get a fixed seat rule; unsold lots vanish because zero is a legal price; and the old collapse to 'shout at the average' is harmless now because bids on unknown lots are worth zero for everyone, so the points come from the twin lots. The weakest finding is that reading silence and bluffing give nothing, so the game plays as 'know your twin, shout just before the crowd, remember the sold row', not as a mind game. The player's information is luck of the deal: at an equal table most of the result is who holds twins. Bot rule used: twin holder shouts at the lot number minus one but never above six; everyone else shouts when the average number (5) minus the price is at least half a point, with timing noise.

Tuning log

  • round 1: first engine had every bot shout at the same fixed number, so 100 percent of lots were tied and the bot that used its twin won 70 percent at four players (even share 25). Added human-like timing noise (a spread in how much each bot thinks the lot is worth, and a 25 percent chance of being one number late). Ties fell to 48 percent of lots at four players but stay between 48 and 60 percent at 3 to 6 players, so the tie rule is a real rule, not a corner case. Tie rule kept deterministic: the shouter nearest clockwise after the caller wins, and the caller rotates, so seat bias stays small (see rows).

  • round 2: the twin holder's best shouting number was tested. Shouting at the lot number minus one but never above a cap: cap 2, 3, 4 give 9 to 13 percent against three cap-5 players, cap 5 is even, cap 6 gives 42, cap 7 gives 39, cap 9 gives 35. Fixed the cap at 6 for the final runs (a bot's rule is 'shout one below the number, but never above six'). Also swept how eagerly a player bids on lots nobody knows: any margin from 0.5 to 4 gives 24 to 26 percent against even 25, and a bot that never bids on unknown lots gets 24.4 percent. So bidding on unknown lots is worth nothing either way, which is the honest answer to the old 'shout at the average' collapse: it is now harmless, because the money is in the known lots.

  • round 3: hand sizes were set so the share of lots where a player holds the twin is 45 to 47 percent (three players with six cards gave only 34, so three players hold eight). Lots per game are fixed so every player calls equally (27, 28, 25, 24 lots for 3, 4, 5, 6 players). Unsold lots fell to 0.0 percent because zero is a legal shout. Then tested reading silence, bluffing and memory (rows below). Reading silence adds 0 to 3 points of win share at equal tables and a bluffing bot loses 8 to 11 points, so reading and bluffing are not skills in this game; remembering which children were sold is (a bot without memory gets 12.9 against 29.0). No rule change was needed, so the game is kept, but the fun rating is held at 6.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Summit Bid (sealed bid, highest serial): here the price falls out loud and the lot is shown by name, so there is no sealed bid

  • The Gala (auction with money cards): there is no money, the price is the count

  • Twin Tracker (hide a twin): this uses the twin as a private fact about the number, not as something to find

  • Going Going Gone (dropped earlier): same count-down shout, but with a private twin signal, a fixed tie rule and no unsold lots

Ratings

from memory: about six rules, one decision (shout now or wait), teach time about three minutes

Setup under one minute and no key card; running score on paper at Levels 2 and 3 costs 1; the caller must keep the number covered with a thumb and count at a steady pace (needs a quick check that a thumb really hides the number on the printed card), which costs 1 because it is a physical trick; ties are frequent so the clockwise rule must be remembered, costing 1; stall rate 0 and downtime under 20 seconds.

The shout is a real moment of tension and the twin makes each player the only one who knows something; but only lots whose twin is held (about 46 percent) have a decision, bids on the other lots are worth nothing, reading the table and bluffing do not pay, and at an equal table the winner is mostly whoever held the twins. Good for a party, thin for repeat play.

Hill Claim

Six hills, one scout, and a secret about which hill is worth the climb.

Inspired by Mint Control (area majority with influence tokens), from memory

FamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 9 / 10Fun 6 / 10

FT-09

2

10 to 15 min (a two-game match)
Age
7+
Dice
1 die (first player and ties)
Pawns
2 (one each)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Place face-down cards on six hills where their suit fits, spend a turn to peek at one hill's secret value, and win each hill with the higher total.

What you need

6 hill cardsAny six cards, shuffled, laid backs up in two rows of three. Number the hills 1 to 6 reading left to right, then top to bottom. A hill's front number (1 to 9) is its secret value.
10 influence cardsFive per player, dealt from the same shuffled deck. Held with fronts to you.
1 dieFirst player, and tie-breaks.
2 pawnsOne each. Your pawn sits on the hill you last peeked at.

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. Lay six cards backs up in two rows of three: these are the hills. Do not look at their fronts.

  • Deal five cards to each player. These are your influence cards. Look at your own fronts and keep them hidden from the other player. The rest of the cards go back in the box.

  • Each player takes a pawn and puts it beside the hills.

  • Both players roll the die. The higher roll goes first (roll again on a tie).

How to play

  1. You get exactly five turns. On each turn you do one of two things.

  2. PLAY: put one influence card face down (front down) on a hill. The card is allowed only if one of the two suits on its front is also on the back of that hill. Your own played cards may be looked at by you at any time.

  3. PEEK: put your pawn on any hill (taking it off the old one) and secretly look at that hill's front. Its number is the hill's value. Your opponent can see where your pawn is but not what you learned.

  4. Cards you did not play after five turns are thrown away. So every peek costs you one card.

How it ends

After the fifth turn of the second player, remove any card that was played on a hill whose back shows none of the card's front suits. Then, hill by hill, turn over the hill card and every card on it. Add the front numbers of each player's cards on that hill. The higher total wins the hill and scores the hill's front number as points. If the totals are equal (including both zero), both players roll the die: higher roll takes the points. Most points wins. Play two games, swapping who goes first, and add the scores for a fair match.

Words in this game

  • hill One of the six cards laid backs up. Its secret value is its front number.
  • influence card A card from your hand that you play onto a hill.
  • peek Spend a turn to move your pawn onto a hill and look at its front.
  • fits A card fits a hill when one of the card's front suits is also on the hill's back.

Common questions

  • Can I look at my own played cards? Yes, any time. You cannot look at your opponent's.

  • What if a card does not fit any hill? It rarely happens (about one hand in 100,000). If it does, you may peek instead, or throw the card away.

  • What if I play a card that does not fit? Nothing happens until the end. Then it is removed and counts as zero. Do not cheat; it wastes your turn.

  • Can I peek at the same hill twice? There is no use, but you may. It costs a turn.

  • Does my pawn do anything else? It shows where you looked. A smart opponent will guess that the hill is worth fighting for or worth ignoring.

  • What if I have no cards left but turns remain? Peek. A turn may not be skipped.

  • Can there be a tie for the whole game? Yes, about one game in 25 ends level on points. Play one more game, or call it shared.

Tips

  • One peek is usually right. One peek beat none 57% of the time and a second peek only 51.5% over one, while a third lost 70% of the time, since each peek costs one of your five cards.

  • Peek on the hill you are most unsure about and where your cards would fit. Your pawn shows where you looked, so move it to a hill you do not care about to bluff.

  • Play your highest cards on the hill with the biggest value after you have peeked, and your low cards on the hills you suspect are small.

  • Check the suit fit before you play. A card on a hill whose back shows none of its suits is removed at the end and counts as zero, which wastes your turn.

  • Always play the two-game match, swapping who goes first. With only ten plays in a game, luck of the deal is large, and a two-game match cuts it.

Worked example

Hills in reading order, backs up: Archana (4), Naresh (3), Dharsh (2), Smaya (8), Nakul (5), Amyra (4). Player one rolled higher and goes first.

  1. The six hills as the players see them: backs only.

  2. Player one peeks: pawn to hill 4. Smaya (8) is a hill worth 8 points. Player two sees only the pawn.

  3. Player two peeks: pawn to hill 2. Naresh (3) is worth only 3.

  4. Player one plays Gowri (9) (a 9) onto hill 4. The card's front shares suit 5 with the hill's back, so it fits.

  5. Player two plays Nysha (8) (an 8) on hill 1, sharing suit 6, and leaves the 3-point hill 2 alone.

  6. Over the next turns, player one plays Anayka (8) on hill 2 and Ajay (2) and Arvind (1) on hill 6. Player two plays Ajay (7) on hill 3, Bn Sharada (7) on hill 5 and Guhan (6) on hill 4, against the 9.

  7. Reveal. Hill 4 (8 points): player one has 9, player two has 6, so player one scores 8. Hill 2 (3): player one 8 against nothing, 3 points. Hill 6 (4): player one has 2 plus 1, which beats nothing, 4 points. Player one has 15. Player two takes hill 1 (4), hill 3 (2) and hill 5 (5) for 11. Player one wins, 15 to 11.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6. Turn all six hills face up from the start. Play your cards face up. No peeking, no pawns. Just add and compare. A grown-up checks that cards fit.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 7 and up. The standard game above, five cards, five turns.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 10 and up. Play a three-game match (swap who goes first each time) and add the scores. The one who goes second in game one goes first in game three.

Solo

Play against the Rival. Deal the Rival five cards face down in a pile. On each Rival turn, roll the die: that is the hill. Play the top Rival card face down there if it fits. If not, try the next hill number (6 goes to 1) until it fits. The Rival never peeks. You take five turns, you go first, and you may peek. Score as normal. A win is Bronze. Win by 4 or more is Silver. Win by 9 or more is Gold (the best-play bot wins about 61 percent, median margin +3, 75th percentile +9).

Two players

This is a two-player game. Three or four players would need more pawns and more hills, and the game would lose its speed.

Maths and skills in this game

Addition of several one-digit numbers, comparing totals, deciding whether information is worth a turn, bluffing by pawn.

Not simulated. Fun, bluffing with the pawn (the bots read where the opponent put their pawn only as a small value hint), and how well a ten-year-old adds six or seven numbers per hill. The gap between smart and greedy is modest at 59 percent, so this is a game of luck and moderate skill. The L1 and L3 versions are not simulated.

Tuning described in tuning_log. Honest read: with only ten plays in a game, luck of the deal matters a lot. The 59 percent edge over a bot that never peeks and the 72 percent edge over random show that the choices matter, but not heavily. A two-game match cuts the luck.

Tuning log

  • round 1: six cards each, seven turns each (peeks cost nothing extra). Second player won 56 percent (last-mover edge) and bots that peeked three times beat bots that peeked once, 81 to 69 percent against a non-peeker. Peeking was nearly free and dominant. Added a free first peek for player one: seat balanced at 50 percent, but peeking was still too strong.

  • round 2: cut to five cards each and exactly five turns each, so every peek costs one unplayed card. Now one peek beats none 57 percent, two peeks beat one 52 percent, three peeks lose to two 70 percent: a real trade-off with the best answer at one or two peeks. The free first peek was no longer needed: with it player one won 58 percent, without it 50.5 percent. Removed it.

  • round 3: tested a Gold Hill (roll the die first and score that hill double). It cut smart vs greedy from 59 to 44 percent and made the seat advantage 57 percent, so it was rejected. The die now breaks ties (about 5 percent of games have one tied hill) and picks the first player. Final: hand 5, five turns, ties by die roll.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Map the Island (building from backs): different; Hill Claim uses the front-suit to back-suit fit as a gate and hidden values for scoring.

Ratings

From memory, similar to Sushi Go in rule count; two actions only; teach time about two minutes.

Teach about two minutes, setup under a minute, no key, no stalls (fixed ten turns), but only two players (-1).

Quick, with a nice reveal at the end and a real question each turn (play or peek, and where). Weakest part: modest skill gap and little choice in the last two turns.

Two-Sided Crew

Every card in your hand is either the money for a camp or the camp itself, and you only learn which by deciding.

Inspired by San Juan (cards are buildings and money) boiled down to one rule; from memory

KidsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 5 / 10
Game code
FT-10
Players
2 to 4
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
6+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each turn take one card, then either build a camp with a card from your hand (paying with other cards whose numbers add up), or hold; first to 60 camp points wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsEvery card is a possible coin (its number is its money), a camp (played face up), or from Level 2 a crate (played face down under a camp).
Open space for a coin pileSpent cards go face up in one pile in the middle.

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal four cards to each player. Players look at their own cards and keep them hidden.

  • Put the rest face down as the deck. Leave room beside it for the coin pile, which starts empty.

  • The youngest player goes first. Play goes clockwise.

How to play

  1. Take a card. Take the top card of the deck, or take the top card of the coin pile (it is face up, so you can see it). Add it to your hand.

  2. Then do one thing, or pass. (a) Build a camp: put one card from your hand face up in front of you. Pay for it by putting cards from your hand on the coin pile. The numbers on the paid cards must add up to at least the number on the camp. No change is given, so paying 9 for a 6 wastes 3. (b) Level 2 only, put a crate: put one card from your hand face down under one of your camps. Its back must show at least one of the two suits on that camp, and a camp can hold only one crate. (c) Pass: do nothing and keep your cards.

  3. Keep five cards. If you hold more than five, put the extra cards on the coin pile. You choose which.

  4. Your score is the total of every camp (its number plus four) and, at Level 2, three for every crate. Say your score out loud after you build. When any player reaches 60 or more, finish the round so everyone has had the same number of turns.

How it ends

The game ends after the round in which someone reaches 60 points (70 at Level 3). Most points wins. If points are tied, the tied player who went earlier in the turn order wins. If the deck runs out, shuffle the coin pile, except its top card, to make a new deck.

Words in this game

  • Camp A card you played face up in front of you. It scores its number plus four.
  • Coin A card you pay with. Its number is its money. You can pay with a card from your hand only on your own turn when you build.
  • Coin pile The face up pile of paid and thrown cards. Its top card can be taken instead of drawing.
  • Crate Level 2: a card face down under a camp. Worth three points.

Common questions

  • Can I build a camp with only one card in my hand? No. You need the camp and at least one other card to pay with. Even a camp with number 1 needs a paying card.

  • Can I build two camps in one turn? No. One thing per turn.

  • Can I pay with a card that has a bigger number than the camp? Yes, but there is no change. That is why holding a big card for a big camp is often better.

  • Can I take the card another player just paid with? Yes. The top of the coin pile is open to everyone on their own turn.

  • Can I look at the cards in the coin pile below the top? No. Only the top card matters.

  • Does the card on the coin pile have to be shown front up? Yes. Put paid and thrown cards face up so everyone sees the front.

  • Two players tie on points. Who wins? The one who went earlier in the turn order.

Tips

  • Hold a big card for a big camp. There is no change, so paying a 9 for a 6 wastes 3. Careful play held on 7 to 30% of the turns it could build, and the bots that were pickier than 1 to 2 points per card beat build-anything 54 to 46.

  • Do not be too picky either. Pickier than 3 points per card lost 26 to 74, so build when the waste is small.

  • Watch the coin pile. The top card is face up and anyone may take it, and at two players you often pick up the card your rival just paid with.

  • Keep five cards at most. Discard the card you need least, and remember the cards you throw go face up for others.

  • Grown-up with a child: build whenever you can and let the child choose the holds. The build-anything bot is a fair picture of a young child's strategy, and an attentive parent will win most games otherwise.

Worked example

Level 2, two players, play to 60. Player A has two camps and a crate, Arvind (8) and Amyra (4), with Dharsh (2) under Arvind (8): 23 points. Player B has Naresh (6) and Dhruv (6), with Amay (1) under Naresh (6): 23 points. Cards in the example come from a real simulated game.

  1. Player A takes the top of the coin pile, Adheesh (9), which Player B just paid with. It is A's only card, and building needs a paying card too, so A passes.

  2. Player B draws Nysha (1) and builds it as a camp, paying with Ammlu (2) (2 is enough for a 1). The camp is worth 1 + 4 = 5. B now has 28.

  3. Player A draws Dhruv (3). A could build Dhruv (3), but would have to pay with Adheesh (9) (9) for a camp that needs only 3. A holds both cards and passes.

  4. Player B draws Adhiraa (6). It is B's only card, so B cannot pay for it and passes.

  5. Player A draws Kanasu (6). Now Dhruv (3) (3) and Kanasu (6) (6) add up to exactly 9. A builds Adheesh (9) as a camp and pays with those two. It is worth 9 + 4 = 13, so A jumps from 23 to 36.

L1 · ages 6 to 7, camps only

Camps only, no crates, play to 60.

L2 · ages 7 to 8, add crates

Add crates: a card face down under a camp whose suit shows on the card's back. Each crate scores three.

L3 · age 9 and up, play to 70

Crates, and play to 70. Players who like a puzzle try to pay exactly and waste nothing.

Solo

Play alone with no other players. Take a card and do one thing each turn exactly as above. Count the turns until you reach 60 (Level 1 or 2). Level 1: Gold 9 turns or fewer, Silver 11 or fewer, Bronze 13 or fewer. Level 2: Gold 9 or fewer, Silver 10 or fewer, Bronze 12 or fewer. (From the careful bot: 10th percentile 9, median 10 to 11, 90th percentile 12 to 13.)

Adding to a target (pay cards that add up to the camp's number, and the leftover is the waste), comparing, saving a card for later, keeping a running total up to 60. At Level 2, matching a suit on a back to a camp.

Tuning log

  • round 1: first version (camp worth its number, play to 20) ended in 4.3 turns each, about 4 minutes. Raised the target to 36 to 40, but then the 'build the biggest thing you can pay for' bot lost 90 percent to the careful bot (even share 50), which is too punishing for a children's game.

  • round 2: tried cheaper camps (pay half, pay number minus one): smart bot still won 70 to 76 percent. Added a flat +4 points to every camp and set the target to 60. Smart bot now wins 69 percent of 2p games against the build-anything bot and 63 percent at 3p (even share 33). Length about 10 turns each.

  • round 3: tried a catch-up rule (trailing player takes an extra card). Seat 2 then won 75 percent of 2p games, so it was rejected. Seat bias with equal turns was 32.5 / 32.3 / 35.1 at 3p; adding 'a tie goes to the player who went earlier' removed the rest. Final: no stalls, tie rate 3 to 6 percent.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Camp Kitchen: both add card numbers to a target; here the same card can be money or a building across turns.

  • Pen and Plume: the grown-up build-or-sell market; this is the simple version of the same idea.

Ratings

From memory: one decision a turn, three rules to learn (take, one thing, five cards), teach time under three minutes; the adding is the hard part.

Teach about 2 min, setup under 1 min, no stalls. Minus one for adding to 60 and paying sums (arithmetic burden). Minus one at 4 players (16 min and waits).

Real hold or build choices (careful bot holds on 7 to 30 percent of buildable turns) and a nice moment when a big card finishes a camp exactly, but low tension and almost no interaction beyond the coin pile. A fine filler.

Inspired by Sushi Go style pick-and-pass drafting and 7 Wonders hand passing (from memory); scoring is original.

The whole game in one line

Everyone holds nine cards, keeps one face up in their album, passes the rest left, and repeats until the cards run out; then you score places in groups, a spread of moods and matching scenes.

What you need

All 54 cardsNine per player (six at level one). Cards not dealt are not used.
Place and Mood keyOne reference card sheet with six place icons and six mood icons, used to sort pictures.
Paper and pencilScore line per player (level two and up). Level one is counted aloud.
1 die (solo only)Rolls which kind of place the ghost removes.

Key cards for this game

Place and Mood key

Place side, six icons with three example pictures each, numbered 1 to 6: 1 Heritage and Worship, 2 Hills and Caves, 3 Museums and Sports, 4 Parks and Wildlife, 5 Streets, Markets and Rides, 6 Water. Mood side, six faces with three example pictures each, numbered 1 to 6: 1 Body and Senses, 2 Brave and Fierce, 3 Delight, 4 Mischief, 5 Startle and Wonder, 6 Think and Notice. Level one uses the Place side only. The groups come from the approved place and mood tags.

Set up

  • Put the Place and Mood key in the middle. Shuffle all 54 cards and deal nine to each player (six at level one). Put any left over back in the box.

  • Look at your own cards. Keep the fronts hidden from the others.

  • Leave space in front of you for your album. Cards in an album lie face up for everyone to see.

  • Write the players' names on the paper (level two and up).

How to play

  1. Choose: pick one card from your hand and put it face up in your album.

  2. Pass: when everyone has chosen, pass the rest of your hand face down to the player on your left. At the same time pick up the hand from the player on your right.

  3. Repeat. Every round your hand is one card smaller. After the last round you have an album of nine cards (six at level one).

  4. Score (level two). Place chapters: for each place type, count your cards of that type. Three cards score 6, four score 8, five score 10, six score 12 (two more points for each extra card). One or two cards score nothing.

  5. Mood spread: count the different moods in your album. Four moods score 2, five score 5, six score 9.

  6. Scenes: each pair of cards with the same place type and the same mood scores 3. A card can be in one pair only. Three cards of the same place and mood make one pair and one spare.

  7. Level one scoring: for each place type, two cards score 1, and three or more score 1 for every card.

How it ends

Play three deals (level one: one deal) and add up the scores. Highest total wins. Tie: most scenes, then most place types, then share the win.

Words in this game

  • album the cards you have kept, face up in front of you.
  • place type which of the six kinds of place the picture shows, read from the Place key.
  • mood which of the six kinds of expression the face shows, read from the Mood key.
  • chapter three or more cards of the same place type in your album.
  • scene a pair of cards with the same place type and the same mood.

Common questions

  • Is the last card forced? Yes. With one card in your hand you keep it. Nine rounds mean eight real choices.

  • Can I look at other albums? Yes, always. Reading the albums and what comes back to you is the skill.

  • Can I remember what I passed? Yes. With n players the hand you started comes back after n rounds with nine minus n cards, so at four players it returns with five cards and at six with three.

  • I cannot tell the place or mood of a picture. Use the key pictures. If still unsure, the group votes, and the answer holds for that card for the whole game.

  • What if fewer than six play? Deal nine each. Unused cards go back in the box unseen, so no one can count the deck.

  • Are albums scored per deal or for the match? Per deal. Add the three deal scores for the match.

  • Can two players play? Yes, with a dummy hand, see two-player mode.

Tips

  • Do not grab the biggest score. The best pick matched the greedy pick only 42% of the time, so keep a second place going.

  • Read the albums. What comes back to you tells you what your neighbours want, and with n players your hand returns after n rounds.

  • Do not spend picks on denying your left neighbour. In simulation denial lost (34% against 41%).

  • Chase chapters of three or more of a place first (3 cards score 6), then fill the mood spread (4 moods score 2, 5 score 5, 6 score 9), then look for scene pairs.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1: six cards, places only, and count aloud. Let them sort their album by place as they go.

Worked example

Level two, four players. You are player A. Place and mood are read from the key. You pass left, and you pick up from your right.

  1. Round 1. Your hand: Amay (8), Adheesh (9), Guhan (6), Pinku (2), Naresh (6), Archana (5), Adhiraa (3), Bn Sharada (2), Kanasu (6). Four are Streets (place 5): Amay (8), Guhan (6), Pinku (2), Naresh (6). You keep Naresh, Streets and Delight. You pass the other eight.

  2. Round 2. The hand from your right has eight cards, including Gowri (9) and Dhruv (6). You keep Gowri, your second Streets card (Streets and Brave). You pass seven cards, including Dhruv, hoping it comes back.

  3. Round 5. Your own round 1 hand returns with five cards left: Adheesh (9), Guhan (6), Pinku (2), Archana (5), Adhiraa (3). Two Streets cards are still there, so nobody to your left needed them. You keep Guhan (Streets, Delight): your fifth Streets card, and a scene with Naresh.

  4. Round 6. Your round 2 hand returns with four cards: Dhruv (3), Anayka (8), Dhruv (6), Amyra (5). Dhruv (Museums and Sports, Startle and Wonder) is still there. You keep it as the first card of a Museums chapter.

  5. Final album: Naresh, Gowri, Arvind, Guhan, Guhan, Dhruv, Ammlu, Gopi, Archana. Streets five cards = 10. Museums and Sports (place 3) four cards = 8. Moods: Delight, Brave, Mischief, Body and Senses, Startle and Wonder, Think and Notice = 6 moods = 9. Scenes: Naresh with Guhan (Streets, Delight) and Dhruv with Ammlu (Museums, Startle) = 6. Total 33.

  6. The other albums score 22, 21 and 29. You win the deal with 33.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5: six cards each. Place side of the key only. Two of a kind score 1; three or more score 1 per card. One deal; ties are fine and everyone cheers.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7: nine cards, place chapters, mood spread and scenes, three deals. A grown-up scores the first deal with the child.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: as level two, but albums are kept in a face-down stack that only the owner may look at. You read the table only by what people pass (not simulated).

Solo

Deal 18 cards face up in three hands of six. For each hand, six turns alternate: you keep one card; then roll the die and remove the leftmost card of that place type (die 1 to 6 = Place key), or the leftmost card if none. You keep three cards from each hand and finish with nine. Score as level two for one deal. Bronze 19, Silver 25, Gold 28 (random play 14 average; a careful greedy player 21 average; a look-ahead bot 22 average, 90th percentile 28).

Two players

Deal three hands of nine and put the third in the middle as the dummy hand. Pass left as usual, with the dummy between you; on every round when the dummy hand arrives, remove its leftmost card face down before passing it on. Works well: skill gap is similar to three players.

Maths and skills in this game

Sorting by two features at once (place and mood), counting in groups, reading a neighbour's collection, and balancing 'more of one kind' against 'one of every kind'.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Simulated Skill is modest: a rollout bot wins 45%/37%/33%/28% at 3/4/5/6p vs greedy bots (even 33/25/20/17); a human-style heuristic wins about the even share plus 8/4/0/1; seat advantage under 1 point.

Not simulated. Real people reading albums and signalling by what they pass, speed of sorting pictures into place and mood, whether a table agrees with the approved mood tags, time per deal. Time estimate: nine rounds at about 12 seconds plus scoring about 90 seconds, so 4 to 6 minutes a deal.

Honest read: the draft is a real choice every round (the score-greedy pick is also the best pick only 42% of the time), but a human-style heuristic gains almost nothing over greedy+, and denial is a mistake. It is a light family drafter with a modest skill edge, not a skill game. Tuning is in tuning_log. Rerun after the approved tags (K11 now Body and Senses, K12 now Think and Notice): the rollout edge over the even share is +11 to +13 points at every size, which sits on the +12 line; the human-style heuristic gains a little at 3 and 4 players and nothing beyond. Level one does not read mood, so its row is unchanged.

Tuning log

  • round 1: album scored by variety of place types (6 types, increasing table), scenes and a penalty for four or more of a kind. Every player reached five or six types in nine cards (99% of albums), so variety was never contested: greedy beat random 79% and my look-ahead bot lost to greedy (3p 27%, even 33%). Replaced by a convex 'more of one place' table: greedy still 80% over random and a card-counting rollout bot (ceiling) lost to greedy at 4p (21%, even 25%). The best pick was simply the one that scored most now.

  • round 2: made scoring threshold-based like Sushi Go sashimi: a place chapter scores only from three cards (6 points, plus 2 per extra card), mood spread scores from four moods (2/5/9). Now the first two cards of a type score nothing, so naive greedy is blind to commitment. Ceiling bot vs greedy+ (greedy with a small bonus for types already held): 4p 33%, 6p 29% (even 25%, 17%), but 24% to 35% of deals tied.

  • round 3: added scenes (two cards with the same place type and the same mood, 3 points per pair) to break ties and to pull against mood spread. Compared three tables (S1 chapters 6/8/10/12, mood 2/5/9, scene 3; S2 chapters 8/10/12, scene 2; S3 chapters 7/9/11, mood 6/12 only). All similar; kept S1 for the lowest tie rate (9-15% before tie-break, 3-6% after) and the cleanest numbers to say aloud.

  • checks: denial (taking a card because the left neighbour would score it) hurts: heuristic bot 34%/23%/16%/13% at 3/4/5/6p with denial 0.5 against 41%/29%/20%/18% with none. Reading what is flowing (does this hand hold more of my type) is worth +8/+4/-1/+2 points at 3/4/5/6p (2000 games each, about 1.5 points of noise), so the 'reading what neighbours pass' pitch is true at 3 and 4 players and small beyond. Not tuned further: hands of nine are fixed by the 54-card deck.

  • tags approved; K11 and K12 mood tags moved; re-ran. Rounds 1 and 2 above were measured before the tags were approved and are kept as history. Final scoring unchanged. Ceiling bot vs greedy+ is now 45/37/33/28% at 3/4/5/6p (700 games each), an edge of +12.1/+11.5/+13.0/+11.3 points over the even share, on the +12 skill line (4p and 6p a fraction under it); the game does not claim skill, so the verdict stands. Seats within 1 point of even (9000 deals each). Tags are now approved.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Passport: also place types, but that is a die roll and a take from a spread; here you draft hands and keep one per pass

  • Team Stock: set collection with a majority at the end; here no majority and scoring is by your own album

  • Blind Pack: keeps five cards judged by backs; here nine cards judged by fronts and picked with open albums

  • Chain Rush: also passes a hand, but one card once then a race; here every round is a pass

Ratings

Two passing rules and three score lines; a four to five minute teach; Sushi Go is about 1.2 and Lost Cities 1.6 (from memory).

10, minus 1 for teach time over three minutes, minus 1 because a key card is read every round, minus 1 for pencil scoring with three tables; no downtime because everyone chooses at once.

Fine filler. Every round is a pick among hands that shrink, passes surprise you, and a scene or a sixth mood feels good, but a plain greedy player is competitive, denial does not pay, and the weakest part is scoring by tables. The reading-the-table skill is small.

Card changes requested: none

Parade of Teams

A parade of explorers walks along the table. Play a card at the tail and the ones that are too small or the wrong colour fall off the front into your pile. Take as few as you can, unless you are taking a whole team.

Inspired by Parade (Naoki Homma), with team-majority scoring

FamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-12
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
1 die
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Add a card to the end of a growing row. Skip the last few cards (as many as your number), then take every card above that which is no bigger than your number or shares the die colour. At the end, the player with the lowest total wins, and holding most of a team makes it cheap.

What you need

All 54 cardsyou play them from your hand into the parade and take them into piles
1 diethe colour die: a plain die read on the Colour key (Ref 3)
Ref 4 (Team key)to read the team of each card by animal name
Pencil and paperto total the scores at the end

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Keep them secret.

  • Put 4 cards face up in a line in the middle. This is the Parade. Read it left to right: the left end is the head and the right end is the tail.

  • Put the rest face down as the draw deck. Each player will build a face-up pile of taken cards in front of them.

  • The player who last went on an adventure goes first (or roll the die, highest first). Play goes clockwise.

How to play

  1. Roll the die. It names a colour (Colour key, Ref 3). Look at the card you plan to play: if the die colour is one of its two colours, that colour is the parade colour. If the die shows neither of its colours, the parade colour is the lower-numbered of its two colours.

  2. Play one card from your hand at the tail of the Parade. Say its number out loud: call it N.

  3. Skip the last N cards of the Parade (counting back from the tail, not counting the card you just played). Those are safe.

  4. Take every card in the rest of the Parade (the head side) that either has a number of N or less, or has the parade colour as either of its two colours. Put them in your pile, face up. They leave the Parade.

  5. Draw one card from the deck. Your turn ends. If the deck is empty, you draw nothing.

How it ends

When a player cannot draw because the deck is empty, the end begins: counting that turn as the first, play 2 turns for every player (so n players give 2n turns), with no drawing. Then everyone scores their pile. 1. Sort each pile by team. 2. For each team, the player (or players, if tied) with the most cards of that team scores just 1 point per card of that team. Everyone else with cards of that team scores the numbers on those cards. 3. Add it all up. The lowest total wins. Ties: the player with fewer cards in their pile; still tied, share the win. Two players: a team majority only counts if you hold at least 2 more cards of that team than your opponent. Otherwise both of you pay numbers for that team.

Words in this game

  • Parade the line of face-up cards. Cards join at the tail and fall off at the head.
  • Tail / head the tail is where you play; the head is the end where cards are taken from.
  • Safe cards the last N cards before your played card. They cannot be taken this turn, whatever their number or colour.
  • Parade colour the colour that counts this turn, picked by the die from the two on your played card.
  • Majority holding more cards of a team than any other player. A majority makes those cards cost 1 each.

Common questions

  • Do I take the card I just played? No. It joins the tail and stays there. Only older cards fall off.

  • What if I take nothing? That is fine, and the best result. A big card played into a long parade is often safe because the safe zone is large.

  • Why would a big card be good? Because N is also the number of safe cards. Playing a 9 protects nine cards at the tail. Playing a 1 protects one card but takes anything of a 1 or the parade colour.

  • Can the colour die help me? Yes. If the die shows neither colour of your card you are stuck with the lower one, so look at which of your cards fit the die before you play.

  • Is it bad to hold lots of cards? Not if they are one team. Twelve cards of a team you lead cost 12 points, not their numbers added up, which could be 70.

  • What if the Parade is shorter than my number? Then every card is safe and you take nothing.

Tips

  • Roll first, then choose. The die is the only thing you cannot plan, so scan your hand for a card whose colour pair matches the roll. A card that takes nothing is worth more than any plan.

  • Play high numbers early when the Parade is long and low numbers late. A 9 in a 4-card Parade protects everything. A 2 in a 12-card Parade is dangerous.

  • Count the colour. Every card shows two colours, so the die colour appears on roughly a third of the Parade. A low card on a colour that nobody holds is a trap for you.

  • Choose a team and lean in. Taking the third and fourth card of a team you already lead is nearly free, because each costs 1 instead of its number.

  • Do not chase a majority that two others are chasing. At four players or more, leaders overlap and the team costs numbers for the losers.

  • In the last 2n turns nobody draws, so you know exactly what you hold. Dump your most dangerous cards early in the end phase while the Parade is still short.

Worked example

  1. Three players. The Parade is Pinku (2), Avika (4), Adhiraa (6), Nysha (8) (head to tail). Player A rolls 3 (yellow) and plays Sharada (3), a 3 whose colours are orange and blue. Yellow is not on it, so the parade colour is the lower one, orange (2). N is 3, so the last 3 cards (Avika (4), Adhiraa (6), Nysha (8)) are safe. The only card left is Pinku (2), a 2, which is 3 or less. A takes it. The Parade is now Avika (4), Adhiraa (6), Nysha (8), Sharada (3).

  2. Player B rolls 5 and plays Guhan (6), a 6 with colours orange and purple. Blue is not on it, so the parade colour is orange. N is 6 and the Parade has only 4 cards, so all 4 are safe. B takes nothing. A big card into a short Parade is a free move.

  3. Player C rolls 1 (red) and plays Ammlu (2), a 2 with colours orange and green. Red is not on it, so the parade colour is orange. N is 2, so the last 2 cards (Sharada (3), Guhan (6)) are safe. Of the older three, Avika (4) has orange as one of its colours, so C takes it. Adhiraa (6) is a 6 (green and yellow) and Nysha (8) is an 8 (red and purple), neither takes. C takes only Avika (4).

  4. Back to A, who rolls 4 (green) and plays Guhan (3), a 3 whose colours are red and green. Green is on the card, so the parade colour is green. N is 3. The last 3 cards are safe, which leaves Adhiraa (6) and Nysha (8). Adhiraa (6) has green as one of its colours, so A takes it, at a cost of 6 or 1. Nysha (8) is an 8 with red and purple, so it stays.

  5. Scoring (a different, shorter game with 3 players). A holds Adhiraa (6) (a Tiger, 6), Adhiraa (3) (a Tiger, 3) and Pinku (2) (a Cobra, 2). B holds Kanasu (3) (a Tiger, 3), Ammlu (2) (a Cobra, 2) and Bharati (4) (a Cobra, 4). C holds Nysha (8) (a Monkey, 8) and Guhan (6) (an Elephant, 6). Tigers: A has 2, B has 1, so A is the majority and scores 2; B pays the number, 3. Cobras: B has 2, A has 1, so B scores 2; A pays 2. Monkeys: only C, so C scores 1 (a majority of one). Elephants: only C, so C scores 1. Totals: A 2 + 2 = 4, B 3 + 2 = 5, C 1 + 1 = 2. C wins with the lowest total.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5, with a helper. Ignore the colour die. You take only cards in the older part of the Parade whose number is the same as or lower than the card you play. Score the numbers in your pile and lowest wins. No teams. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Use the colour die and the full taking rule, but still score only the numbers in your pile. The lowest total wins. Teams are not needed. In the simulation this scoring is where a careful player beats a random one almost every time (95% at 3 players, 99% at 2).

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game with team majorities. One card of a team you lead costs 1, so collecting a team on purpose is the grown-up plan.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about the other players' piles.

Two players

Two players work with the fix: a team majority counts only with a lead of 2 or more cards. Without the fix the reference bot wins just 44% of 2-player games against random play, below the 50% baseline; with the fix it wins 69%.

Maths and skills in this game

Comparing numbers 1 to 9, counting back N places, adding small totals, reading a die colour against two colours at once, and weighing a cost of 1 against a cost of the printed number.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the size of the safe zone, the take-threshold, and the cost of a card you do not lead
ColoursRule the die picks one of the two colours on the card you play; any card in range with that colour is taken
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule majority of a team makes its cards cost 1 each
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour the children walk in the parade
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Win rate of the greedy bot (plays the card that takes the fewest points) against random players: 75% at 3 players, 73% at 4, 66% at 5, 57% at 6 (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%, 17%). Against itself it sits at baseline. (1,500 games a cell, from the original simulation.)

  • As drafted at 2 players the bot won 44% against a 50% baseline. Team-majority scoring rewards taking cards the bot avoids, so for two players the majority needs a lead.

  • New for this page: with the lead-of-2 rule at 2 players the bot wins 69% against random players and 49% mirrored (3,000 games each). Pure numbers scoring with no teams gives 99% and 50%.

  • Length: about 32 to 44 card plays in all at any player count. New run: 22.0 turns each at 2 players and 13.7 at 3 (3,000 games), about 8 to 12 minutes at 15 seconds a turn.

  • Team scoring: in the 3-player run the average total for a smart bot is about 29 points.

  • Without the majority rule at 3 players the bot wins 95% against random, so the majority rule roughly halves the skill gap. It is a swing rule that gives weaker players a way to catch up.

  • Colour die: the die shows one of the two colours of the played card about 1 time in 3 (2 of 6 values), which is why the "lower colour" fallback happens 4 turns in 6.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot plays the card that takes the fewest points and never aims for a team.

  • Not tested: L1 (no colour) and L2 as written, and the 2-player tie-break by pile size.

  • Not tested: whether the end rule (2n turns without drawing) feels fair to the last player.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

PARADE OF TEAMS. Deal 5 each; 4 cards face up = the Parade. Turn: roll the colour die. Play a card at the tail; its number is N. The last N cards are safe. Take every other card with number N or less, or showing the parade colour (the die colour if the card has it, else its lower colour). Draw 1.

Back

END. When the deck is empty, play 2 turns each, no drawing. SCORE. For each team, the player with the most cards scores 1 per card; others score the numbers. Lowest total wins. 2 PLAYERS: a majority needs 2 more cards than your opponent. LEVELS. L1 no colour die, numbers only. L2 colour die, numbers only. L3 team majorities.
