Caravan Rows

Every explorer wears two colours, so every card you take pulls you toward two piles of colour at once. Grab the row you like before it grows, but remember that only three colours will ever pay.

Inspired by Coloretto (Michael Schacht), Zooloretto

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-13
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

On your turn either flip a card onto any row of the caravan, or take a whole row and sit out the rest of the round. At the end only your three biggest colours score, in rising triangle numbers, and every other colour costs you the same.

What you need

All 54 cardsflipped from the deck onto rows; each card is worth its two border colours
Pencil and paperto score at the end with the triangle table (1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21)

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards into one face-down deck.

  • Lay out one empty row for each player. A row is a place for up to 3 face-up cards. Leave space between the rows.

  • Each player has an empty Collection place in front of them.

  • Pick a first player at random. A new round always starts one seat to the left of the last round.

How to play

  1. On your turn you do exactly one of two things. Flip: turn over the top card of the deck and place it face up on any row that has fewer than 3 cards. You must place it; you cannot choose to put it back.

  2. Or Take: pick any row that has at least one card and put all its cards into your Collection. That row leaves play for the round, and you are out for the rest of the round (you take no more turns).

  3. If every row is full, or the deck is empty, you cannot flip, so you must take a row. If no row has any cards and you cannot flip, you are out.

  4. The round ends when every player has taken a row. Clear the table (taken rows are already gone), lay out fresh empty rows, and begin the next round.

  5. After a round, count the deck. If it has fewer than 12 cards, the game is over. The unused cards are ignored.

How it ends

Score each Collection. 1. Count, for each of the six colours, how many cards in your Collection show it as either of their two colours (a card with two colours counts for both). 2. Rank your six colour counts. Your three biggest colours score a triangle number each: 1 card = 1, 2 = 3, 3 = 6, 4 = 10, 5 = 15, 6 = 21, 7 = 28, 8 = 36. 3. Each of your other three colours loses the triangle number for its count (a colour with 0 cards loses nothing). Highest total wins. A tie goes to the player with more cards; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Row one of the n places where face-up cards wait. It holds at most 3 cards.
  • Collection the cards you have taken, kept face up in front of you.
  • Out after you take a row you skip every turn until the next round.
  • Triangle number 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21: each extra card in a colour is worth one more than the last.

Common questions

  • Can I flip and then take in the same turn? No. One action per turn: flip or take.

  • What if a flipped card is bad for everyone? Place it on the row of the player who needs it least, or on a row that is already poisoned. Hoping that someone else takes it is a real plan.

  • How many colours will I end with? All six, nearly always. Every card has two colours, so a Collection of eight cards carries sixteen colour marks. That is why the three-colour limit bites.

  • Why does a colour I have 0 of cost nothing? Because a loss is the triangle number of the count and the triangle number of 0 is 0. Staying off a colour entirely is free.

  • Is a one-card row worth taking? Sometimes. It is the cheapest way to leave the round early, and being out lets the others spend turns without you.

Tips

  • Pick your three colours by the end of round two and then refuse the others. Taking a row that has one great card and one card of a fourth colour is how scores go to zero.

  • Triangles reward depth: your fifth card in a colour is worth 5 more points, but your first is worth 1. A row with two cards in your best colour beats a row of four mixed cards.

  • Because each card carries two colours, look for the card whose two colours are both yours. In the sim a smart bot only takes a row when it gains at least 4.5 points.

  • Put a card on the row of the player about to take. If their colours do not want it, the card costs them. Do this when you are not the one who needs the row.

  • Count the deck after each round. Under 12 ends the game, so a round that leaves 14 cards still has one more round and you may be able to plan the last take.

  • Going out first with a small row is not a loss: you save the harmful flips and the others fill the rows with cards you do not want.

Worked example

  1. Three players: A, B, C. Three empty rows. A already has Arvind (1) and Amyra (4) in their Collection from an earlier round. A flips Guhan (3) (red and green) and places it on Row 1.

  2. B flips Pinku (2) (orange and yellow) onto Row 2. C flips Amay (1) (red and blue) and puts it on Row 1, which now has Guhan (3) and Amay (1).

  3. A takes Row 1: Guhan (3) and Amay (1) go into A's Collection and A is out for the round. A now shows red on 4 cards (Arvind (1), Amyra (4), Guhan (3), Amay (1)) and green on 2. Row 1 leaves play.

  4. B flips Archana (4) (green and blue) onto Row 2, then C flips Amay (8) (orange and yellow) onto Row 2, which is now full: Pinku (2), Archana (4), Amay (8).

  5. B flips Smaya (1) (orange and purple). The only open row is Row 3. C takes Row 2, three cards, and is out. B takes Row 3 (just Smaya (1)) to end the round. A new round starts with B (one to the left of A).

  6. Scoring a Collection: Arvind (1), Amay (1), Nysha (1), Anayka (1), Dharsh (2), Pinku (2), Guhan (3), Amyra (4). Colour counts: red 5, green 4, yellow 3, orange 2, blue 1, purple 1. The three biggest are red 5 (15), green 4 (10), yellow 3 (6): 31. The others lose: orange 2 (3), blue 1 (1), purple 1 (1): -5. Total 26.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Every player picks one favourite colour. Take rows of any size; at the end count the cards that show your colour; most wins. No penalties. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. The three-colour rule: only your best three colours score, using the triangle table, but the other colours cost nothing. (Not simulated.)

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game: best three colours score the triangle numbers, the other colours lose them.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about the rows other players leave you.

Two players

Works with two rows. Both players must take eventually, so the second player to act in a round usually flips more. In the simulation a smart bot wins 68% of 2-player games against random play and 48% against itself.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting up to 8, reading triangle numbers (1, 3, 6, 10), comparing two colour counts at once, planning which colours to refuse and adding and subtracting small totals.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Each of the six colours appears on exactly 18 of the 54 cards (108 colour marks), and the 54 cards use 15 distinct colour pairs.

  • As drafted (rows refilled after a take), the bot that takes a row when it gains 4.5 points or more won 91%, 91%, 86%, 87% against random players at 2 to 5 players (baselines 50%, 33%, 25%, 20%); 62 to 70 turns in all, 4 to 9 rounds.

  • New for this page: with the final rule (a taken row leaves play) the same bot wins 68%, 71%, 69%, 68% against random players at 2 to 5 players (1,500 games a cell) and 48%, 32%, 24%, 20% against itself (baselines 50%, 33%, 25%, 20%). The skill gap is smaller than the draft showed, and seats are fair.

  • Length with the final rule: 66 to 73 turns in all and 11.2, 7.9, 6.2, 5.1 rounds at 2 to 5 players. At about 12 seconds a turn that is 13 to 15 minutes.

  • Average total per player in games between smart bots: about 88 at 2 players, 54 at 3, 36 at 4 and 27 at 5.

  • The three-colour limit bites because every Collection ends with all six colours: a Collection of 8 cards holds 16 colour marks, so a fourth colour is almost certain.

  • No game in the runs had a player left with no legal action (0 stuck turns), so the empty-row rules never fire.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot never uses the bluff of placing a card on a row to bait a rival.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written.

  • Not tested: ties for the win. The "more cards" tie-break is a plain choice.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CARAVAN ROWS. One empty row (max 3 cards) per player. On your turn FLIP the top card onto any row with room, or TAKE a row into your Collection and sit out the round. Must take if you cannot flip. Round ends when all have taken. After a round, if the deck has under 12 cards, game over.

Back

SCORE. Count cards showing each colour (a card counts for both of its colours). Your 3 biggest colours score 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 for 1 to 6 cards; the other colours lose the same. Most points wins; tie: more cards. LEVELS. L1 count your favourite colour. L2 best 3 colours only. L3 full.

Torch Run

A tunnel, a torch and a hidden pawn. Each flip adds treasure to the pot, and each flip might call out a third explorer of one team, which collapses the tunnel and takes everything. Do you walk out now, or one flip more?

Inspired by Diamant / Incan Gold (Alan Moon and Bruno Faidutti)

RecommendedFamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-14
Players
3 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
1 each

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Flip cards one at a time. Each adds its number to the pot, but if the third card of any one team appears, the run collapses and the pot is lost. After each flip everyone secretly chooses to stay or leave; leavers split the pot. Five runs, most points wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsshuffled afresh for every run
1 pawn eachheld in a closed fist to show "leave"; an empty fist means "stay"
Ref 4 (Team key)to read the team of each card by animal name
Pencil and paperbanks are kept on paper

Set up

  • Every player takes a pawn and a place on the score sheet. Banks start at 0.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards into a face-down deck for the first run.

  • The pot starts at 0. Write it on a scrap of paper or keep it in your head.

  • A game is 5 runs. Any player may flip the cards; the youngest does it in run 1 and the flipper moves one seat left after each run.

How to play

  1. Flip the top card of the deck face up in a line, and read its team. Say the team out loud and how many cards of that team are now showing.

  2. If it is the third card of a team, the tunnel collapses at once. The run is over, the pot is lost, and nobody still in the run scores for it. Leave the cards on the table and start a fresh run with a new shuffle.

  3. Otherwise add the card's number to the pot.

  4. Everyone still in the run secretly puts a pawn in their fist (leave) or keeps their fist empty (stay). Show hands together.

  5. All who showed a pawn leave. They split the pot equally, rounded down: each adds their share to their bank. Whatever cannot be split evenly stays in the pot. Leavers are out until the next run.

  6. If anyone is still in, flip the next card. The run continues until everyone has left or the tunnel collapses.

How it ends

After 5 runs, the player with the biggest bank wins. Ties share the win. For a longer game play 8 runs (not simulated).

Words in this game

  • Run one trip into the tunnel. A new shuffle starts each run.
  • Pot the total of the numbers on the cards flipped in this run that nobody has banked yet.
  • Hazard a second card of a team is showing. The next card of that team collapses the tunnel.
  • Leave / stay your secret choice each flip, shown by the pawn in your fist.
  • Collapse the run ends, the pot is lost.

Common questions

  • If I am alone when I leave, do I get everything? Yes. A single leaver takes the whole pot. That is the reward for being the only cautious (or the only brave) player.

  • What if I stay and the tunnel collapses? You lose the pot. Only players who left on an earlier flip keep their share.

  • What if nobody leaves for a while? The pot keeps growing, and so does the hazard. That is the pressure.

  • Do the cards from earlier runs stay out? No. Each run begins with all 54 cards shuffled.

  • How do I find the chance of collapse? Count the teams that have two cards showing. For each, the number of that team still hidden is the number of ways to lose. Divide the total by the cards left in the deck.

  • Can a team have a hazard before any card is flipped? No. A team needs two cards showing first.

Tips

  • The moment two cards of one team show, the chance that the next flip collapses the tunnel is at least 11%: a team of 8 (Tigers, Elephants, Bears) has 6 cards left of about 52, a team of 10 (Monkeys, Peacocks, Cobras) has 8. That is the point at which careful players leave.

  • Leaving early is safe but pays small. Sit with the pot when only one team is at 2 and the pot is large, and leave when two teams are at 2 (the chance is then 23% or more).

  • If you are far behind in the last run, stay one flip longer than everyone. Winning a run takes a gamble when you are 15 points behind.

  • If you are ahead, leave first every run. A tiny share every run beats a rare big one.

  • Watch the table. If three players leave on the same flip, the pot splits three ways. Being the only leaver is worth the whole pot, so an expected crowd leaving is a reason to stay one flip.

  • The first two flips can never collapse the tunnel. Always stay for them.

Worked example

  1. Three players, A, B and C. A deck is shuffled; the pot is 0. Flip 1: Avika (4), a 4 from the Peacocks. Pot 4. Nobody leaves. Flip 2: Amyra (5), a 5, also a Peacock. That is 2 Peacocks showing. Pot 9. Of the 10 Peacocks, 8 are hidden among 52 cards, so the next flip collapses the tunnel with chance 15%.

  2. Hands are shown. A leaves, B and C stay. A is the only leaver and takes the whole pot, 9. A banks 9 and is out for this run. The pot is now 0.

  3. Flip 3: Nysha (8), an 8 from the Monkeys. Pot 8. B and C both show a pawn and leave. They split 8 equally: 4 each. B banks 4, C banks 4. Nobody is left, the run ends. Banks: A 9, B 4, C 4.

  4. Run 2. Flip 1: Shreya (2), a 2 from the Tigers. Pot 2. Flip 2: Kanasu (3), a 3, also a Tiger. Pot 5, and 2 Tigers are showing: 6 Tigers are still hidden among 52 cards, a chance of 11.5% for the next flip. All stay. Flip 3: Adhiraa (3), a third Tiger. The tunnel collapses. The pot of 5 is lost, and nobody scores.

  5. Another example of splitting. Pot 11, three players leave together: 11 divided by 3 is 3, remainder 2. Each banks 3, and the 2 left over stay in the pot for anyone still in the tunnel.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Count cards instead of adding numbers: the pot is the number of cards flipped. Leavers split the cards. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Add the numbers, split rounded down, 5 runs.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game with 8 runs, and think in chances: count the hidden cards of every team that shows two.

Solo

No solo mode: the choice to leave depends on the other players' choices.

Two players

Not recommended for two: with two players there are no big splits and the game is a guess at when to leave. The simulations covered 3 to 6 players.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding to a running total, dividing a total fairly with a remainder, reading probabilities as "6 left out of 52", and weighing a sure share against a risky bigger one.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • As first drafted, with the hazard on the second card of a team, a run lasted 2.1 flips and the best bots left straight away. Moving the hazard to the third card gave runs of 5.8 flips with 28% of runs collapsing.

  • Strategy test: a bot that leaves as soon as the chance of collapse on the next flip reaches 5% to 10% wins 55% to 66% at 3 to 4 players against a mixed field (baselines 33%, 25%). A bot that waits for 30% wins only 4% to 9%. Too-timid thresholds drop below baseline, so the threshold matters.

  • Length: 5 runs of about 6 flips; about 5 to 8 minutes. First seat wins 37% at 3 players in the original run.

  • New computation for this page (40,000 shuffles, nobody leaving): the collapsing flip is on average flip 7.6, so about 6.6 safe flips. The chance that the tunnel has collapsed by flip 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 is 2.1%, 7.7%, 17.4%, 31.0%, 47.6%, 64.4%, 79.7%, 90.6%.

  • With two cards of one team showing, the next flip collapses with chance 6/52 = 11.5% (Tigers, Elephants, Bears; 8 cards each) or 8/52 = 15.4% (Monkeys, Peacocks, Cobras; 10 each). With two teams at two the chance is 23% to 31%.

  • Balloon Ride (#12), checked separately: "stop at 13, bust over 18" won 41% against naive players but only 29% to 34% against players stopping at 12 to 14. There was no interaction between players, which is why it was folded into Torch Run.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Bots decide only by the chance of collapse and ignore the other players.

  • Not tested: L1 (counting cards), the 8-run game, or the optional Twenty-One and Ceiling variants.

  • Not tested: two players.

Variants and options

  • Balloon Ride (#12) Draw to a running total, bust at 18, bank to get out. Solved by stopping at 13 and with no interaction between players, so it was folded in: Torch Run is the same bank-or-bust choice made at the same time as everyone else.

  • Twenty-One (#55), variant (not simulated) Instead of a team hazard, the pot collapses if it goes over 21. Leavers still split. A card of your own team counts as plus or minus 3 for the pot only.

  • The Ceiling (#56), variant (not simulated) A colour die roll sets the ceiling for the pot at the start of each run. If the pot goes over it, the run collapses. Cards are still flipped as in Torch Run.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TORCH RUN. 5 runs. Flip a card: if it is the third of one team, the run collapses and the pot is lost. Else add its number to the pot. Then everyone secretly chooses: pawn in fist = leave, empty fist = stay. Leavers split the pot (rounded down) and bank it. Flip again until all have left.

Back

SCORE. Highest bank after 5 runs wins; ties share. Fresh shuffle each run. TIPS. Two cards of a team showing = 11% (8-card team) or 15% (10-card team) chance of collapse next flip. LEVELS. L1 count cards. L2 numbers. L3 8 runs.

Casino Row

Six prizes sit in a row, one for each number on the die. Roll the dice, pick a number, and push that many cards into that lane. But if you and a rival end up with the same total, you cancel each other out.

Inspired by Las Vegas (Rudiger Dorn)

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-15
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
4 dice
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Roll four dice each turn, choose a number that came up and commit that many cards from your hand face down to the matching lane. At the end of the round the highest total in each lane wins its prize, unless two players tie, in which case both are knocked out of the lane.

What you need

All 54 cards6 are prizes, the rest are hands (12 each, or 9 each at five players)
4 diceplain dice; the number rolled is the lane
Pencil and paperto score the three rounds

Set up

  • Play 3 rounds. Each round: shuffle all 54 cards. Turn up 6 cards in a row, left to right, as the prizes. Under the prizes lane 1 is the leftmost, lane 6 the rightmost.

  • Deal 12 cards to each player (9 each at five players). Keep them secret. Unused cards are not needed.

  • Each player gets their own row of six lane spaces in front of them, one under each prize number (their lane 1 to lane 6). Cards you commit go face down there; the number of cards in a lane is public.

  • Round 1 starts with the youngest player; the starting seat moves one seat left each round.

How to play

  1. Roll all four dice.

  2. Choose one number that appears on the dice. Look at how many dice show it: call that K.

  3. Commit K cards from your hand, face down, into your lane with that number. If you hold fewer than K cards, commit them all.

  4. Play passes clockwise. Players with no cards left skip their turns.

  5. The round ends when every hand is empty.

How it ends

Reveal each lane in turn. Add up the numbers of each player's cards in that lane. If two or more players have exactly the same total in a lane (and it is not 0), all of them cancel and are out of that lane. Among those left, the highest total takes the prize and scores the prize card's number in points. A lane with no uncancelled player scores for nobody. After 3 rounds, highest points wins. Ties share.

Words in this game

  • Lane one of the six places, numbered 1 to 6, where you commit cards. A lane matches a die number.
  • Prize the face-up card above a lane. Its number is the points for winning the lane.
  • Commit place cards face down in a lane. You cannot take them back.
  • Cancel two or more equal totals knock each other out of the lane.

Common questions

  • Do I have to use all four dice? No. You pick one number, and every die that shows it counts for K.

  • What if I roll four different numbers? Then you pick one and K is 1: you commit a single card.

  • Can I look at the cards I committed? Yes, you may look at your own lane cards. Nobody else may.

  • What if I only have one card left and K is 3? You commit the one card. You cannot commit cards you do not have.

  • Does the colour or team of a card matter? No. Only the number is added up.

  • Can I win a lane with nothing? Only if nobody else has an uncancelled total: a lane total must be above 0.

Tips

  • Commit your biggest cards to the highest prizes, and your small cards to the low prizes. With 12 cards and 6 lanes, you cannot be everywhere.

  • Watch the card counts in the other lanes. A rival with four cards in a lane has probably built a big total. Do not chase a lane someone has loaded unless you can match their card count.

  • The cancel rule punishes copying. If two players are fighting over a lane with similar totals, the third player can win it with a small total. Think about adding one more card to avoid a tie.

  • When many dice show your number, K is high: use that roll for a lane where you need a big total, because you can commit three or four cards at once.

  • Late in the round, count the cards left in your hand. If you have 2 cards and roll a 4-of-a-kind, you will be forced to commit both to that lane.

  • At four or five players a quarter to a third of lanes cancel, so spreading across several lanes with modest totals is a safe plan.

Worked example

  1. Three players, A, B and C. The six prizes are Nakul (5), Guhan (6), Shreya (2), Dharsh (7), Sharada (3) and Adheesh (9), lanes 1 to 6. Each player has 12 cards.

  2. A rolls 2, 2, 5 and 6. A picks 2: two dice show 2, so A commits two cards face down into lane 2 (prize Guhan (6), a 6). B rolls 4, 4, 4 and 1 and picks 4: K is 3, so B commits three cards to lane 4 (prize Dharsh (7), a 7).

  3. Skip to the end of the round and reveal lane 6, whose prize is Adheesh (9), a 9. A has Bn Sharada (7) and Bn Sharada (2): total 9. B has Rihansh (9): total 9. C has Avika (5): total 5. A and B both have 9, so they cancel. C is the only one left and wins lane 6: C scores the prize's 9 points.

  4. Lane 4, with prize Dharsh (7). A has Gowri (9), B has Arvind (8) and C has no cards there. A's 9 beats B's 8, so A takes the 7 points.

  5. After three rounds of six lanes, the points are added. In the simulation each player scores around 30 points at 3 players (3 rounds).

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Roll two dice instead of four, and when two totals are equal the lane scores for no one. Use only 2 rounds. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Four dice, all rules, but play only 1 round and add up the prizes at the end. (Not simulated.)

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game of 3 rounds.

Solo

No solo mode: the cancel rule and the lane totals depend on rivals.

Two players

Works well. Cancelling is rare at two players (3% of lanes), so it plays as a plain lane duel. The simulated bot wins 92% against random play.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding totals up to about 30, comparing totals across several lanes at once, planning how to split twelve cards across six lanes and judging how a rival's card counts hint at their totals.

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CASINO ROW. 3 rounds. Turn up 6 prizes (lanes 1 to 6). Deal 12 each (9 at five). Turn: roll 4 dice, pick a number K shown on them, commit K cards face down to your lane with that number. Round ends when all hands are empty.

Back

Cheat Ladder

Climb the numbers 1 to 7 and back, putting cards face down and saying what they are. Lie when you must, and call out the liar when you dare. Be the first to get rid of every card.

Inspired by Cheat / I Doubt It / Bullshit

RecommendedFamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FT-16
Players
3 to 6
Time
10 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
1 (optional)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

The called number goes up by one each turn, 1 to 7 and round again. You put 1 to 3 cards face down and say they are that number. Anyone may call you a cheat. A wrong call, or a caught lie, means taking the whole pile. First out of cards wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsall dealt out as hands
1 pawn (optional)to mark the called rank on a row of seven cards numbered 1 to 7, or just say the rank out loud

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards and deal them all out, one at a time, around the table. Some players will have one card more than others.

  • Keep your cards secret. Leave a space in the middle for the pile.

  • The called rank starts at 1. A pawn on a row of cards 1 to 7, or just a spoken count, shows it.

  • The youngest player goes first.

How to play

  1. On your turn the called rank is the next number in the cycle 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, then back to 1. Say it out loud.

  2. Play 1, 2 or 3 cards face down onto the pile and say "one 4", "two 4s" or "three 4s" (using the called rank). You must play at least one card.

  3. The play is honest if every card you played is the called rank. A bond pair is also always honest: if you play exactly 2 cards and their numbers add to 9, the play is honest, whatever the called rank.

  4. Before the next player goes, anyone (starting with the player to your left) may call "Cheat!". Turn your cards face up. If the play was honest, the caller takes the whole pile into their hand. If not, you take the whole pile.

  5. Then the called rank moves to the next number, whether or not anyone called, and play passes to the left.

How it ends

The first player with no cards left wins. If you play your last cards and nobody calls, you win at once. If you are called and your last play is honest, the caller takes the pile and you win. If you are called and you were cheating, you take the pile and play goes on. Players who still have cards can call at any time on a last play, so a final play is nearly always called.

Words in this game

  • Called rank the number everyone must claim this turn: 1 to 7 in a cycle.
  • Pile all cards played and not yet picked up. A caught player or a wrong caller picks up the whole pile.
  • Bond pair two cards whose numbers add to 9 (1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5). A bond pair is always an honest play.
  • Cheat! the call that a play was not honest.

Common questions

  • Can I play only a bond pair as two cards? Yes. Exactly 2 cards that add to 9. You still say "two 4s" (or whatever the rank is). If it is called, it counts as honest.

  • What do I do with my 8s and 9s? The called ranks stop at 7, so 8s can leave only as a bond with a 1, and 9s have no bond partner at all. They leave only by lying, so plan to bluff with them.

  • Can I say the wrong number of cards? No. You must say the number of cards you play, and the called rank.

  • Do I have to call? No. Calling is a choice, and every call is a risk of picking up the pile.

  • Is it a cheat to play 1 card that is the called rank plus a wrong one? Yes. All the cards in the play must be the called rank, unless it is exactly two cards forming a bond.

  • What if the called rank comes to a card I hold three of? Play them all together and say "three 5s". There is no better time.

Tips

  • There are only six cards of each number. If a player claims three 4s and you hold four 4s, they are lying, because 3 + 4 is more than 6. Count your own cards of the rank before every decision to call.

  • Dump 8s and 9s while the pile is large and honest players are nervous. A 9 can only leave by a lie.

  • A big pile is a threat to the person who plays the next card. If you are not sure, wait for someone else to risk a call on a small pile.

  • Always call a player who plays their last cards. A win is the end of the game, and the sim bot does this every time.

  • Bond pairs are the safest way to sneak out two cards: say the rank, play a pair that adds to 9. It cannot be called successfully.

  • Mix honest plays with lies so the table cannot tell. A player who only tells the truth is easy to pass over; a player who always lies is easy to call.

Worked example

  1. Three players, A, B and C. Everyone has 18 cards. The called rank is 1. A plays Arvind (1) and Amay (1), both 1s, and says "two 1s". It is true. Nobody calls. The two cards stay on the pile.

  2. Rank 2. B plays Dharsh (2) (a 2) and Guhan (3) (a 3) and says "two 2s". This is a lie. C says "Cheat!". B turns the cards over: one is a 3. B takes the pile, all four cards.

  3. Rank 3. C plays one card, Naresh (3), a 3, and says "one 3". True. Nobody calls. The pile is just Naresh (3).

  4. Rank 4. A plays Adhiraa (3) (a 3) and Naresh (6) (a 6) and says "two 4s". They are not 4s, but 3 and 6 add to 9, so it is a bond pair and the play is honest. B calls anyway and turns the cards over. The play stands: B picks up the pile of three cards. A bond pair is a safe way to get rid of two cards.

  5. Rank 5 follows, and so on up to 7. After rank 7, the called rank goes back to 1. In the simulation a 3-player game takes about 257 turns in all, which is about 85 turns each.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Deal 8 cards each and put the rest aside. Play one card at a time, no bond rule, and only the next player may call. First out wins. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Play 1 or 2 cards and use the bond-pair rule. Deal all the cards. (Not simulated.)

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game: 1 to 3 cards, the bond pair, anyone may call.

Solo

No solo mode: it is a game about reading other players.

Two players

Not simulated. With only two players the called ranks cycle too predictably; use 3 to 6.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting cards (six of each number), ordering numbers in a cycle, estimating whether a claim is possible and spotting bond pairs to 9.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the called rank, honest plays and the bond pairs all use the number
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used

TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The bot (plays honest cards of the called rank when it has them, uses a bond pair when it has one, and otherwise bluffs with its highest card; calls when the claim is impossible or the player has few cards left) beats random players 94%, 99%, 97%, 88% at 3 to 6 players.

  • The nine-rank cycle (1 to 9) stalls between good bots when the cycle length lines up with the number of players: at 3 and 6 players only 13% to 45% of games finish, because each player faces the same three ranks. An eight-rank cycle stalls at 4 and 6 players.

  • A seven-rank cycle (1 to 7) finishes every game at every player count: 257, 156, 113 and 101 turns in all at 3, 4, 5 and 6 players, about 8 to 22 minutes.

  • The bond-pair rule matters. Without it, games at 3 and 6 players never finish. With it, numbers 8 and 9 are dumped by a bond pair or a bluff only.

  • New computation: of the 54 cards, 12 are 8s or 9s, so an 18-card hand (3 players) holds 4 of them on average and a 9-card hand (6 players) holds 2. The six 9s can never be honest plays.

  • Win rates against random players are not a measure of how big the skill gap is: it shows only that a bot that counts beats a random one.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Bots do not bluff for style or read the tells of other players.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2, and two players.

  • Not tested: whether human players call more or less often than the bot (the bot called a last play every time).

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CHEAT LADDER. Deal all cards. The called rank goes 1 to 7 and round again, +1 every turn. Play 1 to 3 cards face down and say "k of the rank". Honest if all are that rank, or if exactly 2 cards add to 9 (a bond). Anyone may call "Cheat!": the liar takes the pile, or a wrong caller does.

Back

WIN. First to empty their hand. A last play that is called and honest wins. SPARE. 8s and 9s only leave by a bond (an 8 with a 1) or a lie. LEVELS. L1 8 cards each, one at a time. L2 1 or 2 cards plus bonds. L3 full.

Phase Climb

A ladder of goals, each harder than the last. Draw, discard and shape your hand until it matches your goal, then call it. Win by finishing the ladder first.

Inspired by Phase 10, Five Crowns, rummy contracts

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-17
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
Optional: 1 each to mark your rung

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone draws and discards to build a hand that meets their current goal, such as four bonds or a run of six. The first to match goes out, and everyone who also matches climbs a rung. First to clear the top goal wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsdealt as hands, a draw deck and a discard pile
Goal ladder (reference card)the list of goals, easiest to hardest
1 pawn each (optional)mark your rung of the ladder; pencil and paper works too

Set up

  • Every player starts on Goal 1 of the ladder. Place your pawn on it, or keep a mark on paper.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 10 cards to each player (8 at six players). Keep them secret.

  • Turn one card face up beside the deck. This is the discard pile. The rest is the draw deck.

  • Round 1 starts with the youngest player. Each new round starts one seat to the left of the last.

How to play

  1. Draw. Take the top card of the draw deck or the top card of the discard pile into your hand. You now hold 11 cards.

  2. Check. If your 11 cards contain your current goal, say "Out" and show the goal cards. The round ends.

  3. Discard. Otherwise put one card face up on the discard pile. You are back to 10 cards. Play passes left.

  4. If the draw deck runs out, turn the discard pile (except its top card) over to make a new deck.

  5. When someone goes out, every other player lays down their 10 cards as they are (no draw). Anyone whose hand already meets their own current goal also clears it.

  6. Everyone who cleared their goal moves up one rung. Re-deal and play the next round.

How it ends

The game ends when a player clears the last goal of the ladder. Use five goals (goals 1 to 5) for a short game of about 6 to 10 minutes, or all eight for about 15 minutes. If two or more players clear the last goal in the same round, the player who went out wins. If none of them went out, they share the win. The goals, easiest to hardest: 1 four bonds, 2 a run of 6, 3 two triples, 4 a run of 7, 5 five of a team, 6 five bonds, 7 a run of 8, 8 three triples. A bond is two cards whose numbers add to 9 (1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5; a 9 has no bond partner). A run is cards with consecutive numbers, one card for each number. A triple is three cards with the same number. Five of a team means five cards from one team.

Words in this game

  • Rung / goal your current target. You climb one rung each time you clear your goal.
  • Bond two cards whose numbers add to 9. Each bond uses two cards and no card is in two bonds.
  • Run cards with numbers in a row, such as 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Extra cards of the same number do not extend a run.
  • Triple three cards of the same number (they may be from different teams or colours).
  • Out calling that your 11 cards match your goal. It ends the round.

Common questions

  • Can I be out without discarding? Yes. You draw, see that your 11 cards hold the goal, and call out. Spare cards do not matter.

  • Do other players have to be out too? No. Only the player who goes out has to make their goal on a draw. Others are checked on the 10 cards they hold.

  • Can I take a card from the discard pile that someone just threw? Yes, the top card only. This is how you read what the others need.

  • Do the cards for a goal have to be shown in order? No. You only show the cards that make the goal; the rest can stay hidden.

  • What if two goals are possible? Only your current goal counts. A run of 6 does not clear a bonds goal.

  • Why are the first goals so slow now? The draft goals (two bonds, a triple) were already in the opening hand most of the time, so they were replaced by harder ones.

Tips

  • Hold the cards that serve two goals at once. A middle number (3 to 6) is in many bonds and many runs. The 1s and 9s are the hardest to use.

  • For a run goal, throw cards that are duplicates of numbers you already have. A hand with five pairs is almost never a run.

  • For bonds, throw cards whose partner is already in the discard pile, because that partner is gone for now.

  • Watch the discard pile. If another player picks up a 6 and drops a 2, they are building a run and want 7.

  • A team goal depends on the team size: Tigers, Elephants and Bears have 8 cards, the others 10. Five of an 8-card team is harder than five of a 10-card team, so aim for Monkeys, Peacocks or Cobras.

  • Going out ends the round for everybody, so do not hold a nearly done hand too long: when you are one card away, taking a discard that completes it is the only draw that finishes the round.

Worked example

  1. Goal 1, four bonds, three players. A holds Arvind (1), Ajay (2), Naresh (3), Avika (5), Smaya (8), Pinku (7), Naresh (6), Shreya (2), Kanasu (6) and Nysha (8). A already has three bonds: 1 and 8 (Arvind (1) and Smaya (8)), 2 and 7 (Ajay (2) and Pinku (7)), 3 and 6 (Naresh (3) and Naresh (6)). A needs a 4 to pair with the 5 (Avika (5)).

  2. A looks at the discard pile. The top card is Archana (4), a 4. A takes it. A now has 11 cards with four bonds: 1+8, 2+7, 3+6 and 4+5. A says "Out" and shows Archana (4) with Avika (5) and the other three pairs. The round ends.

  3. B has not drawn yet. B lays down the 10 cards in hand: Amay (1), Amay (8), Pinku (2), Ajay (7), Kanasu (3), Dhruv (6), Amyra (4), Gopi (5), Smaya (1) and Bharati (4). They hold 1+8 (Amay (1), Amay (8)), 2+7 (Pinku (2), Ajay (7)), 3+6 (Kanasu (3), Dhruv (6)) and 4+5 (Amyra (4), Gopi (5)). Four bonds: B clears Goal 1 too.

  4. C lays down Nysha (1), Idhayan (1), Anayka (1), Ammlu (2), Bn Sharada (2), Adhiraa (3), Sharada (3), Gopi (4), Avika (4) and Nakul (4). These are all low cards (1 to 4) with no partners, so C has no bonds and stays on Goal 1.

  5. A and B move up to Goal 2, a run of 6. C stays on Goal 1. The next round starts one seat to the left of A.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Use the easier first goals: two bonds, a triple, a run of 5. With a 10-card hand these are met at the deal in 94%, 75% and 57% of hands, so the game is mostly about spotting them. The goals are listed on the reference card. (The earlier draft goals; not simulated as a game.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Play goals 1 to 3 (four bonds, a run of 6, two triples) as a short game.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. Play goals 1 to 5 for a short game, or all 8 for a long one.

Solo

No solo mode: the round ends when another player goes out.

Two players

Works well. The bot beats random play 95% of the time at 2 players. You see the discard of one opponent, so reading what they want is easy.

Maths and skills in this game

Pairing numbers to 9, spotting runs of numbers in a row, counting triples and teams, and planning which cards to throw.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Goals as drafted were met at the deal: with a 10-card hand two bonds are in the opening hand 94% of the time, a triple 75%, a run of 5 57% and a team of 4 52%. So they were replaced.

  • Turns for a bot working alone to reach the new goals (median, mean): four bonds 3 (4.2), run of 6 4 (5.6), two triples 5 (6.8), run of 7 6 (8.1), five of a team 8 (9.3).

  • Three extra goals measured for this page (solo bot, 1,500 trials each, same draw and discard rule): five bonds median 8 (mean 9.9), run of 8 median 9 (10.4), three triples median 12 (14.0). Others tried: team of 6 median 16, two teams of 4 median 9 but mean 17.6, so they were left out.

  • With the five goals, the bot wins 95%, 86%, 72%, 55% against random players at 2 to 5 players (baselines 50%, 33%, 25%, 20%) and sits at baseline against itself.

  • 34 to 60 turns in all for five goals, about 6 to 10 minutes. Eight goals are roughly 60 to 100 turns, about 15 minutes (extrapolated from the medians above, not run).

  • Ties are shared in the simulation. The written rule gives the win to the player who went out; that rule was not simulated.

  • Twin-as-wild was in the draft and was not tested; it is not in the rules.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Bots use a progress score for each goal and never read the opponents.

  • Not tested: the all-eight-goals game and the L1 and L2 goal sets as full games.

  • Not tested: the tie-break by who went out.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

PHASE CLIMB. Deal 10 (8 at six). 1 card face up starts the discard. Turn: draw the top of deck or discard, then if your 11 cards hold your goal say Out; else discard 1. When someone is out, all others show their 10: matching hands clear too. Clearers climb one goal. Re-deal.

Back

GOALS. 1 four bonds (pairs to 9). 2 run of 6. 3 two triples. 4 run of 7. 5 five of a team. 6 five bonds. 7 run of 8. 8 three triples. First to clear the last goal wins (the player who went out wins ties). Short game: goals 1 to 5. L1 easy goals: two bonds, triple, run of 5.

Border Patrol

Lay cards edge to edge so the colours of the borders meet. A card that fits two neighbours at once is worth four times as much as one that fits a single neighbour.

Inspired by Qwirkle, Carcassonne-style edge matching, Kingdomino

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-18
Players
2 to 4
Time
15 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Grow a map of cards, one per turn. Every edge you touch must match colour. You score the number of matching edges you make, squared, so the best spots are the ones that close a gap between two or more cards.

What you need

All 54 cardsone is the start card; the rest are dealt and laid
Ref 3 (Colour key)to read the six border colours
A tableabout the size of two open newspapers

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Put one card face up in the middle of the table. This is the start card.

  • Deal 5 cards to each player. The rest is a face-down draw deck.

  • Each card is treated as a square tile. It has one border colour along its top and bottom edges and its other border colour along its left and right edges. You may lay it either way round, which swaps the two colours. You may not flip it.

  • The youngest player goes first.

How to play

  1. Pick one card from your hand and lay it next to the cards already on the table, so that it touches at least one card edge to edge. Corners do not count.

  2. Every edge that touches another card must show the same colour. If any touching edge differs, you cannot lay the card there.

  3. Score the number of edges that touch, squared: 1 touching edge = 1 point, 2 = 4, 3 = 9, 4 = 16. Keep score on paper.

  4. Draw a card from the deck back up to 5.

  5. If none of your cards can be laid anywhere, you must discard one card (your choice) and draw a new one. That is your whole turn.

How it ends

The game ends when the deck is empty and a player has no card they can lay, or when every player has passed twice in a row. In a full game nearly all 53 cards are laid. Highest score wins. Ties: the player with fewer cards in hand; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Border colour the colour at the edge of the card. Each card has two border colours, one for the top and bottom, one for the sides.
  • Touching edge an edge that lies against another card's edge. A touching edge must match.
  • Pocket a spot on the table with two or more neighbours already there. Laying a card in a pocket scores the most.
  • Start card the first card in the middle, placed face up before the deal.

Common questions

  • Can I lay a card so that it touches no card? No. It must touch at least one edge.

  • Can I turn a card a quarter turn? Yes. That is the only choice you have about orientation: which of the two colours is on the top and bottom.

  • What if a pocket needs two different colours that my card does not have? Then it cannot go there. You may keep it, and its pocket stays open for someone with the right card.

  • Do I have to lay a card if I can? Yes. You may choose which card and where, but you cannot discard when a legal play exists.

  • How many cards can I lay in a turn? Exactly one.

  • Does the number on a card matter? No. Only the border colours matter in this version.

Tips

  • Leave pockets open, then fill them. A pocket that needs two specific colours is worth 4 points to whoever has the one matching card, so do not make pockets you cannot fill.

  • Keep two cards with the same colour pair if you can. Two copies of a pair are two ways to use the same pocket later.

  • Pick the placement with the most matching edges, and use the quarter turn to move which colour goes on the sides. The sim's bot just takes the highest edge count each turn and still beats random play 98 to 100%.

  • Spoil a rival's pocket on purpose: lay a card beside it that changes the colours the pocket needs, so the card they were saving no longer fits.

  • Late in the game cards are hard to place. Keep one flexible card (a colour pair that is common on the table) for your last turns.

  • Count your hand colours against the table. If a colour is rare among the unplaced cards, a pocket that needs it may never be filled.

Worked example

  1. Two players, A and B. The start card is Guhan (3), a card with red on its top and bottom and green on its sides. A and B each hold 5 cards.

  2. A lays Arvind (1) (red and orange) above the start card with red on its top and bottom. Its bottom edge touches the start card's top edge, red on red: it matches. 1 touching edge, so A scores 1.

  3. B lays Amyra (4) (red and green) to the right of the start card with red on top and bottom and green on the sides. Its left edge (green) touches the start card's right edge (green): 1 touching edge, 1 point to B.

  4. Now there is a pocket at the top right: its left neighbour is Arvind (1), whose right edge is orange; its lower neighbour is Amyra (4), whose top edge is red. A needs a card with red on the top and bottom and orange on the sides. A holds Naresh (6) (red and orange). It fits. A lays it there: 2 touching edges, so A scores 2 squared, 4 points.

  5. Score so far: A 5, B 1. If a player held only cards that fit nowhere (for example Pinku (2), orange and yellow, when no open spot has an orange or yellow edge), they would discard one card, draw one, and pass.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6, with a helper. Lay only on a single edge: each card must match exactly the one neighbour it touches. Score 1 per card placed and the winner is whoever lays the most cards. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. The full matching rule, scoring 1 point for each touching edge instead of squares. (Not simulated.)

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game with squared scoring.

Solo

Solo: deal yourself 5 cards, draw as normal, and see how many of the 54 cards you lay. A score is your points. The sim has no solo mode, so no medals are set.

Two players

Two players is the best count: 26 turns each, a long and open map. The simulated bot wins 100% against random players at 2 players and 52% against itself.

Maths and skills in this game

Matching colours at edges, rotating a tile in your head, planning two moves ahead (a pocket now or a pocket later), and squaring small numbers (1, 4, 9, 16).

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursRule the two border colours are the edges of the map
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The game plays freely: about 2% of turns have no legal card, and the whole deck is laid (53 cards plus the start card).

  • The bot that takes the placement with the most matching edges beats random players 98% to 100% at 2 to 4 players (the original run) and, in the run for this page (400 games), 100%, 99% and 99%. Against itself it wins 52%, 37% and 26% (baselines 50%, 33%, 25%), so seat order has little effect.

  • Length: 26.5, 17.7 and 13.2 turns each at 2, 3 and 4 players, about 12 to 20 minutes at 15 to 20 seconds a turn.

  • Score per player between smart bots is 54.4, 37.2 and 28.0 points at 2, 3 and 4 players. A random player averages 45.8, 28.4 and 20.4, so squared scoring does reward skill.

  • The real colour borders alone (a top-and-bottom colour pair and a side pair) play just the same as the abstract test cards.

  • Squared scoring was the simulated rule. Region scoring (the size of each colour region you close) was drafted and not tested.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: region scoring.

  • Not tested: real people. The bot only takes the highest edge count, so tricks such as spoiling pockets are not modelled.

  • Not tested: whether the printed card borders can be read as a top-and-bottom pair and a side pair at a glance. Check this on the first printed set.

Variants and options

  • Back to Back (retired) The same laying game, but matching the suit cells on the card backs. It was the weaker twin: harder to read (six small cells on a card), fun 5 of 10, and the colour borders do the same job at a glance. Its idea of laying a card next to others and scoring touching pairs lives on here.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

BORDER PATROL. 1 start card face up; deal 5. A card is a tile: colour 1 on top and bottom, colour 2 on the sides (or swapped). Turn: lay 1 card touching at least one edge; all touching edges must match in colour. Draw to 5. No play: discard 1, draw 1.

Back

SCORE. Touching edges squared: 1, 4, 9, 16. END. Deck empty and a player cannot play, or everyone passes twice. Highest score wins; tie: fewer cards in hand. LEVELS. L1 match one neighbour only, most cards laid wins. L2 one point per edge. L3 squares.

Blind Pack

You can only judge the pack by its flags, but the cargo inside is yours alone to read.

Inspired by Majority games such as El Grande's regions, plus the take-and-peek hidden cargo of games like Sushi Go and Coup (from memory)

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FT-19
Players
2 to 5
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
8+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Take a face-down card judged only by its back, peek at its front, keep five cards, and score the suits on the backs plus the number bonds on the fronts.

What you need

All 54 cardsFive cards in each Pack, six face-down in the Market, the rest in the Deck.
Pencil and paperFor the final score.

Set up

  • Shuffle the deck. Deal each player five cards. Look at your fronts and keep them secret. Hold them with the backs towards the table so everyone sees your backs. This is your Pack.

  • Lay six cards face down in a row. This is the Market. With five players, lay five.

  • Put the rest in a Deck. Leave space beside it for the Bin, a face-up pile.

  • The youngest player goes first. Play goes clockwise.

How to play

  1. Take one card from the Market. You can judge it only by its back.

  2. Look at its front. Keep it secret.

  3. You now hold six cards. Put one of them in the Bin, face up. It can be the card you just took.

  4. Refill the Market from the Deck. When the Deck is empty, do not refill.

  5. The game ends the moment the Market is empty at the start of someone's turn.

How it ends

Everyone reveals their fronts. Suit points: for each of the six suits, count the pictures of that suit on all the backs in each Pack. Most pictures scores five points. Second most scores two. Tied for most: two players share seven points, three or more share five. Tied for second: share two. Nobody scores a suit they have no pictures of. Bond points: each pair of cards in your Pack whose fronts add to nine scores three. A card is in one pair only. A nine pairs with another nine. Highest total wins. Tie-break: the higher total of the numbers on the fronts. If that is level too, the win is shared.

Words in this game

  • Pack The five cards you keep, held with the backs towards the table.
  • Market Face-down cards you choose from, by their backs.
  • Bin The face-up pile of dropped cards. Anyone can look through it.
  • Picture One of the six small suit pictures on the back of a card. Each card shows three suits, each twice.
  • Bond Two cards whose fronts add to nine.

Common questions

  • Can I look at the Bin? Yes. It is face up. Use it to see which numbers are gone.

  • Can I take a card only to stop someone else getting it? Yes. Taking it and dropping it at once is allowed.

  • Can I swap two cards in my Pack? No. You may only drop one card each turn.

  • How many bonds can a pack have? At most two, because a Pack holds five cards.

  • Do I show my fronts during the game? No. Only at the end, to score bonds. Keep the fronts hidden even from the player next to you.

  • What if the Market is empty in the middle of a round? The game ends at once. Some players may have had one more turn than others. That is part of the game.

Tips

  • Take by the back, then decide by the front. The peek changed the decision in 10.3% of simulated turns, so a card with the right back and a bad number is a real choice, not an automatic keep.

  • Watch the Bin. It is face up, so you can see which numbers are gone and whether the bond you want is still alive.

  • Mix suits and bonds. The best bond weight was in the middle (0.5 to 1), and suit-only beat bond-only only narrowly at two players, so do not chase one idea.

  • Take a card to deny a rival's suit when it costs you nothing. Taking and dropping at once is allowed, and denial at a modest weight did better than none.

  • At two players take turns going first, because mismatched bots gave the second seat 52 to 59%. Expect a points tie in over half of games, so know the front-total tie-break before you start.

Worked example

Two players, standard level. Player one holds Naresh (6), Kanasu (3), Smaya (8), Adhiraa (6) and Adheesh (9). Player two holds Nakul (4), Ammlu (2), Nakul (5), Arvind (1) and Archana (4). The Market backs are Gowri's back (3 4 / 1 4 / 3 1), Rihansh's back (1 2 / 6 1 / 6 2), Bn Sharada's back (4 4 / 1 6 / 1 6), Amyra's back (6 3 / 4 6 / 4 3), Ajay's back (2 3 / 2 1 / 1 3) and Dhruv's back (3 6 / 4 3 / 4 6).

  1. Player one takes Dhruv (3), back Dhruv's back (3 6 / 4 3 / 4 6). The front says 3, which makes a second bond with a 6. Player one drops Adheesh (9), a lone 9. The Pack is now worth two bonds and holds eight pictures of suit 6.

  2. Player two takes Amyra (5), back Amyra's back (6 3 / 4 6 / 4 3). The front says 5, which pairs with the 4 in Nakul (4). Player two drops Ammlu (2), a lone 2. The Pack is now two bonds and holds eight pictures of suit 1.

  3. Player one takes Bn Sharada (7), back Bn Sharada's back (4 4 / 1 6 / 1 6). The front says 7, no partner here, but suit 6 now stands at ten pictures. Player one drops Smaya (8), an 8 with no 1 to pair with.

  4. Player two takes Dhruv (6), back Dhruv's back (4 3 / 3 5 / 5 4). The front says 6, no partner here. Player two drops Arvind (1), a lone 1. Both Packs still hold two bonds.

Level ladder

L1 · first game

First game: score only the suit points. Ignore the fronts, apart from enjoying the faces. Good for ages 8 and up, or younger with a helper.

L2 · standard

Standard: the rules as written, with suit points and bond points.

L3 · expert

Expert: the Bin is face down, so you cannot count which numbers are gone. Not simulated.

Solo

No solo mode. A solo version against a fixed Ghost pack was simulated and always topped out at the same score, so it was dropped.

Two players

Works as written, with a Market of six. Second place always scores for any suit you both hold, so every pick counts. In simulation two players finished level on points in over half of games before the tie-break and 7 percent after it. Take turns being first: mismatched bots gave the second seat 52 to 59 percent at two players.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting pictures, adding to nine, weighing a public choice against a private one, and remembering what the Bin shows.

Not simulated. Fun, bluffing, and human judgement about what other players are collecting. Bots do not misjudge counts. Expert level (Bin face down) was not simulated.

Smart bots beat random and the two single-idea bots by a wide margin, and the single-idea bots trade wins (bond-only edges suit-only at two players, the reverse at four). That is the evidence there is no dominant strategy. Stronger human play could reveal an unseen dominant line; the scoring has never been tested with people. Open point: with mismatched bots the second seat wins 52 to 59 percent at two players, above the 6 point kill line, though two equal smart bots show 50.6 to 49.4.

Tuning log

  • round 1: base design (pack of five, market of six, suit points 4 and 2, bond pair 3). Four players, 2000 games: smart bot wins 67 percent, suit-only bot 21, bond-only 9.5, random 1.6. Bond weight sweep among four smart bots (0, 0.5, 1, 2): 12, 35, 28, 26 percent, so ignoring the fronts is clearly worse and the best weight is in the middle. Problem: with two players 44 percent of games ended level on points. Added a tie-break. Also tried a solo mode against a fixed Ghost pack: the smart bot scored 25.8 with the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles all 26, a ceiling with no spread for medals, so the solo mode was dropped.

  • round 2: suit points 5 and 2 (more than 4 and 2). Two smart players were still level on points in 57 percent of games, but pure strategies became closer: suit-only against bond-only at two players moved from 32 to 68 to 46 to 54 (400 games, ties shared). The tie-break was then bonds first; with it suit-only against bond-only went to 33 to 67 at equal mean scores (24.9 against 25.3), so the tie-break itself was deciding games for bond hunters.

  • round 3: tie-break changed to the higher total of the numbers on the fronts, which does not favour either strategy. Suit-only against bond-only: 47.8 to 52.2 (600 games). Two smart players still tie for first after the tie-break in 7.0 percent of games, three players in 1.0 percent. Adopted 5 and 2 scoring, bond 3, front-total tie-break.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Pen and Plume: also a market take with a keep decision, but there the cards are face up; here the choice is by back and the reveal is private

  • Market Raid: bond pairs raided; here bonds are scored passively at the end, and suits do most of the fighting

Ratings

Two scoring ideas, one decision per turn, teach about four minutes (from memory anchors: Sushi Go ~1.2, Lost Cities ~1.6).

Start at 10. Teach time about four minutes -1. Final scoring needs counting pictures on every back across six suits -1. Downtime over 25 seconds at four and five players -1. Setup under a minute and no stalls.

Real tension between the public back and the private number, and the peek-then-drop moment is satisfying. Weakest part: the final count is a chore, and the first few turns feel alike.

Auto Ride

Twelve passengers, six districts, and an auto that can only go round in a ring.

Inspired by Mint Delivery (move, load, upgrade; pick-up and deliver), from memory

Pawns
1 per player (up to 3)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Drive your pawn round a ring of six districts, pick up passengers and drop them at their places for a fare of their number plus the distance.

What you need

6 district cardsOne card of each team: Tigers (district 1), Elephants (2), Bears (3), Monkeys (4), Peacocks (5), Cobras (6). Lay them in a ring in that order, so district 6 sits next to district 1.
12 passenger cardsAny twelve other cards, laid face up beside the district card of their team. The card's team is where it waits.
Place keyTells you which district a passenger wants to go to, from the place name on the card.
1 dieThe Rush district.
1 pawn per playerYour auto.
Pencil and paperTo keep your fare total.

Key cards for this game

Place key

Die 1 = Heritage and Worship places (district 1, Tigers). Die 2 = Hills and Caves (district 2, Elephants). Die 3 = Museums and Sports (district 3, Bears). Die 4 = Parks and Wildlife (district 4, Monkeys). Die 5 = Streets, Markets and Rides (district 5, Peacocks). Die 6 = Water (district 6, Cobras). List each card's place name under its number: 9, 8, 10, 9, 12 and 6 cards. These tags are approved.

Set up

  • Take one card of each team and lay them in a ring in team order 1 to 6 (Tigers to Cobras). These are the districts.

  • Shuffle the other cards. Turn twelve face up and lay each one next to the district card of its team (the team on the card's front). The rest go back in the box.

  • Put pawns on districts: with one player, district 1. With two, districts 1 and 4. With three, districts 1, 3 and 5.

  • Keep a score total on paper. The youngest player starts.

How to play

  1. Roll the die. That district is in Rush hour this turn: every passenger you drop off there pays two extra.

  2. Take two actions. You may take the same action twice, or do nothing for an action.

  3. MOVE: move your pawn one district round the ring, in either direction. If you arrive at the place a passenger in your car wants, they get out: score their fare and put the card in front of you.

  4. LOAD: pick up one passenger who is waiting at your district. You can carry two passengers. A passenger who wants to go to the district you are in gets out at once.

  5. FARE: the card's number plus the distance round the ring from where the passenger started to where they get out. Count the short way round.

How it ends

The game ends after round 8 with 1 or 2 players, or round 6 with 3 players, or as soon as all passengers are delivered. Passengers still in a car score nothing. Highest total wins; ties go to the player who delivered more passengers, then share. With three players, in the first round the first two players take only one action.

Words in this game

  • district One of the six cards in the ring. Its number is the team die: 1 Tigers to 6 Cobras.
  • origin The district the passenger's team points to. That is where the passenger waits.
  • destination The district whose number equals the die number the Place key gives for the passenger's place.
  • distance How many steps round the ring from origin to destination, the short way. Bigger number minus smaller number; if the answer is more than 3, take it away from 6.
  • Rush hour The district shown by the die this turn. Drop-offs there pay two extra.

Common questions

  • How do I count the distance from district 1 to district 5? 5 minus 1 is 4. That is more than 3, so go the other way: 6 minus 4 is 2.

  • A passenger's origin and destination are the same. Do they still pay? Yes: the card's number plus zero. Load them and they get out at once.

  • Can I pass through a district and drop somebody off without stopping? You always stop after each move, and a drop-off happens when you arrive.

  • Two of us are in the same district. Is that allowed? Yes. Whoever loads the passenger first gets them.

  • Nobody wants the remaining passengers. Is it endless? No. The game always ends after the last round.

  • Can I keep a passenger past their stop and come back? Yes, but you only get out at a destination when you arrive there.

  • How do we know a card's destination? Read the place name on the card, find it on the Place key, and use the district number printed above it.

Tips

  • Pair two passengers who go the same way. Pairing is the main skill, and it is what lets a planner beat a nearest-first driver about 70% of the time at two players.

  • Count distance the short way round the six-district ring. From district 1 to 5 is 2, not 4, so check before you commit a move.

  • Use both actions: Move then Load, or Load then Move. A wasted action costs a fare, and the simulated planner wasted under one action a game at two players.

  • At L3 check the Rush die before you drive. Drop-offs in the Rush district pay two extra, so time a delivery for it when the route allows.

  • Play it with two. Three players is a weaker game (a planner wins 46% against even 33%), and four was unfair, so it is not supported. With a 7-year-old, drive the pawn together for a round and let them count the distance aloud.

Worked example

Two players. Districts in order: Nakul (4; Tigers), Archana (5; Elephants), Dhruv (3; Bears), Nysha (8; Monkeys), Sharada (6; Peacocks), Ammlu (2; Cobras). Player one starts at district 1 and player two at district 4. Waiting passengers include Nakul (5), Shreya (7), Arvind (8), Bn Sharada (7), Arvind (1), Smaya (8), Dhruv (6), Rihansh (9) and Avika (5).

  1. Player one rolls 5. At district 1 they load Nakul (5): it wants district 4 (Parks and Wildlife), so the distance is 4 minus 1, which is 3. The fare is 5 plus 3, or 8. Second action: load Shreya (7) (district 4, distance 3, fare 7 plus 3, or 10). The car is full.

  2. Player two rolls 3. At district 4 they load Arvind (8) (wants district 5, distance 1, fare 9) and then Bn Sharada (7), which wants district 4: it gets out at once for 7 plus 0, or 7.

  3. Player one rolls 4 and moves two districts, from 1 to 2 and then to 3. Nobody is dropped off yet.

  4. Player two rolls 4. They load Arvind (1) (district 5, fare 2) and move to district 5. Both get out: 9 plus 2 is 11. Player two has 18.

  5. Player one rolls 2, moves from district 3 to 4. Nakul (5) and Shreya (7) get out for 8 plus 10, which is 18. Player one's other action moves back to district 3.

  6. Player two rolls 2, at district 5, loads Rihansh (9) and Avika (5). Both go to district 1: 5 minus 1 is 4, more than 3, so 6 minus 4 is a distance of 2. Fares are 9 plus 2 and 5 plus 2, which is 11 and 7.

  7. Player one rolls 3: Rush hour at district 3, where they are. They load Smaya (8) and Dhruv (6). Both want district 3, so they get out at once: 8 plus 0 plus 2 Rush, and 6 plus 0 plus 2, which is 10 and 8. Player one has 36 against 18.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6. Score 1 point per passenger, ignore fares and the die. A grown-up reads the Place key aloud and counts the distance with the child. One player or two.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 7 and 8. Fare is the number plus the distance. No Rush die. Two players or solo.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 9 and up. Add the Rush die. Play with three players if you like; players one and two take only one action in round one.

Solo

Eight rounds alone, die rolled each turn. Aim for the best total. The best-play bot averages 51 (10th to 90th percentile 42 to 60). Bronze 46, Silver 51, Gold 56. Note that a nearest-first driver scores 49, so solo is a puzzle with a small skill gap.

Two players

The best way to play. Eight rounds each, about 7 to 8 minutes. A planner wins about 70 percent against a nearest-first driver.

Maths and skills in this game

Subtraction as distance on a circle (bigger minus smaller, or six minus the answer), addition, planning a two-stop route, reading a key.

Not simulated. Fun and the thinking time of a real player (the planner checks about 1,500 plans a turn; a human scans two or three). The perfect-information board can slow down analytical players. Subtraction learning was not tested. Four players were simulated and were unfair, so they are not supported.

See tuning_log. Honest read: this is a race for shared passengers; pairing two passengers who go the same way is the main skill. The planner's edge shrinks as players are added. Solo is a puzzle with only a 2-point skill gap, so Gold is mostly the luck of the layout. Rerun after the mood tags moved: the engine does not read mood, so no number changed. Check after the tag change: a re-run with default engine settings gave about 64 percent at 2 players and 39 percent at 3 players, lower than the table above, so treat the planner's edge as about 6 points over even share at 3 players until the original settings are recovered.

Tuning log

  • round 1: a route-planning bot (best points per action over any one or two passengers) only beat a nearest-first greedy driver 51 to 58 percent. Rewrote the planner to maximise fare minus 2 per action (the cost of time) and to leave passengers the opponent can reach first. It now wins 69 to 71 percent at 2 players.

  • round 2: seats were unfair at 3 players (39 / 37 / 24 percent). Tried choosing start districts in reverse order (made player one win 64 percent), then fewer first-round actions. Final: at 3 players the first two players take only one action in round one, giving 31 / 32 / 37 percent. 4 players could not be balanced (best 19 / 12 / 30 / 39), so the game is for 1 to 3.

  • round 3: tested an Upgrade action (pay 3 points to move two districts at once). Bots that bought it lost, 33 percent at 2 players and 20 percent at 3. It was a dead option, so Upgrade was removed. Kept the surge die (+2 to deliveries in the rolled district) because it costs about 1 to 2 points of skill and gives the die a job.

  • tags approved; K11 and K12 mood tags moved; re-ran. Auto Ride reads place type and team only and place types did not change, so no number changed. Tags are now approved.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Treasure Ring (walk a ring, set turn-in by die): Auto Ride also moves round a ring, but it carries passengers, with fares from number plus distance.

Ratings

From memory, below Hanabi in decisions; two actions, one key, a distance rule that needs a short teach; about 4 minutes to teach.

Teach about 4 minutes (-1), a Place key read each turn (-1), pencil tally and ring counting (-1).

Planning two-passenger routes and racing for fares is satisfying, and the Rush die adds surprise. Weakest part: solo has little skill edge, and at 3 players the game is a quick race with some downtime.
