Rug Hunt

The trail guide rolls two dice and the whole camp dives for the right face in the right place.

Inspired by From memory: Spot It style hunts and Dobble-like grabbing, plus the pick-a-card reflex floor games used in many classrooms.

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasyComplexity 1.1 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FL-01
Players
2 to 8
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
2 dice (Place die and Mood die, read off the Place key and Mood key)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Roll a Place die and a Mood die, then race to put a hand on a face-up card that shows that kind of place and that kind of face.

What you need

All 54 cardslaid face up in a rectangle on the rug, every card within reach of every player
2 diceone is the Place die, one is the Mood die (agree which colour is which)
Place key and Mood keytwo key cards that say which place type and which mood each die number means
1 reference cardthe quick rules and the rolls-per-player table

Key cards for this game

Place key

One card with six pictures and words. Die 1 = Heritage and Worship (palaces, forts, temples, old gates). Die 2 = Hills and Caves. Die 3 = Museums and Sports. Die 4 = Parks and Wildlife. Die 5 = Streets, Markets and Rides. Die 6 = Water (lakes, tanks, rivers, boats). Each place type also has a small picture so a five year old can match it.

Mood key

One card with six faces and words. Die 1 = Body and Senses (hungry, sleepy, sour, cold, hot, smelly). Die 2 = Brave and Fierce. Die 3 = Delight (laughing, cheering, happy). Die 4 = Mischief (cheeky, sneaky, shy). Die 5 = Startle and Wonder (scared, awestruck, surprised). Die 6 = Think and Notice (puzzled, listening, counting).

Set up

  • Lay all 54 cards face up in six rows of nine. Leave a little gap between cards so a hand can land on one card.

  • Everyone sits or kneels around the rug. Put the Place key and the Mood key where everyone can see them.

  • Children aged five and under are little hunters. Everyone else is a hunter. A little hunter picks the Place die or the Mood die for the whole game (the Mood die is easier for most five year olds because they read faces).

  • The youngest player rolls first. The roller changes after every roll, clockwise.

  • Each player will roll a fixed number of times: 2 players 12 each, 3 players 8, 4 players 6, 5 players 5, 6 players 4, 7 or 8 players 3.

How to play

  1. The roller rolls both dice and reads them aloud with the keys: 'Water and Mischief'.

  2. Everyone hunts at once. A hunter needs a card whose place is the Place die type AND whose face is the Mood die type. A little hunter needs a card that fits only the die they chose.

  3. Catch-up: if you hold two or more cards fewer than the player with the most cards, you may use either die (a card that fits the Place die OR the Mood die).

  4. To claim a card, put your flat hand on it. The first hand on a fitting card takes it and keeps it face up in front of them. If hands land together, the hand that is lowest, touching the card itself, wins. If it is still a tie, the player with fewer cards wins.

  5. A wrong touch (the card does not fit your rule): put the card back and sit out the rest of this roll.

  6. If you think no card fits both dice, call 'None!'. Everyone stops. The table checks. If you are right, you take any one card of the Place die type from the rug as your prize (if there is none, any card). If you are wrong, a fitting card exists: put one of your cards back on the rug face up (if you have none, nothing happens) and the hunt goes on.

  7. A roll that nobody settles after a slow count of twenty is called off by the roller, who points out the fitting card or says 'None'. Then the next player rolls.

  8. Exactly one card leaves the rug on every roll.

How it ends

After everyone has rolled their share (see setup), the game ends. The player with the most cards wins. Equal cards: those players share the win (it is a party game).

Words in this game

  • Roller The player who rolls both dice this time. The roller hunts as well.
  • Hunter / little hunter A little hunter is aged five or under and needs a card that fits only one die. Everyone else is a hunter.
  • Fits A card fits when its place type matches the Place die and its face matches the Mood die, as the keys say.
  • Catch-up Two or more cards behind the leader: either die is enough.
  • None! The call when no card on the rug fits both dice. It happens about one roll in four.

Common questions

  • Two hands land at the same moment. Who wins? The hand lowest on the card, touching the card itself. If that is a tie, the player with fewer cards. If that is a tie too, the younger player.

  • I called 'None!' and a fitting card exists. What now? Put one of your cards back on the rug, face up. The hunt goes on and the fitting card is still there for anyone.

  • We disagree about whether a face is 'scared' or 'surprised'. Both are in Startle and Wonder. If it is still unclear, the grown-up decides in five seconds. The key text is the rule.

  • A child keeps rolling the dice softly and nothing happens. Each die must tumble clear of the cards. Roll it into a lid, a box or a cleared patch of rug.

  • Nobody finds a card and nobody calls None! After a slow count of twenty the roller says what is on the rug or says 'None'. No card leaves on this roll, and the roller still counts as having rolled.

  • Can I play without the dice or the keys? Yes. A grown-up calls from the call list below instead of rolling. Each call has at least two fitting cards, so nobody is stuck. Call list: 1 Water and a brave face. 2 Water and a happy face. 3 Hills and a cheeky face. 4 Hills and a scared face. 5 Museum or sports and a scared face. 6 Museum or sports and a thinking face. 7 Street or market and a hungry, sleepy or sour face. 8 Street or market and a happy face. 9 Street or market and a cheeky face. 10 Park and a brave face. 11 Park and a cheeky face. 12 Old palace or fort and a hungry, sleepy or sour face. 13 Water and a cheeky face (nothing fits: the answer is None!).

Tips

  • Check the pair of dice before you hunt. 4 of the 36 Place and Mood pairs have no card at all, and about 11% of rolls on a full rug find nothing, so call None! only after a quick scan of the whole rug.

  • Expect more None! calls as the rug thins. Nothing fits 16% of the time at 48 cards and 31% at 36, so late in the game 'None!' is often right.

  • Use the catch-up rules. A player two or more cards behind may use either die, and a 5-year-old uses only one, which brought a mixed table within 1.0 to 1.24 largest-to-smallest share in simulation.

  • Land the flat of your hand lowest on the card. If hands land together, the hand touching the card wins, then the player with fewer cards.

  • With a 5-year-old, let them pick the Mood die and read faces, since it is easier for most children. Use the call list to skip the dice for the very youngest, and roll the dice into a lid so they tumble clear.

Worked example

Three players on the rug: Asha (aged 5, little hunter, uses the Place die), Bilal (aged 8, hunter) and Chitra (a grown-up, hunter). Real seeded run. Each roll shows the Place die type and the Mood die type.

  1. Roll 1. Place die 6 (Water), Mood die 6 (Think and Notice). No Water card has a thinking face. Chitra calls None! before anyone has touched a card. The table checks and agrees, so she takes a Water card as her prize: Amay (1).

  2. Roll 2. Place die 6 (Water), Mood die 1 (Body and Senses). The only card that fitted both, Amay (1), was taken last roll, so nothing fits both dice. Asha is a little hunter and needs only the Place die. She touches Amyra (5), a Water card, and keeps it. The cards are now Asha 1, Bilal 0, Chitra 1.

  3. Roll 3. Place die 5 (Streets, Markets and Rides), Mood die 6 (Think and Notice). Only Shreya (2) fits both dice. Bilal puts his hand on it first and keeps it.

  4. Roll 4. Place die 1 (Heritage and Worship), Mood die 1 (Body and Senses). Three cards fit both: Sharada (3), Pinku (7) and Rihansh (9). Bilal touches Sharada (3) first. The cards are now Asha 1, Bilal 2, Chitra 1.

  5. Roll 18. Place die 2 (Hills and Caves), Mood die 1 (Body and Senses). Nothing fits both. Before this roll the counts are Asha 4, Bilal 6, Chitra 7, so Asha is three cards behind the leader and may use either die. She touches Dharsh (2), a Body and Senses face, and keeps it.

  6. Roll 20. Place die 4 (Parks and Wildlife), Mood die 6 (Think and Notice). Smaya (1) fits both dice, but Asha, a little hunter, is first to Shreya (7). It is a Parks card, so it fits her one die and she keeps it.

  7. After roll 24 the rug has 30 cards left. Asha has 9 cards, Bilal 8 and Chitra 7, so Asha wins.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Little hunters use one die only (their choice) and take any card that fits it. Play 3 players and read the keys aloud for them.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Both dice, with the catch-up rule. Call None! for the prize.

L3 · age 8 and up

Both dice and no catch-up unless the table is mixed. A wrong None! costs a card. Add the Colour die for a third condition: the card must also have that colour.

Solo

Roll the two dice 24 times. For each roll, find a fitting card within a slow count of ten, or call None! within the count if nothing fits. Each success is one point (24 possible). The rug starts with all 54 cards and every found card leaves. From the model with assumed scan speeds: Bronze 10, Silver 15, Gold 19. Age 8 usually lands around 13, an adult around 18.

Two players

Each player rolls 12 times. Catch-up applies. A five year old against a grown-up ends within a few cards of level (simulated shares 50% and 50%).

Visual scanning, reading expressions, categorising places, fast and fair turn-taking, quick checking and calling.

Real reflex speed (the scan speeds are my assumptions), whether a five year old really reads place pictures quickly, rug arguments and grabbing, how often someone calls None! wrongly, and the fun of shouting. The tags are approved, but every fit still depends on them and a table may still argue about a face.

Bots here are search models, not a decision game: each player scans the rug in a random order at its speed and the earliest hand wins. There is no skill gap to measure other than reading speed, which the catch-up rules are built to cancel. The three rounds changed the handicap rule and the game end (see tuning log). Rerun after the approved tags (K11 now Body and Senses, K12 now Think and Notice): one fewer empty pair on the full rug, None! about 2 points lower, shares unchanged within noise.

Tuning log

  • round 1: everyone needs a card matching both dice. Simulated scan speeds (assumed: age 5 = 1.2 cards per second, age 8 = 2.8, adult = 4.5). The adult takes 45 to 89% of the cards, the five year old 4 to 11% (largest share divided by smallest = 7 to 11 across 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 players). Rejected: it is not a game for a mixed rug.

  • round 2: let all small children use one die, or either die. Works for a five year old but overshoots for a six year old (49% of the cards at a four child table). A rule that only helps the trailing players (leaders need both dice, everyone else either) evens the shares but removes the 'None!' call almost completely.

  • round 3: grid of 27 combinations of age 5 rule, age 6 rule and catch-up gap. Chosen: age 5 and under use ONE die; anyone two or more cards behind the leader may use either die; everyone else needs both. Largest share divided by smallest is 1.0 to 1.24 at 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 players. Also changed the end: playing until 24 cards were left gave 'None!' on 32% of rolls (the rug starves). Now the game is 24 rolls total, one card leaves per roll (a correct None! takes a consolation card), so the rug ends at 30 cards and None! is 24 to 26% of rolls.

  • tags approved; K11 and K12 mood tags moved; re-ran. The full rug now has 4 empty Place x Mood pairs instead of 5 (K11 moved to Body and Senses, K12 to Think and Notice), so None! falls about 2 points (24 to 26% of rolls in a 24 roll game, 39% at 30 cards). Shares and the catch-up rules are unchanged within noise (1500 games per table). Tags are now approved.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Jungle Totem (reflex grab on matching top cards): this one uses the whole deck face up and picture tags, not a match between two top cards

  • Charades Camp (acting the expression): this one reads the expression instead of acting it

Ratings

From memory, about like Snap or Dobble: two minute teach, one idea, no hidden information.

Start 10, minus one for reading two key cards on every roll, minus one for touch disputes on a crowded rug. Teach about two minutes, setup under a minute, no waiting, works from 2 to 8.

Shouting, diving hands and the None! call make a loud party game; a grown-up can play with a five year old fairly. Weakest part: the rug starves in the last third (None! reaches 39%) and the whole game depends on place and mood tags that a table may still argue about.

Bond Slap

Nine cards on the camp table: the first hand down on a pair that fits takes the pair.

Inspired by Snap-style table slapping and Ghost Blitz style grabbing; the None! call is original (from memory)

KidsFamilyEasyComplexity 1.1 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FL-02
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
None
Pawns
Up to 3 pawns as deal markers

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Tap two face-up cards that make 9 and share what the level asks for, before anyone else; if you see no such pair, shout None!.

What you need

All 54 cardsNine face up in a three by three grid, the rest a face-down stack. Fronts only.
3 pawnsCount deals won. The winner of a deal takes one.

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Put cards face up in two rows: three per row at level one (six cards), four per row at levels two and three (eight cards). Everyone must be able to reach every card.

  • Put the rest face down in a stack beside the grid. Put the pawns beside the stack.

  • Each player picks a level (see Levels). In a family with mixed ages, everyone picks their own level.

  • Each player has an empty pile in front of them. Cards you win go there, face down.

How to play

  1. There are no turns. Everyone looks at the grid at the same time. A pair is good for you if it fits your level: level one is two cards that make 9; level two is two cards that make 9 and share a colour; level three is a bond, or three cards, that share one colour and add up to exactly 9.

  2. The first player to tap a good pair with a finger on each card (or a hand on both) says the numbers aloud and takes the cards into their pile.

  3. Fill each gap with the top card of the stack, in the same place.

  4. If you think there is no good pair for you, shout None!. Everyone checks. If you are right, take the top card of the stack without looking at it into your pile. Then the two cards in the left column go in the discard and two new cards from the stack fill the column.

  5. If you shout None! and a good pair is there, put one card from your pile in the discard. The round goes on.

  6. If you tap cards that are not good, put one card from your pile in the discard. The cards stay where they are. If your pile is empty, nothing happens.

  7. Two hands tap at the same moment: the player with fewer cards in their pile wins it. If equal, the younger player wins.

  8. A deal ends when the stack has three cards or fewer. Count the piles. The biggest pile takes a pawn. Shuffle all 54 cards and start the next deal.

How it ends

First player with two pawns wins (so a match is two or three deals). If two players tie for the biggest pile, both take a pawn. If everyone has the same number of pawns after three deals, play one more deal. At level one, play one deal only and the biggest pile wins.

Words in this game

  • bond two cards whose numbers add up to 9: 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5. A 9 makes a bond only with another 9.
  • grid the face-up cards in two rows (six at level one, eight at levels two and three).
  • good pair cards you may take at your level.
  • None! the call that means there is no good pair for you on the grid.

Common questions

  • Can I take a pair and a bigger group? No. At levels one and two you take exactly two cards. At level three you take a bond, or three cards that add to exactly 9, and all of them share one colour.

  • How do 9s work? A 9 makes a bond only with another 9 (there are six 9s). Two 9s at level two must also share a colour. A 9 never goes in a group of three.

  • I shouted None! but a younger player found a pair at their lower level. None! is about your own level. If there is no good pair for you, you are right. The younger player may still take their pair, so whoever acts first wins that round.

  • What if I am slow and the table changes? The first completed tap wins. Changes to the grid happen only after someone takes cards or a None! is confirmed.

  • Two grown-ups and a five-year-old are playing. It is not fair. Use the mixed age rules in Levels: everyone picks their own level, grown-ups say the numbers aloud before touching, and whoever won the last round sits out the next one when three or more play.

  • What if the stack runs out in the middle of a refill? The deal is over as soon as the stack has four cards or fewer, so this does not happen.

  • What if the stack runs out in the middle of a refill? The deal is over as soon as the stack has three cards or fewer, so this does not happen.

Tips

  • Find a number's partner first, then check the colour. Look for 1 with 8, 2 with 7, 3 with 6, 4 with 5 and 9 with 9.

  • Scan the grid in order, left to right, so you do not keep re-reading the same cards. The only skill is not missing a pair.

  • Do not shout None! early. A wrong None! costs a card, and a grid has at least one good pair 83% to 92% of the time, so shout only after a full scan.

  • With mixed ages, let each player choose their own level and let grown-ups say the numbers aloud before touching. In the simulation a fast player won every deal until the sit-out and say-it-aloud rules were added.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1 with six cards and one deal. Let them point and say 'one and eight' before tapping, and lose a few pairs on purpose rather than winning every deal.

Worked example

Level two, three players (A, B and C), eight cards in two rows of four. Good pairs make 9 and share a colour.

  1. Top row Arvind (1), Naresh (6), Ajay (2), Gowri (9); bottom row Bharati (5), Ammlu (2), Nysha (8), Smaya (1). Two good pairs: Arvind (1; Red+Orange) with Nysha (8; Red+Purple) (1 and 8, both Red) and Smaya (1; Orange+Purple) with Nysha (8; Red+Purple) (both Purple). Player B taps Arvind (1) and Nysha (8) first and takes them. Pinku (2) and Adheesh (9) fill the gaps.

  2. Now the top row is Pinku (2), Naresh (6), Ajay (2), Gowri (9) and the bottom row Bharati (5), Ammlu (2), Adheesh (9), Smaya (1). The only bond that looks possible is Gowri (9; Red+Yellow) with Adheesh (9; Orange+Blue), two 9s, but they share no colour. 2s need 7s, 5 needs a 4, 6 needs a 3, 1 needs an 8: none are there. Player C shouts None! and is right. C takes the top stack card unseen. The left column (Pinku (2), Bharati (5)) is discarded and replaced by Dhruv (3) and Anayka (8).

  3. Top row Dhruv (3), Naresh (6), Ajay (2), Gowri (9); bottom row Anayka (8), Ammlu (2), Adheesh (9), Smaya (1). Two good pairs: Dhruv (3; Orange+Yellow) with Naresh (6; Red+Orange) (3 and 6, both Orange) and Anayka (8; Orange+Blue) with Smaya (1; Orange+Purple) (8 and 1, both Orange). Player A taps Dhruv (3) and Naresh (6) and takes them. Rihansh (9) and Arvind (8) fill the gaps.

  4. Top row Rihansh (9), Arvind (8), Ajay (2), Gowri (9); bottom row Anayka (8), Ammlu (2), Adheesh (9), Smaya (1). Now Rihansh (9; Orange+Green) with Adheesh (9; Orange+Blue) is a good pair: two 9s that both have Orange. Player B taps Anayka (8) and Smaya (1) first (8 and 1, Orange) and takes them. Nysha (1) and Bn Sharada (7) fill the gaps.

  5. Top row Rihansh (9), Arvind (8), Ajay (2), Gowri (9); bottom row Nysha (1), Ammlu (2), Adheesh (9), Bn Sharada (7). Four good pairs: Rihansh (9) with Adheesh (9) (9 and 9, Orange), Arvind (8; Yellow+Green) with Nysha (1; Yellow+Green) (8 and 1, Yellow and Green), Ajay (2; Red+Purple) with Bn Sharada (7; Green+Purple) (2 and 7, Purple) and Ammlu (2; Orange+Green) with Bn Sharada (7; Green+Purple) (2 and 7, Green). Player A, in a hurry, taps Gowri (9; Red+Yellow) and Rihansh (9; Orange+Green): two 9s but no shared colour. That is a wrong tap, so A puts one card from their pile in the discard. Player C then takes Rihansh (9) and Adheesh (9).

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5: six cards in the grid, any two that make 9 (a grown-up keeps the bond strip 1 8, 2 7, 3 6, 4 5, 9 9 on the reference card). Play one deal. Spoken help allowed.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7: eight cards, two cards that make 9 and share a colour. Play to two pawns.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: eight cards, a bond or three cards that add to exactly 9, all sharing one colour. Play to two pawns.

Solo

Lay out the grid for your level and play one deal alone with no time pressure. Take a good pair whenever you find one and call None! when you are sure there is none (a wrong None! costs you one card). Your score is the cards in your pile at the end. Bronze, Silver, Gold: level one 33, 38, 42; level two 31, 36, 40; level three 33, 38, 42 (the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of simulated solo deals). The only skill is not missing a pair, so this is practice, not a puzzle.

Two players

Works well at two players. A fast player beats a slow one every time, so use the say-it-aloud rule for different ages (the sit-out rule applies only at three or more players).

Maths and skills in this game

Number bonds to 9 at speed (level one), colour matching alongside number (two), adding two or three numbers to a target (three), scanning a grid systematically.

Tuning log

  • round 1 (before the 9+9 fix): nine-card grid gave None! 13% (L1), 21% (L2), 20% (L3). With 9 and 9 now a bond, the same grid gives 3.7%, 10.9%, 9.4%: too few None! calls.

  • round 2: tried smaller spreads with the fixed bond. Six cards: L1 20 to 23%, L2 39 to 42%. Seven cards: L1 11 to 13%, L2 26 to 32%. Eight cards: L1 6 to 7%, L2 18 to 22%, L3 15 to 17%. Survivors that did not pair stay on the table, so rates in play are higher than for a fresh spread.

  • round 3: chose a spread size per level (six cards at L1, eight at L2 and L3) and a correct None! swaps the left column of two cards. None! is now 22% (L1), 22% (L2), 18% (L3). Level three is a bond or three cards adding to 9, all sharing one colour. Mixed ages: a 3.6 times speed gap still gives the fast player 100%; sit-out plus say-it-aloud gives 47/53/0 for adult, eight-year-old, five-year-old.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Jungle Totem: also a grab on a match, but this one searches nine cards for a bond and has a None! call

  • Camp Raid: also uses a bond to snatch cards, but that is from a stash, this is from a shared grid

  • Nine Hunt: bonds to 9 again, but asked for in turns, not in a race

10 minus 1 for the left-column swap on a correct None!, minus 1 because mixed ages need house rules; teach time under 3 min, setup under 30 s, no stalls.

Chain Rush

Link the animals and the numbers into one long chain before the next camp does.

Inspired by Hand-building races like Rummikub runs and Dominoes chains, with a pass phase like Sushi Go (from memory)

RecommendedFamilyEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
FL-03
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
5+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone holds nine cards, passes one left, then races to lay a chain where each neighbour is on the same team or the two numbers make a bond.

What you need

All 54 cardsNine per player (six at level one). At five players or fewer the spare cards are not used, except in solo.
Paper and pencilOne score line per player for the match.

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards and deal nine to each player (six each at level one). Any left over form a face-down stack and are not used in a group game.

  • Everyone looks at their own cards. Nobody shows their front.

  • Write the players' names on the paper for the score.

How to play

  1. Pass: everyone chooses one card and puts it face down in front of the player on their left. At the same moment each of you picks up the card from the player on your right. With two players you swap one card each.

  2. Race: everyone lays cards face up in a row in front of them, all at once. Each card must link to the card beside it. Two cards link if they are on the same team, or if their numbers make a bond (1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5, 9 and 9).

  3. The first player to lay a chain of five (level one: three; level three: six) shouts Chain!. Everyone else stops talking and keeps laying while the table counts slowly to five aloud (level three: to three).

  4. Check the caller's chain. If a link is wrong, the caller scores 0 this round and is out for the round. The count of five then starts again for everyone else.

  5. Score: the caller scores the chain length plus 2. Everyone else scores the number of cards in the longest unbroken linked row they have laid when the count ends.

  6. Stuck: any player may say Stuck! Count slowly to ten. If nobody says Chain!, the round ends and everyone scores the length of their longest laid row.

  7. Collect all the cards, shuffle, deal again and play the next round.

How it ends

Play five rounds (level one: three). Add up the scores. Highest total wins. Tie: the player with the most Chain! calls wins; if still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • link two cards that can sit side by side: same team, or numbers adding to 9. Two 9s also link, because 9 and 9 is a bond in this deck.
  • chain a row of cards where every neighbour pair is linked.
  • pass the first step: one card face down to the player on your left.

Common questions

  • Can I rearrange my row? Yes, at any time before Chain! is shouted. Once someone shouts, the row you have on the table is the row that counts.

  • Can I use the same card twice? No. A chain uses each card once.

  • What if two players shout Chain! together? Both check. Both score the length plus 2 if both chains are right.

  • Do the extra cards in my hand count? No. Only the linked row you have laid counts. Cards in your hand are ignored.

  • Can I look at the card I am passing before I choose? Yes, you hold all your cards and may look at them. You may not look at the card you receive until the pass is finished.

  • How do 9s link? A 9 links to another 9 (a bond) or to any card on the same team. A pair that is both the same team and a bond is just a link. Nothing extra is scored.

  • Should the caller be allowed to rearrange after shouting? No. The row on the table when Chain! is shouted is the row that is checked.

Tips

  • Pass the card that links to the fewest others. Smart passing lifted the chance of reaching five from 70% to 85% and won 42% of matches against three random passers (25% is even).

  • Group by team first, then look for bonds. Teams link whole runs at once, and a 9 only links to another 9 or by team.

  • Do not shout Chain! on a doubtful link. A wrong chain scores 0 and puts you out of the round, while a right one scores the length plus 2.

  • Keep laying while the count runs. Everyone else scores their longest linked row when the count ends, so a four-card row is worth having.

  • With a 5-year-old, play L1: six cards and a chain of three. Let them sort their cards by animal first, and say 'Stuck!' for them if both of you run out of links.

Worked example

Level two, three players (A, B and C), chain of five. Player A holds nine cards.

  1. Player A's hand: Sharada (6), Nakul (5), Anayka (1), Arvind (1), Gowri (9), Dharsh (2), Adheesh (9), Anayka (8), Dhruv (3). A's best chain is only four.

  2. A passes Nakul (5; Tigers) to B; dropping it costs A nothing from the best chain. A receives Dharsh (7; Elephants) from C.

  3. A lays: Anayka (1; Elephants), Dharsh (2; Elephants), Dharsh (7; Elephants), Anayka (8; Elephants), Arvind (1; Monkeys). Links: 1 and 2 same team, 2 and 7 same team and make 9, 7 and 8 same team, 8 and 1 make 9.

  4. A shouts Chain!. B has laid Guhan (6; Elephants), Archana (5; Elephants), Archana (4; Elephants) and Nakul (5; Tigers). During the count of five B lays Kanasu (6; Tigers); the row is five and every link is right. C has laid Gopi (4; Peacocks), Gopi (5; Peacocks), Bharati (4; Cobras) and Bharati (5; Cobras).

  5. Scores for the round: A scores 5 plus 2, which is 7. B scores 5. C scores 4. B's chain used the Nakul (5) that A passed.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5: six cards each, chain of three, three rounds. Linked pairs are shown on the reference card with pictures (same animal, or two numbers that fill the 9 strip). A grown-up may help.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7: nine cards, chain of five, five rounds.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: nine cards, chain of six, count of three, five rounds.

Solo

Deal nine cards. Turn the top card of the spare stack face up. You may swap it for one card in your hand, once per deal. Lay your longest chain. Play five deals and add up the chain lengths. Bronze 28, Silver 32, Gold 36 (perfect play with the swap averages 32.3, without the swap 27.8).

Two players

Works with two players: the pass is a swap, about 2% of rounds are stuck (use the Stuck! rule), and the match takes about the same time.

Maths and skills in this game

Number bonds to 9 used as a link, team identification, planning a path through a set (graph thinking) and choosing what to give away.

Not simulated. Real laying speed (the bot counts edge looks at one per second), mistakes in checking links, the fun of the pass, how children read teams on cards, and how a human searches (people group by team first, which is faster than the bot).

Re-run after the bond fix; no rule had to change. Pawn per round scoring tied too often; points with a catch-up count fixed it. The pass is the only decision beyond speed. Speed still matters (59% for the fastest of four). Mixed ages at one table share one level; giving children a smaller chain target than grown-ups was not tested.

Tuning log

  • round 1: nine cards each, link = same team or make 9, race to a chain of five, one pawn per round. Reach-five is 70% per player, 10% of two-player rounds were stuck, and with five rounds the match was tied 35% of the time. Fix: points, not pawns.

  • round 2: added a pass (everyone passes one card left at the same time) so there is a decision beyond speed: a smart passer lifts reach-five from 70% to 85% and cuts two-player stuck rounds from 9.7% to 2.1%. Scoring changed to: caller scores chain length plus 2, everyone else scores the longest chain they have laid when a slow count of five ends. Ties fell from 35% to 11%.

  • round 3: re-run after the fix that makes 9 and 9 a bond (more links: mean longest chain 5.54, was 5.23). Targets still fit, so no rule changed: level two chain of five reaches 85% after the pass, level three chain of six 66% (was 57%), level one six cards and three 87%. Leader after three of five rounds wins 65%, which is just what five independent deals give (no carry-over). The fastest of four wins 59% with the count of five (the earlier 68% to 58% effect of the count was not re-measured).

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Llama Trek: also a race but a shedding game; this is path building

  • Nine Hunt: bonds again, but here bonds are just one of two kinds of link

  • Quiet Climb: ordering race, but silent and cooperative

Ratings

Four rules (pass, link, race, score); a three to four minute teach (from memory against Sushi Go 1.2 and Lost Cities 1.6).

10 minus 1 for teach time over three minutes, minus 1 for pencil score keeping, minus 1 because mixed ages need the same level and speed gaps show.

The pass gives a real choice, finding a chain is a satisfying small puzzle, and everyone is busy all the time. Weakest part: quick thinkers still win most rounds and the five-count can feel anticlimactic.

Storm Warning

The storm front is closing. Turn and swap your camp until the flags link up, and shout before anyone else.

Inspired by Real-time puzzle racers such as Rush Hour races and Dobble, and the Map the Island patch idea in this box (from memory)

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FL-04
Players
2 to 6

about 10 min
Age
5+
Dice
2 dice (one for the suit, one for the target; the suit die is read on the Suit key)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone rebuilds their own 3 by 3 block of card backs at once, and the first to link enough pictures of the rolled suit into one patch shouts Storm.

What you need

54 cards (nine per player)Each player lays nine cards backs up in a 3 by 3 block. With fewer than six players the spare cards stay in the box.
2 diceOne die names the suit (find it on the Suit key). The other adds to your target.
Suit keyShows the picture for each suit number.
Pencil and paperFor the score.

Set up

  • Deal nine cards face down to each player. Do not look at the fronts. Put spare cards back in the box.

  • Each player has a pile of nine cards and some table space.

  • Pick someone to be the first roller. The roller changes every round, clockwise.

How to play

  1. Lay out. Everyone shuffles their nine cards, then lays them backs up in three rows of three, edge to edge, with every card long side up and down. Lay each card the way it lands. The block is six pictures wide and nine pictures tall.

  2. Roll. The roller rolls both dice. The first die is the suit number. The second die adds to your target: 1 or 2 adds one, 3 or 4 adds two, 5 or 6 adds three.

  3. Count. Each card shows a suit twice or not at all. Count your cards that show the rolled suit. Call this your count. Your target is your count plus the add. With two players, take one off the target. If your target is more than twice your count, you cannot score this round.

  4. Go. Everyone moves at once. A move is turning one card half way round, or swapping two cards. Make as many moves as you like.

  5. A patch is pictures of the rolled suit that touch side to side or top to bottom. Pictures on different cards touch if they sit next to each other across the card edge. Corners do not count.

  6. Shout Storm when one patch in your block holds your target number of pictures or more. Everyone stops moving. Point at each picture in your patch and count out loud. The others check.

  7. A right shout wins the round: score one point. A wrong shout: lose one point and sit out the rest of the round.

  8. If you think nobody can finish, say Calm. When everyone still in the round has said Calm, the round is void. Nobody scores.

How it ends

Play ten rounds. The highest score wins. If you are tied, the tied players share the win, or play one more round to settle it.

Words in this game

  • Block Your nine cards laid in three rows of three. Six pictures wide, nine pictures tall.
  • Picture One of the six small suit pictures on the back of a card.
  • Patch Pictures of the rolled suit that touch side to side or top to bottom, also across card edges.
  • Count How many of your nine cards show the rolled suit.
  • Target The patch size you must reach: your count plus the add from the second die.
  • Storm What you shout when your patch reaches your target.
  • Calm What you say when you think nobody can finish.

Common questions

  • Do pictures touching at a corner count? No. Only side to side or top to bottom.

  • Can I look at the fronts? The fronts never matter. Keep your cards backs up all game.

  • My target is bigger than I can ever reach. What now? If the target is more than twice your count, you cannot score this round. Watch the others and be the checker.

  • Can two people shout together? Whoever the group heard first goes first. If that shout is wrong, the next shouter is checked.

  • Do I have to leave my block in the same place for the next round? No. Everyone shuffles and lays out again each round.

  • Is turning a card the same as flipping it over? No. Turning is half way round on the table. The back always stays up.

  • What if the patch is bigger than my target? That is fine. Your target is the smallest patch you need.

Tips

  • Count first. Your target is your count plus the add, so count how many of your nine cards show the rolled suit before you touch anything.

  • If the target is more than twice your count, stop and be the checker. You cannot score that round.

  • Look for the two cards that nearly touch. The median needs only 2 moves from a random layout, and 96% of solvable cases need 3 moves or fewer.

  • Turn a card half way round before you swap. A turn changes which pictures sit on the edge, and it is often cheaper than moving two cards.

  • Do not shout early. A wrong shout loses a point and sits you out, while a right one scores one. At two players take one off the target, which is built in. For a 5-year-old play L1 where the target is just the count.

Worked example

Level 2, four players. You are one of them. Your nine cards are laid out and the roller rolls suit 2 on the first die and 2 on the second die.

  1. Second die 2 adds one. You count the cards that show suit 2: Adheesh (9), Rihansh (9), Arvind (1), Smaya (1) and Avika (4). Your count is five, so your target is six.

  2. Your block, row by row: Adheesh (9), Rihansh (9), Gopi (5) then Arvind (1), Bharati (5), Smaya (1) then Sharada (6), Idhayan (1), Avika (4). Adheesh (9), Arvind (1), Bharati (5), Smaya (1) and Avika (4) lie turned round. Your biggest patch is two pictures. You need six.

  3. Move one: swap Adheesh (9) with Bharati (5). Your biggest patch is now five.

  4. Move two: swap Gopi (5) with Avika (4). Your biggest patch is now six. That is your target.

  5. You shout Storm, point at the six pictures and count them out loud. The others check along the grid. You score one point.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5: one die only, for the suit. Your target is your count, with nothing added. Nobody loses a point for a wrong shout. Play six rounds, and a grown-up helps count.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7: the rules as written, with the second die adding to the target.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: the target is your count plus the add plus one. Play with five or six players. A wrong shout costs two points.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is a race. For one player, play Quilt Solo, the quiet puzzle version of the same block.

Two players

Take one off the target. Without that, 41 percent of two-player rounds had nobody who could finish with a simple search.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting to nine, adding a small number, spotting connected pictures, turning shapes in your head, and checking a friend's claim by counting out loud.

Not simulated. Reflex speed and the human search itself. Greedy and exact search bracket what a person does; real players plan better than the greedy bot and worse than the exact search. Fun was not measured. Speed races reward quick pattern spotters, which a simulator cannot rate.

Round start is a freshly shuffled layout, as in the rules. The greedy bot numbers are an upper bound on difficulty, so some rounds will void. The Calm rule exists for that. Three players use the standard target: exact search voids 10 percent of rounds, the greedy bot 29 percent. Taking one off at three players cut voids to 2 and 11 percent but made small hands win 36 percent against 17 percent for large hands, so it was not adopted.

Tuning log

  • round 1: fixed target (second die plus two cells). Per-player solvable within four moves 67 percent, which is on brief, but the win share by hand is lopsided: a hand with only two cards of the suit wins 2 percent of rounds, a hand with eight wins 55 percent (4 players, fair share 25). Deal luck decides the game. Rejected.

  • round 2: cap the target by the hand (the smaller of the fixed target and twice your count minus one). The win share by hand becomes U shaped: two cards 38 percent, four cards 15.5 percent, eight cards 53 percent. Rejected.

  • round 3: make the target relative to your own hand: target = your count of cards showing the suit plus (die 1 or 2: one, 3 or 4: two, 5 or 6: three). Win share by hand is flat: two cards 22, four 25, six 27, eight 19 percent. Per-player solvable within four moves 57 percent; at least one solver in 94 percent of rounds at four players. Kept. A greedy-bot check showed 2 players had too many voided rounds (41 percent with no greedy solver) so the 2-player rule takes one off the target (19 percent). Layout is re-shuffled every round so the sim start matches play.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Map the Island: also builds a patch from backs, but by laying overlapping cards, not by re-arranging a fixed block against a roll

  • Pack the Rucksack: also calls a symbol over nine cards, but with flips and memory, not a patch

Ratings

Seven short rules, one count and one addition per round, teach time about three minutes (from memory anchors: Dobble ~1.1, Uno ~1.1).

Start at 10. Teach time a little over three minutes -1. The Suit key must be read every round -1. Count and add every round is light bookkeeping -1. Setup under a minute and no downtime.

Tension and shouting are real and the hand-strength luck is flattened, but searching alone is quiet, one slow solver makes rounds drag, and players who count slowly start behind. Weakest part: some rounds void at two or three players.

Peel Race

Everyone builds their own crossword camp at once, and every time someone finishes, the whole camp gets one more tent to fit in.

Inspired by Bananagrams (build a private crossword, call Peel, everyone draws), from memory

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FL-05
Players
2 to 4
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
9+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone races to arrange all their cards into one valid crossword; the first to finish says Peel and everyone draws one more card, until the pile is nearly gone.

What you need

All 54 cardsOnly the letter on the front is used. Cards are laid face up on the table in each player's grid.
Reference cardThe rules in short and the list of names that count as words.
A clear table area for each playerAbout the size of a placemat. No pencil or paper needed.

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player 7 cards face up in front of them (6 cards each at four players). Leave the cards in a loose heap, not yet in a grid.

  • Count out the pile and put it face down in the middle: 20 cards at two players, 21 at three, 24 at four. Put any other cards back in the box. They are not used.

  • Agree what counts as a word: any ordinary word you would find in a children's dictionary, plurals allowed. The names on the reference card also count. The Q card spells QU and fills one square.

  • Everyone says Go together.

How to play

  1. All players play at the same time. Lay your cards in your own grid: words read left to right and top to bottom. Every word needs three or more cards. Every card is part of at least one word, the whole grid is joined up, and words may cross by sharing a card. Cards that touch side by side must form a word.

  2. The first player whose grid uses every card says Peel. Everyone, including that player, takes one card from the pile and fits it in. Keep going.

  3. Stuck? Dump. Put one card into the pile, shuffle the pile, then take two cards from it. You may dump only while the pile has at least two more cards than there are players. You may rearrange your whole grid at any time.

  4. When another player says Peel, you do not have to be finished. Take your card and keep working.

  5. If a word or the grid is wrong when someone says Peel, that player must fix it while everyone else keeps building. Nobody takes a card until the grid is right.

  6. Name bonus: if your finished grid contains a name from the reference card when you say Peel, you do not take a card this time.

How it ends

When someone says Peel and the pile has fewer cards than there are players, nobody takes a card. If that player's grid is right, they win the race and the game. If the grid is wrong, they fix it while everyone else keeps going. Ties cannot happen: someone finishes first. For a longer match, play three races and count wins.

Words in this game

  • Peel Said by the first player whose grid uses all their cards. Everyone then takes one card.
  • Dump Swap one card you cannot use for two cards from the pile.
  • Grid Your own crossword: all your cards laid out so that every row and column of touching cards is a word.

Common questions

  • May two words run side by side? No, unless every pair of touching cards also makes a word. Keep it simple: leave a gap.

  • May I use a word that is not in a children's dictionary? Only if the other players agree. A name from the reference card always counts.

  • May I look at other players' grids? Yes, they are face up. Peeking costs time.

  • I have no vowels. What now? Dump a hard card as soon as you see it. Q, X, Z and J are the usual trouble, and Q needs a U next to it.

  • Can I dump after a Peel has been called? Yes, at any time while the pile has at least two more cards than there are players.

  • What if a player is far behind? A slow player still takes a card at every Peel and can dump. A late card often fits easily, so a slow start is not the end.

Tips

  • Dump Q, X, Z and J early. A hard card ruins a grid, and dumping gives you two cards back, and the simulated games had about one dump per player.

  • Build a tree-shaped crossword, each new word crossing exactly one other. That is the easiest shape to rearrange when a new card arrives.

  • Start by finding a long word. A 7-card start hand is buildable only 40 to 77% of the time depending on vocabulary, so if you cannot build it, rearrange it, or dump.

  • Keep building when someone else says Peel. You still take your card and a late card often fits easily, so a slow start is not the end.

  • Two players is the weakest count (8% of stages have nobody able to finish), so use three or four. Use L1 (five cards, pile of twelve) with younger spellers, and let a grown-up call the word list.

Worked example

Two players, A and B. A holds Nysha [A], Anayka [X], Rihansh [Q], Archana [K], Bn Sharada [T], Idhayan [Y], Smaya [O]. B holds Gopi [P], Naresh [A], Ajay [E], Adhiraa [H], Amay [E], Smaya [L], Pinku [B]. The pile has 20 cards. The cards drawn below come from a real run of the engine with the 2,700-word kids dictionary.

  1. Go! B quickly sees HELP and ABLE: HELP down, ABLE across, sharing the L. B uses Gopi [P], Naresh [A], Ajay [E], Adhiraa [H], Amay [E], Smaya [L] and Pinku [B]. A has Q, X and K and cannot build a grid, so A dumps the Q: Rihansh [Q] goes into the pile, A shuffles the pile and takes Adheesh [R] and Anayka [H].

  2. B says Peel. Both players take one card: A takes Nysha [E], B takes Guhan [J].

  3. A now holds 9 cards and builds EXTRA across with HEY and OAK down, crossing at the E and the A. B holds a J (Guhan [J]) and cannot fit it. B dumps it, shuffles the pile and takes Dharsh [E] and Dhruv [I].

  4. A says Peel first. Both take a card: A takes Shreya [D], B takes Arvind [S]. The pile has 14 cards left.

  5. B rebuilds with the new cards: BASE down, HELPS across (sharing the S), LIE down. B says Peel, and both take another card, Gowri [Z] and Amay [O]. The game continues until the pile has fewer cards than players.

Level ladder

L1 · first game

First game (untested variant): deal 5 cards, pile of 12, and dump as often as you like. Use only three-card words. A grown-up helper may spell.

L2 · standard

Standard: as written.

L3 · expert

Expert (untested variant): no names count as words and there is no name bonus.

Solo

Deal yourself 7 cards and a pile of 8. Build, then Peel yourself: take one card and fit it in, until the pile is empty. If you ever cannot build, dump. Count your dumps. Gold: no dump. Silver: one dump. Bronze: two dumps. About 83 percent of bot games finish; if you cannot finish, start again.

Two players

Works as written with a pile of 20: about ten Peels. This is the weakest count: 8% of stages have nobody able to finish, and everyone dumps.

Not simulated. Human speed (who finishes first is the whole race), how people physically rearrange cards, whether the strict adjacency rule trips people up, the name bonus, disputes over words, and fun. The builder is conservative: it builds only tree-shaped crosswords where each new word crosses exactly one existing card and nothing touches sideways, so people can build more than the sim shows. The race winner in the sim is the player with the least search effort times a random factor, which stands in for speed and is not a human measure.

The builder tries every dictionary word that the tile set can spell, then every word that crosses one tile already placed, with a node cap of 1,500 to 3,000. Players who cannot build dump one hard card (rarest letter first) while the first finisher calls Peel; if nobody can build, everyone dumps. Dictionaries are the supplied lists cleaned of acronyms and names; real play lies between the 2,700 and 10,000 word figures. The 29,600-word dictionary is an upper bound and contains obscure words. Weakest part: with a narrow vocabulary the game stalls, so it needs players who know everyday words.

Tuning log

  • round 1: first design with 7-card start hands (6 at four players), a pile of 20/21/24 cards, dump = return one card to the BOTTOM of the pile and take two. Sim showed the last seat winning only 26% of 3-player games (first seat 37%). Cause: dumped hard cards sat at the bottom and were drawn last, in seat order. -> dumped card is shuffled into the pile. After the fix seats win 35/32/33% (3p, 450 games) and 27/22/26/26% (4p, 400 games).

  • round 2: hand size. At 3 players, 6 cards: start hand buildable 48%, 1.14 dumps per player, 0.17 stuck stages per game. 7 cards: 56%, 0.88, 0.07. 8 cards: 61%, 0.82, 0.33 and 1% of games not finished. 4 and 5 cards are poor starts (13% and 42% buildable) because 4 cards need one four-letter word. -> 7 cards (6 at four players, to keep the pile at 24).

  • round 3: pile size. A full 36-card pile would mean grids of 20+ cards. Solo with a 20-card pile (27-card grid) finished only 63% of games, with 8 cards 83%. -> pile 20/21/24 gives 5.6 to 9.6 Peels and grids of 12 to 17 cards. Also found: with only a 2,700-word vocabulary, stuck stages rise from 0.76 to 2.9 per 2-player game and 5% of games do not finish, so the 10,000-word everyday vocabulary matters.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Signal Fire (spell one real word with the beacon letter, race): this builds a whole crossword from all your cards and repeats after every Peel.

  • Wordwalk (word game, not re-read): assumed a different format.

Ratings

From memory, a little above Bananagrams: four rules (grid, Peel, dump, end), no hidden information, teach time about three minutes.

Teach time about 3 minutes, setup under one minute, no key card. Minus one for needing a big table area per player, minus one for word disputes, minus one for the 2-player game having stuck stages in 8% of rounds.

Real-time building with a shared groan at every Peel is a proven shape and the dump rule rescues bad hands. Weakest part: the winner is simply the fastest word-builder, so the game rewards vocabulary and speed over choices, and a child who knows fewer words can fall behind early.

Card changes requested: none

Target Chef

Four ingredient cards and one target card. Whoever first cooks the target out of the ingredients, using plus, minus and times, takes the round. And if you think the dish cannot be cooked, you can say so.

Inspired by Krypto and The 24 Card Game

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
FL-06
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Flip five cards: four ingredient numbers and one target. Use each ingredient at most once, combining them with add, subtract and multiply, to hit the target. First correct call scores. You may also call No way!

What you need

All 54 cardsnumbers are the ingredients, and at L3 the serial is the target
A way to count to 20aloud, or a sand timer, for No way! calls
Pencil and paperto keep score

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards and put them face down in the middle as the deck. Nobody holds a hand.

  • Choose a level (see Levels). Play to 8 points, or for a number of rounds you agree on before you start.

  • Decide who calls the cards each round. Nobody should look before the flip.

How to play

  1. Flip. Turn up 4 cards in a row as the ingredients and then 1 more card next to them as the target. At L3 the target is the serial (1 to 54) of the target card. At L2 it is the card's big number.

  2. Think. Everybody thinks silently. You may use any of the ingredient numbers, each at most once, joined with +, - (always the bigger minus the smaller) and x. You can combine in any order, one step at a time. Division is not allowed.

  3. Call. The first player to say Chef! must show the working. If it is right, they score 1 point, or 2 points if it uses all four ingredients. If it is wrong, they are out for the round and play goes on.

  4. No way! If you think no combination of the ingredients reaches the target, call No way!. Everybody counts slowly to 20. If someone shows a correct dish in that time, that player scores 2 and the caller loses a point (never below 0). If nobody does, the caller scores 1.

  5. Discard the five cards and flip five new ones. Reshuffle the discards when the deck runs out.

How it ends

The first player to reach 8 points wins. If two players reach 8 in the same round, the one with more 2-point rounds wins; still tied, play one more round.

Words in this game

  • Ingredient one of the four number cards in a row. Its big number is the number you use.
  • Target the number you are cooking. At L3 it is the serial of the fifth card; at L2 its big number.
  • Chef! the call to show a working that reaches the target.
  • No way! the call that says no combination works.

Common questions

  • Do I have to use all four cards? No. Any two, three or four cards will do. Using all four scores 2 points instead of 1.

  • Can I take away a bigger number from a smaller one? Yes, but you always subtract the smaller from the bigger, so every answer stays positive. 3 - 8 is treated as 8 - 3 = 5.

  • Can I divide? No. Only add, subtract and multiply.

  • Can I use a result more than once? No. Each ingredient is used once. A result may be used in the next step, once.

  • What if the caller says No way! and somebody finds a dish after the count? The count is what matters. A dish shown after the count does not change the score. That is why you should call No way! only when you have checked the big products.

Tips

  • Look at the target first. If it is near a product of two ingredients (for example 6 x 8 = 48), subtract or add the rest to move it to the target.

  • Big targets need multiplication, because adding four numbers of at most 9 each reaches 36 at most. At L3 check the big products first.

  • Check small solutions first. A three-card answer is quicker to find than an all-four answer, and the one-point lead is worth more than a risky two.

  • Check your answer once before you say Chef! A wrong call puts you out of the round and gives everybody else the time you spent.

  • Use No way! sparingly at L2: only about 6% of L2 deals have no answer. At L3 about 1 deal in 4 has none, so No way! is a real weapon there.

  • Practise the products of 6, 7, 8 and 9 until they come quickly: most answers at L3 use one of them.

Worked example

  1. Level 3. Flip four ingredients: Sharada (6), Amay (8), Ajay (2), Bn Sharada (7). The target card is Archana (4), whose serial is 34.

  2. P1 looks for a big product. 6 x 8 = 48. 48 is 14 more than 34, and 2 x 7 = 14. So (6 x 8) - (2 x 7) = 48 - 14 = 34, using all four ingredients. P1 shouts Chef! and shows it. Correct: 2 points.

  3. P0 had found a shorter one: (6 x 7) - 8 = 42 - 8 = 34, using three ingredients. But P1 called first, so P0 gets nothing this round. If P0 had called first, they would have scored 1 point.

  4. Next round: ingredients Avika (4), Dharsh (7), Ajay (7), Idhayan (8), target Ammlu (2) with serial 40. P2 thinks it cannot be done and calls No way! Everybody counts to 20. Nobody finds 40 (4 x 8 = 32 and 7 x 7 = 49 are both near, but 32 + 7 = 39 and 49 - 8 = 41 miss it). P2 scores 1 point.

  5. A wrong call: in the first round, a player who shouted Chef! with (6 x 7) - 7 = 35 would be out for that round, because it uses the 7 twice and also misses 34 by one.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 6. Flip five ingredients and one target; the target is the card's big number. Use two ingredients and one operation, + or -. A round is solvable about 77% of the time, so No way! is a real call.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Four ingredients, target is the card's big number, and you may use +, - and x with any number of ingredients. About 94% of deals can be solved.

L3 · age 8 and up

Four ingredients and the serial of the target card (1 to 54) as the target. About 76% of deals can be solved, and using all four scores 2.

Solo

Solo: flip ten deals at L2 or L3. For each, say aloud Chef! with your working, or No way!, and check with the full rules. Score 1 for each dish you can show (2 if it uses all four ingredients); skip a deal if you find nothing in one minute. A score of 12 or more in ten deals is a gold chef. (The medal line is a suggestion; solo is not tested.)

Two players

Works as written. Two players can also play each deal as a duel: both write the dish and compare.

Maths and skills in this game

Mental addition, subtraction and times tables up to 9 x 9, and planning backwards from a target. It also teaches that some questions have no answer, which is a real mathematical skill.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the ingredients, and the target at L1 and L2
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule the target at L3
NamesFlavour the children whose cards you are cooking with
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Solvability (chunk 2, 1,500 deals per target type): with a random target, using all four cards solves 64% of deals if the target is the serial (1 to 54), 81% if it is a card number and 80% if it is the sum of two extra cards. Using any of the cards, 76%, 95% and 93%. Adding only, with two cards, works just 10% to 35% of the time.

  • My re-check for this page (200,000 random deals, exact search over every combination with +, - as larger minus smaller, and x): L3 serial target, any cards 76.2%, all four 65.9%; L2 number target, any cards 94.0%, all four 80.7%. These agree with the chunk 2 figures.

  • So the No way! call is true about 24% of the time at L3 (100 - 76.2) and 6% at L2. At L1 (five ingredients, target a card number, any two ingredients with + or -) my check gives 76.8% solvable, 23% No way!.

  • The idea list suggested that at L1 the target should be the sum of two flipped cards 'so it always works'. My check shows that is not true: with four ingredients and + - x it is solvable 93% to 80% of the time, not 100%. So L1 here uses a plain number target and keeps No way! as a legal call.

  • Skill is solving, not luck: the deal is random and the fastest correct solver wins. No bot-versus-bot win rates were run for this game, because the contest is who finds a solution first.

  • Length is set by the players: at about 30 to 60 seconds a round, 8 points is 8 to 12 rounds, so 8 to 12 minutes. This is an estimate.

  • Subtraction as larger minus smaller keeps every intermediate result positive, so there are no negative numbers to explain to a child.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Speed of solving, and how often players wrongly call No way!, depend on the table.

  • Not tested: the 8-point scoring and the 2-point bonus; they are a first draft.

  • Not tested: L1 as written, or the solo medals.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TARGET CHEF. Flip 4 ingredient cards and 1 target card. L3 target = the target card's serial; L2 = its big number. Combine ingredients with + - x (bigger minus smaller), each at most once, in any order, to reach the target. First to say CHEF! with correct working scores 1 (2 if all four used). Wrong call: out for the round.

Back

NO WAY! Call it if no dish exists; count to 20. A solution found: finder scores 2, caller loses 1. None: caller scores 1. First to 8 wins. LEVELS. L1 five ingredients, two cards, + or - . L2 four ingredients, number target, + - x. L3 serial target. Solo: ten deals, 12 or more is gold (untested).

Sum Hunt

Everyone can see what you are carrying, but only you know what it is worth.

Inspired by Liar's Dice (from memory), with the Perudo-style raise and challenge loop

RecommendedFamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
PN-01
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
8+
Dice
None (L1 uses 1 die)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round, claim that the front numbers of all cards showing a chosen suit on their back add up to at least a total, then raise or call the previous claim a lie, and the loser gives up a card.

What you need

All 54 cardsEveryone's hands are dealt from them each round. You hold your cards with the backs facing out.
Suit keyStandard key card, so players can say suit numbers 1 to 6 and match them to the back icons.
One die (L1 only)Chooses the suit for the round.

Set up

  • Pick your starting hand size: 2 players hold five cards, 3 players four, 4 to 6 players three.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player a hand of that size. Look at your own fronts. Do not look at your own backs.

  • Hold your cards fanned with the backs facing out, so everyone else can see the backs and only you can see the fronts.

  • The youngest player makes the first claim.

How to play

  1. On your turn you either make a claim or, if there is already a claim, you may challenge it instead.

  2. A claim names one suit by its number (1 to 6) and a total, for example: suit 4, at least 30. It means: take every card in play (in all hands) that shows suit 4 anywhere on its back, add up the numbers on their fronts, and the result is at least 30.

  3. The first claim of a round can name any total. Each later claim must beat the one before it by at least three, for example from 30 up to 33 or more. The suit may change every time.

  4. Instead of raising, you may challenge: say Liar. Everyone turns their cards over and the real total for the claimed suit is added up.

  5. If the real total is at least the claimed total, the claim was true and the challenger loses. If it is lower, the claim was false and the player who made it loses.

  6. The loser permanently loses one card from their hand size. A player with no cards left is out.

  7. Collect and shuffle all cards. Deal the new hand sizes. The loser makes the first claim of the next round (if they are out, the next player in turn order does).

How it ends

The last player with cards left wins. Rounds cannot tie, because each round has exactly one loser. If you want a quicker game, stop when two players are left and the one with more cards wins; if they hold the same number, play one more round.

Words in this game

  • counting card A card with the claimed suit anywhere on its back. A back shows three suits, each twice, so a counting card counts once, not twice.
  • claim A suit number plus a total. It says the counting cards' front numbers add up to at least that total.
  • Liar The challenge call. It ends the round.
  • hand size How many cards you are dealt each round. It shrinks by one every time you lose.

Common questions

  • I cannot see the backs of my own cards. How do I know if they count? You do not. That is the game. You know your numbers, you can see everyone else's backs, and nobody may tell you about your own backs. Remember each of your own cards counts for a given suit about half the time.

  • Can I ask another player what their fronts are? You may ask, but they do not have to answer and may lie. Nobody may tell you what your own backs show.

  • A back shows suit 4 twice. Does the card count twice? No. It counts once, with its front number.

  • What if a claim is higher than anything possible? It is just a false claim. The next player may challenge it, and the claimant loses.

  • What if the real total equals the claim exactly? The claim was true (at least means equal or more). The challenger loses.

  • Do lost cards come back? No. Your hand size is lower for the rest of the game, but you are dealt a fresh random hand each round.

  • Players who are out have to wait. What can they do? They may sit beside a player, keep score of the claims, and take over a seat if there is a new game. Games at 2 to 4 players have little waiting.

Tips

  • Count the other players' backs first, then add your own numbers. A bot that used the visible backs beat one that ignored them 63 to 85% of the time.

  • Remember your own cards count for a given suit about half the time. Treat each of your own cards as half a card when you estimate.

  • Open low and raise by the minimum. A smart player raised about twice and then called Liar, so a high opening claim only helps the player after you.

  • Call Liar when the claim needs more than the visible cards can plausibly supply. Humans will call by feel, so the skill gap is smaller than the bots show.

  • Younger players: play L1 with cards 1 to 4 only, the die picking the suit, hand of 3 and raises of 1. Say each total aloud as you add the cards, to build mental addition.

Worked example

Three players, A, B and C, each hold four cards. A holds Sharada (6), Amyra (5), Nysha (1) and Gopi (4). B holds Adhiraa (6), Kanasu (3), Avika (5) and Nakul (4). C holds Ajay (2), Bn Sharada (2), Gopi (5) and Adhiraa (3). Each player sees only their own fronts. A makes the first claim.

  1. B and C look at A's backs. All four show suit 6 somewhere, so all four of A's cards count for suit 6.

  2. A opens with: suit 1, at least 29.

  3. B can see which of A's and C's cards show suit 4 and knows B's own numbers. B raises by at least three: suit 4, at least 32.

  4. C sees that seven of the eight cards in A's and B's hands show suit 6. C holds 2, 2, 5 and 3 in the hand. C raises: suit 6, at least 35.

  5. A is not sure and challenges C's claim: Liar. Everyone turns their cards over. Cards with suit 6 on the back: Sharada (6) 6, Amyra (5) 5, Nysha (1) 1, Gopi (4) 4 (A, 16); Adhiraa (6) 6, Kanasu (3) 3, Avika (5) 5 (B, 14); Bn Sharada (2) 2 (C, 2). The total is 32.

  6. 32 is less than 35, so C's claim was false. C loses a card and is dealt three cards next round. A and B still have four. All cards are shuffled and C makes the first claim.

Level ladder

L1 · ages 6 to 8 (kids game)

Ages 6 to 8. Use only the cards numbered 1 to 4 (24 cards). Roll the die at the start of each round: that suit is the only suit for the round. Everyone holds three cards. A new claim only has to beat the old one by one.

L2 · age 10 and up (standard)

Age 10 and up. The standard game above: any suit may be claimed, each raise beats the last by at least three.

L3 · expert

Expert. Each raise only has to beat the last by two, which allows many more small steps and finer reading.

Solo

Eight rounds. Each round deal yourself three cards (fronts to you) and six cards in a row face up showing their backs. Roll the die: that is the suit. Write down a total you think will be reached by the counting cards among your nine cards. Turn everything over. If the real total is at least your claim, score your claim. If not, score zero. Add up eight rounds. Best sensible play (a bot that picks the claim that maximises claim times chance) scores about 111 on average, with the middle half between 94 and 129. Bronze 95, Silver 110, Gold 130.

Two players

Each player holds five cards, so a game is about seven rounds. Both players see the other's backs, so the game is a duel of reads, and the opening claim is the main chance to bluff.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding several numbers in your head, estimating a total, thinking about what other people can and cannot see, probability sense (is this likely enough to call?).

SerialNot used

ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Reference card

Sum Hunt

Claim: cards with suit X on their back add to at least N. Raise by 3 or more, or call Liar. Loser loses a card.

  • Backs out. See others' backs, your own fronts.
  • A back counts once per suit.
  • Shuffle and redeal each round.
  • Last player with cards wins.
2 to 6 players10 to 20 min
L1

Cards 1 to 4 only. Die picks the suit. Hand 3. Raise by 1.

L2

Any suit. Raise by 3. Hands 5/4/3 for 2/3/4 to 6 players.

L3

Raise by 2.

Solo 8 rounds, claim a total for 9 cards, score it if true.

Count the other players' backs first, then add your own numbers.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Simulated Smart bot beats random 93 to 99 percent and a back-ignoring guesser 63 to 85 percent at 2 to 4 players; no stalls, seats within 3 points of even.

SettingResult
2 players, hand 5: smart vs random / vs guesser99% / 85% (even share 50%)

Seat advantage, all-smart, 1000 games, 4 players25.5 / 25.1 / 25.8 / 23.6%
Length, rounds (about 70 s each): 2p / 3p / 4p / 6p7.2 / 10.4 / 10.7 / 16.4 (about 8 / 12 / 12 / 19 min)

Kids L1 (cards 1 to 4, die suit, hand 3), 3 players: smart vs random / vs guesser96% / 44% (even 33%)
Solo, 8 rounds, best-play botmean 111, 25th to 75th percentile 94 to 129 (guesser mean 102)
Stalls (game not finished in 400 rounds)0 in all runs

Not simulated. Fun. Real players bluff, tell and read faces in ways the bots cannot. Humans cannot compute the odds, so they will challenge more by feel and the skill gap will be smaller than the bots show. The actual speed of adding twelve cards by hand is not measured. The expert L3 and the kids L1 settings were simulated only lightly.

The guesser bot ignores the visible backs (it treats every unseen card as half-counting). The smart bot uses the backs and its own numbers and gives a normal-approximation probability. A reading-of-claims bot added only 1 to 2 points, so the information that matters is on the table, in the backs. Claims above the real possible maximum are allowed (they are just false). No rule had to be changed after round 1.

Tuning log

  • round 1: raise step (how much a new claim must beat the old one) tested at 1,2,3,4,5 with 3 players. Smart vs greedy win rate was 60, 62, 70, 77, 70 percent; raises per round were 4.6, 3.3, 2.7, 2.1, 2.0. Chose 3 as the standard (real bluffing exchanges, still a clear skill gap). Step 2 kept as the L3 expert setting.

  • round 2: challenge threshold of the smart bot swept from 0.40 to 0.60. Calling less often (0.40) was best, so the smart bot gives claims the benefit of the doubt. Used 0.40 in all later runs. No rule change.

  • round 3: tested a bot that reads opponents' claims as hints about their hidden numbers (weights 0.2, 0.4, 0.7). It gained only 1 to 2 points of win rate over the plain smart bot, which is inside noise. Rule kept as is. The big edge comes from reading the visible backs, not from reading claims.

  • start hand sizes set so total cards in play stay near 10 to 12: 2p 5, 3p 4, 4 to 6p 3 each. Seat advantage checked with 1000 all-smart games at 3p and 4p: within 3 points of even.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Tall Tales (suit-count bluffing, Liar!): Tall Tales counts suit icons, which are all visible or all counted. Sum Hunt asks for a sum of hidden numbers, so every card has a public half (back) and a private half (front) and nobody can check a claim alone.

Ratings

From memory, close to Liar's Dice (about 1.2) plus the sum, a few extra rules about backs and fronts; teach time about 4 minutes.

Teach about 4 minutes (-1), setup under a minute, no key to read, no stalls, but eliminated players wait at 5 to 6 players (-1).

Split information (you see my backs, I see my fronts) gives a real read on every claim, and the reveal is a good moment. Weakest part: adding up to twenty or more numbers at the reveal, and waiting if you are out early.
