Fake Photographer

One of the photographers never saw the brief, but the album still has to look right.

Inspired by A Fake Artist Goes to New York (from memory); also close to Fox in the Camp in this rulebook

FamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
PN-02
Players
4 to 9 (one is the Keeper)
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
8+
Dice
3 dice (Team key, Colour key, suit number)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

The Keeper secretly rolls a theme; everyone adds cards that fit it, except the Fake, who must guess the theme from the cards and bluff.

What you need

Cardsup to 54, all shuffled together; each player has a hand and a row of played cards
3 dicethe Keeper rolls them out of sight for the theme
Team key and Colour keythe standard keys, read by the Keeper only
The reference cardfor the Keeper and anyone who forgets what fits

Set up

  • Choose the Keeper. The Keeper does not play cards, runs the round and knows the secret. Everyone else is a photographer.

  • Count photographers. Three to five photographers have one Fake. Six to eight photographers have two Fakes.

  • The Keeper shuffles all cards and deals one card face down to each photographer, glancing at each card's serial number while dealing. The photographer with the lowest serial is a Fake (the two lowest if there are two Fakes). The Keeper collects these cards and shuffles them back in.

  • The Keeper rolls the three dice hidden in a hand. Die one is read on the Team key, die two on the Colour key, die three is a suit number. This is the theme: one team, one colour and one suit number.

  • Everyone hums loudly with fingers in their ears. The Keeper taps one photographer at a time, who takes a hand away and listens. The Keeper whispers the theme to each honest photographer. The Keeper whispers only "you are the Fake" to a Fake. Nobody else hears.

  • Deal hands. Three photographers: three cards each. Four or five photographers: four cards each. Six to eight photographers: three cards each. Put the rest in a face-down draw pile. Give each photographer space for a row of face-up cards.

How to play

  1. Go clockwise from the Keeper's left. On your turn draw one card, then play one card from your hand face up at the end of your row. Your row is your part of the collage.

  2. An honest photographer plays a card that fits the theme if they have one. A card fits if it is the theme team, or has the theme colour, or has the theme suit number. If nothing fits, play any card.

  3. A Fake does not know the theme. Look at the cards already played, work out what they share, and play a card that you think fits.

  4. Do not speak about the theme or about what fits while cards are being played. You may groan.

  5. Play goes round the table twice (three photographers) or three times (four or more photographers). Then everyone has finished their row.

  6. Talk for one minute. Honest photographers can point at a card and say it is wrong or odd. The Fake can say anything.

  7. Count down from three and everyone points at one other photographer at once. Most pointed at is accused. Ties for the most: all tied photographers are accused. With two Fakes, the two photographers with most votes are accused; if two or more are tied for second place, none of those tied for second are accused.

How it ends

The Keeper reveals the theme and says which accused photographers are Fakes. Each accused Fake secretly tells the Keeper two of the three theme parts (for example Bears and Green). If both are in the theme, that Fake guessed right. The photographers win if at least one Fake was accused and no accused Fake guessed right. Otherwise the Fakes win. Nobody is out. Pass the Keeper job on and play again; count each person's wins after everyone has been Keeper once.

Words in this game

  • Keeper the player who rolls the theme, runs the round and does not play cards
  • Theme one team, one colour and one suit number, set by the three dice
  • Fits a card fits if it is the theme team, has the theme colour or has the theme suit number
  • Fake a photographer who was told nothing about the theme
  • Row the face-up cards you have played; all rows together are the collage

Common questions

  • I am honest and nothing in my hand fits. What do I do? Play any card. It will look odd, so be ready to say nothing. This is uncommon (honest players misfit about 0.1 times per game).

  • Can the Fake play a card that happens to fit? Yes, and that is the Fake's whole plan. A Fake that fits every time cannot be caught by the cards alone.

  • What if the Fake guesses right after being accused? The Fakes win. With two Fakes, the photographers lose if any accused Fake guesses right.

  • With two Fakes, can the Fakes tell each other? No. Fakes do not know each other. Another Fake's cards just look like honest cards to them.

  • Do the Keeper's cards count? The Keeper holds no cards and does not vote.

  • What if two photographers are tied for the most votes and one is a Fake? Both are accused. The photographers still need the Fake not to guess right.

  • The draw pile runs out. It cannot at eight photographers: 8 hands of 3 plus 24 draws uses 48 cards.

Tips

  • As an honest photographer, play a card that fits more than one theme part (the team, the colour or the suit number). It proves you know the theme without giving all of it away to the Fake.

  • As the Fake, copy what you see. Look at the first cards played, find what they share, and play a card you think fits. A Fake that fits every time cannot be caught from the cards alone.

  • If you are accused, name the two theme parts that the cards agree on. The simulation shows an accused Fake guessed right 7% of the time with three photographers but 25% with five, so the more cards on the table the more likely you are right.

  • Do not point at the player who fits least. Honest players misfit only about 0.07 to 0.17 times a game, but the Fake misfits 0.58 to 0.9, so look for the odd card, and then check it against the others.

  • Keeper: say as little as possible while whispering the theme, and keep the talk to one minute. Start new players on L1 (colour only). Play with 4 to 8, since nine photographers was dropped and five or more favours the Fake.

Worked example

Four photographers (P1 to P4) and a Keeper. The Keeper rolled Bears, Green (colour 4) and suit 3. P4 is the Fake. Each has a hand of four and draws one each turn.

  1. P1 plays Nysha (1; Yellow+Green). It has Green, so it fits.

  2. P2 plays Bn Sharada (2; Green+Blue). Green again, so it fits.

  3. P3 plays Naresh (3; Bears). It is a Bears card, so it fits. It also has Green and suit 1+6.

  4. P4, the Fake, sees Green, Green and Bears so far. P4 plays Adheesh (9; Bears), a Bears card. It fits, so P4 hides well.

  5. Second round. P1 plays Anayka (1; Green+Purple) and P2 plays Idhayan (8; Green+Purple). Both have Green and fit. P3 plays Ajay (7; Orange+Green), which also has Green.

  6. Last round. P4 has to guess again and plays Shreya (2; Blue+Purple). It is not Bears, has no Green and no suit 3, so it does not fit. The other photographers noticed.

  7. The vote: three photographers point at P4 and P4 points at P2. P4 is accused and secretly names two theme parts to the Keeper. The Keeper says at least one is wrong, so the photographers win.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5, with a grown-up as buddy: the Keeper rolls only the Colour die. A card fits if it has that colour. One Fake. Not simulated.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7: roll the Team die and the Colour die. A card fits if it has the team or the colour. Not simulated.

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up: the full theme of team, colour and suit number, with the rules as written.

Solo

No solo mode. A hidden role needs at least four people (a Keeper and three photographers).

Two players

Not playable. The minimum is three photographers plus a Keeper.

Maths and skills in this game

Matching on colour, team and suit number; hiding and spotting what you know; stating a guess under pressure.

Fake Photographer

The Keeper rolls a secret theme. Honest players add cards that fit it. The Fake guesses the theme from the cards and bluffs. Vote for the Fake. A caught Fake can still win by naming two theme parts.

  • Fits: theme team, or theme colour, or theme suit number
  • Dice: Team die, Colour die, suit die

  • 6 to 8 players: two Fakes
4 to 9 (one is the Keeper) players15 to 20 min

Colour die only.

L2

Team die and Colour die.

L3

Team, colour, suit number.

Solo Needs 4 people.

Play cards that fit more than one theme.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Partly simulated Photographers win 58% (3), 44% (4), 38% (5) with one Fake; 51% (6), 47% (7), 38% (8) with two Fakes; 22% at nine (dropped).

SettingResult
3 photographers, hand 3, 2 turns, one Fake (500 games)Photographers win 58%; Fake accused 63%; accused Fake guesses right 7%
4 photographers, hand 4, 3 turns, one Fake (500)Photographers win 44%; accused 54%; guess right 18%
5 photographers, hand 4, 3 turns, one Fake (500)Photographers win 38% (Fake side 62%, just over the 60% target); accused 50%; guess right 25%
6 / 7 / 8 photographers, hand 3, 3 turns, two Fakes (400 each)Photographers win 51% / 47% / 38%; at least one Fake accused 77% / 74% / 69%
9 photographers, two Fakes (400)Photographers win 22%: unsupported, dropped
Fit rate of a random card with the dice themeabout 63%. Honest misfits 0.07 to 0.17 per player per game; Fake misfits 0.58 to 0.9
Detective quality, 5 photographers, hand 3, 3 turns (500)careful table 32%, sloppy table (noisy, kids) 27%, random pointing 18%
Seats and lengthFake seat random. 12 to 24 card plays, about 5 to 7 minutes plus whispering and a one-minute talk

Not simulated. Whether people actually check each card against three theme parts, how honest players hint or hesitate, the one-minute talk, humour, L1 and L2 theme sizes, and the ablation of a random Fake bot in hand mode (the flag was not wired in; only the Bayesian Fake was measured).

Engine sims/fake_photographer.py. Fake bot: Bayesian posterior over all 216 themes, picks the card that fits most posterior mass. Honest bot: plays the fitting card that leaves the posterior of the true theme lowest. Detective bot: counts misfits per player with shared discussion noise (sd 0.5) plus personal noise (sd 0.3); kids noise is 2.5 times larger. Caught Fake guess: best pair of theme parts by posterior. Balance depends on table size, so rules vary by count. Table size and tie rules were tuned, see tuning_log.

Tuning log

  • round 1: first design had a secret theme of one value out of 24 (6 teams, 6 colours, 6 place types, 6 moods), cards from private hands. A card fits one value only 17 to 33% of the time, so honest players often held no fitting card (0.9 to 1.4 misfits per honest player per game) and could not be told from the Fake. Detective side won 9 to 35% (3 to 9 players). A shared camera roll of 6 or 8 cards and a one-time Blur (pass) did not help (3 to 44%).

  • round 2: theme became three values, one team, one colour and one suit number, from three dice. A card fits if it has any of them (fit chance about 63%). Honest misfits fell to 0.07 to 0.17 per player. Place and mood were dropped (no provisional tags needed; results with them were the same within noise). Guess rule: naming one theme part let a caught Fake win 25 to 80% of the time, so a caught Fake must now name two parts.

  • round 3: with one Fake, 6 to 9 players hid the Fake too well (detectives 11 to 30%). Two Fakes who do not know each other at 6 to 8 players brought detectives to 38 to 51% (win if at least one Fake is accused and no accused Fake guesses). Ties at the top of the vote now count as accused (+3 to 7 points). Hand and turns set per table size: 3 players hand 3 and 2 turns, 4 or 5 players hand 4 and 3 turns, 6 to 8 players hand 3 and 3 turns. Nine players (22% detectives) dropped.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Fox in the Camp: also a hidden odd-one-out, but there every player holds one card, here the evidence is a collage that builds turn by turn, the theme is three things from dice, and a caught Fake can win by guessing the theme from the cards

Ratings

From memory: about Coup level. Six rules, three dice values to hold in mind, teach about 3 minutes.

Setup about 90 seconds (serial check, whispering). Keeper must check serials. Misfit and fit checks against three parts each turn. Works from 4 to 8 people; nine unsupported.

The bluff, the groan when a card does not fit and the last-second guess should land well with kids. Weakest part: after the first two cards the Fake can often just fit, so rounds end on a one-card slip, and checking three theme parts each turn is a chore for younger children.

Card changes requested: none

Expression Tales

A clue that is not too obvious and not too strange. Say what a face or a place makes you think of, and see who finds your card in a row of look-alikes.

Inspired by Dixit, Rory's Story Cubes

RecommendedKidsFamilyEasyComplexity 1.2 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
PN-03
Players
3 to 6
Time
20 to 35 min
Age
L1 from 5, L3 from 8
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

The Narrator secretly picks a card and gives a clue about its expression or place. Everyone else plays a card from their own hand that fits the clue. All the cards are shuffled and laid out; everyone except the Narrator votes for the Narrator's card.

What you need

All 54 cardsevery card has its own face, expression and place, so there are 54 different pictures
Pencil and paperfor the score, or use pawns on a number line

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the draw pile.

  • Pick a first Narrator at random. The role passes left every round.

  • Everyone looks at their own cards only. Look at the expression on each face and the place behind it: these are your clues.

How to play

  1. Clue. The Narrator picks one card from their hand, keeps it face down, and gives a clue: a word, a sentence, a sound or an action that fits the card's expression or place. It must not be too obvious ('wink') or too hidden ('Tuesday'). The Narrator puts the card face down in the middle.

  2. Match. Every other player secretly picks one card from their own hand that also fits the clue, and puts it face down in the middle.

  3. Lay out. The Narrator shuffles all the cards (their own plus one from each other player) and lays them face up in a row, left to right. Number them aloud, 1 upward.

  4. Vote. Everyone except the Narrator secretly picks the number of the card they think is the Narrator's. You cannot vote for your own card. Then all show with fingers at the same time.

  5. Score and refill. See below. Everyone draws back up to 5 cards. Pass the Narrator seat left.

How it ends

Scoring each round. If every voter or no voter found the Narrator's card, the Narrator scores 0 and every other player scores 2 (the clue was too easy or too hard). Otherwise the Narrator scores 3, and each voter who found the card scores 3. Besides that, each player other than the Narrator scores 1 for every vote that went to their own card. The game ends when each player has been Narrator twice (once at L2). If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile. Highest score wins. Ties are shared.

Words in this game

  • Narrator the player whose turn it is to give a clue.
  • Clue anything that is not a printed name on the cards: a word, a phrase, a sound or a movement.
  • Decoy a card another player chose to look like it fits the clue.
  • Row the shuffled cards laid face up, numbered from the left.
  • Found a voter picked the Narrator's card.

Common questions

  • Can the clue be a name? No. Use anything but a printed name of a face on the table.

  • Can I play the twin of the Narrator's card? If you hold one. Twin cards show the same child with a different expression and place, so they make excellent decoys.

  • Can the clue be a number? No: the numbers are not part of the picture. Use the pictures.

  • Do I have to play a card that really fits? Pick the one that fits best; a vague fit is fine because decoys should be believable.

  • What if I cannot think of a clue? Say the first thing the picture makes you feel. A mood word works well.

Tips

  • Aim for a clue that the player on your left would get, but the one on your right would not. That is the sweet spot that scores 3.

  • Twin pairs are decoys with a built-in contrast: one wink, one raspberry. If you hold the twin of an expression in a clue, play it as a decoy.

  • As a voter, think about who the Narrator is and what they would say, not only the picture.

  • As a player of decoys, look for the one card whose expression or place almost fits the clue.

  • Play to get votes on your own card: a good decoy earns 1 point per vote, and enough decoys beat a Narrator who scored 0.

Worked example

  1. 4 players. The Narrator (Seat 0) holds Dhruv (6), a Dhruv with both hands on the head, eyes huge, mouth open, in front of the Government Museum courtyard.

    The clue: 'Whoa!'.

  2. Seat 1 plays Dharsh (7) (Dharsh, awestruck, jaw dropped). Seat 2 plays Naresh (6) (Naresh, an 'aha!' moment, huge grin, finger raised). Seat 3 plays Bharati (4) (Bharati, whispering a secret).

  3. The Narrator shuffles the four cards and lays them out: 1 is Naresh (6), 2 is Dhruv (6), 3 is Bharati (4), 4 is Dharsh (7).

  4. Votes: Seat 1 cannot vote for 4 (their own card) and votes 2. Seat 2 votes 4. Seat 3 votes 2. Two of three found the Narrator's card.

  5. Scores: the Narrator scores 3, and Seats 1 and 3 each score 3 for finding it. Seat 1's card got one vote (from Seat 2), so Seat 1 scores 1 more, for 4. Seat 2's and Seat 3's decoys got no votes. Round total: Seat 0 3, Seat 1 4, Seat 2 0, Seat 3 3.

  6. Had all three voted 2, the clue was too easy: Seat 0 scores 0 and everyone else scores 2.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Story match (age 5 with a helper). Hands of 3. The Narrator tells a tiny story about their card. Everyone else plays the card from their hand that fits it best; the Narrator then points to the card that is most like the story and that player scores 1. No voting. First to 5.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Full rules with 5 cards and one turn as Narrator for everyone.

L3 · age 8 and up

Full rules, two turns as Narrator for everyone, and the clue must be a single sentence.

Solo

No solo mode: the game needs other players to guess.

Two players

Not supported: with two players there is only one voter and no decoy.

Maths and skills in this game

Language, description, perspective-taking (guessing what others notice), and judging how obvious a clue is.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour faces are the people in the stories
ExpressionRule the main source of clues; every card has a different one
PlaceRule a second source of clues; every card has a different one

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Not simulated. A story game is played by talking; there is no bot to test it. The numbers below are exact counts from the deck.

  • The deck has 54 distinct expressions and 54 distinct places. Every face has an A and a B expression that contrast (for example a cheeky wink against a raspberry), so each twin pair is a ready decoy.

  • Light is split 27 morning and 27 golden hour, so a clue about the light can fit about half the cards. It is a weak clue, so it makes a useful decoy.

  • The chance that the twin of the Narrator's card is in another player's hand: 5 cards each for the other players out of the 53 unseen: 19% at 3 players, 28% at 4, 38% at 5, 47% at 6 (exact count).

  • Hand of 5 and refill each round: with reshuffled discards the deck never runs out; a game is 6, 8, 10, 12 rounds at 3, 4, 5, 6 players (twice as Narrator each).

  • Length is an estimate: about 2 to 3 minutes a round gives 15 to 30 minutes.

Not tested:

  • Not tested at all with real people. Scoring is borrowed from Dixit and not tuned for this deck.

  • Not tested: whether twins as decoys are too dominant.

  • Not tested: the L1 story-match variant.

Variants and options

  • #10 Fib Table The tall-tale bluffing idea was dropped as a duplicate of this game's clue-and-vote core.

Front

EXPRESSION TALES. 3 to 6 players, 5 cards each. Narrator picks a card and gives a clue (word, phrase or sound, no printed names). Others each play a card that fits. Shuffle, lay out and number. Everyone but the Narrator votes secretly (not your own card).

Back

SCORING. All or none found it: Narrator 0, others 2. Otherwise Narrator 3, each who found it 3. Each decoy vote: 1 point to its owner. Everyone has two turns as Narrator. LEVELS. L1 story match, no voting. L2 one turn each. L3 two turns.

Where Are We

Everyone knows where you are except one player. Ask clever questions that prove you know, without telling the spy, and catch the one who is faking it.

Inspired by Spyfall

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
PN-04
Players
3 to 6 players and a Keeper
Time
20 to 35 min (5 to 10 min a round)
Age
L1 from 7, L3 from 10
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Eight places lie face up. All but one player are told where they are; the spy is not. Players take turns asking each other questions about the place. Catch the spy before the timer ends, or the spy names the place and wins.

What you need

All 54 cards8 are the Atlas (the list of places); the rest are the secret location and spy cards
A timera phone or watch for 6 minutes a round
Pencil and paperfor the score

Set up

  • The Keeper lays out the Atlas: eight cards, one with each number from 1 to 8, face up in two rows of four, so everyone can read their places. The Keeper changes the Atlas for every game.

  • The Keeper secretly picks one Atlas card: the secret place. Call its number k.

  • From the rest of the deck the Keeper takes one card numbered k for each player except one, and one card numbered 9. For example at 4 players: three cards numbered k and one 9. They are shuffled face down and dealt, one to each player.

  • Every player looks at their own card: the number is all that matters. If it is 1 to 8, that is the Atlas card where you are. If it is a 9, you are the spy and you do not know the place. The pictures on the dealt cards do not matter. Keep it hidden.

  • The Keeper starts the timer at 6 minutes. A random player asks first.

How to play

  1. Ask. The player whose turn it is asks any other player one question about where you are, for example 'What do you hear here?'. Not allowed: naming a place or asking 'Are we at X?'.

  2. Answer. The player answers the question. They must say something that is true of the place without being so exact that the spy finds out where they are.

  3. The answerer then asks a question of any other player, except the player who asked them (no immediate back-and-forth).

  4. Accuse. At any time a player may say 'I accuse (name)'. All players except the accused vote at once with a thumb up or down. If all vote yes, the accused shows their card.

  5. Spy's guess. At any time the spy may turn their card face up and point to one Atlas card. If it is the secret place, the spy wins; if not, the non-spies win.

How it ends

The round ends when the spy is exposed by an accusation, or the spy guesses, or the timer runs out. Scoring. If the accused is the spy: each non-spy scores 1 and the accuser scores 2. If the accused is not the spy: the spy scores 2. If the spy guesses the place correctly: the spy scores 3. If the timer runs out with no accusation, the spy scores 2 and then the non-spies get one final vote on who the spy is; a right vote means no score for the spy. Play one round per person (the Keeper rotates each round, so everyone is Keeper once if you have one more person than the player count); highest score wins.

Words in this game

  • Atlas the eight face-up cards, numbered 1 to 8, whose places are the possible locations.
  • Keeper the person running the round. Not a player in that round.
  • Secret place the Atlas card with number k.
  • Spy the player dealt a 9. They do not know where they are.
  • Accusation naming a player as the spy and calling a vote.

Common questions

  • Who is the Keeper? Someone who does not play this round, picks the place, deals the cards and keeps the time. The role passes to the next person each round.

  • Why numbers instead of pictures? A card has only one picture, but several players need to know the same place. The Keeper deals cards with the same number, so each player can read the same Atlas card.

  • Can the spy see the dealt cards of others? No. Every card stays face down in front of its owner.

  • Can I answer 'I do not know'? Not if you are a non-spy. A non-spy who dodges looks like a spy.

  • What if the vote is not unanimous? Then the accusation fails and the round carries on.

Tips

  • As a non-spy, answer with something specific that fits only a few places but would help the spy only a little. 'Birds' fits many places.

  • As the spy, listen for the places the answers could not be and cross them off in your head. Start by asking easy questions to learn more.

  • Ask questions that depend on the place: sounds, smells, crowds, light, who sits there.

  • Do not accuse too early. A wrong accusation scores the spy 2.

  • As the spy, guess the place when you are 50 percent sure: waiting for 100 percent will often run past the timer.

Worked example

  1. 4 players and a Keeper. The Atlas: 1 Smaya (1) (Cubbon Park bamboo grove), 2 Pinku (2) (VV Puram food street), 3 Guhan (3) (Namma Metro station), 4 Amyra (4) (Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace), 5 Amyra (5) (Lalbagh lake footbridge), 6 Naresh (6) (Tiffin stall courtyard), 7 Shreya (7) (Cubbon Park statue), 8 Smaya (8) (Janapada Loka folk museum).

  2. The Keeper picks Atlas card 7, Shreya (7) (k = 7), then deals three cards numbered 7 (Pinku (7), Ajay (7), Ammlu (7)) and one numbered 9 (Rihansh (9)), shuffled. Seat 3 gets the 9 and is the spy.

  3. Seat 0 asks Seat 1: 'Is it busy here?' Seat 1: 'Only at weekends.' Seat 1 asks Seat 3: 'What would you be carrying here?' Seat 3, the spy, says 'A bag', which fits every place. The others notice that Seat 3 gave a safe, plain answer.

  4. Seat 2 asks Seat 0: 'Is there food nearby?' Seat 0: 'Not close.' That rules out the food street, the tiffin courtyard and the folk museum's cafe. Seat 3 listens and crosses places off.

  5. Seat 2 accuses Seat 3. The other three vote yes. Seat 3 shows Rihansh (9), a 9: the spy. Seats 0, 1 and 2 each score 1, and Seat 2, the accuser, scores 2 in all.

  6. Had Seat 3 turned the card over and pointed at Shreya (7) before the accusation, the spy would have scored 3.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Four places only (Atlas cards 1 to 4), no timer, and the spy is given a hint: the Keeper says which row the place is in. Ask only yes or no questions.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Eight places, 8-minute timer, free questions.

L3 · age 8 and up

Eight places, 6-minute timer, and the spy may not ask 'Why?'.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about talking.

Two players

Not supported: you need at least three players and a Keeper.

Maths and skills in this game

Asking precise questions, inference from partial information, and keeping a straight face.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the dealt card's number names the secret place, and a 9 names the spy
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour faces are the people in the place
ExpressionNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Not simulated: this is a conversation game. The numbers below are exact counts.

  • There are 54 distinct places and twins never share one. A spy guessing blindly from all 54 has a 1.9% chance. From a shortlist of 12 places it is 8.3%, and from the Atlas of 8 used here it is 12.5%. The final-cut table asked for a shortlist of 12; the Atlas is 8 because the numbers 1 to 8 are what name a place on a card.

  • Each number 1 to 9 appears on six cards. One is in the Atlas, so five others can be dealt as 'k' cards: that caps the table at 6 players (5 cards numbered k and one spy).

  • The spy card is a 9, so the Atlas can use only numbers 1 to 8. Over many games, the Atlas has 6 possible cards for each of the eight positions, so there are 6 to the power 8 = 1,679,616 different Atlases.

  • Length is an estimate: 2 to 8 minutes a round plus a minute of setup; a full game of one round per person is 15 to 30 minutes.

  • Scoring (1 for each non-spy, 2 for the accuser, 2 or 3 for the spy) is borrowed from the shape of Spyfall and not balanced.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: balance between spy and non-spies. That needs real conversation.

  • Not tested: whether the Keeper role makes the game too slow for 4 people.

  • Not tested: the Atlas of 8 against the 12 in the plan.

Front

WHERE ARE WE. 3 to 6 players + a Keeper. Atlas: 8 cards numbered 1 to 8 face up. Keeper picks a place k, deals one card numbered k to all but one player and a 9 to the last. A 9 is the spy. Take turns asking each other questions about the place. 6-minute timer.

Face Codenames

Sixteen faces on the table, six of them yours. Give one word and a number so your team finds them all, and steer clear of the face that ends the game.

Inspired by Codenames (with ideas from Decrypto and Just One)

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
PN-05
Players
4 to 8
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
L1 from 7, L3 from 10
Dice
1 die
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Two teams. Sixteen cards lie face up in a grid. A hidden key says which belong to which team. Each team's clue-giver says one word and a number; teammates point at cards. First team to find all its cards wins; touch the trap and you lose.

What you need

All 54 cards16 key cards, 16 grid cards, and 22 spare
1 dieto choose which team starts
Team keyRef 4, for team words in clues (optional)

Set up

  • Make the key deck from 16 cards, chosen by number: all six 1s (North's cards), five 2s (South's cards), four 3s (neutral) and one 4 (the trap). Shuffle them face down and lay them in a 4 by 4 grid. This is the key grid.

  • Shuffle the other 38 cards face down. Deal 16 of them, face up, in a 4 by 4 grid next to the key grid, in the same direction. This is the word grid. Each key card sits at the same place as the grid card it describes.

  • Split into two teams: North and South. Each team picks one clue-giver. The two clue-givers sit side by side, facing their teams, and look at the key grid; the others must not see its fronts.

  • Roll the die. The higher roll is the starting team and needs 6 cards; the other team needs only 5, which is why the key has one fewer 2 than 1s.

How to play

  1. Clue. The clue-giver whose team is up says one word and one number, such as 'Water, 2'. The word is a hint to the cards in the grid that belong to their team; the number says how many cards the hint touches. The clue can be about anything on a card: a name, place, expression, mood, letter, number, colour, team animal or what a face reminds you of. It may not be a name printed on a grid card, and no spelling, gestures or sounds.

  2. Guess. The team discusses and points at a grid card. The clue-giver turns the matching key card face up on top of that grid card. If it is a 1 (North) or a 2 (South) for the team that is guessing, it is theirs: they may guess again.

  3. Guess a card that belongs to the other team: it counts for them and your turn ends. A 3 is neutral: your turn ends. The 4 is the trap: your team loses at once.

  4. A team may guess up to one more card than the number (for the leftovers of earlier clues) and may stop earlier. At least one guess must be made.

  5. Then the other team gets a clue. Keep going until a team has found all its cards.

How it ends

The game ends when a team has found all of its cards (North 6, South 5), or when a team touches the trap: the other team wins. If a team runs out of time to agree, pick the card the clue-giver would most likely mean. If the grid has no cards left for a team, that team has already won.

Words in this game

  • Clue-giver the player who sees the key and gives one word and a number.
  • Key grid 16 face-down cards; the number on the front says whose card the grid card is.
  • Word grid the 16 face-up cards the teams guess from.
  • Trap the 4 in the key; guessing its card loses the game.
  • Neutral a 3: no team's card, ends the turn.

Common questions

  • Why are the key cards chosen by number? So the key is always balanced and needs no extra pieces. The six 1s, five 2s, four 3s and one 4 are picked out of the deck.

  • Can the clue be a team animal like Monkeys? Yes, if no printed name is that word. The team animal is on every card.

  • Can the clue use two words? No. One word only; a hyphenated word counts as one.

  • What if the clue-giver accidentally gives a face away? Turn the guessed card over and carry on; the other team may add a clue.

  • Can I ask the clue-giver questions? No. They sit silent and keep a straight face.

Tips

  • Use the team animal and the number for sure things. A team word like 'Monkeys 3' is clean when your cards hold all the Monkeys in the grid, which is rare.

  • Free-form clues carry the game. Plan clues about the place or the mood of the faces, such as 'water', 'festival' or 'sleepy', rather than a printed attribute.

  • Say a smaller number than you could. Three cards at once is risky; two with a very clean clue is safe.

  • Look at where the trap sits before you clue. Any clue that fits the trap card as well as your cards is out.

  • Guessers: take the clue-giver's number as the most they intend. Stop early when your confidence drops.

Worked example

  1. The key grid and word grid are laid out. North's cards in the grid are in positions: Shiva statue (Pinku (7)), Lalbagh (Bn Sharada (7)), the railway platform (Guhan (6)), Hebbal Lake (Nysha (8)), safari (Nakul (4)) and Diwali (Arvind (8)). The trap is Adheesh (9) (Devarayanadurga hill).

  2. North's clue-giver says: 'Monkeys, 3'. Bn Sharada (7), Nysha (8) and Arvind (8) are the only Monkeys in the grid, and all three belong to North. The team points at Arvind (8), then Nysha (8), then Bn Sharada (7); each key card is turned face up and shows a 1, so North scores three. They stop; three cards are enough.

  3. South's clue-giver says: 'Water, 2', meaning the waterfall of Anayka (8) and the lake of Adheesh (9). South guesses Anayka (8): a 2, South's. Then Adheesh (9): the key shows a 3, a neutral card. South's turn ends. South has found 1 of 5.

  4. North's clue-giver says: 'Safari, 1'. Nakul (4) (Bannerghatta safari) shows a 1. North has found 4 of 6 and chooses to stop.

  5. South says 'Fort, 2', which touches Ajay (7) (Makalidurga fort ruins) but also Archana (4) (Bangalore Fort gate, neutral) and Adheesh (9), the trap hill (Devarayanadurga hill is a fort-like hill). The team guesses Ajay (7) first, which is a South card, then hesitates. A clue that fits the trap is a risk. They stop.

  6. If a team ever pointed at Adheesh (9), its key card shows the 4 and that team would lose at once.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

All players work together as one team (age 7 with a helper). One clue-giver, no rival team, no trap. Use the six 1s only as the key: find all six faces in the grid in as few clues as possible.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Two teams, with a trap, but the clue can be a team animal, number or colour (clean, simple clues).

L3 · age 8 and up

Full game: any one-word clue, North starts with 6 and South needs 5.

Solo

No solo mode: it needs a clue-giver and guessers.

Two players

Not tested at fewer than 4 players. As a two-player co-op, one gives clues and the other guesses against the clock of 6 clues.

Maths and skills in this game

Finding links between pictures and words, choosing a clear clue, estimating risk, and reading a teammate's thinking.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the key: 1 is North, 2 is South, 3 is neutral, 4 is the trap
ColoursFlavour a source of clues
Suit pairFlavour a source of clues
Back patternNot used
TeamFlavour the animal can be the clue
Letter tileFlavour a source of clues
SerialNot used
NamesRule a printed name cannot be used as a clue
ExpressionFlavour the main source of free clues
PlaceFlavour the main source of free clues

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Not simulated as a game. The numbers below come from counting the deck.

  • Attribute clues alone are thin. On a 16-card grid where 6 are your cards, the best clean clue (touching only your cards) covers 2.05 cards on average, 3 or more in 23% of grids and 4 or more in 4% (computed for the final-cut table). By one attribute: number covers 1.4, letter 1.3, team 0.9, age group 0.65, colour and suit about 0.15. So free-form clues have to carry the game.

  • The key built from the six 1s, five 2s, four 3s and one 4 uses 16 cards and leaves 38 for the grid, with numbers 3 to 9 only (counts: 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 5, 5: 6, 6: 6, 7: 6, 8: 6, 9: 6).

  • Over 100,000 random grids (computed for this page): 92% hold at least one twin pair (two cards of the same face), the largest team group in a grid averages 4.5 cards, and 94% of grids have 4 or more cards from one team.

  • The starting team needs 6 cards and the other team 5, the same trade-off Codenames makes with 9 and 8 cards.

  • Length: unmeasured; clues and discussion run about 1 to 3 minutes a turn, so 15 to 25 minutes is an estimate.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: everything about play. No bot can give a clue like a person. The claim 'free-form clues carry the game' comes from the thin attribute counts, not from play.

  • Not tested: whether 6 versus 5 is fair for the starting team.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

FACE CODENAMES. 4+ players, two teams (North, South). Key grid: six 1s (North), five 2s (South), four 3s (neutral), one 4 (trap), face down 4x4, seen only by the two clue-givers. Word grid: 16 other cards face up in the same layout. Clue: ONE word and a number. Guessers point; clue-giver puts the key card on the grid card.

Back

Own card: guess again (up to the number + 1). Other team's card: counts for them, turn over. 3: turn over. 4: you lose. Clue may be about anything on a card but not a printed name. North needs 6, South 5. LEVELS. L1 one team, six cards. L2 team and number clues only. L3 full.

Party nights · Deduction · Fronts

Face Whodunit

Three cards are hidden: a face, a place and a number. Every card in your hand is a clue for somebody else, and every question you ask gets a private answer.

Inspired by Clue, Deduce or Die and Dead Drop

FamilyKidsMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
PN-06
Players
3 to 6
Time
15 to 40 min
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Three hidden cards name the culprit, the place and the number. Ask about one face, one place and one number. The first player to hold a matching card shows you one in secret. Cross off what you learn and accuse when you are sure.

What you need

All 54 cardssorted at set-up into a face pile, a place pile and a number pile
Pencil and paperone notepad each, to cross off faces, places and numbers

Set up

  • Build the three piles. Shuffle all 54 cards. Turn them over one at a time from the top. Put each card in the first pile that wants it: the Face pile (one card from each of the first 4 teams, from the Tigers up to the Monkeys) first; then the Place pile (again one from each of teams 1 to 4); then the Number pile (one card of each number 1 to 6). Skip any card whose twin is already in a pile, and any card nobody needs. Stop when you have 4 faces, 4 places and 6 numbers. That is the small line, 14 cards.

  • In the full line (L3) use all 6 teams in the Face and Place piles and numbers 1 to 9: 6 faces, 6 places and 9 numbers, 21 cards.

  • A card is judged only by its pile. A Face card is its name only. A Place card is its place only. A Number card is its number only.

  • Shuffle each pile separately. Without looking, take the top card of each pile and put the three together face down. This is the Envelope.

  • Mix the other cards from the three piles together and deal them out evenly to the players. Sort your cards into three small fans: faces, places and numbers.

  • Each player takes a pencil and writes the full list of faces, places and numbers in play, ready to cross off.

How to play

  1. On your turn you do one of two things: ask a question, or accuse.

  2. Ask. Say one face from the line, one place from the line and one number from the line. For example: "Adhiraa, Visvesvaraya Museum, number 5." You may name items you hold yourself.

  3. Answer. Going clockwise from the asker, the first player who holds at least one of the three named cards shows one of them to the asker only, face up for a moment. If a player holds several matches, they choose which to show. Other players only see that somebody showed a card, and who. Stop at the first player who shows. If nobody can show a card, nothing is shown.

  4. Note it. Cross off what you see. A shown Face card crosses off that name. A shown Place card crosses off that place. A shown Number card crosses off that number. Also cross off the cards in your own hand.

  5. Accuse. When you think you know all three, say "I accuse" instead of asking. Say your face, place and number, then look at the Envelope in secret. If you are right, you win. If you are wrong, you are out, but you keep your cards and still show them when asked.

How it ends

The first player to make a correct accusation wins. If every player is out or nobody has solved it after each player has taken 12 turns on the small line (or 20 on the full line), open the Envelope: the game is a draw and you play again. If nobody can show a card in answer to your question, the three you named are the Envelope, unless you hold one of them yourself.

Words in this game

  • Envelope the three hidden cards, one from each pile
  • Line the cards in play: faces, places and numbers
  • Small line 4 faces, 4 places, 6 numbers; the shorter game
  • Accuse name all three hidden items and look in the Envelope
  • Fan your cards, sorted into faces, places and numbers

Common questions

  • Does the Number pile card count as its face too? No. A card is only the thing its pile says. A Number card is just a number, even if it also shows a child's face.

  • Why skip twins? If both cards of a child were in play, a name could mean two cards. One of each child keeps every name unique.

  • Can I ask about something I hold? Yes, to throw others off. But the player on your left may show a card that tells them something.

  • What if two players could show? Only the first clockwise from the asker shows. The others do not.

  • What if I accuse wrongly? You are out for the game but you still show cards when you are asked.

Tips

  • Mix your questions. Ask about two unknown items and one you already know, so a card you hold hides which are your real doubts.

  • Count the shows. When a player passes (cannot show), you know they hold none of the three named items. That helps all three players, not just the asker.

  • If you ask and nobody can show a card, you have named the Envelope in all three categories, or you hold one of the cards yourself. Check your own hand and accuse.

  • Ask for numbers you do not hold. A number you hold teaches you nothing new.

  • With 5 or 6 players the cards are spread thin. Pay attention to who showed what, even when it is not your question.

  • Keep your own fan tidy and cover the cards you hold when you show; the others should only see what you choose to show.

Worked example

  1. 3 players, small line. The Envelope holds Smaya (8) (Smaya, Bears), Idhayan (1) (the Cubbon Park toy train) and Pinku (2) (number 2). Seat 0 holds Amay (8) (face), Nakul (4) and Anayka (1) (places) and Sharada (3) (number 3). Seat 1 holds Archana (5) (face), Kanasu (6), Nysha (1) and Gopi (5) (numbers 6, 1, 5). Seat 2 holds Adhiraa (3) (face), Dhruv (3) (place) and Amyra (4) (number 4).

  2. Seat 0, turn 1: asks "Adhiraa, Visvesvaraya Museum, number 5." Seat 1 holds the number 5 card and shows it. Seat 0 crosses off 5.

  3. Turn 2: "Adhiraa, Cubbon Park toy train, number 6." Seat 1 shows the number 6 card. Cross off 6.

  4. Turn 3: "Archana, Cubbon Park toy train, number 1." Seat 1 shows Archana (5) (Archana). Cross off Archana.

  5. Turn 4: "Smaya, Cubbon Park toy train, number 4." Seat 1 has none of the three, so seat 2 shows the number 4 card. Cross off 4. Turn 5: "Adhiraa, Visvesvaraya Museum, number 1": seat 1 shows number 1. Turn 6: "Smaya, Visvesvaraya Museum, number 2": seat 1 has none; seat 2 shows Dhruv (3) (Visvesvaraya Museum). Turn 7: "Adhiraa, Cubbon Park toy train, number 2": seat 2 shows Adhiraa (3) (Adhiraa). (Seats 1 and 2 take their turns in between.)

  6. Seat 0's notes: faces left: only Smaya (Amay is in their own hand, Archana and Adhiraa were shown). Places left: only the Cubbon Park toy train (Bannerghatta and KR Market are in their hand, Visvesvaraya Museum was shown). Numbers left: only 2 (3 is in hand; 5, 6, 4 and 1 were shown). Seat 0 accuses "Smaya, Cubbon Park toy train, number 2" and the Envelope matches. Seat 0 wins on turn 8.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Who Am I (age 5, folds in idea #26). Each player holds a card against their forehead so others can see it. Ask yes or no questions to the group: "Is my number a bond with 6?" "Is my team the Bears?" "Is my number more than 5?" Name the child and the number to win. Keep questions about the card's number, team or colours.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The small line (14 cards: 4 faces, 4 places, 6 numbers). Use scoring pads with all items listed. For ages 8 and up.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full line (21 cards: 6 faces, 6 places, 9 numbers). A longer game, 25 to 35 minutes.

Solo

No solo mode: other players hold the clues.

Two players

Not designed for 2 players. With two players one holds all the other cards, which makes it a pure guessing game. Use 3 to 6.

Maths and skills in this game

Logical elimination: crossing off cases until one remains, and keeping organised notes. Remembering what each player has shown.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the number named in the question and one of the three hidden items
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule chooses the cards for the lines, one from each team
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesRule the face is the culprit
ExpressionNot used
PlaceRule the place is the second hidden item

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • As first written, with the three hidden cards chosen from the whole deck, the game is unsolvable: a number from 1 to 9 has six copies and the hidden card's own number is never fully seen. It can only be cut down by seeing 48 of the other 51 cards, and no bot solved a game in 120 rounds, with 27 faces and 54 places, or with 6 faces, 6 places and numbers 1 to 9.

  • With every hidden item picked from a laid-out line of unique cards (6 faces, 6 places, 9 numbers) the bots solve about half the games (48% to 56%) within 60 turns each, at a median of 13 to 23 turns each (about 10 to 35 minutes).

  • A smaller 4, 4, 6 line solves 46% to 68% of the games at 8 to 12 turns each (about 6 to 17 minutes).

  • Those bots only read cards shown to them; they do not use the fact that nobody could show a card, so people should be faster.

  • New computation for this page: a bot that picks a random question among the items it has not crossed off, and accuses only when certain, solved 100% of 300 games at each of 3, 4, 5 and 6 players on the small line (accusing only when certain never loses). The median solving turn was 9, 9, 10 and 10 for the winner's own turns, mean 8.8 to 10.3.

  • The small line is 14 cards and the full line 21. At 3 players the small line leaves 11 cards to deal, about 4 each.

  • Folding in Who Am I: its yes/no questions on a forehead card become the L1 game, so there is no separate game for it.

Not tested:

  • Nobody could show a card (an automatic solution) is a rule for people; the bots ignored it.

  • Human play. The bots do not read who passed or who showed.

  • The 12 and 20 turn limits are suggestions.

  • Who Am I as L1 was not simulated.

Variants and options

  • Who Am I (#26) Folded in as the age-5 mode: each player wears a card and asks yes or no questions about its number or team.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

FACE WHODUNIT. 3 to 6 players. Build 3 piles from the deck, one of each child only: Faces (teams 1 to 4), Places (teams 1 to 4), Numbers (1 to 6). Hide the top card of each pile as the Envelope. Deal out the rest. Your turn: ASK (name one face, one place, one number) or ACCUSE. The first clockwise player holding a match shows ONE card to you in secret. Cross off what you see.

Back

ACCUSE: name all three, look in the Envelope. Right = you win. Wrong = out, but keep showing your cards. If nobody can show a card, the three named are the Envelope (unless you hold one). Full line: 6 faces, 6 places, numbers 1 to 9. L1: Who Am I with a card on your forehead. Limit 12 turns each on the small line.

Forehead Words

Every explorer wears a letter on their forehead, and only their friends can read it.

Inspired by Letter Jam (cooperative clue words about hidden letters) and forehead-card party games, from memory

FamilyHardComplexity 1.8 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
PN-07
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 20 min
Age
10+
Dice
None
Pawns
3 pawns (the miss row)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone wears one letter on their forehead; each round a giver taps cards that spell a word, and the players who were tapped work out the letter they cannot see.

What you need

All 54 cardsEach player holds one on their forehead, letter facing out. The rest are the supply; one new card is flipped face up each round.
3 pawnsThe miss row. Each wrong guess puts one pawn on the table.
Reference cardHas the letter table: how many copies of each letter are in the deck.
A way to hold a card on your foreheadYour hand, a hair band or a tall rubber band. Only your hand is needed.

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. Deal one card to each player. Without looking, hold it against your forehead with the letter facing out. Everyone else can read it. You cannot.

  • Put the rest of the cards face down as the supply. Flip the top card face up in the middle. This is the first public card.

  • Put the three pawns beside the supply. This is the miss row.

  • Agree a dictionary: any word you would find in a children's dictionary, including plurals. No names, no short forms.

  • The player with the earliest birthday in the year gives first. Play passes clockwise.

How to play

  1. The giver looks at every card they can read: all other players' cards, all public cards, and all solved cards (including their own card once it is face up). The giver's own unsolved card is the one card they cannot read.

  2. The giver silently picks a real word of three or more cards, spelled with cards they can read, each card used once. Q is the Qu card and counts as one card that spells QU. If no word helps anyone, the giver says Pass.

  3. The giver taps the cards of the word in order, slowly, twice. Tap a public card by touching it. The giver says nothing at all, not even how long the word is.

  4. Each player whose own card was tapped and is not solved is a holder. A holder knows which place in the word is theirs and can read all the other letters. The holder works out which letters could fill their gap to make a real word. A letter is ruled out if every copy of it is already on a card the holder can read (use the letter table on the reference card). Remember the answer. Later clues must also fit.

  5. Clockwise from the giver, each holder either says Pass or names a letter. If right, turn the card face up and put it in the middle: it is solved and now everyone can use it. If wrong, put a pawn in the miss row. A wrong letter is never your letter, so cross it off in your head.

  6. At the end of the round flip one new card from the supply face up. The next player clockwise is the giver. A round where the giver passes still counts as a round.

How it ends

You win together if every card held on a forehead is solved by the end of round five. You lose if a third pawn goes into the miss row or any card is still unsolved after round five. Rate the win: solved in four rounds or fewer with no pawn is Gold, in five rounds with no pawn is Silver, otherwise Bronze. There are no individual winners or ties.

Words in this game

  • Giver The player whose turn it is to give a clue by tapping cards.
  • Holder A player whose unsolved card was tapped in this round's word.
  • Public card A card flipped face up in the middle. Everyone can read it and any giver can tap it.
  • Solved A holder named the letter correctly and turned the card face up. It stays in the middle and is public.
  • Miss row The three pawns. Each wrong guess places one pawn here.

Common questions

  • Two cards show the same letter. Which one does the giver tap? Either. The giver taps the card whose holder it wants to help. Both holders of a repeated letter can be tapped in the same word.

  • What if I am not sure but think I know? You may guess when two or three letters are left, but every wrong guess costs a pawn. You may also Pass and wait for a better clue.

  • How do I know a letter is ruled out? Use the letter table. If the table says there is one B and you can read a B on another card, your card is not a B.

  • May the giver use their own card? Only once it is solved and face up. Before that the giver cannot read it.

  • Can people who were not tapped say anything? No. No talking, hints, hmms or faces. Untapped players still watch: the word tells them what the giver is thinking.

  • What if the supply runs out? It cannot. The game lasts five rounds, so at most five cards are flipped, and the supply never drops below 40.

  • What does the Q card do? It spells QU and uses one card. The reference card says there is one Q and one U in the deck.

Tips

  • As giver, choose a word where only one letter fits the gap. A smart giver (the most informative word) won 71 to 85% against 31 to 47% for a random valid word.

  • Use the letter table. If there is one B in the deck and you can read a B on someone else's forehead, your card is not a B, so cross it off in your head before you guess.

  • Do not guess with five letters left. Pass and wait for a better clue, because every wrong letter costs a pawn, and three pawns lose the game.

  • Tap a word that helps two holders at once. A repeated letter lets both holders be tapped in one word.

  • Hold the cards steady and say nothing at all while tapping. Start with L1 (six rounds, five pawns) for a first game. Two players is the hardest setting (47 to 66% for a perfect solver), so start with three or more.

Worked example

Four players. Adhiraa holds Adhiraa [H], Amay holds Amay [E], Archana holds Archana [M] and Nakul holds Nakul [A]. Everyone reads the other three cards but not their own. The first public card is Sharada [E]. Archana gives first. This is a real run of the engine with the 3,000-word kids dictionary.

  1. Round 1. Archana reads H, E, A and the public E. She cannot spell a useful word of three cards, so she says Pass. Flip Smaya [O] as the second public card.

  2. Round 2. Nakul gives. He reads H, E, M and the public E and O. He taps Adhiraa, then the public Smaya, then Archana, then Amay, twice. The word is H O M E.

  3. Amay sees H O M and a gap: only E fits (HOME). Amay names E, it is right, and Amay turns face up. Adhiraa sees a gap then O M E and finds C, H or S (COME, HOME, SOME). Archana sees H O, a gap, E and finds L, M or P (HOLE, HOME, HOPE). Both say Pass and remember their short list. Flip Gopi [S] as the third public card.

  4. Round 3. Adhiraa gives. He taps the public Gopi, then Amay, then the public Sharada, then Archana, twice. The word is S E E M. Archana sees S E E and a gap. Many letters fit by themselves (SEED, SEEM, SEEN), but only M is also on her round 2 list. She names M and Archana turns face up. Flip Kanasu [R] as the fourth public card.

  5. Round 4. Amay gives; their card is solved, so they can read everything. Amay taps Nakul, then the public Gopi, then Adhiraa. The word is A S H. Nakul sees a gap then S H: only A fits. Adhiraa sees A S and a gap and checks his round 2 list of C, H, S: only H fits. Both name their letters, both are right. All four cards are solved in four rounds with no pawn: Gold.

Level ladder

L1 · first game

First game (untested variant): six rounds and five pawns. The giver may also say how many cards are in the word. Use only the cards on the table to rule letters out, ignore the letter table.

L2 · standard

Standard: five rounds, three pawns, giver says nothing, use the letter table.

L3 · expert

Expert (untested variant): four rounds, two pawns, and a guess with three letters left costs two pawns.

Solo

Not possible. The game needs a hidden letter and a second person to read it. For practice alone, lay out five cards face up, cover one with a finger and work out its letter from a word you build around it.

Two players

Works, but is the hardest setting (a smart team wins 47 to 66 percent, depending on dictionary). Players take turns as giver. The giver can read only one player card plus the public cards, so many rounds are passes (about 2.5 per game in the sim).

Maths and skills in this game

Spelling, vocabulary, pattern completion, logical elimination, giving a clue that has only one answer.

Hold your card to your forehead, letter out. The giver taps cards that spell a word. Tapped holders find their missing letter and name it. Right: flip it up for all. Wrong: add a pawn. Solve every card in five rounds before three pawns.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Simulated A perfect-solver team wins 47 to 92 percent in five rounds (2p to 6p, by dictionary size); a smart giver beats a greedy giver by about 10 points and a random giver by about 35; deals are solvable 99 percent.

Not simulated. Human speed and memory (holders must keep earlier candidate lists in their head), how long the giver needs to find a good word, whether groups argue about the dictionary, and whether it is fun. The bot is a perfect dictionary solver, so real win rates will be lower. The supplied word lists were cleaned against a standard English word list (most acronyms and names removed), but they still hold some obscure words and a few names.

The bot giver tries every word from the dictionary that the visible cards can spell and picks the one that leaves the most holders with a single possible letter. Holders use exact logic: each clue is intersected with the earlier ones and letters whose every copy is visible are ruled out. A holder guesses when two letters are left. Q is the Qu tile. Dictionary size is the main uncertainty: a bigger dictionary gives the giver more words and gives holders more candidates. The three dictionaries bracket real play. Win rate rises with player count because the giver can read more cards, and 2 and 3 players are clearly the hardest.

Tuning log

  • round 1: one card per player, giver spells a word from the cards it can see, holder needs a unique completion. Solved-all rate in 12 rounds: 3p 0%, 4p 9%, 5p 19%, 6p 34% (kids list). Cause: with 3 players the giver sees only 2 cards and words need 3 cards. -> added public cards.

  • round 2: two fixed public cards: solved-all 32% to 55%, still stalls on rare letters (Q X Z J V). -> flip one NEW public card every round (round 1 has one, round 5 has five) so rare letters get fresh partners.

  • round 3: set the clock and the safety valve: five rounds for every player count, and a guess is allowed when two letters are left, with three pawns as misses. Smart team now wins 47% to 92% (2p to 6p, by dictionary size) and the deal is solvable without any guess 99 to 100% of the time given 14 rounds. (All numbers re-run after cleaning acronyms and names out of the word lists; the first rounds of tuning ran on the unclean lists.)

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Signal Fire (spell a real word, race): this is cooperative and about the letters you cannot see.

  • Perfect Camp (Hanabi-like co-op): same shape of hidden own card, but here the clue is a word, not a number or colour.

  • Wordwalk (word game): not re-read, assumed a solo or race word game.

Ratings

From memory, a little under Hanabi: four steps per turn, one new idea (reasoning about what the giver could have chosen), teach time about five minutes.

Teach time 4 to 5 minutes (-1), the letter table is read while deducing (-1), giver thinks up to a minute while others wait (-1), weaker at 2 players (-1), no setup or stalls (0).

The moment a holder says a letter and flips it right is a real payoff, and giving a clue with only one answer is a good puzzle. Weakest part: the giver's word search is hard for humans, and the game is five rounds, so a lost game feels like bad luck in the first flip.

Card changes requested: none

Flag Words

Plant a word flag where the first letter says you may, and out-spell your rivals for the best hills.

Inspired by Area majority games such as El Grande and Cottage Garden, with the word laying of Scrabble; from memory.

FamilyHardComplexity 1.8 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
PN-08
Players
2 to 4
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
8+
Dice
None (solo uses 1 die)
Pawns
6 (territory markers)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Spell words of three or more cards and lay them at the territory named by your first card's suits; the player with the most cards at a territory scores it, over three rounds.

What you need

All 54 cardsHand, draw pile and the words you lay.
6 pawnsStand in a row as the six territories, 1 to 6.
1 dieSolo only: the ghost's territory.

Key cards for this game

Territory key

Territory 1 and 2 are worth 3 points. Territory 3 and 4 are worth 4 points. Territory 5 and 6 are worth 5 points.

Set up

  • Stand the six pawns in a row in the middle of the table. From left to right they are territory 1 to 6. Keep the Territory key beside them.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal seven cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the draw pile. Look at your own fronts only.

  • The youngest player starts the first round. In later rounds the start moves one player to the left.

  • Each player takes the same number of turns in a round: six turns each at two players, four at three players, three at four players.

How to play

  1. Choose one of two things.

  2. Lay a word. Pick three or more cards from your hand that spell a word. Lay them in a row in front of you, reading left to right. The first card is your flag card. Look at the two suit numbers on the front of the flag card. Put your word beside the pawn of either of those territory numbers, on your side of the table. You may have several words at one territory; keep each word in its own row.

  3. Or swap. If you cannot or do not want to lay a word, put up to three cards from your hand on the discard pile and draw the same number.

  4. Then draw cards until you hold seven again. If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile to make a new one.

  5. After the last turn of the round, score every territory. Count the cards each player has laid there. The player with the most cards scores that territory's points from the Territory key. If two or more players tie for most, nobody scores it.

  6. Clear the table, gather all 54 cards, shuffle and deal again. Play three rounds.

How it ends

After three rounds the player with the most points wins. Tie: the player who won more territories wins; if still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • flag card The first card of your word. Its two front suit numbers say which territories you may lay the word at.
  • territory One of the six pawns. A territory is worth the points on the Territory key.
  • swap Discarding up to three cards and drawing as many instead of laying a word.
  • round A full deal and a fixed number of turns, then a count of the territories.

Common questions

  • Can I add cards to a word I already laid? No. Words stay as they are. To add more cards at a territory, lay a new word of three or more cards there.

  • Can two players lay at the same territory? Yes. That is the fight. Only the player with the most cards there scores.

  • What counts as a word? Any ordinary dictionary word. No names. The Q card counts as the two letters Qu and uses one card.

  • My flag card shows suits that are not the territory I wanted. May I change the order of my word? Yes. Any word you can spell from your hand works, so a different first letter may open a different territory.

  • What if a territory ties? Nobody scores it, so a rival can stop you by matching your cards.

  • Is Y a vowel? It does not matter. Spell however you like.

Tips

  • The territory is the game, not the word. A bot that weighed value and rivals beat a territory-blind bot 95% of the time, so choose where to lay before you choose what to spell.

  • Points are 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5 for territories 1 to 6, and territories 3 to 6 drew most of the points in simulation. Contest the 5s, but do not ignore the 3s, because rivals do.

  • Tied territories score for nobody, so match your rival's count at a territory you cannot win, and stop them cashing it.

  • Plan your first letter. The first card's two suit numbers decide where the word may go, so a different word can open a different territory.

  • Swap rather than force a word. 11% of turns had no legal word and swapping up to three cards is free. For younger players, play L1 (one round) and let them lay a three-letter word at any territory they like.

Worked example

Three players, Asha, Ben and Cara, first six turns of round one (real seeded run). Territory points: 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5.

  1. Asha lays NOSE at territory 5: Arvind [N] Amay [O] Gopi [S] Ajay [E]. The flag card Arvind shows suits 3 and 5 on its front, so territory 5 is allowed. Asha now has 4 cards there. Asha draws back up to seven.

  2. Ben lays LED at territory 6: Smaya [L] Ammlu [E] Amyra [D]. The flag card Smaya shows suits 5 and 6 on its front, so territory 6 is allowed. Ben now has 3 cards there. Ben draws back up to seven.

  3. Cara lays READ at territory 6: Adheesh [R] Guhan [E] Nysha [A] Shreya [D]. The flag card Adheesh shows suits 3 and 6 on its front, so territory 6 is allowed. Cara now has 4 cards there. Cara draws back up to seven.

  4. Asha lays AGE at territory 1: Naresh [A] Adheesh [G] Amay [E]. The flag card Naresh shows suits 1 and 6 on its front, so territory 1 is allowed. Asha now has 3 cards there. Asha draws back up to seven.

  5. Ben lays ACT at territory 3: Amyra [A] Pinku [C] Bharati [T]. The flag card Amyra shows suits 3 and 4 on its front, so territory 3 is allowed. Ben now has 3 cards there. Ben draws back up to seven.

  6. Cara lays HAVE at territory 3: Adhiraa [H] Nakul [A] Adhiraa [V] Nysha [E]. The flag card Adhiraa shows suits 1 and 3 on its front, so territory 3 is allowed. Cara now has 4 cards there. Cara draws back up to seven.

  7. Picture after six turns, territory 1: Asha 3; territory 3: Ben 3, Cara 4; territory 5: Asha 4; territory 6: Ben 3, Cara 4. Nobody has scored yet. Points are counted only when the round ends (here after twelve turns in all).

Level ladder

L1 · first game

First game: play one round only and use any words. Count it as the whole game.

L2 · standard

Standard game: three rounds as written.

L3 · expert

Expert: the player with the second most cards at a territory, if not tied, also scores half its points, rounded down.

Solo

Play three rounds of five turns. After each of your turns, roll the die and put the top four cards of the draw pile face up at that territory as the ghost's cards. At the end of a round you score each territory where you have more cards than the ghost. Bronze 26, Silver 31, Gold 36 (from 300 runs of a bot that knows the kids word list: a bot that picks territories at random scored a median of 26, the smart bot a median of 36).

Two players

Six turns each per round. The smart bot beat a territory-blind bot 95% of the time at two players, so the territory choice is the whole game; play fast.

Maths and skills in this game

Spelling. Counting a row of cards. Planning where to commit limited cards.

Not simulated. Real vocabulary: bots find every word in a 3,000 word list; people find far fewer, so humans will swap more and lay shorter words, and the first-card suit rule will often be the harder constraint than spelling. Table talk, how fast a group counts rows, and whether the swap turns feel frustrating.

Tuning: three rounds as listed in the log. The first design (cover a shorter word with a longer one) collapsed into longest word wins; stacking fixed that. Values 3,3,4,4,5,5 keep the low territories alive. Skill gap is large because the bot plans which territory to commit to; a human table will see a smaller gap. Ties are common enough to need the territory tie-break.

Tuning log

  • round 1: one word per territory; a longer word covers a shorter one (cover/extend rules). Three bots (longest word first, value first, mixed) all scored 29 to 37 percent at three players and the longest-word-first bot was never beaten: the game was just a longest word contest and the territory barely mattered. Cut.

  • round 2: replaced covering with stacking. Every card you lay stays; each territory goes to the player with the most cards there (tie scores for nobody). A territory-blind bot (longest word, random legal territory) now loses to a bot that weighs value against rivals (93% to 4% at three players); a bot that always rushes the biggest territory also loses.

  • round 3: territory values were 1 to 6 and the bots left territories 1 and 2 almost unscored (0.3 of 3 points a game). Changed to 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5 so every territory is worth a fight. Territory 1 now scores 4.4 of 9 points per game. Skill gap stayed large (78% for the smart bot against two blind bots at three players).

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Map the Island: also a majority game but built from card backs, not words.

  • Signal Fire and Wordwalk: one word at a time; Flag Words spreads many words across six territories.

  • Boundary Stones: a 2-player lane duel; Flag Words has six shared territories and 2 to 4 players.

Ratings

From memory, close to Hanabi (about 1.8): three rules to learn (lay, swap, count) and a tactical layer; teach in about three minutes.

10 minus 1 for counting rows of cards at every territory, minus 1 for word-hunting downtime at four players, minus 1 for a territory key read each round.

Choosing which hill to commit your cards to is a real, visible decision and ties give small stand-offs. Weakest part: vocabulary and the 11% of turns with no legal word decide a lot, and the pawns on the table add little.

Wordwalk

Eight letter cards lie face up on the table. Spell a real word from them, take the cards, and the row fills up again. Cards that match in colour and suit side by side earn a bonus.

Inspired by Scrabble, Quiddler, with a shared market row as in a draft

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
PN-09
Players
2 to 5
Time
about 15 min
Age
L1 from 7
Dice
1 die (first player in round 1)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Spell a word of three or more letters using cards from a shared row of eight, one card for each letter. You score the numbers on the cards, plus 3 for every neighbouring pair of letters whose cards share both a colour and a suit. Most points wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsthe letter tile on each card is its letter, the number is its score
A dictionaryany ordinary dictionary, a book or a phone app, to settle doubts
1 dieto pick the first player in round 1
Pencil and paperto keep scores (or use scoring piles)

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Lay 8 cards face up in a row. This is the River.

  • The rest is the face-down draw deck.

  • Each player has a face-up scoring pile next to them.

  • Agree on a dictionary. Roll the die: the highest roll plays first in round 1.

How to play

  1. Do one of these on your turn.

  2. Spell. Make a real word of 3 or more letters from the River, using one card for each letter, each card once. Names, abbreviations and non-words do not count. Take the cards into your scoring pile in word order, then refill the River to 8 from the deck.

  3. Swap. If you cannot (or will not) spell, discard one River card and refill the River to 8.

  4. If another player doubts your word, check it in the dictionary. If it is not there, you lose your turn: the cards go back into the River and nothing else changes.

  5. A round is one turn for every player. In each new round, the player with the fewest points plays first, then play goes clockwise. Ties: roll the die.

How it ends

When the deck cannot refill the River to 8, finish the round and stop. Word score: add the numbers on the word's cards, then add 3 for every neighbouring pair of letters in the word whose two cards share both a colour and a suit (at least one colour in common, and at least one suit in common). Most points wins. Ties: the player whose pile holds the card with the highest number; equal numbers, the higher serial.

Words in this game

  • River the row of 8 face-up cards that everyone spells from.
  • Neighbouring pair two cards that sit side by side in your word, such as the H and E of HERD.
  • Link a neighbouring pair that share at least one colour and at least one suit. Each link adds 3 points.
  • Swap discarding one River card when you do not spell.

Common questions

  • Can I use the same card twice in a word? No. One card for each letter, each card once. A word with two Ts needs two T cards.

  • What if I do not know if a word is real? Another player may doubt it. If the dictionary says it is not a word, you lose your turn. If it is a word, the doubter loses nothing, so doubt freely.

  • Do I have to put the cards in the order of the word? Yes, in word order, into your pile. Links count only between neighbours in that order.

  • Who plays first each round? The player with the fewest points. This keeps the opening River from favouring the first seat.

  • Is it fair for a child? Mostly vocabulary decides it. Help younger players by letting them use the level 1 or 2 rules, or agree a handicap such as 5 free points.

  • What is the best word? A longer word uses more cards, so more numbers and more chances for links. The X, Q, J and F cards can stay in the River for a long time.

Tips

  • Go for longer words. Every extra card adds its number (1 to 9) and gives another chance for a link bonus.

  • Look for neighbouring pairs: cards that share a colour and a suit. Reorder your idea of the word to put matching cards side by side where the word allows.

  • Hard letters (X, Q, J, F) sit in the River for a long time. Use them when a good word lets you, or leave them as safe blocks for other players.

  • Do not worry about leaving the next player a poor River. In the simulation, trying to do that gave no edge.

  • The player with the fewest points goes first, so the leader moves last in each round. If you are well ahead, play for a safe long word rather than racing.

  • A swap is not wasted when the River is poor: it brings in a fresh card and costs you only a turn.

Worked example

  1. Three players. The River is Adhiraa (3) (H, 3), Amay (8) (E, 8), Adheesh (9) (R, 9), Amyra (4) (D, 4), Rihansh (9) (T, 9), Anayka (8) (H, 8), Avika (4) (H, 4) and Adhiraa (6) (V, 6).

  2. Seat 0 spells HERD with Adhiraa (3), Amay (8), Adheesh (9) and Amyra (4). The numbers add to 3 + 8 + 9 + 4 = 24. Links: E and R (Amay (8) and Adheesh (9)) share orange and also suit 6, so that is a link and adds 3. H and E share only a suit, and R and D share nothing. Score 27. The four cards go to seat 0's pile.

  3. The River is refilled with Amay (1), Ajay (2), Naresh (3) and Dhruv (6). It now holds Rihansh (9) (T), Anayka (8) (H), Avika (4) (H), Adhiraa (6) (V), Amay (1) (O), Ajay (2) (L), Naresh (3) (A) and Dhruv (6) (T).

  4. Seat 1 spells THAT with Rihansh (9), Anayka (8), Naresh (3) and Dhruv (6). Numbers: 9 + 8 + 3 + 6 = 26. T and H (Rihansh (9) and Anayka (8)) share orange and suit 4, so that is a link: +3. The others have no link. Score 29.

  5. Seat 2 cannot find a word they like in Avika (4), Adhiraa (6), Amay (1), Ajay (2) and the four new cards, and discards Adhiraa (6) (the V) as a swap. The River is refilled to 8. Scores after round 1: 27, 29, 0. Seat 2 has the fewest points, so seat 2 plays first in round 2, then seat 0, then seat 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Age 5 to 6 (or beginner spellers), with a helper. Only 3-letter words. Score the number of cards you take, ignore the numbers and links. (Not simulated.)

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Ages 6 to 7. Words of 3 or more letters, score the numbers, no link bonus. (Not simulated.)

L3 · age 8 and up

Age 8 and up. The full game with link bonuses. For a shorter game of about 14 minutes, cap words at 4 letters and use a River of 6 (derived from the simulation, not played).

Solo

No solo mode: the game is a race for the shared River.

Two players

Works well. Without the "fewest points first" rule, the first player won 71% of two-player games because the opening River is the richest. With it, the split is 49 to 51.

Maths and skills in this game

Spelling, anagram-spotting, adding numbers up to 9 several times, and comparing the colours and suits of two cards at once.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the points of each card in the word
ColoursRule one half of the link bonus
Suit pairRule the other half of the link bonus
Back patternNot used
