Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • A fresh River of 8 has a legal word 99% of the time, and a player has to swap about 11% of turns.

  • A game is about 11 turns and 11 minutes at 15 seconds per action plus 45 seconds for each word; that is below the 15 to 25 minute target. A bigger River only makes it shorter.

  • With a link bonus of 3, links make about 20% of a typical score.

  • Without "fewest points plays first", the first player won 71% of two-player games, because the opening River is richest. With it, the split is 49 to 51 at two players and about even at 3 to 5.

  • Skill is mostly vocabulary: a player who knows obscure words beats an ordinary-dictionary player 61% of two-player games (500 to 2,000 games a cell, with a bot that plays its best-scoring word).

  • Trying to leave the next player a poor River gave no edge. A simultaneous version, where everyone picks a word at once and clashing words cancel, was worse: too short, and 70% to 85% of words cancelled.

  • Spelling a child's name from a fresh River is possible only 1% to 4% of the time, so there is no name bonus.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot plays its best-scoring word and knows every word in its list; humans will fall short.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written, and the 4-letter cap with a 6-card River.

  • Not tested: dictionary disputes and how often a doubt happens in a real game.

Variants and options

  • Rainbow Words (retired) A letter rummy with a colour bonus. Its idea of a bonus for matching colours is the link bonus here (a shared colour plus a shared suit). The rest of Rainbow Words was a weaker twin of Wordwalk and was dropped.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

WORDWALK. 8 cards face up (River). Turn: SPELL a real word of 3+ letters, one River card per letter, then take those cards in word order and refill to 8; or SWAP: discard one River card, refill. Doubted word not in dictionary = lose the turn. Fewest points plays first each round.

Back

SCORE. Card numbers plus 3 for each neighbouring pair sharing a colour AND a suit. END. Deck short: finish the round. Most points wins; tie: highest card. SHORTER GAME. Words of 4 letters at most, River of 6. LEVELS. L1 3-letter words. L2 no links. L3 full.

Inspired by Modern Art by Reiner Knizia, with the Decktet idea of cards as both goods and money

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round the Dealer puts up one card for sale. Everyone else bids a card in secret. The highest bid wins the sale and the bid card goes to the Dealer's purse. At the end the six teams are ranked by how many cards were sold, and the best teams pay the most.

What you need

All 54 cardseach card is a lot (its team is what it is worth) and also money (its number is what it bids)
Ref 4 (Team key)to read the team of each card by animal name
Pencil and paperto total the scores at the end

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Keep them secret. Put the rest face down as the draw deck.

  • Each player makes two places in front of them: a Collection (face up, for lots they win) and a Purse (face down, for money they earn).

  • Pick the first Dealer at random. The Dealer role passes to the left after every round.

  • Find the number (the big one) and the serial (the small one in the pill) on a card. The number is the bid. The serial only breaks ties.

How to play

Each round, run by the Dealer:

  1. Offer. The Dealer puts one card from their hand face up in the middle. This is the Lot. What matters about it is its team.

  2. Bids. Every other player secretly picks one card from their hand, or no card, and puts it face down. When everyone is ready, turn them over together. A bid's strength is its number. Equal numbers: the higher serial is stronger.

  3. Result. The strongest bid wins. The winner puts the Lot in their Collection. Their bid card goes face down into the Dealer's Purse. Every other bidder takes their card back. If nobody bid, the Dealer keeps the Lot in their own Collection.

  4. Refill. Everyone draws back up to 5 cards, Dealer first, then clockwise. The Dealer role moves one seat to the left.

  5. A player with no cards cannot bid. A Dealer with no cards skips their turn as Dealer.

How it ends

The game ends at once when the draw deck runs out during a refill (about 24 rounds at 2 players, 20 at 3, 17 at 4, 15 at 5). Now count. 1. Across everyone's Collections, count the cards of each of the six teams (read the Team key). 2. Rank the teams by that count. Equal counts: the team with the higher total of card numbers ranks higher; still equal, the lower team number on the Team key. 3. The teams ranked 1st to 6th are worth 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 0 points. 4. Each card in your Collection scores its team's value. 5. Add up the numbers of the cards in your Purse, divide by 4, drop any remainder. Your total is 3 + 4. Highest total wins. A tie goes to the player with more cards in their Collection.

Words in this game

  • Lot the card the Dealer puts up for sale. Its team is what counts.
  • Collection the face-up cards you have won. They score by team rank at the end.
  • Purse the face-down bid cards other players paid you when you were Dealer. A quarter of their numbers is your score.
  • Bid one card from your hand, played face down. Its number is its strength.
  • Team rank which of the six teams has the most cards across all Collections at the end.

Common questions

  • Why would I offer a card that helps my rivals? Every sold card raises its team's count for everybody, not only the winner. Offer cards from teams you already hold and try to win them yourself, or offer a card whose team nobody else wants.

  • Does it matter what team my bid card is? No. A bid card goes to the Dealer's Purse, where only its number counts (a quarter of it). Only Lots score by team.

  • What if I am Dealer and nobody bids? You keep the Lot in your Collection and nobody pays anything. That is the cheapest way to take a card, so a Lot nobody wants is a gift to the Dealer.

  • Can I bid a card of the same team as the Lot? Yes. A bid is just a number. The card goes to the Purse, not your Collection, so it does not count for the team.

  • Why is the draw deck so important? It ends the game without warning for the player who is counting on one more round. Count the deck. A round ends with a refill, and the game ends when the deck runs out in that refill.

Tips

  • Count the draw deck before every offer. The game ends the moment a refill runs dry (15 rounds at 5 players, 24 at 2), so the last few Lots are cheap for anyone who sees the end coming.

  • Offer a Lot from a team you already hold, then bid to win it yourself. Every sold card lifts that team for everyone, so only offer teams where you are likely to take the card.

  • Spend the cheapest card that can win. A bid card is worth only a quarter of its number in the Purse (the smart bot works from this), so a 9 thrown at a 1-point Lot is a loss.

  • Teams have 8, 8, 8, 10, 10 and 10 cards, so the big teams rank first slightly more often (18% against 15% in testing). Do not assume the 8-card teams are doomed, but do favour the 10-card teams when two Lots look equal.

  • When you are Dealer and a Lot is unwanted, nobody may bid and you keep it for free. A Lot from a team nobody else is chasing is a gift, so offer it when you want a quiet round.

Worked example

3 players, a real game from the simulation. Deal 5 each. P0 is the first Dealer. All facts below are checked against the card list.

  1. Round 1. P0 is Dealer and offers Kanasu (6) (number 6, a Tiger, serial 7). P1 bids Adhiraa (6) (number 6, a Tiger, serial 47). P2 bids Rihansh (9) (number 9, a Peacock). Turn them over: 9 beats 6, so P2 wins. Kanasu (6) goes to P2's Collection and Rihansh (9) goes face down into P0's Purse. P1 takes Adhiraa (6) back.

  2. Round 2. P1 is Dealer and offers Pinku (2) (number 2, a Cobra). P2 bids Naresh (6) (number 6, a Bear). P0 bids Adheesh (9) (number 9, a Bear). P0 wins. Pinku (2) goes to P0's Collection and Adheesh (9) goes into P1's Purse.

  3. Round 3. P2 is Dealer and offers Anayka (1) (number 1, an Elephant). P0 bids Nysha (8) (number 8, a Monkey). P1 bids Adhiraa (6) again (number 6). P0 wins with the 8, takes Anayka (1), and Nysha (8) goes into P2's Purse. A cheap lot for a big card is not always a good deal. P0 bid an 8 for a Lot worth at most 4 points.

  4. Scoring (the same game, after 20 rounds). Across all Collections: Peacocks 4 cards (numbers total 17), Bears 4 cards (13), Tigers 3 (11), Cobras 3 (11), Elephants 3 (6), Monkeys 3 (4). Peacocks and Bears tie on 4 cards, so the higher number total ranks first: Peacocks 1st (4 points), Bears 2nd (3). Tigers and Cobras tie on cards and on number total (11 each), so the lower team number goes first: Tigers 3rd (2 points), Cobras 4th (1). Elephants and Monkeys score 0.

  5. P1's Collection is Amyra (4), Sharada (3), Amyra (5) (three Peacocks, 4 points each, 12), Kanasu (3) (a Tiger, 2), and Naresh (6) and Smaya (1) (two Bears, 3 each, 6): 20 points. P1's Purse holds seven cards whose numbers add to 52, and 52 divided by 4 is 13. P1 totals 33 and wins over P2 (20) and P0 (17).

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

The easiest teaching round. Play with open hands and no secret bids: the Dealer offers, then everyone says aloud which card they would bid and why. Count teams on the table, ignore the Purse (treat it as 0 points). Play only until the deck has 10 cards left.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Bids are secret. The Purse scores, but as the sum of the numbers divided by 4. Play to the end of the deck. Rank only the top three teams (4, 3, 2 points).

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: all six teams rank, 4/3/2/1/0/0, tie-breaks as written, Purse divided by 4.

Solo

Race the Caravan. You are the only player. The Caravan is the other Dealer and has no hand. Deal yourself 5 cards. Each round flip the top card of the deck as the Lot and the next card as the Caravan's bid. You may play one card from your hand that beats the Caravan's bid (higher number; equal numbers, higher serial). If you do, the Lot goes to your Collection and your card goes into the Caravan's Collection (it counts for its team there). Discard the Caravan's bid card. If you do not, the Caravan takes the Lot into its Collection and its bid card goes into your Purse. Then refill to 5. Stop when the deck cannot supply two cards. Score both sides as in the normal game (team ranks from both Collections together, your Purse divided by 4). Medals by your lead over the Caravan: Bronze ahead by 1 or more, Silver by 6, Gold by 11.

Two players

Play the normal game with two. One opponent bids in each round (so only one bid is ever made), the game is about 24 rounds and the Dealer swaps every round. It is a fair duel: with equal players the first Dealer wins half the games. Bid when the Lot matters more to you than the card you give up.

Maths and skills in this game

Comparing numbers up to 9, dividing by 4 and dropping the remainder, ranking six teams by a count, using a total as a tie-break, and simple expected-value thinking: a big card is worth only a quarter of its number in the Purse, so spend it on a Lot that gains you more than that.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the bid strength, and a quarter of it is the Purse score
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule what a Lot is worth: teams are ranked by cards sold, and a Collection card scores its team's value
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks ties between equal bids
NamesFlavour the children are the traders on the road
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random bots 83% at 3p, 76% at 4p, 69% at 5p (even: 33, 25, 20), 15 to 24 rounds, seats fair within 1.5 points

SettingResult
2p smart v random / simple94% / 98% (even 50%), 24 rounds
3p smart v random / simple83% / 81% (even 33%), 20 rounds
4p smart v random / simple76% / 70% (even 25%), 17 rounds
5p smart v random / simple69% / 63% (even 20%), 15 rounds
All smart, seat share3p 33.5/32.8/33.7; 4p 24.9/26.2/24.4/24.4; 5p 19.7 to 20.6
Score median (quartiles), all smart2p 32 (29 to 35); 3p 24 (20 to 28); 4p 16 (13 to 19); 5p 11 (9 to 15)
Solo medals (lead over Caravan)Bronze 1, Silver 6, Gold 11 (quartiles 0 / 6 / 11)
Rule change: extra count for teams 1 to 3with it 8-card teams rank first 20.7% on average vs 12.6% for 10-card; without 15% vs 18%

  • Three bots were used: random (any legal bid or none), simple (offers its most-held team, bids a big card half the time when it holds the team) and smart (works out how much a Lot raises its own and its rivals' team score, and bids the cheapest card likely to win). Each setting was 2,000 games on the real card list.

  • Smart against random bots won 94% at 2 players, 83% at 3, 76% at 4 and 69% at 5 (fair share 50, 33, 25, 20). Smart against simple bots won 98%, 81%, 70% and 63%. With all smart bots, seats were within 1 to 1.5 points of an even share (for example 3p 33.5 / 32.8 / 33.7). The first Dealer is random.

  • Length: 24 rounds at 2 players, 20 at 3, 17 at 4, 15 at 5. At about a minute a round that is 15 to 24 minutes. Ties for the win: 0.1 to 2.5% before the Collection tie-break.

  • Score spread (all smart, median with quartiles): 3p 24 (20 to 28), 4p 16 (13 to 19), 5p 11 (9 to 15), 2p 32 (29 to 35). The Collection gives about 54 to 60% of a typical score and the Purse the rest.

  • Testing removed the rule 'teams 1 to 3 count as having one extra card' because it over-corrects. It was meant to help the 8-card teams, but with it the 8-card teams ranked first 31.6% / 20.4% / 10.2% (smart 4p) against 6.5% to 19.7% for the 10-card teams (averages 20.7% and 12.6%). Without it 8-card teams rank first on average 15% of games against 18% for 10-card teams (4p, all smart), which is much closer. The ranking tie-break is unchanged (number total, then lower team number), and the rule is one line shorter on the card.

  • Other tie-break orders were tried (smaller team first, or higher serial). None was clearly fairer, so the current order stays.

  • Solo, Race the Caravan: a bot that bids the cheapest card that beats the Caravan when the gain is worth the card beat the Caravan in 74% of games. Lead over the Caravan (quartiles): 0 / 6 / 11. A bot that bids at random loses to the Caravan 79% of the time. These set the medals.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots bid from fixed formulas; humans read each other and bluff by offering a bad card, which is not modelled.

  • Not tested: the solo Caravan with people. Only a bot has played it.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 separately. They are variants of the same rules.

  • Five players ran in the simulations, but with only 15 rounds each player is Dealer 3 times. If that feels thin, play with 3 or 4.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

SILK ROAD. A caravan auction. Every card is a crate to sell and a coin to spend. Deal 5 each. Collection face up, Purse face down. Each round the Dealer puts up a Lot. Everyone else bids one card (or none) in secret. Turn them over together. Highest NUMBER wins; equal numbers, higher serial. The winner takes the Lot into their Collection. The bid card goes face down to the Dealer's Purse. Others take theirs back. Refill to 5. Dealer moves left. No bids: the Dealer keeps the Lot. The game ends when the deck runs out.

Back

SCORING. Count the cards of each team in all Collections (Ref 4). Rank the teams: most cards first; ties go to the higher total of numbers, then the lower team number. 1st to 6th are worth 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 0. Each Collection card scores its team's value. Purse: add the numbers, divide by 4, drop the remainder. Highest total wins; a tie goes to more cards in the Collection. LEVELS. L1 open hands, no Purse. L2 secret bids, top three teams score. L3 the full game. SOLO: Race the Caravan. Medals by your lead: Bronze 1, Silver 6, Gold 11.

GA

Grown-ups · Game 2 of 13 · Auction with a money squeeze · Fronts

The Gala

Tonight's guests pay with the same cards they hope to be remembered for, and the host quietly notices who has gone home with nothing left.

Inspired by High Society by Reiner Knizia

Grown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-02
Players
2 to 5 (best with 3 or 4)
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
12+ (L1 from 10)
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Turn up a lot each round and bid by putting out money cards. Prizes are won by the highest bid, Disgraces and the Scandal are dodged by being the first to give in. The game ends at the fourth red card. Highest score wins, but the poorest guest loses 10 points.

What you need

All 54 cards17 become the lots; the rest are money, worth their number
Pencil and paperfor the end score

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Build the Lot deck of 17 cards, face down, from the 54: 10 PRIZES (any ten cards numbered 2 to 8), 3 PEERAGES (three of the nines), 1 SCANDAL (the fourth nine), 3 DISGRACES (three of the ones). Shuffle it.

  • Every other card is money, worth its number. Shuffle it and deal each player 14 cards at 2 players, 11 at 3, 8 at 4, 7 at 5. Put the rest of the money away unseen.

  • Choose the first player. Each player keeps their money in hand, and will keep their won lots in a face-up row.

  • Peerages and the Scandal are the red cards. Mark them by putting a pawn or a note beside the Lot deck: you will count four.

How to play

Each round, turn up the top lot.

  1. Prize or Peerage: a normal auction. Starting with the player whose turn it is, each player in turn either raises or passes. A bid is the total number on all the money cards you have put in front of you in this auction. A raise must beat the highest bid so far, using cards already out and any you add. If you pass, take your cards back and drop out of this auction. The last player left wins the lot and discards the money they put out. If everyone else passes at once, the last player left wins the lot free.

  2. Disgrace or Scandal: a reverse auction. Each player in turn either adds money cards face up or passes. The first to pass takes the lot and keeps the cards they put out. Everyone else loses the cards they put out (discard them). Cards added need not beat anyone. A player with no cards must pass.

  3. The player to the left of the player who won (or had to take) the lot starts the next round.

  4. When the fourth red card (a Peerage or the Scandal) is turned up, the game ends at once. That card is not auctioned.

How it ends

Score: add the numbers on your prizes. Each Peerage you won doubles that total. The Scandal halves it, rounding down. Each Disgrace you took is minus 5, taken off after the doubling and halving. Then count the money cards left in each player's hand, by number. The player with the least money loses 10 points. Ties for poorest: fewer cards is poorest; still tied, the lower score; still tied, the player furthest clockwise from the first player. Highest score wins. A tie goes to the player with more money.

Words in this game

  • Lot the card turned up to be bid for or dodged.
  • Prize a card numbered 2 to 8 used as a lot. Its number is points.
  • Peerage a nine used as a red lot. It doubles your prize total.
  • Scandal the fourth nine, a red lot. It halves your prize total. Nobody wants it.
  • Disgrace a one used as a lot. Minus 5 points.
  • Bid the numbers of the money cards you have put out in front of you in this auction.
  • Poorest the player whose money left in hand adds up to the least at the end. They lose 10 points.

Common questions

  • Can I put out more money than I need? Yes, but once the auction is won your cards are discarded. Money is also your shield against being poorest, so spend with care.

  • What if everyone passes on a Prize? The last player to pass, the one still in, wins it for free. Late seats get free prizes, which is why passing on a good prize is a risk.

  • Do I have to bid on Peerages? No, but a Peerage is the only way to double a big prize total, and it is cheap early on. Rivals will chase later ones.

  • Can the poorest player still win? Yes. They lose 10 points but may still have the best score. In the simulation the leader was the poorest player in about a third of games at 4 players, and the penalty changed the winner in about one game in five.

  • What happens to money I put out in a reverse auction? If you pass first you take the Disgrace or Scandal and keep your cards. If someone else passes first, you lose what you put out. So adding cards is paying to make someone else take it.

Tips

  • Watch the money, not just the prizes. The poorest guest loses 10 points, and in testing the leader was also the poorest in about a third of 4-player games, so keep your hand total just above the poorest rival.

  • Bid hardest on a Peerage when you already hold big prizes. It doubles your whole prize total, so it is worth more to the player with more prizes and cheap early on.

  • In a reverse auction (Disgrace or Scandal), the first to pass takes the lot and keeps their cards. Adding cards only pays to make someone else take it, so add only when the rival will give in before you do.

  • Passing on a Prize is a risk because the last player left wins it free. If everyone else is about to pass, one more pass from you can hand a late seat a free prize.

  • Neither hoarding nor dumping everything on the first lot won more than 0.5% of games, so spend steadily. Put money out only on lots that move your score by more than the 10 points you risk.

Worked example

4 players, real cards from the deck. Lots (in order) begin {K44}, {K11}, {K54}. P3 is first. Money in hand: P0 has {K04}, {K08}, {K14}, {K21}, {K30}, {K27}, {K25}, {K38}. P3 has {K01}, {K17}, {K23}, {K22}, {K31}, {K39}, {K43}, {K46}.

  1. Round 1. The lot is the prize Nysha (8) (number 8). P3 puts out Ajay (7) (7). Bid 7.

  2. P0 puts out Pinku (7) (7) and Nysha (1) (1). Bid 8, which beats 7. P1 passes. P2 passes.

  3. P3 adds Naresh (3) (3) to the Ajay (7) already out. The bid is 10, which beats 8. P0 passes and takes Pinku (7) and Nysha (1) back.

  4. P3 is the last player left. P3 wins Nysha (8), discards Ajay (7) and Naresh (3), and keeps Arvind (1), Nakul (4), Bharati (4), Naresh (6), Smaya (8), Anayka (8), which add up to 31. P0, to P3's left, starts round 2.

  5. A later round. The lot is the Disgrace Anayka (1) (number 1, minus 5). P0 adds Nysha (1) and P1 adds Shreya (2). P2 passes at once, so P2 takes Anayka (1), keeps the cards they put out (none), and P0 and P1 lose the cards they put out.

  6. End of the game. P2 won prizes Arvind (8) (8), Guhan (6) (6) and Bharati (5) (5), which make 19, and the Peerage Rihansh (9), so the total doubles to 38. P2 also took two Disgraces, Anayka (1) and Amay (1): 38 minus 10 is 28. P2 has only Smaya (1) (1) and Pinku (2) (2) left, 3 points of money, the least of anyone. P2 loses 10 points and finishes on 18.

  7. P3 won prizes Nysha (8) (8), Idhayan (8) (8), Kanasu (3) (3) and Archana (5) (5): 24 points and no multipliers. P3 wins with 24, though P2 had the better raw score (28). The 10-point penalty decided it.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. Use only the 10 prizes and the 3 Peerages (13 lots). The game ends at the third Peerage. No Disgraces, no Scandal, and nobody loses points for being poorest.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add the 3 Disgraces and the Scandal (the full 17 lots). The game ends at the fourth red card. Still no penalty for being poorest.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: the poorest player loses 10 points.

Solo

Lone Guest. Deal yourself 11 money cards. Build the 17-card Lot deck. Keep the rest of the money as the pile. For each lot, flip two cards from the pile and add their numbers: that is the price. A Prize or Peerage: you may win it by putting out cards worth more than the price (discard them), or you may pass. A Disgrace or Scandal: you may dodge it by putting out cards worth at least the price (discard them), or you must take it. Discard the two flipped cards each round and shuffle the discards back if the pile runs out. The game ends at the fourth red card. Score as usual, and lose 10 if the money left in your hand is under 10. Medals: Bronze 3, Silver 12, Gold 27.

Two players

Deal 14 money cards each. The rules do not change. With two players, the poorest-player penalty applies to one of you every game, so the money you keep is decisive: spend it only on lots that move the score by more than the 10 points you risk.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding several numbers, comparing totals, deciding if a lot is worth its price, and a little expected-value thinking: a Peerage doubles the total you have, so it is worth more to a player with more prizes. Doubling and halving with whole numbers, and keeping a running balance of what you can afford.

ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used only for tie-breaks in the unlikely case of exactly equal bids, which cannot happen because a raise must beat the last bid
NamesFlavour the children are the guests at the Gala
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random 81% at 3p, 75% at 4p (even 33, 25); poorest-loses-10 changes the winner in about 1 game in 5 (poorest-out rule: 1 in 3 at 4p)

SettingResult
Poorest OUT, smart v random2p 63%, 3p 76%, 4p 72%, 5p 67%
Poorest LOSES 10, smart v random2p 89%, 3p 81%, 4p 75%, 5p 69%
Leader is poorest (OUT rule decides)2p 80%, 3p 54%, 4p 34%, 5p 28%
Penalty flips the winner (LOSE 10)2p 7%, 3p 23%, 4p 22%, 5p 21%
Length (actions, lots)2p 46, 3p 68, 4p 78, 5p 93 actions; 13.4 lots

  • Bots were random, simple (bids up to a fixed multiple of the prize) and smart (sets a ceiling from the value of the lot and keeps its money near the poorest rival's), on the real card list and 17-lot deck, 1,500 games per setting for each rule. Two rules for the poorest player were compared. With 'poorest is out', the poorest player was the raw leader in 80% of 2-player, 54% of 3-player, 34% of 4-player and 28% of 5-player games (smart bots), so the rule decided that share of games. With 'poorest loses 10', the penalty changed the winner in 7% (2p), 23% (3p), 22% (4p) and 21% (5p).

  • Skill, one smart bot against random bots (fair share 50 / 33 / 25 / 20): 'out' 63 / 76 / 72 / 67%; 'minus 10' 89 / 81 / 75 / 69%. At 2 players 'out' is a coin-flip with a lot of luck (the poorer player loses automatically); 'minus 10' is far better. At 3 to 5 the skill is about equal, within the noise. Testing chose 'minus 10', and it is the rule in the game.

  • Seats are fair. All-smart win shares: 3p 34.7 / 33.1 / 32.1; 4p 24.6 / 27.3 / 23.0 / 25.1; 5p 17.9 to 21.8; 2p 51.1 / 48.9. Ties for the win: 0.07% (2p), 0.2% (3p), 0.9% (4p), 0.8% (5p).

  • Hoarding (never bidding) won 0.2 to 0.3% of games and dumping all money on the first lot won 0.2 to 0.5%, with either rule, so neither extreme is a dominant move.

  • Length: 13.4 lots per game on average; 46 / 68 / 78 / 93 auction actions at 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 players, which is about 15 / 23 / 26 / 31 minutes at 20 seconds an action and 9 to 19 minutes at 12 seconds. Testing changed prizes from 12 to 10 (deck 19 to 17 cards) for this reason: lots per game fell from 14.8 to 13.4, actions from 84 to 78 at 4p, and the score spread (standard deviation) from 11.6 to 9.8.

  • Smart against simple bots was at or a little below an even share (2p 35%, 3p 33%, 4p 22%, 5p 14%), so the smart bot's edge over a simple 'bid up to a multiple of the prize' bot is not shown. The measured skill is against random play only. Score median (quartiles), all smart 4p: 8 (2 to 14).

  • Solo, Lone Guest: a bot that wins a lot when the price is at most twice its value and keeps at least 10 of money had a median of 12 (quartiles 2 / 12 / 27) over 3,000 games.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots follow fixed ceilings. People bluff, and a clever player passes on a prize to watch rivals empty their hands.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 (no Disgrace, no penalty).

  • Not tested: smart play beating simple play. The claim that good players win more rests on the random-bot results.

  • Two players with the 10-point rule worked in simulation, but with only two players the poorest-player penalty hits one of you every game.

  • Not tested: the solo Lone Guest with people. Only a bot has played it.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

THE GALA. A guest list that pays in the same cards. 17 lots: 10 prizes (2 to 8), 3 Peerages and 1 Scandal (nines), 3 Disgraces (ones). The rest is money, worth its number. Deal 11 (3p), 8 (4p), 7 (5p). Turn up a lot. Prize or Peerage: raise (beat the highest bid) or pass and take your cards back. Last in wins and discards their cards. Disgrace or Scandal: add cards or pass. First to pass takes it and keeps theirs; the others lose theirs. The winner's left starts the next round. The fourth red card (Peerage or Scandal) ends the game.

Back

SCORE. Prize numbers added. Each Peerage doubles. The Scandal halves (round down). Each Disgrace minus 5. The poorest player (least money left) loses 10. Highest wins; a tie goes to more money. LEVELS. L1 prizes and Peerages only, no penalty. L2 add Disgraces and the Scandal. L3 full game with the 10-point penalty. SOLO. Lone Guest: price = two flipped cards; win a prize by paying more, dodge a Disgrace by paying at least. Lose 10 if you finish with under 10 money. Medals: Bronze 3, Silver 12, Gold 27.

Grown-ups · Game 3 of 13 · Simultaneous bidding, ties by dice · Fronts

Market Raid

The camp market opens at dawn. Everyone slips one card to a stall at the same moment, and the watchmen are listening for a bargain that adds up to nine.

Inspired by Razzia (the older bar-and-police dice-duel game)

Grown-upsHard
Game code
GU-03
Players
2 to 6 (2 and solo with the Inspector)
Time
25 to 30 min
Age
Grown-ups (L1 teaches in 7 min)
Dice
1 die (duels; at L3 also read on the Colour key)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round, everyone secretly puts one card at a stall at the same time; two cards at a stall that add up to 9 are raided and both lost, otherwise the highest number takes the prize, and ties are settled by a dice duel.

What you need

All 54 cardsYour stock of 6, the prizes on the stalls, and the prizes you win
1 plain dieDice duels for ties; at L3 also the hot colour, read on the Colour key (Ref 3)
Pencil and paperA running score across the days

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • A game is 1 market day (L1), 2 days (L2) or 3 days (L3). Each day is set up the same way.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards and deal each player 6 cards: your stock. Look at it, keep the fronts hidden.

  • Set out the stalls in a row: 3 stalls with 2, 3 or 6 players; 4 stalls with 4 or 5 players. The rest of the cards are the draw pile (with 6 players the stock and 3 stalls use all 54 cards).

  • L3: roll the die and read it on the Colour key. That is today's hot colour: a prize that shows it is worth double.

  • Play 6 rounds per day, one for each card in your stock.

How to play

Each round:

  1. Prizes: turn up one card from the draw pile above each stall. A prize is worth its number.

  2. Choose: everyone picks one card from their stock and puts it face down next to a stall. When everyone has chosen, turn the cards over together.

  3. Raid (L2 and L3): at each stall, if two cards add up to 9, the watchmen take both. Remove them: those players win nothing at this stall. Check again for more pairs. If a card could pair with more than one card, take the card with the lowest serial number that has a partner, and pair it with its partner of lowest serial.

  4. Win: the highest number left at the stall wins the prize. A lone card wins automatically.

  5. Dice duel: if two or more highest cards are tied, those players roll the die. The highest roll wins; roll again on a tie. If no card is left at a stall, the prize goes in the box.

  6. Played cards go in the box. The winner keeps the prize card face up in front of them. After round 6, the day is over.

How it ends

After each day add up your prize numbers; at L3 hot-colour prizes count double. L3 bonus: +5 for every pair of prizes you won that day whose numbers add to 9 (each prize can be in one pair only). Add the day scores. Highest total wins. Ties: more prize cards won, then the highest serial among your prizes.

Words in this game

  • Stock Your 6 cards for the day. Each round you use one.
  • Stall A place where cards compete for one prize.
  • Raid Two cards at a stall that add up to 9. Both are removed.
  • Dice duel The tie-break among equal top cards: roll the die, highest wins.
  • Hot colour The colour rolled on the Colour key at L3. Prizes showing it count double.
  • Bond pair Two prizes whose numbers add to 9, worth a bonus at L3.

Common questions

  • Can I put my card on a stall where I think nobody else will go? Yes. A lone card wins at once, even a 1. That is the whole game: guess where the others will go and send your high cards where the prizes are big and the crowd is small.

  • What if three cards are at one stall and two of them add up to 9? The two are raided and removed. The third wins the stall if it is the only one left. If all three are in two overlapping pairs (for example 4, 5, 5), take the card with the lowest serial that has a partner and pair it with its lowest-serial partner. Check again.

  • Does a 9 get raided? Only by a 0, and there are none, so a 9 is never raided. But a 9 meeting another 9 is a tie and goes to a dice duel.

  • Do the spare cards matter at the end? No. After 6 rounds you have used all your stock. The draw pile gives the prizes.

  • Is the dice duel fair for the player who rolled the hot colour? The hot colour is only about prizes. The duel is a plain die: highest wins.

Tips

  • Send your high cards where the prize is big and the crowd is small. A lone card wins at once, even a 1, so a 9 on a busy stall is often wasted.

  • Remember that a 9 can never be raided (there is no 0), but two 9s at one stall go to a dice duel. A card whose partner is likely to arrive (a 4 next to a likely 5) is the one in danger.

  • Do not always follow the biggest prize. The smart bot was tuned on the cost of spending a high card, and raising that cost lifted its win rate against random play at 3, 4 and 6 players.

  • At L3 check the hot colour before round 1: a prize showing it counts double, so plan which stall that colour will land on and send a good card there.

  • At 5 or 6 players expect many raids (6.4 and 9.3 per game), so spread bets and do not rely on one stall. At 2 or 3 players raids are rare, so go for plain highest-card play.

Worked example

Six players, 3 stalls, L3, hot colour Red.

  1. The prizes are Pinku (7) (7), Bharati (5) (5) and Dhruv (3) (3). Pinku (7) and Bharati (5) both show Red, so they are worth 14 and 10. Dhruv (3) does not show Red, so it is worth 3.

  2. Stall 1: Ann puts Bharati (4) (4) and Ben puts Amyra (5) (5). 4 + 5 = 9, so the watchmen raid it. Both cards go, and the 14-point prize Pinku (7) goes in the box.

  3. Stall 2: Cy puts Amay (8) (8) and Dee puts Arvind (8) (8). No raid (16, not 9). It is a tie, so they roll the die. Cy rolls 5 and Dee rolls 2: Cy wins Bharati (5) and scores 10.

  4. Stall 3: Eli puts Bn Sharada (7) (7) and Fay puts Archana (5) (5). 7 + 5 = 12, not a raid. Eli has the higher number and wins Dhruv (3) for 3.

  5. Later that day, if Eli also wins Naresh (6) (6), then Dhruv (3) (3) and Naresh (6) (6) add to 9: a bond pair, +5 bonus.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. 1 day. No raids: highest number wins, ties by dice duel. No hot colour, no bonus.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

2 days. Raids with cards that add to 9.

L3 · age 8 and up

3 days. Raids, a hot colour each day (the Colour key), and the bond-pair bonus.

Solo

Solo: play against the Inspector. He has his own 6-card stock, face down, and each round plays the top card on the stall with the biggest prize (leftmost if tied). He is scored like a player and takes part in raids and duels. Play 3 days (L3). Medals on your total: Gold 106, Silver 89, Bronze 72. You also win if you beat him. A bot beat him 53% of the time.

Two players

Two players plus the Inspector as a third player (3 stalls). He plays exactly as in solo. Two humans with the Inspector won 75.5% of games between them (67% would be even), so he is a gentle third player. Without the Inspector, two players at 3 stalls works but has few raids (about one per game).

Maths and skills in this game

Number bonds to 9, comparing and estimating where the others will go (probability), adding prize scores, doubling.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule Highest number wins; two cards that add to 9 are raided; bond pairs of prizes score a bonus.
ColoursRule At L3 the Colour key sets a hot colour whose prizes count double.
Suit pairNot used Not used.
Back patternNot used Not used.
TeamNot used Not used.
Letter tileNot used Not used.
SerialRule Picks which pair is raided first, and breaks final ties.
NamesFlavour Prizes are the stall goods; names are just who sells.
ExpressionNot used Not used.
PlaceNot used Not used.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random 93% at 4p L3 (25% even), 2p 96%; 3 days about 19 to 23 min

SettingResult
2p L3 (3 days)smart vs random 96% (50% even); raids 1.1, duels 3.9 per game; median 91 points
3p L391% (33%); 5.4 duels; median 62
4p L393% (25%); 3.9 raids; median 50; raw ties 1.3%

6p L366% (17%); 9.3 raids; median 29

4p L1 (1 day, no raids)71% (25%); median 9
Solo vs Inspector L3bot wins 53%; points 72/89/106 at 25th/50th/75th

  • Skill counts everywhere, and least at 6 players with only 3 stalls (up to 9 raids per game). Smart bot vs random bots (2,000 games per setting; fair share in brackets), L3 3 days: 2p 96% (50%), 3p 91% (33%), 4p 93% (25%), 5p 86% (20%), 6p 66% (17%); L2 2 days: 94%, 82%, 82%, 72%, 56%; L1 1 day: 87%, 71%, 71%, 62%, 45%.

  • No seat has an advantage. With all-smart bots the seat win shares are flat (4p L3 24.1 to 25.9%; 6p 14.7 to 18.4%). Raw ties on score are 0.8 to 2.4% at L3 and 1.7 to 5.9% at L1, all settled by the prize-count and serial tie-breaks.

  • Raids and duels per L3 game (3 days): 2p 1.1 raids and 3.9 duels; 3p 2.3 and 5.4; 4p 3.9 and 7.0; 5p 6.4 and 7.9; 6p 9.3 and 9.0. Raids grow with the number of players, so the game gets chaotic at 6.

  • Testing changed the game from one day to 3 days at L3 (2 at L2) because one day is about 7 min, under the 10 to 25 min target. A round takes 55 s with 3 stalls and 65 s with 4 (about 20 s to choose plus 10 s per stall to resolve), so 18 rounds take 19 min with 2, 3 or 6 players and about 23 min with 4 or 5 (4 stalls); two days back to back (L2) would be 12 to 15 min.

  • Testing replaced the earlier L3 bonus (+3 for a pair of prizes that are twins, the same face), which fired only 0.16 to 0.39 times per game, with a bond-pair bonus (two won prizes that add to 9) worth +5, and added the hot colour (doubles). The bond bonus still fires rarely, 0.2 to 0.7 pairs per game in all, because the smart bot does not chase it, so it is a small extra for human collectors, not a core rule; the effect of the hot colour alone was not isolated.

  • The smart bot was tuned on the cost of spending a high card; the version kept raised its win rate vs random bots at 3p, 4p and 6p to 89%, 87% and 61% in a 500-game trial.

  • Inspector: one bot vs the Inspector over 3 days wins 53% (50% would be even); points 10th/25th/50th/75th/90th = 57/72/89/106/121. Two bots plus the Inspector win 75.5% between them (66.7% even).

  • No stalls or loops: each round ends after every player has played one card, so all rounds are a fixed length.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Bots choose with an estimate of winning each stall against random opponents; real opponents bluff and follow patterns, so tells and second-guessing are untested.

  • Not tested: the effect of the hot colour on its own, and the effect of the bond-pair bonus on a bot that chases it.

  • Not tested: games with 2 players and no Inspector (only the Inspector variant was run).

  • Not tested: whether the more chaotic five- and six-player games are fun.

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

MARKET RAID. The market opens at dawn. Everyone sends one card to a stall at the same time. NEED: 2 to 6 players, all 54 cards, a die. SET UP: Each day shuffle and deal 6 cards (your stock). Lay 3 stalls (4 stalls with 4 or 5 players). PLAY (6 rounds a day): Turn up one prize card above each stall. Everyone puts one card face down at a stall, then all turn over together. Two cards at a stall that add to 9 are raided: both are out (lowest serial pairs first). The highest number left wins the prize. A tie goes to a dice duel. SCORE: prize numbers; the hot colour (Colour key, L3) counts double; a pair of your prizes adding to 9 gives +5.

Back

LEVELS. L1: 1 day, no raids. L2: 2 days, with raids. L3: 3 days, hot colour and bond-pair bonus. TIES: more prizes, then the higher serial. SOLO: play against the Inspector, who plays his top card on the stall with the biggest prize. L3 medals: Gold 106, Silver 89, Bronze 72. TWO PLAYERS: add the Inspector as a third player. COLOUR KEY (Ref 3): Red 1, Orange 2, Yellow 3, Green 4, Blue 5, Purple 6. TIPS: a lone 1 beats a crowded 9; send your high cards where the big prize is but the crowd is small.

Grown-ups · Game 4 of 13 · Bluffing and counting · Fronts

Tall Tales

Around the campfire everyone swears the tale is true. Somebody is stretching it.

Inspired by Perudo and Liar's Dice

RecommendedGrown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-04
Players
2 to 6 (best with 3 to 5)
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
12+ (L1 from 10)
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each player holds a few cards no one else can see. Take turns claiming how many cards of a suit lie on the whole table, raising the claim or calling 'Liar!'. Whoever is wrong loses a card. The last player with cards wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsshuffled and dealt fresh every round
Ref 4the Suit key: suits are claimed by number 1 to 6

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Choose how many cards each player starts with: 5 cards at 2 or 3 players, 4 at 4 players, 3 at 5 or 6 players.

  • Each round, shuffle all 54 cards and deal each player their current number of cards. Set the rest aside unseen. Look only at the fronts of your own cards.

  • Every card shows two suits. A card carries a suit if either of its two suits matches. Every suit is on exactly 18 of the 54 cards.

  • Pick the first opener. The opener passes to the left each round.

How to play

Each round:

  1. A claim is a number and a suit: "at least Q cards carry suit S", counting every card in every hand. Say it aloud, for example "at least 6 of suit 4".

  2. The opener makes the first claim. The opener has nothing to call, so they must claim. Then, going clockwise, each player must either:

  3. Raise. Make a higher claim. That is a larger Q with any suit, or the same Q with a higher suit number.

  4. Call "Liar!". Everyone shows their cards and counts the real total of the claimed suit. If the real count is at least Q, the claim was true and the caller loses. If it is below Q, the claim was false and the claimant loses.

  5. If no higher claim exists, you must call. There is no "spot on".

  6. The loser of the challenge has one fewer card in every later round. At 0 cards you are out.

How it ends

The last player with cards wins. Players who are out watch, and may help count.

Words in this game

  • Claim "at least Q cards carry suit S" across all hands at the table.
  • Carry a card carries a suit if either of its two suits is that suit.
  • Raise a bigger claim: more cards, or the same number and a higher suit number.
  • Liar the call that ends the round. Cards are shown and counted.
  • Opener the player who makes the first claim of a round. It cannot be called.

Common questions

  • How do I know how many to claim? Your own cards are the only hard facts. Each suit is on one card in three, so with N cards dealt the average for one suit is N/3 (see the counting table on the reference card). Claim the suit you hold most of, since you know that part is there.

  • Can I raise the same number with a lower suit? No. The same number needs a higher suit number. 6 of suit 4 can be raised to 6 of suit 5, but not to 6 of suit 3.

  • What if my claim is exactly right? A claim is true if the real count is at least Q, so exactly Q is true. The caller loses.

  • Can I call the opener's first claim? Yes. The player after the opener may raise it or call "Liar!" on it. Only the opener cannot call, because there is nothing to call yet.

  • Is it a long wait if I am out early? A little. Knocked-out players wait about 2 to 3 minutes at 4 players. Count along: you are still learning the cards.

Tips

  • Each suit is on exactly 18 of the 54 cards, so about one card in three carries it. With N cards on the table, N/3 is your starting estimate, and your own cards are the only hard facts. Claim the suit you hold most of.

  • Raise by suit number when you can. The same count with a higher suit is a legal raise, so a small step up (6 of suit 4 to 6 of suit 5) costs little and keeps the pressure on the next player.

  • Call when the claim sounds more than your own cards plus an even share of the rest. The smart bot calls when the chance a claim is true is under 42% and raises when the next claim is at least 50% likely.

  • A claim is true if the real count is at least Q, so exactly Q means the caller loses. Do not call a claim that is merely tight.

  • The bots never bluff, so their edge is a lower bound. A well-timed bluff on a suit you hold none of is where a human can do better than the 60% to 97% the bots show.

Worked example

4 players, 4 cards each, a real round from the deck. Seat 0 holds {K14}, {K45}, {K28}, {K23}. Seat 1 holds {K16}, {K43}, {K27}, {K18}. Seat 2 holds {K51}, {K05}, {K47}, {K09}. Seat 3 holds {K04}, {K37}, {K19}, {K11}.

  1. Seat 0 opens: at least 5 of suit 3. Seat 0 holds two cards with suit 3 (Adhiraa (3) and Nakul (4)), so that is a claim of 5 across 16 cards.

  2. Seat 1 raises: 5 of suit 5. The same number with a higher suit number is a raise. Seat 1 holds two cards with suit 5 (Sharada (3) and Kanasu (3)).

  3. Seat 2 raises: 6 of suit 5. A larger number is a raise. Seat 2 holds one card with suit 5, Arvind (8).

  4. Seat 3 raises: 7 of suit 5. Seat 3 holds two cards with suit 5 (Amyra (4) and Bn Sharada (2)) and is hoping for five more.

  5. Seat 0 calls "Liar!" Everyone shows their cards. The cards carrying suit 5 are Archana (5), Sharada (3), Kanasu (3), Arvind (8), Amyra (4) and Bn Sharada (2): 6 cards. That is below 7, so the claim was false. Seat 3 loses a card and has 3 cards next round. Seat 1 opens round 2.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. Play with open hands on the table (helper sets the count). Everyone has 3 cards. Claims use only the numbers, not the suit order. One challenge and the game restarts with the loser's hand a card smaller.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Normal rules with 5 cards each at any table size, and the counting table is on the table. Players can use pencil and paper.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: starting cards by table size (5, 5, 4, 3, 3), no counting aids.

Solo

Lone Teller. Play 6 rounds. Each round deal yourself 5 cards and deal 15 more face down in a row. Look only at your 5. Name a suit and a number Q. Reveal the 15 and count every card carrying that suit among all 20. If the count is at least Q, score +Q. If it is below Q, score minus Q. Add your 6 rounds. A bot that picks the best expected score had a median of 35. Medals: Bronze 20, Silver 30, Gold 36.

Two players

Each player starts with 5 cards. The rules do not change; the table has only 10 cards, so claims are small and quick (a game takes about 9 minutes). The player who loses a challenge gets one card fewer; play to 0. For more depth, play best of three.

Maths and skills in this game

Estimating a proportion (one in three), averages and spread, counting across hidden sets, deciding if a claim is likely, and the idea that a total of cards is a sum of what you know and what you guess.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used card numbers do not matter; the claim uses its own number Q
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule a card carries a suit if either of its two suits matches; each suit is on exactly 18 cards
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour the children are the tellers of tall tales
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

  • Bots were random (random raise or call), simple (claims from its own count plus an even share of the rest) and smart (works out the exact chance a claim is true from its own cards and calls when that is under 42%, raises when the next claim is at least 50% likely). The smart bot assumes about two extra matching cards in the other hands, a bias found by tuning against simple bots. It does not bluff, so the skill gap is a lower bound. The real card list was used (each suit on exactly 18 cards).

  • Length by player count and starting hand (all smart bots, 600 games, rounds / auction actions): 2p start 5: 6.7 / 28; 3p start 5: 12.0 / 57; 4p start 4: 13.7 / 69; 5p start 3: 13.2 / 67; 6p start 3: 16.2 / 88. At 20 seconds an action that is 9 / 19 / 23 / 22 / 29 minutes.

Before, 4 players took 17.2 rounds and 90 actions (30 minutes at 20 seconds), 5 players 22 rounds and 122 actions (41 minutes). After: 4 players 13.7 rounds and 69 actions (23 minutes), 5 players 13.2 rounds and 67 actions (22 minutes). Skill is nearly unchanged: smart v simple 60.5% before, 59.5% after at 4 players.

  • Skill (one smart bot, starting hands as now, 600 games): v random 100 / 99 / 97 / 92 / 89% at 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 6 players; v simple 88 / 70 / 60 / 46 / 42% (even 50 / 33 / 25 / 20 / 17). All-smart seats are even: 4p 26.8 / 26.3 / 24.7 / 22.2; 3p 33.2 / 33.0 / 33.8. No stalls or endless games in any run (the 400-round guard was never hit).

  • A fixed strategy of always calling or always raising the least likely suit does not beat smart play. Claims per round: about 2.7 for simple play, 4 for smart.

  • Solo, Lone Teller: a best-expected-score bot scored a median of 35 over 6 rounds; 95% of games reached 20, 68% reached 30, and at least a quarter reached 36.

  • There is no 'Spot on' call: a trivial spotter beat the bots and made game length swing from 3 to over 30 rounds.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real bluffing. The smart bot never bluffs, and the simple one claims honestly; real players bluff and read each other's raises. People may beat the bots' skill gap in either direction.

  • Not tested: L1 (open hands) and L2.

  • Not tested: whether players find 3 starting cards at 5 or 6 players too small a hand to feel the skill.

  • Not tested: a points version, which an early check suggested favoured chance over skill at 5 and 6 players.

  • Not tested: solo Lone Teller medals with people. They come from a bot that maximises expected score; a human may take more risks.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TALL TALES. Each round shuffle all 54 and deal 5 (2 or 3 players), 4 (4 players) or 3 (5 or 6 players) cards each. Look at your own only. A CLAIM is "at least Q cards carry suit S", counting every hand. A card carries a suit if either of its two suits matches (suits are read on the Suit key). The opener claims first. Then each player RAISES (a bigger Q, or the same Q with a higher suit number) or calls "LIAR!". Show all cards. Real count at least Q: the caller loses a card. Below Q: the claimant does. At 0 cards you are out. Last one standing wins.

Back

COUNTING. Each suit is on 18 of 54 cards (one in three). Average count of one suit and its spread, by cards dealt: 6 cards, 2.0 (1.1); 9, 3.0 (1.3); 12, 4.0 (1.5); 15, 5.0 (1.6); 16, 5.3 (1.6); 18, 6.0 (1.6). LEVELS. L1 open hands. L2 counting table out. L3 full game. SOLO: Lone Teller. Deal yourself 5, 15 more face down, claim Q of a suit, score +Q if right or minus Q if wrong; 6 rounds. Medals: Bronze 20, Silver 30, Gold 36.

Grown-ups · Game 5 of 13 · Secret bets, elimination race · Fronts

Jungle Derby

Six animal teams race through the jungle. Secretly back two of them, then push your favourites on and trip up the rest.

Inspired by Colossal Arena

Grown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-05
Players
3 to 6 (2 with the Referee, or solo)
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
Grown-ups (L1 teaches in 10 min)
Dice
1 die (Team key, for ties)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Secretly bet on two teams, then take turns adding to a team's strength with its own cards or knocking another team down; the weakest team is out each round and only bets on the last three teams pay.

What you need

All 54 cardsYour hand, your secret bets, and the six team columns
1 plain dieRolled and read on the Team key (Ref 4) to break ties between teams
Pencil and paperTo keep each team's running strength

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Make six team columns side by side in the order of the Team key: 1 Tigers, 2 Elephants, 3 Bears, 4 Monkeys, 5 Peacocks, 6 Cobras. Each starts at strength 0. Write the strengths on paper.

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 8 cards to each player. The rest is the draw pile.

  • Each player secretly chooses 2 cards of two different teams and puts them face down in front of them: your bets. The team on a bet card is the team you back. Bet cards are not played. (L3: 3 bets, three different teams.) You keep a hand of 6 (L3: 5).

  • The youngest player starts round 1. The start moves one seat left each round.

How to play

There are 4 rounds. In each round take turns round the table:

  1. Add: play one card from your hand face up on its own team's column (the team named on the card). Add the card's number to that team's strength.

  2. Sabotage (L2 and L3): instead, play one card sideways on a different team that is still racing. Subtract the card's number from that team's strength. Strength can go below 0. A card of a team that is already out can only be played this way.

  3. If you cannot play (empty hand, or no legal card), pass. If everyone passes in a row, the round ends.

  4. A round ends as soon as every team still racing has had at least one card played on it this round (adding or sabotage).

  5. At the end of rounds 1, 2 and 3, the team with the lowest strength is out: turn its column face down. On a tie for lowest, roll the die and read the Team key until a tied team comes up: that team is out. Round 4 is the final sprint: no team goes out. Everyone draws back up to 6 cards (L3: 5) from the draw pile.

How it ends

After round 4 the three teams left are ranked by strength (ties: roll the die on the Team key; the first tied team that comes up ranks higher). Everyone turns over their bets. A bet scores 5 if its team finished first, 3 if second, 1 if third, and 0 if the team was knocked out. Most points wins. Ties: the higher total of numbers on your bet cards (you gave up more), then the lowest serial on a bet card.

Words in this game

  • Bet A face-down card whose team you back. It is not played.
  • Racing A team not yet knocked out.
  • Strength A team's running total of added numbers minus sabotage.
  • Sabotage Playing a card sideways on another team to subtract its number.
  • Sprint The last round, where no team is knocked out and the final order is set.

Common questions

  • Can I bet on a team and then sabotage it? Yes, nobody can tell, and sometimes you must, to stop the lowest team being yours. But the card you play sideways must be from a different team than the one it lands on.

  • Why would the round end before I play? The round ends the moment the last racing team gets its first card. Be quick to put cards where you want them.

  • What if a team's cards all run out? You can still push or knock it down with cards of other teams, using sabotage, and cards of your own team on it only when you hold them. Teams have 8, 8, 8, 10, 10 and 10 cards, and some are bets or in hands you cannot see.

  • What do the backs tell me? Nothing about the team. You can see the backs of other players' hands but a back never shows a team.

  • How do I know who is winning bets? You do not. Bets stay face down until the end. Watch what people sabotage and protect.

Tips

  • Back two different teams, but think about which pair can both reach the last three. Only a first, second or third place pays (5, 3 or 1), and a team knocked out pays 0.

  • Keep your bets quiet. Sabotage your own bet team once in a while, since nobody can tell, and the tie-break is the higher total of numbers on your bet cards, so a low-number bet card also keeps you ahead on ties.

  • Play fast on a team you want to stay in. A round ends the moment the last racing team gets its first card, so you may not get a second turn to protect it.

  • Aim your sabotage at the lowest team that is not yours. Strength can go below 0, and each of rounds 1 to 3 knocks out the lowest, so a rival's bet can be removed by pushing it under.

  • Do not spend cards on a team already safe. Raw score ties happen in 17% to 31% of games, so one extra point from a good third place can be the whole result.

Worked example

Three players: Ann, Ben, Cy. L2.

  1. Bets: Ann has Nakul (4) (Tigers) and Dhruv (6) (Bears). Ben has Amay (8) (Monkeys) and Archana (5) (Elephants). Cy has Pinku (2) (Cobras) and Avika (4) (Peacocks). Nobody sees these.

  2. Ann plays Shreya (7) (7, Tigers) on the Tigers: Tigers 7. Ben plays Dharsh (7) (7, Elephants): Elephants 7. Cy plays Sharada (3) (3, Peacocks): Peacocks 3. Ann plays Smaya (8) (8, Bears): Bears 8.

  3. Ben wants Cy's Peacocks lower. He plays Guhan (3) (3, an Elephants card) sideways on the Peacocks: 3 - 3 = Peacocks 0.

  4. Cy plays Arvind (1) (1, Monkeys): Monkeys 1. Ann plays Ammlu (2) (2, Cobras): Cobras 2. Now all six teams have had a card, so the round ends.

  5. Strengths: Tigers 7, Elephants 7, Bears 8, Monkeys 1, Peacocks 0, Cobras 2. The lowest is the Peacocks, so they are out, and Cy's bet Avika (4) is dead.

  6. At the end, suppose the last three finish Bears first, Tigers second, Elephants third. Ann scores 5 (Bears) + 3 (Tigers) = 8. Ben scores 1 (Elephants) + 0 (Monkeys out) = 1. Cy scores 0.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. No sabotage: cards only add. A card of a team that is out can be added to any team still racing. 2 bets each.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The full game: sabotage allowed, 2 bets.

L3 · age 8 and up

3 bets each (and a hand of 5), so every team matters more and your bets can fight each other.

Solo

Solo: play against the Referee. Show him your bets (turn them face up). He has a face-down stack of 6 cards. On his turn he flips the top card and plays it sideways on whichever of your backed teams that is still racing is strongest (not the card's own team). Play L2 with 2 bets or L3 with 3. Medals on your points: L2 Gold 8, Silver 5, Bronze 3. L3 Gold 9, Silver 8, Bronze 6. A bot beat the Referee 81% of games at L2 and 90% at L3.

Two players

Add the Referee as a third player. His bets are the first 2 cards of his stack (face down, stack of 8), and his stack then has 6 cards. On his turn he flips the top card and plays it on its own team's column (if that team is out, sideways on the strongest racing team). He rarely wins (8% of games), so he mostly stirs the race.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding and subtracting with negative numbers, comparing running totals, probability of an unseen bet, bluffing.

  • The smart bot's edge shrinks as the table fills: with 5 or 6 players, hidden bets and shared turns make it more of a lottery. Smart bot vs random bots (2,000 games per setting; fair share in brackets), L2 with sabotage: 3p 84% (33%), 4p 66% (25%), 5p 54% (20%), 6p 42% (17%); L3: 3p 83% (33%), 4p 66% (25%), 5p 51% (20%), 6p 38% (17%); L1: 3p 79% (33%), 4p 65% (25%), 5p 53% (20%), 6p 42% (17%).

  • Cards played per game at L2: 3p 31, 4p 32, 5p 32, 6p 32. At about 20 s a play plus 1.5 min for the bets, 4 eliminations and the reveal that is 12 to 15 min, so the estimate is 13 to 16 min.

  • Testing added a 4th 'sprint' round with no knock-out because 3 rounds gave only 28 plays (about 11 min); the game now has 31 plays. Requiring every racing team to get 2 cards per round was rejected: hands ran dry and rounds stalled in most test games, because 54 cards must cover hands, bets and refills. Two Derbies back to back would be 26 to 30 min, too long.

  • Testing added tie-breaks because scores are only 5/3/1/0 per bet, so about 13 to 36% of games tied on points at L2 and L3 before any tie-break. The first tie-break is the higher total of numbers on your bet cards, then the lowest serial, so no game stays tied.

  • Testing changed L1 because, when cards could only add to their own team, a hand of cards from an out team could not be played and rounds stalled (a round had to be ended by everyone passing in nearly every game). L1 now lets a card of an out team be added to any racing team, and pass-out rounds fell to a few percent. Random bots also choose two bets of different teams, as the rules require.

  • Solo: the first Referee (playing his own card on his own team) lost nearly every game, with the bot getting the perfect 8 points in about 93% of games and so no medal scale. Testing changed him to play sideways on your strongest backed team; the bot now beats him 81% at L2 (score 25th/50th/75th = 5/5/8) and 90% at L3 (score 8/8/9). Medals are set at the bot's 75th, 25th-to-50th and lower levels, since a human is weaker than the bot.

  • Two players: bots with the Referee win 92% of games between them (67% even); points 10/25/50/75/90th = 1/4/6/8/8.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot bets on the teams it holds most points of and values moves by the projected ranking; it does not bluff or read other players' sabotage.

  • Not tested: bets that are both on the same team, because the rule forbids it.

  • Not tested: the 6-player game with a draw pile of 6; hands are refilled only partly, so late rounds can be thin.

  • Not tested: how readable the strengths are at the table; pencil and paper are assumed.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

JUNGLE DERBY. Six animal teams race through the jungle. NEED: 3 to 6 players, all 54 cards, a die, paper. SET UP: Lay six team columns in the order of the Team key. Deal 8 cards each. Secretly put 2 cards of different teams face down: your bets. Keep 6. PLAY: Play a card on its own team's column to add its number, or (L2) sideways on another racing team to subtract it. When every racing team has had a card, the round ends and the lowest team is out (tie: roll the Team die). 4 rounds; round 4 knocks nobody out. SCORE: your bets score 5, 3, 1 if their team finishes first, second, third; 0 if out. Most points wins.

Back

LEVELS. L1: cards only add; cards of an out team add to any racing team. L2: sabotage. L3: 3 bets each, hand of 5. TIES: higher total of numbers on your bet cards, then the lowest serial. TEAM KEY (Ref 4): 1 Tigers, 2 Elephants, 3 Bears, 4 Monkeys, 5 Peacocks, 6 Cobras. SOLO: the Referee plays sideways on your strongest backed team. L2 medals: Gold 8, Silver 5, Bronze 3. L3 medals: Gold 9, Silver 8, Bronze 6. TWO PLAYERS: add the Referee as a third player; he plays his top card on its own team.

Grown-ups · Game 6 of 13 · Exact-bid trick-taking · Fronts

Switchback

The trail doubles back on itself, and you have promised exactly how many steps you will take before it does.

Inspired by Oh Hell (and the Decktet habit of giving every card two suits)

Grown-upsHard
Game code
GU-06
Players
2 to 5 (best with 3 or 4)
Time
25 to 30 min
Age
12+ (L1 from 10)
Dice
1 die (Team key; Suit key for the Weather variant)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Bid exactly how many tricks you will win in a hand. The leader names one of their card's two suits, everyone follows, and a die picks a trump team. Hit your bid exactly and you score big, miss and you lose the difference.

What you need

All 54 cardsa hand is dealt from them; the rest are set aside unseen
1 dieread on the Team key (Ref 4) to pick the trump team; on the Suit key for Weather
Ref 4Team key (animal names) and Suit key (suit 1 to 6)
Pencil and paperto keep the score

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • A game is two hands. Deal 12 cards each at 2 or 3 players, 9 each at 4 players, 7 each at 5 players. Set the rest aside unseen. Pick a first dealer; the player to their left deals the second hand.

  • At the start of each hand the dealer rolls the die and reads it on the Team key (Ref 4). That team is trump for the hand: every card of that team is a trump card.

  • Look at your cards. Keep them secret. Each card shows two suits on it. Read them by number on the Suit key.

  • Card strength: a higher number beats a lower one. Equal numbers: the higher serial wins. So any two cards can be compared.

How to play

Each hand:

  1. Bid. Starting left of the dealer, each player says how many tricks they expect to win this hand (0 up to the hand size). The dealer bids last and may not make all the bids add up to the hand size, so at least one player must miss. If the other bids already add up to more than the hand size, the dealer may bid anything.

  2. Lead. The player left of the dealer leads the first trick. After that the winner of a trick leads the next. The leader plays any card and names ONE of its two suits as the led suit.

  3. Follow. Everyone else must play a card that has the led suit as either of its two suits, if they have one. If they have none, they may play anything.

  4. Win the trick. The trick goes to the highest trump card in it (a trump card wins whether or not it followed the led suit). If there is no trump, it goes to the highest card that followed the led suit (the leader's card counts). Equal numbers: higher serial.

  5. The hand ends when all cards are played. Keep your tricks face down in a pile. Score the hand, then deal the second hand with a new die roll.

  6. Weather (optional). See the Weather note under Level 3 in the ladder. It changes how trump is chosen.

How it ends

Scoring each hand. Made your bid exactly: 10 plus 2 for each trick you bid. Missed: lose 1 point for each trick you were over or under. Keep scores on paper. Highest total after two hands wins. Ties: more exact bids, then more tricks won in the second hand. A tie after that is shared.

Words in this game

  • Trick one card from each player, and one winner.
  • Led suit the suit the leader names, out of the two on their card.
  • Trump the team the die picks for the hand. Its cards beat everything else.
  • Exact bid winning exactly the number of tricks you said.
  • Set aside the undealt cards, never looked at. They make it harder to count what is out.

Common questions

  • I have a card with the led suit as its second suit. Must I play it? Yes. Either of a card's two suits counts as following. If you have any card showing the led suit, you must play one.

  • Does a trump card have to follow suit? A trump card that has the led suit must follow like any other. If you have none of the led suit, you may play a trump card (or anything) and it wins.

  • Why can the dealer not bid the total to the hand size? So that somebody misses. If every bid could be exact, nobody would ever need to take a risk.

  • Is bidding zero a good plan? It is safe but small: you score 10 for a 0 bid. In the simulation a bot that bids zero and plays low wins less than 1 game in 14.

  • Do I have to win my tricks early? No. A bid is a plan to be flexible: keep a few low cards to lose on purpose and a few high ones to win when you must.

Tips

  • Bid for the tricks you can hold, not the tricks you hope for. Smart bots make the exact bid in only 32%, 41% and 50% of hands at 3, 4 and 5 players, so a bid one trick too bold is the usual miss.

  • Count the high cards. Only six of each number exist, so once a few 8s and 9s have been played you know which cards can still beat yours. Also remember that the cards set aside unseen make the count harder.

  • Use the two suits. A card names either of its suits when you lead, so lead the suit where you hold the fewest cards, or the one other players are most likely to be forced to follow.

  • Keep a few low cards to lose on purpose and a few high ones to win when you must. A trick won by mistake costs as much as one missed (you lose a point for each trick over or under).

  • Do not hide at zero. A 0 bid only scores 10, and a bot that bids 0 and plays low won under 7% of 3-player games and under 1% at 4 or 5 players.

Worked example

3 players, hand of 12, the die gives Monkeys: trump is the Monkeys team. P0 is the dealer. A real hand from the simulation. Checked against the card list.

  1. Bids, starting left of the dealer: P1 bids 6, P2 bids 5. The other two bids add to 11, so the dealer P0 may not bid 1 (that would make 12). P0 bids 3. The bids add to 14.

  2. Trick 1. P1 leads Nysha (8) (number 8, a Monkey, suits 2 and 6) and names suit 2. P2 plays Gowri (9) (number 9, suits 2 and 3). P0 plays Shreya (2) (number 2, suits 2 and 4). Nysha (8) is a trump card, so it beats the 9. P1 wins.

  3. Trick 3. P1 leads Avika (5) (number 5, suits 3 and 6) and names suit 3. P2 follows with Dhruv (6) (number 6, suits 3 and 5). P0 has no card showing suit 3, so P0 may play anything and plays Idhayan (1) (number 1, a Monkey, suits 4 and 6). It is trump, so a 1 wins the trick. P0 wins.

  4. Trick 4. P0 leads Gowri (9) (number 9, suits 4 and 5) and names suit 4. P1 follows with Gopi (5) (number 5, suits 1 and 4). P2 follows with Arvind (1) (number 1, a Monkey, suits 1 and 4). The Monkey is trump, so P2 wins with a 1.

  5. After all 12 tricks P0 has won 2, P1 6 and P2 4. P1 bid 6 and made it exactly: 10 + 2 x 6 = 22. P0 bid 3 and won 2, one under: minus 1. P2 bid 5 and won 4: minus 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. One hand only, 5 cards each. Bids are called aloud while everyone's cards are visible to the helper. Just try to win the number you said. No dealer restriction.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Two hands, the dealer restriction and exact scoring, but no trump (do not roll the die).

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: trump team from the die each hand. Weather variant (optional): instead of a trump team for the hand, the leader rolls the die before every trick and reads it on the Suit key. That suit is trump for that trick: any card showing it (as either of its two suits) beats any card that does not. Among trump cards, highest number wins. No team trump when Weather is on. Best with 2 to 4 players; ties become more common at 4 and 5.

Solo

Lone Hiker. Play against three Ghost hands. Deal 9 cards each to you and three Ghosts (face down, never looked at). Roll for trump. You bid on your own hand and lead the first trick. A Ghost leads its lowest card and names its lower suit number. A Ghost follows with its lowest legal card, or its lowest card if it has none of the led suit. Ghosts bid nothing and score nothing. Play two hands and add your two scores. Medals: Bronze 5, Silver 13, Gold 16.

Two players

Deal 12 cards each, set 30 aside, and play two hands. The dealer rule still applies (the dealer may not make the bids add to 12). With only two players exact bids are harder (about 1 in 4 in the simulation), so 3 or 4 is the better game.

Maths and skills in this game

Estimating how many tricks a hand will win, comparing numbers up to 9, tracking which cards are out, working out how many 8s and 9s remain (only six of each), and scoring with a bonus for exactness and a loss for a miss.

Variants and options

  • Weather (optional variant). Roll the die before every trick, read it on the Suit key (Ref 4): that suit is trump for the trick (any card carrying it, as either suit, beats a card that does not; highest number among trump cards wins; no team trump). Exact-bid play still works (bid accuracy 40% at 3p, 43% at 4p), but ties rise, so use it with 2 to 4 players.

Back patternNot used
TeamRule the die picks the trump team for each hand
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks ties between equal numbers
NamesFlavour the children are the hikers on the trail

PlaceNot used

Settings used 2,000 games for team trump and Weather, 1,500 for the others, on the real card list. Smart bots make the exact bid in 32% / 41% / 50% of hands at 3 / 4 / 5 players with team trump (hand 12 / 9 / 7), and 28% at 2 players. A simple bot makes 25 / 36 / 45%.

  • Trump rule compared with no trump and a suit trump for the whole hand (4 players): exact bids 39.0% (no trump), 40.9% (team die), 43.3% (suit die); smart v simple 24.9 / 26.0 / 28.9 (even 25). At 3 players: 34.3 / 32.2 / 35.5% and 30.5 / 35.1 / 32.0. The differences are small, so the team die stays.

  • Weather variant (die rolled every trick, read on the Suit key, replaces team trump): bid accuracy holds up and improves at 2 to 4 players: exact 40.0% (3p), 43.0% (4p), 33.8% (2p) against 32.2 / 40.9 / 27.6% for team trump; at 5 players it is 45.5% against 50.0%. It is therefore an optional variant for 2 to 4 players, not for 5.

  • Solo, Lone Hiker (three ghost hands): a smart bot hits the exact bid in 41% of hands; two-hand score quartiles -2 / 13 / 15 over 3,000 games (team trump); with Weather 13 / 14 at the median and top.

  • A bot that always bids 0 and plays low won under 7% of 3-player games and under 1% of 4- or 5-player games. This was not repeated with the final rules.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bots bid from a table of card strengths; they do not read each other's bids.

  • Not tested: the L1 five-card hand, the L2 no-trump game, and the 'a tie after tie-break is shared' rule.

  • Not tested: Weather at 5 players, or the effect of a die per trick on game length (it adds a die roll per trick: 12 more rolls per hand at 3 players).

  • Not tested: the Lone Hiker ghost rules with people. Only a bot has played them.

  • Not tested: a full game of one hand per player.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

SWITCHBACK. Two hands. Deal 12 each (2p, 3p), 9 (4p), 7 (5p); set the rest aside unseen. Roll the die on the Team key: that team is trump. Left of the dealer bids first: how many tricks will you win? The dealer bids last and may not make the total equal the hand size. The player left of the dealer leads any card and names ONE of its two suits. Others must play a card with that suit (either of its two) if they can. Highest trump wins the trick; if none, the highest card that followed. Equal numbers: higher serial. Winner leads.

Back

SCORE. Exact bid: 10 + 2 per trick bid. Miss: minus 1 for each trick over or under. Highest after two hands wins; ties: more exact bids, then tricks in hand 2. WEATHER (optional, 2 to 4 players): no team trump; the leader rolls the die before each trick and reads it on the Suit key; that suit is trump for the trick. LEVELS. L1 one hand, helper, aloud. L2 no trump. L3 trump or Weather. SOLO: Lone Hiker against three Ghost hands that always play their lowest legal card. Medals: Bronze 5, Silver 13, Gold 16.
