Grown-ups · Game 7 of 13 · Press your luck, share the pain · Fronts

Cauldron

Three witches' cauldrons bubble on the camp fire. Add a little, but whoever makes one boil over has to take the whole brew.

Inspired by Poison

RecommendedGrown-upsFamilyMedium
Game code
GU-07
Players
3 to 6 (2 with the Troll, or solo)
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
Grown-ups (L1 teaches in 10 min)
Dice
None (L3: 1 plain die)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Play cards onto three cauldrons without letting any total pass the limit; whoever tips one over takes its cards, and at the end the cards you hold of each colour either hurt you or, if you hold the most of that colour, are safe.

What you need

All 54 cardsHands, three cauldron piles, and the cards you take
Pencil and paperTo tally the colour scores at the end of each round
1 plain die (L3 only)Read as a plain number 1 to 6 to set the limit

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Play 3 rounds with 3 or 4 players, 2 rounds with 5 or 6. Before each round, shuffle all 54 cards.

  • Turn 3 cards face up in a row. Each starts a cauldron. The first card of a cauldron is its bottom card; it stays the bottom card until the cauldron boils over.

  • Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest back in the box for this round.

  • Each player keeps a taken area in front of them, face up. The youngest player starts round 1; the start moves one seat left each round.

  • The limit is 15. (L3: roll the die at the start of each round; the limit is 12 plus the roll.)

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Play one card from your hand onto a cauldron. You must pick a cauldron whose bottom card shares at least one border colour with your card. If your card matches none of the three, you may pick any cauldron.

  2. Add up the numbers of every card in that cauldron, including yours. If the total is the limit or less, nothing more happens. Your turn is over.

  3. If the total is over the limit, the cauldron boils over. You take every card that was in it except the one you just played and put them face up in your taken area. The card you played stays and becomes the cauldron's new bottom card.

  4. L3 only, twin potion: if the card you play is the twin of a card already in that cauldron (the same child's other card), the cauldron is blessed. Check this before adding up. Put every other card from it in the box. Your card stays as the new bottom card. Nobody takes anything.

  5. The round ends when all hands are empty. Cards left in the cauldrons go in the box. Then score the round.

How it ends

Score each round, then add the rounds. Lowest total wins. Look at your taken area. A card counts once for each of its two colours. For each of the six colours, the player (or players) with the most cards showing that colour are safe for it. Everyone else pays 1 point for each card they hold showing that colour. A card numbered 9 pays 2 instead of 1. If you did not take a single card that round, you pay nothing. Ties: fewer cards taken in all rounds wins; still tied, the player whose taken cards include the higher serial number loses; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Cauldron One of the three piles. It starts with one face-up card.
  • Bottom card The card that started a cauldron. Your play must share a colour with it.
  • Boil over The total passes the limit. The player who did it takes the cards that were already there.
  • Safe You hold the most cards of a colour (or share the most), so you pay nothing for that colour.
  • Twin The other card of the same child. Twin numbers always add to 9.
  • Limit 15 normally; 12 plus the die at L3.

Common questions

  • Do I have to play a card that matches? Yes, if one of your cards matches a cauldron's bottom card in colour you must play such a card on a cauldron it matches. If no card in your hand matches any cauldron, you may play any card on any cauldron. If one card matches several cauldrons, you choose.

  • Does my own card count when I boil a cauldron over? Yes, it is in the total that went over. But you do not take it. It stays and starts the cauldron again, so the next player faces a low total.

  • Why is it good to take lots of one colour? Because the most cards of a colour are safe. Taking five Blue cards costs you nothing if nobody holds more Blue. It is when you are spread thin, with one or two of every colour, that you pay the most.

  • Can nobody lose? Yes, and it happens. If a round has no boil-overs, nobody pays. The next round you may need to be braver.

  • Which cards come back after a round? All of them. Shuffle all 54 for the next round; cards you took last round go back into the deck.

Tips

  • Collect colours, do not spread. The most cards of a colour are safe, and having one or two of every colour is where you pay the most, so take cards that deepen colours you already hold.

  • Boiling a cauldron over is not always a loss. You take the cards but your own card stays as the new bottom card, so a boil-over that gives you a heavy pile of one colour can be a good trade.

  • Look at which cauldrons are close to the limit before you play. If no card in your hand matches any bottom card you may play anywhere, so a hand with nothing matching is a chance to dump a card safely.

  • The 9s pay 2 instead of 1, so avoid taking 9s in a colour you will not win. The 9s are also the cards that push a total over the limit fastest.

  • Rounds with no boil-overs cost nobody anything, so being the first to play safe leaves the next round to be braver. Smart bots won 82% to 90% against random players, mostly by choosing which cauldron to overflow.

Worked example

Three players: Ann, Ben and Cy. Limit 15, L2 scoring.

  1. The three cauldrons start with Guhan (3) (3), Avika (4) (4) and Dhruv (6) (6).

  2. Ann plays Amyra (4) (4) on Guhan (3). Both show Green and Red, so it matches. The total is 3 + 4 = 7, under 15.

  3. Ben plays Gopi (5) (5). It shows Green and Orange, so it matches Guhan (3) (Green) and Avika (4) (Orange), but not Dhruv (6). He chooses Avika (4): 4 + 5 = 9.

  4. Cy plays Amyra (5) (5) on Dhruv (6). Both show Blue and Purple. The total is 6 + 5 = 11.

  5. Ann plays Bn Sharada (7) (7). It shows Green and Purple, so it matches Guhan (3) and Dhruv (6). She puts it on Dhruv (6): 6 + 5 + 7 = 18, over 15. The cauldron boils over. Ann takes Dhruv (6) and Amyra (5) and keeps them. Bn Sharada (7) stays as the new bottom card, total 7.

  6. At round end, say Ann holds Dhruv (6) and Amyra (5), Ben holds Nakul (5) and Naresh (6), Cy holds Nakul (4). Ann has 2 Blue and 2 Purple, Ben 2 Orange and 2 Red, Cy 1 Purple and 1 Yellow. Ann is safe on Blue and Purple (most), Ben on Orange and Red, Cy on Yellow (nobody else has any). Cy pays 1 for Purple, because Ann holds more Purple. Round scores: Ann 0, Ben 0, Cy 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. 2 rounds, no colour scoring: just count the cards you took, fewest wins. 9s are ordinary cards. Ties: fewest cards in the second round, then the serial rule.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The full game as written above: colour scoring, 9s pay 2, limit 15.

L3 · age 8 and up

Adds the twin potion (a twin blesses the cauldron) and the die limit (12 plus a roll each round).

Solo

Solo: play against two Trolls and try to finish with fewer points than both. Each Troll has a face-down stack of 5 cards. On his turn he flips the top card and plays it on the matching cauldron where the total gets highest without going over the limit (leftmost if tied). If every matching cauldron would go over, he plays on the leftmost matching one and takes the cards. Trolls are scored like players. Medals (L3, 3 rounds, your own points): Gold 1 or less, Silver 2 or less, Bronze 4 or less, and you must also beat at least one Troll. The bot beat both Trolls 66% of the time.

Two players

Add one Troll as a third player (he sits after both of you in turn order, same rules as solo). 3 rounds. You are really racing each other; the Troll fills the cauldrons so that boil-overs happen. The Troll lost to a human-level bot about 1 game in 6, so he is gentle.

Maths and skills in this game

Addition to a limit, estimating what other people can safely add, risk and set counting: counting the most of each colour (a small-set 'majority' count). Reading card colours quickly.

Variants and options

  • Poison-style colour majority scoring (taken cards grouped by colour, not by cauldron)

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule The numbers add up to the limit; a 9 pays double.
ColoursRule Which cauldron you may play on, and the six colour counts at scoring.
Suit pairNot used Not used.
Back patternNot used Backs are not part of this game.
TeamNot used The team is not used.
Letter tileNot used Not used.
SerialRule The last tie-break: the higher serial among your taken cards loses.
NamesRule At L3 a twin (the same child's other card) blesses a cauldron.
ExpressionNot used Not used.
PlaceFlavour The camp fire and the kitchen of the camp; no rule.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random 90% at 4p L2 (25% even), 18 to 23 min, ties under 3% after tie-breaks

SettingResult
3p L2 (3 rounds)smart vs random 82% (33% even); 45 turns, about 18 min; ties 0.1%
4p L2 (3 rounds)90% (25%); 60 turns, about 23 min; ties 0.1%; median score 7
5p L2 (2 rounds)84% (20%); 50 turns, about 20 min; ties 1.8%
6p L2 (2 rounds)87% (17%); 60 turns, about 23 min; ties 2.6%
4p L3 (twin + die)88% (25%); 60 turns; median score 6
4p L1 (count only)95% (25%); 40 turns; ties 0.7%
2 players + Troll L3humans beat the Troll 85% (67% even)
Solo vs 2 Trolls L3bot beats both 66% (33% even); points 25th/50th/75th = 1/2/4

  • A careful player beats a careless one almost every time. Smart bot against random bots (2,000 games per setting; fair share in brackets), L2: 3p 82% (33%), 4p 90% (25%), 5p 84% (20%), 6p 87% (17%); L3: 83%, 88%, 83%, 83%; L1: 96%, 95%, 92%, 91%.

  • No seat has an advantage. With equal bots at L2 the seat win shares are flat (4p 24.0 to 25.6%, 6p 16.0 to 17.0%, from 2,000 games), and the winner is not decided before the end.

  • Games fit the 15 to 25 minute target. 3 rounds of 5 cards = 45 turns at 3p, 60 at 4p; 2 rounds = 50 turns at 5p, 60 at 6p; at about 20 s a turn plus 1 min scoring per round that is 18 min (3p), 23 (4p), 20 (5p), 23 (6p). Two games back to back would be 36 to 46 min, too long for one sitting.

  • Boil-overs happen 12 to 19 times per game (about 3 turns in 10 at 4p L2 end in a boil-over). Nobody is ever stuck: a player with no matching card may play anywhere, so there are no stalls.

  • Testing changed the scoring from grouping taken cards by cauldron (A, B, C) to grouping them by the six colours, because ties were too common: with only three groups most players were safe in most groups, and 63% of 3p games and 38% of 4p games ended in a tie at 0 points. With colours, raw ties are 15% at 3p and 10% at 4p, below 3% after the two tie-breaks, and the smart bot's win share over random bots rose (3p 75% to 82%, 4p 76% to 90%).

  • Testing shortened the game because of time: 6-card hands and 3 rounds meant 54 to 108 turns (18 to 36 min at 20 s). Hands are now 5 cards, and 2 rounds are played with 5 or 6 players: 45 to 60 turns.

  • Testing made the Troll stronger because the first one was too gentle: he played the top card on the leftmost match, and a bot playing against two of him won 82% of the time. Now he plays on the fullest matching cauldron that stays under the limit: the bot wins 66 to 68% against two Trolls (33% is even) and about 83 to 85% as a pair against one (67% is even), and a bot's score against two Trolls over 3 rounds is 25th percentile 1, median 2, 75th 4 (L3).

  • At L3 the twin potion blessed a cauldron about once a game (0.9 at 3p, 1.2 at 4p, 1.3 at 6p, with bots that do not chase it) and left the bot's lead over random players about the same (83 to 88%). The die limit makes the limit 13 to 18, so some rounds are tense and some are calm.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people at the table. All numbers are from bots; the smart bot is greedy with one-turn lookahead and does not read what opponents hold.

  • Not tested: whether the colour count at scoring feels fair when a card counts for two colours at once; a pencil-and-paper tally is needed.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CAULDRON. Three witches' pots bubble on the fire. Add a little, but whoever makes one boil over takes the brew. NEED: 3 to 6 players, all 54 cards, pencil and paper. SET UP: Shuffle. Turn 3 cards up: the cauldrons. Deal 5 each. Limit is 15. PLAY: Play 1 card on a cauldron that shares a border colour with its bottom card (any, if none match). If the total is over 15, you take the cards already there; your card stays as the new bottom. When hands are empty, score: for each colour, the most cards are safe; others pay 1 per card with that colour, a 9 pays 2. Lowest total after 3 rounds wins (2 rounds with 5 or 6 players).

Back

LEVELS. L1: 2 rounds, just count the cards you took, fewest wins. L2: full colour scoring. L3: a twin of a card in a cauldron blesses it (everything else goes to the box, nobody takes), and the limit is 12 plus a die roll each round. TIES: fewer cards taken, then the higher serial among your taken cards loses. SOLO: play against two Trolls; each flips his top card and plays it on the fullest matching cauldron that stays under the limit. L3 medals by your points: Gold 1 or less, Silver 2 or less, Bronze 4 or less. TWO PLAYERS: add one Troll as a third player.

Grown-ups · Game 8 of 13 · Push your luck, set collection · Fronts

Harbour Day

The quay is full of crates. Load your ship with matching goods for the best price, but a heavy ship may not make it through the storm.

Inspired by Medici: The Card Game

Grown-upsFamilyMedium
Game code
GU-08
Players
2 to 6 (or solo)
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
Grown-ups (L1 teaches in 10 min)
Dice
1 die (Suit key for the premium suit, plain die for the storm)
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Take crates from the quay one at a time into your ship's hold, then sail to bank them; the more icons of one suit you have the better they score, but past weight 12 each new crate risks sinking the ship and losing the day.

What you need

All 54 cardsThe quay, and the crates in your hold
1 plain dieRolled once a day for the premium suit (Suit key, Ref 4), and rolled for storms
Pencil and paperDay scores

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Play days: 2 players 6 days, 3 players 4 days, 4 or 5 players 3 days, 6 players 2 days. Solo: 3 days. Shuffle all 54 cards before each day.

  • Turn 6 cards face up in a row: the quay. The rest is the draw pile.

  • L2 and L3: roll the die and read it on the Suit key. That suit is today's premium suit.

  • Each player has a hold (a row of cards in front of them). A hold starts empty.

  • The youngest player starts day 1. The start moves one seat left each day. After each full turn round the table the order reverses (the last player to act goes again first), so the seats are fair.

How to play

On your turn, do one of these:

  1. Take: choose a card from the quay and add it to your hold. Fill the quay back to 6 from the draw pile. Then check your weight (below).

  2. Sail: bank your hold. Your day is over and you score it (see scoring). You need at least 1 card to sail.

  3. Weight is the total of the numbers in your hold. L3 only, twin ballast: a card and its twin (the same child's other card) in the same hold weigh 0 together.

  4. Storm check: after a take, if your weight is more than 12, roll the die. You sink if the roll is less than or equal to the weight minus 12, divided by 3, rounded up: weight 13 to 15 sinks on a roll of 1; 16 to 18 on 1 to 2; 19 to 21 on 1 to 3; 22 to 24 on 1 to 4; 25 to 27 on 1 to 5; 28 or more always. (L1: no die, you sink at once if the weight is over 15.)

  5. If you sink, put your whole hold in the box. You score 0 for the day and take no more turns. The day ends when every player has sailed or sunk.

How it ends

Score a ship that sailed: each card shows two suits. Count the suit icons in your hold for each of the six suits (read them on the Suit key, 1 to 6). At L2 and L3 the premium suit counts double for each card that shows it. Square each suit's count and add the six squares. Example: counts 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0 score 9 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 15. Add your day scores. Highest total wins. Ties: the player who sank on fewer days; still tied, the player with the lowest serial among cards in their last sailed hold; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Quay The 6 face-up cards you can take from.
  • Hold The cards you have taken today.
  • Weight The total of the numbers in your hold.
  • Sail Bank your hold and end your day.
  • Premium suit The suit rolled each day (L2, L3). Its icons count double.
  • Twin ballast L3: twins in one hold weigh nothing together.

Common questions

  • Why square the counts? Because a set is worth more than the sum of its parts. Four icons of one suit score 16, but four different suits score only 4. Aim for a big pile of one or two suits.

  • Can I take a card and then sail in the same turn? No. Take is one turn and Sail is another. After you take, you have to survive the next player's turn first, and the storm check happens straight after your take.

  • Does a card with the premium suit count double for both icons? Each card shows two different suits, so a card can show the premium suit only once. That one icon counts as 2.

  • What if the quay runs out? It never does in practice: the draw pile has 48 cards and a day uses about 12. If it does, you can only sail.

  • Is it better to sail early? Only if the cards you can take would push you over 12. The best moves are crates that add icons to a suit you already hold and do not add much weight (low numbers).

Tips

  • Chase one or two suits. Counts are squared, so four icons in one suit score 16 but four in different suits score only 4. Take crates that add to a suit you already hold.

  • Prefer low numbers. The best crates add icons without adding much weight, and weight 12 is the limit before the storm die starts to matter.

  • Know the sinking odds: weight 13 to 15 sinks on a roll of 1, 16 to 18 on 1 or 2, and so on. The ship sank on about 1 day in 4 for the smart bot, so sail when the next take would cross a band.

  • Check the premium suit at the start of the day (L2 and L3). A card showing it counts its icon double, so it can be worth a slightly heavier hold.

  • At 6 players only 2 days are played and the last seat wins 13% (17% is fair). Seat does matter there, so play 3 to 5 players when you want a fairer game.

Worked example

The premium suit is 3 (Suit key). You start with an empty hold.

  1. You take Kanasu (6) (6). It shows suits 3 and 4. Weight 6. Icons: suit 3 counts double = 2, suit 4 = 1. Score if you sailed now: 4 + 1 = 5.

  2. Next turn you take Dhruv (6) (6), suits 3 and 5. Weight 12, still no storm check. Icons: suit 3 = 4, suit 4 = 1, suit 5 = 1. Score if you sail: 16 + 1 + 1 = 18.

  3. You take Idhayan (1) (1), suits 4 and 6. Weight is now 13, so you roll the die. You sink on a 1 only. Icons: suit 3 = 4, suit 4 = 2, suit 5 = 1, suit 6 = 1. If you survive and sail the score is 16 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 22.

  4. At L3 with twin ballast, if you later held Kanasu (6) (6) and its twin Kanasu (3) (3), those two cards would weigh 0 together.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. No premium suit, no storm die: sink at once if your weight is over 15. Score is the squares of the six suit counts.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The full game above: premium suit and the storm die.

L3 · age 8 and up

Adds twin ballast: a card and its twin in the same hold weigh 0 together.

Solo

Solo: play 3 days alone and add your days. Medals (your total): L2: Bronze 60, Silver 90, Gold 115. L3: Bronze 75, Silver 110, Gold 155. The ship sank on about 1 day in 4.

Two players

Play 6 days (2 players). The game is swingy and tense: ties are almost impossible. There is no neutral third player; the 5 face-up crates on the quay are the only competition.

Maths and skills in this game

Addition against a limit, risk and probability (the storm die), squares and totals, collecting a set.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule The weight of a crate; the 12 limit.
ColoursNot used Not used.
Suit pairRule The two suits on a card are the goods it carries; the Suit key sets the premium suit.
Back patternNot used Not used.
TeamNot used Not used.
Letter tileNot used Not used.
SerialRule The last tie-break.
NamesRule At L3 twins weigh 0 together.
ExpressionNot used Not used.
PlaceFlavour The quay and harbour.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: Simulated. smart beats random 95% at 4p L2 (25% even), 14 to 21 min; L1 and L3 also simulated

SettingResult
2p L2 (6 days)smart vs random 99.5% (50%); 52 actions, about 17 min; ties 0.7%
3p L2 (4 days)98% (33%); 52 actions, about 17 min; ties 1.2%
4p L2 (3 days)95% (25%); 51 actions, about 17 min; median total 57
5p L2 (3 days)94% (20%); 63 actions, about 21 min
6p L2 (2 days)86% (17%); 50 actions, about 17 min; last seat wins 13%
4p L1 (squares, hard 15)99.8% (25%); ties 8.9%; median total 42
4p L3 (twin ballast)95% (25%); 62 actions, about 21 min; median total 76
Solo L2 / L3 (3 days)25th/50th/75th = 61/88/117 and 73/111/155; sank on 25 to 27% of days

  • The skill gap is very wide: a careful player beats a careless one almost always. Smart bot vs random bots (2,000 games per setting; fair share in brackets), L2: 2p 6 days 99.5% (50%), 3p 4 days 98% (33%), 4p 3 days 95% (25%), 5p 3 days 94% (20%), 6p 2 days 86% (17%); L3: 99.6%, 98%, 95%, 94%, 85%.

  • Seats are close to fair except at 6p. With all-smart bots, seat shares for 3p L2 are 33 to 35%; for 6p they are 12.6 to 19.3% even with the rotating start and reversed order, and the last seat wins 13% in the 2-day game (17% is fair). This is a known weakness; 3 days at 6p was tried (seat shares 13.9 to 19.9%, not clearly better, about 25 min), so 6p stays at 2 days.

  • Testing changed the start rule because of seat bias. Before, the start moved one seat left each day and at 6p seat 6 won 11% and seat 2 won 26%; now the order reverses every lap round the table and the start still rotates, giving seat 6 12.7 to 13.9% and seat 1 about 18 to 19%. Better but not fixed.

  • Counted actions per game at L2: 2p 4 days 35 (about 12 min at 20 s), 3p 4 days 52 (17 min), 4p 3 days 51 (17 min), 5p 2 days 42 (14 min), 6p 2 days 50 (17 min). Testing changed the number of days because of this: 2p from 4 to 6 days (52 actions, 17 min, was 12) and 5p from 2 to 3 days (63 actions, 21 min, was 14); two days back to back at 6p would be 34 min, too long. L3 adds about 20% more actions (ballast keeps people loading longer): 2p 6 days 64, 4p 62, 5p 3 days 76 (25 min), 6p 2 days 60.

  • The ship sank on 24 to 27% of all days at L2 and L3 (expected, since the bot gambles at the threshold). There were no stalls in any simulated run: every day ends because each take refills the quay and a sail or sink eventually happens.

  • Raw tie rate on total score is 0.9 to 3.2% at L2 (2p 0.9%, 4p 2.1%, 6p 3.2%), 0.4 to 1.7% at L3 and 4 to 15% at L1 (low counts), all settled by the tie-breaks. Scores at L2, 4p all-smart, 10/25/50/75/90th percentile = 25/40/57/75/91 over 3 days; solo L2 25/50/75th = 61/88/117 (medals 60/90/115); solo L3 = 73/111/155 (75/110/155).

  • Three L1 variants were tested. (a) Score = icon count, hard sink over 15: very tied (16 to 34% of 3 to 6p games tie), 99% bot win rate, solo median 22, too dull. (b) Squares of suit counts, hard sink over 15, no premium: ties 4 to 15%; bot beats random 100% at 2p 4 days and 3p, 99.8% at 4p, 98% at 5p, 96% at 6p; solo 25/50/75th = 40/50/58. (b) was chosen: it keeps a one-line rule (a sure sink at 15), teaches squaring, and the sink never fires for a sensible bot (0% sunk). (c) Squares with the storm die: bot wins 91% at 4p, ties 7.5%, solo median 46; that is simply L2 without the premium, so not a step down.

  • L3 twin ballast (twins weigh 0 together) raised the median total by a third (4p 57 to 76) and widened the spread (90th/10th percentile of totals 5.7x vs 3.6x); the sink rate went from 25% to 27%. The bot beats random 95% at 4p (95% at L2), seat shares are flat at 24 to 28% at 4p, and ties are 1.1%; it adds weight-checking work for the table.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The smart bot sails by expected value; humans may fear the storm sooner or later than it does, and may chase a suit.

  • Not tested: the premium suit on its own (L2 minus premium), or separately from squaring.

  • Not tested: whether the reversed-order rule is easy to remember at the table.

  • Not tested: 2 players over 6 days beyond the smart-vs-random run (99.5%); a human duel may still feel long.

  • Not tested: how often a twin ballast pair forms.

  • Not tested: taking a card from the quay while another player is next to take the one they want; the bot does not treat the quay's contents as a resource for opponents.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

HARBOUR DAY. The quay is full of crates. Load your ship, but a heavy ship may sink. NEED: 2 to 6 players, all 54 cards, a die. SET UP: Shuffle. Turn up 6 cards: the quay. Roll the die and read it on the Suit key: today's premium suit. PLAY: On your turn TAKE a card from the quay into your hold (refill the quay), or SAIL to bank your hold. Over weight 12 after a take? Roll the die. You sink if the roll is at most (weight minus 12) divided by 3, rounded up. A sunk ship scores 0. SCORE: count suit icons in your hold, premium suit double, square each of the six counts and add them.

Back

LEVELS. L1: no die, sink at once over weight 15, no premium suit. L2: the full game. L3: a card and its twin in the same hold weigh 0 together. DAYS: 2 players 6, 3 players 4, 4 or 5 players 3, 6 players 2. ORDER: after each lap round the table, the order reverses. TIES: fewer sunk days, then the lower serial. SOLO: 3 days. L2 medals: Bronze 60, Silver 90, Gold 115. L3 medals: Bronze 75, Silver 110, Gold 155. SINK TABLE: weight 13 to 15 sinks on 1; 16 to 18 on 1 to 2; 19 to 21 on 1 to 3; 22 to 24 on 1 to 4; 25 to 27 on 1 to 5; 28 up always.

Grown-ups · Game 9 of 13 · Cooperative deduction · Fronts (hold them facing your teammates)

Perfect Camp

The whole expedition must raise six camps up the mountain, from 1 to 9, and nobody is allowed to look at their own cards.

Inspired by Hanabi (Antoine Bauza)

FamilyGrown-upsHard
Game code
GU-09
Players
2 to 5
Time
25 to 35 min
Age
10+
Dice
1 die (Storm counter)
Pawns
6 Radio tokens (pawns)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Hold your cards facing out so only your teammates can see them, give each other clues, and play cards onto six camps in order from 1 up to 9. Three wrong plays end the game.

What you need

All 54 cardsHands, the draw deck, the discard pile and the six camps.
6 pawnsRadio tokens. Each clue spends one; a discard wins one back.
1 dieThe Storm counter: it counts mistakes.
A flat tableSix camp columns, one for each suit 1 to 6.

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • The six camps are six empty columns, one for each suit 1 to 6 (read the suits on the Suit key, Ref 4). They are built up 1, 2, 3 and so on to 9.

  • Deal each player 5 cards (2 or 3 players) or 4 cards (4 or 5 players). The rest is the draw deck, face down.

  • Hold your cards so that your teammates can see the fronts and you see only the backs. Never look at your own fronts.

  • Put all 6 pawns in the middle. Set the die to 1: it counts mistakes.

  • Pick a first player. Go clockwise.

How to play

On your turn, do exactly one of these:

  1. Play a card. Choose one of your cards and put it on a camp without looking at it. It must fit: its number is exactly one more than the camp's top card (1 for an empty camp) and the camp is one of the card's two suits. If it fits two camps, you choose (L3) or it goes on the lower-numbered suit (L1 and L2). If it fits neither, it is a mistake: turn the die up by one and put the card face up in the discard pile. Then draw a replacement.

  2. Radio. Spend a pawn. Pick one teammate and tell them one fact: a number (1 to 9), a colour (red, orange, yellow, green, blue or purple; Ref 3) or a suit (1 to 6; Ref 4). You must point at every card of theirs that matches, and at least one must match. A card matches a colour if either of its two colours is that one, and matches a suit if either of its two suits is that one. Everyone hears the clue.

  3. Discard. Show one of your cards face up in the discard pile. Take a pawn back (never more than 6). Draw a replacement.

  4. The first time the draw deck runs out, shuffle the discard pile face down to make a new deck, once only.

How it ends

The game ends at once when the die would show 4 (three mistakes), or when all 54 cards are in the camps. It also ends when the new deck runs out and every player has had one more turn. Your score is the number of cards in the camps. A three-mistake ending still scores the cards placed. A perfect 54 has never been reached by any simulated table (see Sims), so it is a goal, not a promise. Bands: Camper 22 or fewer, Ranger 23 to 26, Guide 27 to 29, Summit-ready 30 or more.

Words in this game

  • Camp One of the six columns, built 1, 2, 3 up to 9 in one suit.
  • Radio A clue: one fact about a teammate's cards, which costs a pawn.
  • Storm The die. Each mistake turns it up by one; at 4 the game ends.
  • Fits A card fits a camp when it is exactly one number above the camp's top and the camp is one of its two suits.
  • Twin The other card of the same child. A pair adds up to 9.

Common questions

  • Can I ever look at my own fronts? No. You see your own backs, and the backs tell nothing about the front. You learn only from clues and from the cards you can see on the table, in the camps and in the discard pile.

  • Can I give a clue that points at nothing? No. At least one of your teammate's cards must match, and you must point at all that match.

  • Is it bad to discard? It is how you win pawns back, so you need to. But a discard destroys that card for ever (until the one reshuffle), so discard cards you know are useless, such as a number already in its camp.

  • Can I guess a play? You can, but in the bots' games a player who guesses ends the game with three mistakes within about eight turns. With one random player in a 3-player table the score fell from 27 to 8.

  • What if a card fits two camps? At L3 you choose which camp. At L1 and L2 it goes on the lower-numbered suit.

Tips

  • Never guess a play. In testing a player who guessed ended the game with three mistakes within about eight turns, and one random player cut a 3-player score from 27 to 8.

  • Give the clue that makes the most certain plays. Pointing at every matching card matters, because the clue also tells your teammate which of their other cards do not match.

  • Only about 40 clues are given in a game, so do not waste them. Discard cards you know are dead (such as a number already in its camp) to win a pawn back.

  • Remember that a colour or suit clue matches either of a card's two colours or suits. A card can be a 'blue' card by its second colour, so think about both values before you play on a clue.

  • Count the camp tops, the discard pile and your teammates' cards. The bots reach about 27 by working out what each of their own cards could be, and people will probably score lower, so aim for Ranger or Guide first.

Worked example

3 players, tokens start at 6. P0 holds {K40} {K17} {K48} {K23} {K45}. P1 holds {K52} {K42} {K34} {K02} {K30}. P2 holds {K16} {K49} {K04} {K11} {K08}. Each player sees the other two hands but not their own.

  1. P0 radios P1: number 1. It points at Amay (1) only. Tokens 5.

  2. P1 plays Amay (1) (number 1, suits 2 and 3) on camp 2. Correct. (It could also have gone on camp 3.)

  3. P2 discards Gowri (9) (a number 9). Tokens back to 6.

  4. P0 radios P2: number 1. It points at Nysha (1) only (number 1, suits 1 and 3). Tokens 5.

  5. P1 discards Bn Sharada (7) (a 7). Tokens 6.

  6. P2 plays Nysha (1) on camp 1. Correct.

  7. P0 radios P2: number 2. It points at Bn Sharada (2) and Ajay (2). Tokens 5. Then P1 radios P2: colour 5. It points at Sharada (3) and Bn Sharada (2). Tokens 4.

  8. P2 knows Bn Sharada (2) is a 2 with colour 5. Only two cards in the whole deck are a 2 with colour 5, Bn Sharada (2) and Shreya (2), and each fits camp 1 or camp 2 (both read 1). P2 plays Bn Sharada (2) on camp 1. Correct.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching game: do not reshuffle the discard pile. When the deck runs out, give every player one more turn and stop. Cards go on the lower-numbered suit if they fit two camps. A table of bots scored about 16 to 17, so aim for Ranger at 14 to 17.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The full reshuffle (once), with cards placed on the lower-numbered suit. A table of bots scored about 27.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: reshuffle once, and you choose the camp when a card fits two. About one point better than the automatic rule for a 4-player bot table.

Solo

Not available. The game needs teammates who can see your cards, because you may never look at your own fronts. For one person, play the two-player game with a helper who takes the second hand.

Two players

Works with 5 cards each. Scores are about the same as with 3 or 4 players (median 27) but the game takes more turns (about 124 plays, 25 to 30 minutes).

Maths and skills in this game

Logical deduction (what could this card be, given what I know?). Number order and counting up to 9. Using a limited resource (pawns). Working together and communicating what matters.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule Camps are built 1 to 9; a number clue is the strongest clue.
ColoursRule A clue can name a colour; a card matches if either of its two colours matches.
Suit pairRule Camps are suits. A card fits two camps, and a suit clue matches either suit.
Back patternNot used You see your own backs, but they tell you nothing about the front.
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour Each child is a member of the expedition.
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour Camps are pitched at the places on the cards.

  • A perfect 54 was never reached. The best single game was 34, in the 2-player games; every game ended by the deck running out, never by three mistakes, because the bot never guesses. The limit is the 6 pawns: only 40 or so clues are given in a game, and a lower sureness threshold (60% instead of 99%) did not raise the score (27.4 vs 27.2 at 3 players) and led to mistakes.

  • Co-op score at 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 players (500 / 500 / 300 / 300 games): mean 26.5 / 27.4 / 26.9 / 25.8; median 27 / 28 / 27 / 26; quartiles 24 and 29 / 26 and 29 / 26 and 28 / 25 and 27; 90th percentile 31 / 30 / 29 / 28; best 34 / 33 / 32 / 29. Reaching 30 or more: 21% / 17% / 8% / 0%.

  • The bot tracks what each of its own cards could be from the clues it has had and from every card it can see, plays only when sure (a card that must fit), gives the clue that makes the most certain plays, and discards cards it knows are dead. It never played a card it was not sure of: zero mistakes in thousands of games on the real 54-card list.

  • Score bands are set from these numbers: Camper 22 or fewer is below the bot's 10th percentile (22 to 24); Ranger 23 to 26 is a bit below its median; Guide 27 to 29 is its median to 75th percentile; Summit-ready 30 or more is reached by only 8 to 21% of bot games at 2 to 4 players and none at 5. At 5 players subtract 2 from each band.

  • Letting the table choose a camp (a simple rule: use the suit with fewer other cards of that number still around) gave a 4-player mean of 27.6 against 26.9 for the automatic lower-suit placement (150 and 300 games), so L3 uses the choose rule and L1 and L2 the automatic rule.

  • Length: 124 / 103 / 103 / 90 plays at 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 players. At 10 to 15 seconds a play (most plays are short clues) that is 20 to 30 minutes, over the 25-minute target at 2 players. L1 (no reshuffle): median 16 at 2 players and 17 at 4 (100 games each), 67 to 77 plays, about 15 minutes. No stall seen: all games ended by the deck or by mistakes.

  • A table with one random player: 3 players median 7 (59 of 60 games ended by three mistakes); 4 players median 15 (45 of 60 ended by mistakes). The game depends on nobody guessing.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: human play. The bot's perfect memory is better than most people's, so real scores will probably be lower; the bands should be checked after play.

  • Not tested: whether a different clue style (for example only number clues first) would reach 30 more often.

  • Not tested: 5-player bands beyond one bot design; they are an estimate.

  • Not tested: a solo mode.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

PERFECT CAMP. Raise six camps, one per suit 1 to 6, from 1 up to 9. Hold your cards so teammates see the fronts and you see only backs. Deal 5 each (2 or 3 players) or 4 (4 or 5 players). Six pawns are Radio tokens; the die starts at 1 and counts mistakes. On your turn do ONE of: PLAY a card on a camp where it is the next number and one of its two suits (wrong: die up one, at 4 the game ends); RADIO a teammate one number, colour or suit, pointing at every match (costs a pawn); DISCARD a card and take a pawn back. Draw after a play or discard.

Back

Score = cards in the camps. When the deck runs out, shuffle the discards once. BANDS: Camper 22 or fewer, Ranger 23-26, Guide 27-29, Summit-ready 30 or more (5 players: subtract 2). A perfect 54 has not been reached. LEVELS. L1 no reshuffle. L2 reshuffle, camp placed on the lower suit. L3 you choose the camp. SOLO: none. Tip: clue a card so the player is SURE, not just touched. Do not guess.

Grown-ups · Game 10 of 13 · Cooperative trick-taking · Fronts

Twin Tasks

Every child in the deck has a twin. The team's mission is to get each task card's twin into exactly the right pair of hands.

Inspired by The Crew by Thomas Sing

RecommendedFamilyGrown-upsHard
Game code
GU-10
Players
2 to 5 (best with 3 or 4)
Time
10 to 15 min a mission
Age
12+ (L1 from 10)
Dice
None
Pawns
1 pawn (the team pass)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone is on one team. Task cards are turned up and claimed; each task is done when the twin of that card is won by the player who claimed it. Play tricks to arrange it, and use the one-time team pass to rescue a missed twin.

What you need

All 54 cardsdealt as hands; the rest are the remainder where the tasks come from
1 pawnthe team pass; put it aside when you use it
Ref 3the Colour key: colours are named by name (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple)
Ref 4the Suit key for the Radio rule

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player a hand: 18 cards each for 2 players, 15 for 3, 12 for 4, 10 for 5. The undealt cards are the remainder (18, 9, 6 or 4 cards).

  • Choose K, the number of tasks, from the difficulty table below. It cannot be more than the number of cards in the remainder whose twin was dealt to a player. Turn up K cards from the remainder as the Task cards, choosing only cards whose twin was dealt to a player. If there are not enough such cards, shuffle and deal again.

  • A twin is the other card with the same face (the same child). The numbers on twins add up to 9. The twin of a Task card is its target. Tasks are public.

  • A random player is the commander. Starting with the commander and going clockwise, each player in turn claims one unclaimed task, until all are claimed. A player may end up with none.

  • Put the pawn in the middle. It is the team pass.

How to play

Each trick:

  1. The commander leads the first trick. After that the winner of a trick leads the next. The leader plays any card and names ONE of its two colours as the led colour (read on the Colour key).

  2. Everyone else must play a card showing that colour (either of its two) if they can. If they cannot, they may play anything.

  3. The highest card that followed the colour wins (the leader's card counts). Equal numbers: the higher serial wins. There is no trump.

  4. Radio (once per player per mission). Between tricks, place one card from your hand face up on the table and say whether it is your highest, your lowest or your only card showing one of its suits (a card counts for either of its two suits, read on the Suit key). You may not talk about your hand in any other way.

  5. Team pass (once per mission, for the whole team). When a trick contains a Task card's twin, the trick's winner may give the credit for that twin to the task's owner. Put the pawn aside when you use it.

  6. Stop playing as soon as the last task is done or the mission is lost.

How it ends

The mission is won when every task's twin has been won by that task's owner, or credited to them by the pass. It is lost the moment a twin is won by someone else and the pass cannot or will not be used to give it to the owner. A mission is short: 8 to 12 minutes. Play several in a row and raise K after each win.

Words in this game

  • Task a card turned up from the remainder. Its twin is the target.
  • Twin the other card of the same child. The two numbers add to 9.
  • Owner the player who claimed a task.
  • Commander leads the first trick and claims first.
  • Radio once each, show a card and say it is your highest, lowest or only card in one of its suits.
  • Team pass one per mission: the winner of a trick that holds a task's twin gives the credit to the owner.

Common questions

  • Do I need to win the trick myself? The owner of a task must win the trick that contains its twin, or the winner must use the team pass for you. If you hold the twin, you decide when to play it.

  • Can we say what is in our hands? Only through the Radio. Once per player per mission you show a card and say if it is your highest, lowest or only card of a suit. Nothing else about your hand.

  • Can I hold the twin of my own task? Yes. Then you only have to win the trick that holds it yourself, with no help needed. Many players pick a task whose twin they hold.

  • I hold the twin of someone else's task. What should I do? Keep it until the owner can win the trick, or until the owner is already winning and you can play it as a low card. Do not play it to a trick someone else will win unless you are ready to spend the pass.

  • Why is there a pass at all? Without it a 4-player mission with 3 tasks is won about 1 time in 5. With one pass it is won about 2 times in 3.

Tips

  • Keep the team pass for a real emergency. Without it a 4-player mission with 3 tasks is won only 19% of the time and with it 67%, so it is the thing that makes missions winnable, but you get one per mission.

  • Claim a task whose twin you hold yourself when you can. Then you only have to win the trick that holds it, with no help needed.

  • If you hold the twin of someone else's task, keep it until the owner can win the trick. Playing it into a trick the owner will lose forces the pass or loses the mission.

  • Use Radio early and spend it on a card that tells the team something useful (highest, lowest or only card in a suit). The bots used no Radio, so a table that uses it well should beat the quiet-team numbers.

  • Start with a low K and raise it after each win. For a 4-player table the sim shows K=2 at 87%, K=3 at 67% and K=4 at 45%, so K=2 is a good first target and K=4 a real challenge.

Worked example

4 players, K = 2, 12 cards each. The tasks are {K31} (twin {K17}) and {K26} (twin {K22}). P3 is the commander and claims {K26}, so P0 claims {K31}. A real mission from the simulation. We start at trick 3, with P0 leading. Checked against the card list.

  1. Trick 3. P0 leads Bharati (4) (number 4, colours 2 and 6) and names colour 2. Bharati (4) is the twin of Bharati (5), which P3 owns. P1 plays Nakul (5) (number 5, colours 1 and 2). P2 plays Avika (4) (number 4, colours 2 and 3). P3 plays Dhruv (3) (number 3, colours 2 and 3).

  2. Everyone followed colour 2. The highest is Nakul (5), so P1 wins the trick. The trick holds Bharati (4), and P1 is not its owner. P1 uses the team pass and gives the credit to P3. The pawn is put aside. P3's task is done.

  3. Trick 4. P1 leads Bn Sharada (2) (number 2, colours 4 and 5) and names colour 4. P2 plays Naresh (3) (number 3, colours 3 and 4), the twin of Naresh (6), which P0 owns. P3 plays Nysha (1) (number 1, colours 3 and 4). P0 plays Avika (5) (number 5, colours 4 and 6).

  4. Avika (5) is the highest card that followed colour 4. P0 wins the trick that holds Naresh (3), so P0's task is done. Both tasks are done and the mission is won. Notice that P2 played the twin when P0 was already going to win, and nobody had to spend a second pass.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching version. K = 1 task, hands open on the table for the first mission. Pass allowed. No Radio. The team nearly always wins and learns how a twin is won.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Normal rules, K = 2, the pass, and Radio.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game. Pick K from the difficulty table (below), and play missions in a row, raising K by 1 after each win.

Solo

Two-handed puzzle. Deal two hands of 18 cards, face up in front of you, and a remainder of 18. Pick K tasks. You are two players: claim the tasks between the two seats as you like. Play both hands honestly (no looking ahead at the cards you will receive). You have the pass. Medals (by the largest K you win): Bronze K = 3, Silver K = 5, Gold K = 6. These follow the two-player bot's results with a full-information player, which is easier than a bot; a first-time group may need the hint of a lower K.

Two players

Deal 18 cards each (remainder 18). Both players are on the team. The pass works as usual. A 2-player mission is short (6 to 9 tricks at the highest K).

Maths and skills in this game

Reasoning about which of 54 cards are still out, pairs that add to 9, planning who will win a trick, and working out whether a card is safe to lead. The twins of K tasks are a small logic puzzle every mission.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule strength in a trick, and twins add to 9
ColoursRule the leader names one of a card's two colours; others follow either of theirs
Suit pairRule only for the Radio call (highest, lowest, only in a suit)
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks ties between equal numbers
NamesRule the twin of a card is the other card of the same child
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

  • Length: a mission with K = 2 or more is 19 to 39 card plays (5 to 10 tricks), which is 5 to 13 minutes at 15 to 20 seconds a card (a K = 1 mission is 6 to 32 plays). A mission is shorter than the 10 to 25 minute target, so play several in a row.

  • Feasibility is the chance the remainder has enough cards whose twin was dealt. 3 players: K = 5 99%, K = 6 88%. 4 players: K = 3 98%, K = 4 98%, K = 5 74%. 5 players: K = 3 89%, K = 4 89%, and K = 5 is impossible (the remainder has only 4 cards). Testing added 'if there are not enough such cards, shuffle and deal again' and a cap of K = 4 at 5 players for this reason.

  • A 2-player mode (18 cards each) was added and run: the pass is still needed (K = 3: 71% without, 98% with). Radio was not simulated; it is estimated to add at most 3 points.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real groups. The bots do not talk or use Radio; a table that uses Radio well should beat these numbers, and a first-time table will probably be below the simple-team column.

  • Not tested: the campaign idea (raise K after every win).

  • Not tested: Radio, and solo medals (the thresholds follow the two-player bot, not a solo bot).

  • Not tested: whether tables will trust the shuffle-and-redeal rule in 5p K = 4 (it is needed 1 deal in 9).

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TWIN TASKS. One team. Deal 15 (3p), 12 (4p) or 10 (5p). Turn up K Task cards from the remainder whose twins were dealt. A twin is the other card of the same child; numbers add to 9. Players claim a task each in turn. A task is done when its TWIN is in a trick won by its owner. The leader plays a card and names ONE of its two colours; others follow that colour if able. Highest follower wins and leads; equal numbers: higher serial. Radio, once each: show a card and say highest, lowest or only in a suit. Team pass, once: the winner of a trick that holds a twin can give its credit to the owner.

Back

DIFFICULTY (win rate of a good team, with the pass). 3 players: K=2 96%, K=4 75%, K=5 59%. 4 players: K=2 87%, K=3 67%, K=4 45%. 5 players: K=2 76%, K=3 46%, K=4 22%. 2 players: K=4 93%, K=5 87%, K=6 78%. L3 pick K from the table and raise it after each win. SOLO: two hands of 18. Medals: Bronze K=3, Silver K=5, Gold K=6.

Grown-ups · Game 11 of 13 · Rising trails and a shared discard · Fronts

Two-Way Trails

Two explorers cut trails through the same jungle, and every card could start a path in either of two directions.

Inspired by Lost Cities (Reiner Knizia), with the idea from the Decktet that every card belongs to two suits

RecommendedGrown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-11
Players
2 (or solo)
Time
15 to 20 min
Age
10+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Build rising trails of numbers, one per suit. Each trail you open costs you 14 points, so only open the ones you can climb high.

What you need

All 54 cardsHands, the draw deck and the six fire piles. Every card is on two suits, so it can go in two places.
A flat tableRoom for six fire piles in the middle and six trail columns in front of each player.
Pencil and paperFor adding up the score at the end.

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 7 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the draw deck.

  • Lay six empty spots in a row in the middle: the fire piles, one for each suit 1 to 6 (read the suits on the Suit key, Ref 4). Fire piles are face up and shared.

  • In front of each player, leave room for six trail columns, one for each suit 1 to 6. They start empty.

  • Pick a first player. The seats are fair, so anyone can start.

How to play

A turn is Play, then Draw:

  1. Play one card from your hand, either way. Trail: put it on your own trail column for one of its two suits, but only if its number is higher than the top card of that column. An empty column takes any number. Overlap the cards so every number stays visible. Fire: put it face up on the fire pile of one of its two suits.

  2. Draw one card. Take the top card of the draw deck, or the top card of any fire pile except the one you just put a card on.

  3. Now it is your opponent's turn.

  4. Equal is not higher: a 5 cannot go on a 5. Only you may add to your own trail columns.

How it ends

The game ends the moment the last card of the draw deck is drawn, or when each player has had 30 turns, whichever comes first (the 30-turn stop is a safety stop; in the bots' games it only bites if both players keep swapping fire cards). Score each trail you opened: add its numbers, then subtract 14. A trail of 5 or more cards earns +12. Every twin pair with both cards in your own trails earns +3. Highest total wins. A tie goes to the player with more cards in trails; still level, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Trail One of your six columns. A trail only goes up: each new card must be higher than the one before.
  • Fire pile A shared face-up pile for one suit. Cards you do not want go here, and either player may take the top card.
  • Opening a trail Putting the first card on an empty column. It costs 14 points, which you win back by adding up the numbers.
  • Twin pair The two cards of one child. They always add up to 9 (the double-nine children are 9 and 9).

Common questions

  • Can I put a card on my opponent's trail? No. Trails are private to the player who builds them. You only affect your opponent by what you put on, or take from, the fire piles.

  • I fired a card. Can I take it straight back? No. You may not draw from the fire pile you just put a card on. You may draw from any other fire pile.

  • A card has two suits. Which trail does it go on? Your choice, as long as its number is higher than the top card of that column. It only ever goes on one.

  • Why would I ever not open a trail? Every trail you open starts at minus 14. A trail whose numbers add up to less than 14 loses points, so open only the suits you can climb past about 20.

  • Do twin pairs have to be in the same trail? No. The two cards of one child can be in any two of your trails. Both just have to be in your trails, not in your hand or on a fire pile.

Tips

  • Open only the trails you can climb past about 20. Each trail costs 14, and smart players open about 4.7 of the 6 suits. A bot that opened everything lost 76% to 24%, and one that opened very few lost about 81%.

  • Remember a card can go on either of its two suits. Play it on the trail that wastes the least, and fire it on the suit pile that helps you least.

  • Think about the fire piles as a gift. Anything you fire can be drawn by your opponent (but never by you straight away), so do not fire a card that fits their trail.

  • Mind the skipped numbers. A bot that put less weight on skipped numbers lost 90% to the tuned one, so do not jump from a 2 to a 9 if you can wait for the middle cards.

  • Look at the twin bonus, but do not chase it. It is worth only about 10 points to a good bot, so build for the +12 on a trail of five or more cards first.

Worked example

One side of a game. Player 0 starts with {K14} (3), {K45} (8), {K28} (5), {K23} (4), {K16} (3), {K43} (8) and {K27} (5). Player 1's hand is not shown.

  1. Player 0 plays Sharada (3) (number 3, suits 5 and 6) on trail 6, which was empty, then draws Avika (5) from the deck.

  2. Player 1 plays Nysha (1) (number 1, suits 1 and 3) on trail 3, which was empty.

  3. Player 0 plays Gopi (5) (number 5, suits 1 and 4) on trail 4, which was empty, then draws Adheesh (9) from the deck.

  4. Player 1 fires Kanasu (3) (number 3, suits 2 and 5) onto fire pile 2.

  5. Player 0 plays Nakul (4) (number 4, suits 3 and 6) on trail 6. Four is higher than three and 6 is one of its suits, so trail 6 now reads 3, 4.

  6. Player 1 fires Idhayan (1) (number 1, suits 4 and 6) onto fire pile 4.

  7. Player 0 plays Smaya (8) (number 8, suits 2 and 4) on trail 4. Trail 4 now reads 5, 8: a sum of 13, which is minus 1 after the 14 is taken off. It needs more cards to pay.

  8. Player 1 plays Pinku (2) (number 2, suits 1 and 3) on trail 3, which now reads 1, 2.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching game. Ignore the +12 for a long trail and the twin bonus. Each trail you open scores its numbers added up minus 14. Hold 7 cards and play it open-handed if you like.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add the +12 for a trail of 5 or more cards. Ignore twin pairs.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: the +12 for a long trail and +3 for every twin pair held in your trails.

Solo

Solo (30 turns). Deal 7 cards, set up the fire piles and your trails as usual, and play 30 turns alone: play a card, then draw (from the deck or any fire pile except the one you just used). There is no opponent, so use the fire piles as a place to park cards you may want back. Then score as in the full game. Bronze 80, Silver 100, Gold 115. These come from 2,000 bot games (a decent bot scored 79 / 98 / 117 at the 25th / 50th / 75th percentile; a very simple bot scored 13 in the middle). Scores swing by about 26 points from luck, so judge yourself over a few games.

Two players

This is a two-player game at heart. Seats are fair: the first player wins 50% of games between equal bots. Three or more players are not supported.

Maths and skills in this game

Ordering numbers and keeping a rising sequence. Adding a column of numbers and subtracting 14 (negative numbers appear when a trail is too short). Expected value: is this trail worth the 14-point cost? Number bonds to 9 through the twin cards.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule Trails must rise; the score is the sum of the numbers.
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule Each card can start or extend a trail in either of its two suits, or sit on either suit's fire pile.
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used Ties are broken by cards in trails, not by serial.
NamesRule The two cards of one child (twins) score +3 when both are in your trails.
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour The trails are laid through the places on the cards.

  • Smart bots beat random bots 2,000 to 0 and simple bots (which extend trails but fire at random) 1,991 to 9 (99.5%). A simple bot beat a random one 98%. Skill clearly beats luck. Each setting was 2,000 games on the real 54-card list.

  • Equal smart bots finished 1,002 to 992 with 6 ties (0.3%). The first player won 50.0% of decided games, so the seats are fair.

  • A typical game is 40 plays (20 each). At about 20 seconds a play that is about 13 minutes, so the game is given as 12 to 18 minutes.

  • Scores between smart bots had quartiles 46 / 59 / 72, with a median winning margin of 19 points.

  • Opening is balanced, not dominant. Smart players open 4.7 of 6 trails. A bot that opens every trail lost 76% to 24% to the smart bot, a bot that opens very few lost about 81%, and one that never opens lost 100%. Winners opened 4.6 trails on average, losers 4.9.

  • Testing added the 30-turn stop as a safety stop. Random players keep drawing fire cards and never exhaust the deck (mean 124 plays, and every random game ends on the stop). Smart games always end at the deck (mean 40 plays, none reached the stop), so the stop costs smart play nothing.

  • Level scores for equal smart bots (600 games each): L1 (no bonus, no twins) quartiles 22 / 30 / 37; L2 (+12 only) 36 / 48 / 61; L3 (full) 46 / 59 / 72. The seat split was about 51 / 49 at all three, so every level is fair.

  • Solo, 2,000 games of 30 turns: a decent bot scored 62 / 79 / 98 / 117 / 132 at the 10th / 25th / 50th / 75th / 90th percentile (standard deviation 26); a simple bot had a median of 13; a random bot a median of minus 24. Skill separates about 85 points of score from luck's 26, which supports Bronze 80, Silver 100, Gold 115.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: human players. The bot's weight on skipped numbers in a trail mattered a lot (an untuned version lost 90% of games to the tuned one), so a strong human may find a better opening policy.

  • Not tested: how far humans play for the twin bonus. It is worth only about 10 points to a good bot, so humans may play for it more.

  • Not tested: solo medals with people. They were set from a bot.

  • Not tested: three or more players. The game is designed for two.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

TWO-WAY TRAILS. Two explorers, six jungle trails, and every card points two ways. Deal 7 each. The rest is the deck. Six fire piles sit in the middle, one per suit 1 to 6, and each of you has six trail columns of your own. Turn: PLAY one card, then DRAW one. Play it on YOUR trail for either of its two suits, only if its number beats that trail's top (an empty trail takes any number). Or FIRE it onto either of its suits' piles. Draw from the deck or from any fire pile except the one you just fired onto. The game ends when the last deck card is drawn.

Back

SCORING. Each trail you opened: add the numbers and subtract 14. A trail of 5 or more cards: +12. Each twin pair with both cards in your trails: +3. Highest total wins; tie goes to more cards in trails. LEVELS. L1 no bonuses, L2 add the +12, L3 everything. SOLO. 30 turns alone, then score. Bronze 80, Silver 100, Gold 115. Tip: open only the trails you can take past about 20.

Grown-ups · Game 12 of 13 · Market take, build or sell · Fronts

Pen and Plume

Two rival camp-keepers fill their pens with the best animals at the market, or sell them for coin before the fair closes.

Inspired by Emu Ranchers (P. D. Magnus, a Decktet game), with a market take in the style of Reiner Knizia's games

Grown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-12
Players
2
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
10+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Take a card from a market of five, then start a pen, add to a pen (higher number, shared suit) or sell the card for coins. Tall pens score big, but every pen costs upkeep.

What you need

All 54 cards14 go back in the box each round without looking; 40 are played.
A flat tableA market row of five, up to four pens each, and a face-down Sales pile each.
Pencil and paperFor adding up pens and coins at the end of each round.

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Without looking, put 14 back in the box. Lay 5 cards face up in a row as the market. The other 35 are the draw deck, face down.

  • Each player has up to 4 pens (stacks where you can see the top card; overlap them so every number shows) and a face-down Sales pile.

  • Pick a first player. In round 2 the other player goes first.

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Take one card from the market. Fill the empty spot from the draw deck.

  2. Then do exactly one of these with the card: Start a new pen with it (if you have fewer than 4 pens). Add it to one of your pens: its number must be higher than the pen's top card and share at least one suit with it. It becomes the new top card. A 9 on top ends a pen, because nothing can follow. Sell it: put it face down in your Sales pile. A sold card is worth coins equal to its number.

  3. When the market cannot be filled back up to 5, the round ends once both players have had the same number of turns.

  4. Pay upkeep. Each pen of 3 or more cards costs 3 coins, taken from your Sales (coins are the numbers on your sold cards). Pay for your longest pen first, then the next longest. A pen you cannot pay for is lost.

  5. Score the pens. Each pen of 3 or more cards that you kept scores the sum of its numbers, plus 4 if one suit is on every card of the pen. Pens of fewer than 3 cards score nothing and cost nothing.

  6. Spare coins: every 2 coins you have left over scores 1 point.

  7. Play two rounds, shuffling again for round 2, and add the scores.

How it ends

After round 2, add both rounds. Highest total wins. If it is a tie, the player with more surviving pens wins; if that is level too, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Market The row of five face-up cards that both players take from.
  • Pen A stack of your cards in rising order that all share suits link by link. You see only the top card.
  • Sales pile Face-down cards you have sold. Each is worth coins equal to its number.
  • Upkeep 3 coins per pen of 3 or more cards, paid from your sales at the end of the round.
  • Link Two cards next to each other in a pen: the second has a higher number and shares a suit with the first.

Common questions

  • Do all the cards in a pen need to share the same suit? No. Each card only has to share a suit with the card just below it. If one suit is on every card of the pen, you earn the +4 bonus.

  • What if I cannot pay for my pens? Pay for the longest pen first. A pen you cannot pay for is lost and scores nothing. Sell low cards early to keep enough coins; the bots almost never fell short.

  • Do I have to build a pen? No, but a player who only sells loses almost every game. Selling everything wins about 10% of games against the smart bot.

  • Can I take a card and then not use it? No. You must start, add or sell it. Selling is always possible, so you are never stuck.

  • Why does it matter what the market shows my opponent? They see the same five cards. Taking a card they need, even to sell, can deny them a good link.

Tips

  • Balance pens and sales. A bot that built one tall pen lost 85% of its matches and a bot that sold everything lost 89%, so build two or three pens and sell the cards that do not fit.

  • Sell low cards early to keep coins. Upkeep (3 coins per pen of 3 or more cards) almost never bit the smart bot, but it is the reason not to build four tall pens with no sales.

  • Take a card that helps your opponent even if you only sell it. Both of you see the same five cards, and denying a good link is a real move.

  • Aim for one suit on every card of a pen. That is +4, and each card only has to share a suit with the one below it, so plan the first two cards with a suit you can keep.

  • A 9 on top ends a pen because nothing can follow. Save a 9 for the very end of a long pen, or sell it for 9 coins.

Worked example

Start market: {K16} (3), {K38} (7), {K35} (6), {K09} (2) and {K24} (4).

  1. Player 1 takes Pinku (2) (number 2, suits 1 and 3) and starts a pen. The market refills with Ajay (7).

  2. Player 2 takes Archana (4) (number 4, suits 2 and 3) and starts a pen. The market refills with Naresh (6).

  3. Player 1 takes Kanasu (6) (number 6, suits 3 and 4) and adds it to the pen: 6 is higher than 2 and both show suit 3. The market refills with Ammlu (7).

  4. Player 2 takes Pinku (7) (number 7, suits 4 and 6) and sells it face down for 7 coins. The market refills with Rihansh (9).

  5. Player 1 takes Rihansh (9) (number 9, suits 1 and 5) and sells it for 9 coins. The market refills with Idhayan (1).

  6. Player 2 takes Ammlu (7) (number 7, suits 2 and 5) and adds it to the pen with Archana (4): 7 is higher than 4 and both show suit 2. The market refills with Gowri (9).

  7. Now Player 1 has one pen (Pinku (2), Kanasu (6)) and 9 coins; Player 2 has one pen (Archana (4), Ammlu (7)) and 7 coins.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching game: play one round only, and skip the upkeep. Pens of 3 or more cards just score their numbers (plus 4 for one suit on every card). Spare coins still score 1 point per 2.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Play two rounds, still without upkeep.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: two rounds, 3 coins upkeep per pen of 3 or more cards, longest pen paid first.

Solo

Solo (two rounds). Play both rounds alone: take a card from the market and start, add or sell, with the same rules and upkeep, until the market cannot be filled (about 36 turns a round). Nobody takes cards from you, so scores are higher than in a two-player game. Add the two rounds. Bronze 260, Silver 275, Gold 290. Bot results over 2,000 games: a decent bot scored 262 / 277 / 289 at the 25th / 50th / 75th percentile; a bot that only sells scored about 196; a random bot about 192.

Two players

This is a two-player game. The player who goes second in round 1 goes first in round 2, which removes the first-turn edge.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding long runs of numbers. Comparing a sure coin value to a bigger but risky pen. Halving coins (every 2 spare coins is 1 point). Planning ahead for a rising sequence with matching suits.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule Pens rise; scores are the sum; sale value equals the number.
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule A card links to a pen if it shares either of its two suits with the top card; one suit on every card earns +4.
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour The animals in the pens are named after the children on the cards.
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour The market stalls are the places shown on the cards.

  • The smart bot beat a random bot 2,000 to 0. Against a simple bot (takes the highest card, adds if it can, sells the rest) it won 1,782 to 208 with 10 ties (89%). Equal smart bots finished 993 to 984 with 23 ties (1.2%), so there is no seat advantage. The smart bot values a pen by its sum, its room to grow and the coins it holds, and also considers what the card is worth to the opponent.

  • Each row is 2,000 two-round matches on the real 54-card list, with round 1 and round 2 swapping the starter.

  • No single plan dominates. A bot that builds one tall pen and ignores selling lost to the smart bot 1,696 to 280 (85%). A bot that sells everything lost 1,789 to 198 (89%). Neither extreme beats the balanced plan, and they win only 15% and 10%.

  • A match is 72 market takes (36 per round, 18 each per round). At about 15 to 20 seconds a take that is 18 to 24 minutes, so the game is given as 18 to 24. One round alone is about 9 to 12 minutes.

  • Upkeep almost never bites: smart bots lose 0.00 pens per round, and even a tall-pen bot loses only 0.12. Testing 1 coin per card instead of a flat 3 changed little (the tall bot loses 0.19 pens a round and still loses the match 90 to 10 against smart; equal bots split 995 to 988), so the flat 3 stays. Upkeep is a small tax.

  • With 23 cards removed instead of 14, the round shrinks to 56 takes, scores fall to about 80 and tall pens lose 0.33 per round. Smart wins 90% there, so 14 stays.

  • Bot weights mattered more than rules: how a bot values an unfinished pen changes the pen-versus-coins balance a lot. In a head-to-head of 300 matches, a bot that valued unfinished pens at 0.30 instead of 0.35 of their sum lost 256 to 42; at 0.45 it lost 193 to 103. The balanced play sits in a narrow band, and the best weight (0.38) is used for every number here.

  • Scores: equal smart bots total 115 / 130 / 144 over two rounds (quartiles); a random bot 62 / 73 / 85. Solo, 2,000 two-round games: a decent bot 262 / 277 / 289 (25th / 50th / 75th percentile, sd 20); a tall bot median 228; a sell-everything bot 196; random 192. The gap between a decent bot and random is 85, so skill is visible in solo.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

PEN AND PLUME. Five cards lie face up in the market. On your turn take one, then do exactly one thing with it. START a new pen (up to 4). ADD it to a pen if its number is higher than the pen's top card and they share a suit. SELL it face down for coins equal to its number. Refill the market from the deck after each take. When the market cannot refill, finish the round so both players have had the same number of turns. Then pay 3 coins for each pen of 3 or more cards (longest first). A pen you cannot pay for is lost.

L1 one round, no upkeep. L2 two rounds, no upkeep. L3 full. SOLO. Play both rounds alone. Bronze 260, Silver 275, Gold 290. Tip: sell your high cards you cannot use.

Grown-ups · Game 13 of 13 · Tile laying, balance your tracks · Fronts

Six Roads

Lay the roads across the map: every card is a stretch of two roads, and your expedition is only as good as its weakest road.

Inspired by Ingenious (Reiner Knizia)

Grown-upsMedium
Game code
GU-13
Players
2 to 4 (best with 2)
Time
15 to 25 min
Age
10+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Place cards like dominoes on a shared map and score along lines of matching suits into six tracks, one per suit. You are scored mostly on your weakest track, so spread your points. New: the rules are still settling, see the testing notes.

What you need

All 54 cardsA shared map on the table, plus a hand of 5 each and a draw deck.
Pencil and paperEach player keeps six tracks, one for each suit 1 to 6, each from 0 to 18.
A tableA 10 by 10 square of room for the map.

Fronts of the cards are private, backs are public. Reference cards are the seven small cards in the box (Ref 1 to 7).

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Turn one card from the deck face up in the middle: the start card.

  • A card has two squares, one for each of its two suits (read the suits on the Suit key, Ref 4). A card is two squares long and one square wide.

  • The whole map may never be wider or taller than 10 squares.

  • Each player writes six tracks, suit 1 to suit 6, each starting at 0.

  • Pick a first player.

How to play

On your turn:

  1. Place one card from your hand flat on the table, either way up, horizontally or vertically, so that it touches a placed card side to side. It must stay inside the 10 by 10 limit.

  2. Score it. For each of the card's two squares, look out from that square in the three directions that do not pass through the card's other square (straight on, left and right). Count the squares in a row, starting next to your square, that show the same suit as it. Stop at the first square that differs or is empty. Count at most 4 squares in any one line. Add the count to your track for that suit, up to a maximum of 18.

  3. The first time one of your tracks reaches 18, take another turn straight away.

  4. Draw back to 5.

  5. If you cannot place any card, pass.

How it ends

The game ends when the deck is empty and the player to move cannot place a card, or when everyone passes in a row. Cards left in hands do not count. Score = your lowest track plus half your second-lowest track (to avoid halves, work out 2 x lowest + second lowest). Highest wins. If tied, the next lowest track decides, and so on; if your sorted tracks match exactly, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Track Your score for one suit, kept on paper, from 0 to 18.
  • Square Half a card. It shows one suit.
  • Line Squares of the same suit in a row, starting next to the one you just placed.
  • Weakest track The track with the lowest number. It counts most at the end.

Common questions

  • Which directions do I count? From each of the card's two squares, three ways: straight on, left and right. Never back through the card's other square.

  • Why count at most 4 squares? Without the cap, a single column of one suit paid 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, and one suit ran away. The cap keeps a long column from being worth more than a spread of points.

  • Why am I scored on my weakest track? To win you must score in all six suits. Look for placements that score in two suits at once, and avoid handing a rival a long open line of a suit they need.

  • Do I have to place a card? Yes, if you can. If no card in your hand can be placed inside the 10 by 10 limit, pass.

  • Can a card go on top of another? No. Cards never overlap.

Tips

  • Your score is mostly your weakest track (2 x lowest + second lowest at L3), so when two placements are close, choose the one that lifts your lowest suit.

  • Look for placements that score in both squares at once. A card has two suits, and scoring on two tracks in one turn is the fastest way to bring up the weak ones.

  • Do not hand a rival a long open line of a suit they need. With a cap of 4 squares in a line, a single placement is worth at most 4 per direction.

  • Play this at 2 players if you can. The balancing bot beat a points-maximiser 54% there, while at 3 and 4 players the board is crowded and the lowest tracks are only 1 to 5.

  • Hitting 18 on a track gives an extra turn, but only once per track. Keep a card back for the turn when a track reaches 18, and fill the other tracks first.

Worked example

2 players, the start card {K50} in the middle: its left square shows suit 1 and its right square shows suit 2. Cards are placed below it one after another. Lines of at most 4 squares are counted.

  1. A places Bharati (5) (suits 1 and 2) directly under Adheesh (9), suit 1 under suit 1 and suit 2 under suit 2. +1 to track 1 and +1 to track 2.

  2. B places Naresh (6) (suits 2 and 6) under Bharati (5). The 2 sits under two 2s: +2 to track 2. The 6 sits under a 1: 0.

  3. A places Dharsh (2) (suits 2 and 6) under Naresh (6). The 2 sits under three 2s: +3 to track 2. The 6 sits under a 6: +1 to track 6.

  4. B places Amay (1) (suits 2 and 3) standing up under the right-hand column. The 2 sits under four 2s in a column: +4 to track 2. The 3 is at the far end: 0.

  5. A places Gopi (4) (suits 2 and 6) standing up above Adheesh (9) on the right. The 2 sits above five 2s, but only 4 count: +4, not 5, to track 2.

  6. Tracks, suits 1 to 6: A has 1, 8, 0, 0, 0, 1 and B has 0, 6, 0, 0, 0, 0. Both still score 0 for the lowest tracks, because suits 3, 4 and 5 are empty. Next, they should go there.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teaching game: count the whole line (no limit of 4) and score only your lowest track. Two players are easiest.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add the limit of 4 squares in a line. Still score only your lowest track.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: limit of 4, and score = lowest track plus half the second lowest.

Solo

Solo. Deal yourself 5 cards, put one in the middle and play every turn alone until the deck is empty and you cannot place (about 46 turns). Keep six tracks and score 2 x lowest + second-lowest (the top is 54). Bronze 48, Silver 52, Gold 54 (every track full). These are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of a balancing bot over 300 games (48 / 52 / 54, standard deviation 4). A bot that just scores points scored 44 / 48 / 54, and a random bot about 4. It is easy to reach the top, which is why Gold is a full set.

Two players

The best way to play. Skill shows most: a balancing bot beats a plain points-maximiser 54% of games against a fair 50%. With 3 or 4 players the board is crowded and the lowest tracks are small (1 to 5), so who wins is less in your control.

Maths and skills in this game

Counting along lines. Adding to six running totals. Choosing between a big gain in one suit and a small gain in two. Planning to bring up the weakest total.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule Each card is two squares, one for each suit; you score each square separately.
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceFlavour The map is the lands the cards come from.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Status: New, rules still settling. No version clearly improved; limit of 4 plus lowest and half the second lowest chosen; balancer beats a points bot 54 / 52 / 42% at 2 / 3 / 4 players (fair 50 / 33 / 25); about 46 plays, 12 to 20 min

Version (balancer vs maximiser)Win % at 2 / 3 / 4 playersWinner has most points %, 2 / 3 / 4
Current rule54 / 50 / 3557 / 47 / 28
(a) at most 4 in a line53 / 53 / 4755 / 33 / 39
(b) lowest plus half second lowest58 / 42 / 3750 / 41 / 29
