Solo (2 x lowest + second)48 / 52 / 54quartiles of a balancing bot

  • Results come from simulation on a real 10 by 10 board with the real 54-card deck, with all placements (both ways up, both directions) tried. A game is about 46 plays in total at every player count: 12 to 16 minutes at 15 to 20 seconds a play, and nearer 20 when counting lines slowly.

  • Testing was prompted by an earlier version of the rules, which took about 47 turns and in which a smart bot beat a simple bot 71% / 50% / 38% at 2 / 3 / 4 players (fair: 50 / 33 / 25). It played as a points race rather than a balance game, so four versions were simulated: the previous rule; (a) at most 4 squares in a line; (b) score = lowest + half the second lowest; (a) and (b) together.

  • No version clearly beat the others, and the rules are still settling. Differences between versions are inside the noise of 100 to 120 games (about 4 to 5 points), and the previous rule already made the weakest track matter (the points leader loses 27 to 53% of games). What the numbers do support: the 4-square limit removes most extra-turn chains, and half the second lowest makes the scores finer and the order less tied at 3 and 4 players.

  • Bots: a balancing bot (weights each placement by how much it lifts the weakest tracks), a points-maximiser and a random bot; 120 games per equal-skill cell and 100 per balancer-versus-maximiser cell. Balancer vs random wins every game in all four versions at 2, 3 and 4 players (100%), so it does not separate the versions. Balancer vs points-maximiser wins (fair 50 / 33 / 25): previous rule 54 / 50 / 35; (a) only 53 / 53 / 47; (b) only 58 / 42 / 37; (a)+(b) 54 / 52 / 42.

  • How often the winner is also the player with the most total points (lower means balance matters more), balancer vs maximiser at 2 / 3 / 4 players: previous 57 / 47 / 28%; (a) 55 / 33 / 39%; (b) 50 / 41 / 29%; (a)+(b) 47 / 34 / 32%. Between two balancers: previous 73 / 42 / 38%; (a) 67 / 56 / 36%; (b) 73 / 51 / 46%; (a)+(b) 70 / 47 / 48%. Under the previous and (a) rules the winner always has the best lowest track, because the lowest track is the score; under (b) the best lowest track won 92 to 100%. Equal balancers at 2 players averaged 1.85 tracks at 18 per game with the previous rule, 0.87 with (a), 1.26 with (b) and 0.52 with (a)+(b); at 3 and 4 players it is under 0.8 in every version.

  • Testing kept (a)+(b) together. It cuts the runaway (extra turns from hitting 18 on a track) the most, has the lowest winner-is-top-scorer rate against the maximiser at 2 players (47%) and a near-lowest one at 3 (34%), and keeps a clear skill gap at every count (54 / 52 / 42 against a fair 50 / 33 / 25). The score is also less lumpy: at 4 players the lowest track alone is only 2 / 3 / 4 (quartiles) and a random opponent leaves it at 0, while with half the second lowest added the equal-skill score is 4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5.

  • Seats: equal-skill seat shares in the chosen version were 52 / 48 at 2 players, and between 22 and 37% at 3 and 4 players (120 games, so only roughly fair). Ties are under 1.2% in every version because tied tracks are broken by the next lowest. Skill fades with more players: 3 and 4 players are much more crowded and the lowest tracks are about 3 to 5, so the game is best at 2.

  • Solo, 300 games: balancing bot 48 / 52 / 54 (quartiles), points bot 44 / 48 / 54, random about 4.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: human play.

  • Not tested: differences between the four versions beyond the noise at 100 to 120 games.

  • Not tested: 4-player seat shares beyond a rough estimate.

  • Not tested: two cards per turn (a way to lengthen the game).

  • Limit: the solo medals are close to the cap, so there is little spread.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

SIX ROADS. Put one card flat on the map, touching a placed card side to side, inside 10 by 10. Each card has two squares (its two suits). For each square look out in the three directions not through its own card (straight, left, right). Count squares of the same suit in a row, at most 4, starting next to your square. Add that count to your track for that suit (max 18). Hit 18 for the first time: take another turn. Then draw back to 5. Pass if you cannot place. The game ends when the deck is empty and the player to move cannot place.

Back

SCORE = lowest track + half the second lowest (work in doubles: 2 x lowest + second lowest). Highest wins; ties go to the next lowest track. LEVELS. L1 no limit on line length, score only the lowest track. L2 limit of 4, lowest track only. L3 full. SOLO. Play alone to the end of the deck. Bronze 48, Silver 52, Gold 54 (2 x lowest + second lowest). Tip: score in two suits at once, and do not leave a long open line of a suit your rival needs.

Mind games · Deduction · Both

Number Cipher

Your cards stand in a row from low to high, and you can see them. Your opponent can only see their backs. Guess what they are, one number at a time, and be the first to crack the whole row.

Inspired by Coda, Da Vinci Code and Fugitive

RecommendedGrown-upsKidsMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-01
Players
1 to 4
Time
about 10 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each player keeps a hidden row of cards sorted from low to high. On your turn you draw a card, then try to guess a number in an opponent's row. A right guess turns it up; a wrong one turns up your own new card. Last player with a hidden card wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsa row in front of each player and a draw pile
Colour key (Ref 3)to read the colour numbers when two cards have the same number

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. At 2 players deal 4 cards to the first player and 5 cards to the second player (the extra card offsets the first-move edge). At 3 or 4 players deal 4 to each.

  • Look at your cards and stand them in a row in front of you, fronts toward you so opponents see only the backs. Put them in order: lowest number on the left.

  • If two cards have the same number, the one with the lower first colour number goes to the left (Red 1, Orange 2, Yellow 3, Green 4, Blue 5, Purple 6, using the lower of a card's two colours). If that is also equal, the lower serial goes left.

  • Put the rest of the cards face down as the draw pile. The player with 4 cards goes first.

How to play

  1. Draw. Take the top card of the draw pile and slide it into the right place in your row, using the same order. It is still hidden from opponents.

  2. Guess. Point at one hidden card in an opponent's row and name its number (1 to 9).

  3. If you are right, the opponent turns that card face up where it stands. You may then guess again (at any hidden card) or stop.

  4. If you are wrong, you must turn the card you drew this turn face up in your own row. Your turn ends. If you did not draw (the pile is empty), turn up any one of your hidden cards.

  5. Cards that are face up stay in their places. They are clues for everybody.

How it ends

A player whose cards are all face up is out. At 2 players, the first player to have every card face up loses; the other wins. At 3 or 4 players, the last player who still has a hidden card wins. If the draw pile runs out, you carry on without drawing.

Words in this game

  • Row your cards in order from the lowest number on the left to the highest on the right.
  • Hidden card a card in a row that is face down toward the other players.
  • Face up a card that has been guessed or revealed. Everyone can see its number.
  • Tie order for the same number: lower first colour number to the left; if still equal, lower serial to the left.

Common questions

  • How do my opponents see my cards? They see only the backs. Fronts face you. When a card is revealed you turn it round so its front faces everybody.

  • Can I guess a card that is already face up? No. You may only guess a hidden card.

  • Why does the order of equal numbers matter? Because a position is a clue. If two 7s are next to each other, you know the left one has a lower colour number than the right one.

  • If I guess right three times, do I get anything extra? No, but every right guess takes you one card closer to winning and gives you information. The risk is that you must reveal your own new card if you are wrong at the end.

  • Do I need to guess in order? No. Guess any hidden card you like in any row.

Tips

  • Use the order. If the card to the left of a hidden card is a face-up 6, the hidden card is 6 or more. The row is a ladder, so every revealed card narrows its neighbours.

  • Count the copies. There are six cards of each number. If you hold two 7s and two more are face up, only two 7s are left in the whole game.

  • Guess the extremes. The leftmost hidden card is low and the rightmost is high. A guess of 9 at the far right is often safe.

  • Stop when it gets uncertain. The bot only keeps guessing after a right guess when it believes its next guess is better than 50% likely. Stop earlier and keep your drawn card hidden.

  • Your drawn card is your price for a wrong guess. A card in the middle of your row is more valuable to hide than one at the end, because it hides a number that is hard to guess.

  • Think about colours. Two face-up cards with the same number tell you the order of their first colours. A third card next to them narrows down which colour it has.

Worked example

  1. Two players. P0 (4 cards, first) has Ammlu 2, Shreya 2, Amyra 4 and Gowri 9: Ammlu (2), Shreya (2), Amyra (4), Gowri (9). The two 2s are in colour order: Ammlu has the lower colour number (Orange 2), Shreya's lower colour is Blue 5, so Ammlu is on the left. P1 (5 cards) has Archana 5, Pinku 7, Anayka 8, Adheesh 9 and Rihansh 9: Archana (5), Pinku (7), Anayka (8), Adheesh (9), Rihansh (9). Adheesh (Red 1) goes left of Rihansh (Yellow 3).

  2. P0 draws Ammlu (7) (Ammlu, 7) and slides it between the 4 and the 9. P0's row is now 2, 2, 4, 7, 9. P0 looks at P1's backs: the last two cards are the right end of an ascending row. P0 guesses the fifth card is a 9. Right: Rihansh (9) is turned up.

  3. P0 guesses the fourth card is also a 9. Right: Adheesh (9) is turned up. P0 is on a roll and guesses the first card is a 6. Wrong, it is a 5 (Archana (5)). P0 must turn up the card they drew this turn: Ammlu (7), the 7. P0's turn ends.

  4. P1 draws Rihansh (9) (Rihansh, 9, Orange 2) and slides it between the two 9s already in the row, because its first colour number (2) is between Adheesh's 1 and the other Rihansh's 3. P1 sees that P0's face-up 7 sits in the fourth place, so the fifth card is at least 7. P1 guesses a 9. Right: Gowri (9) turned up.

  5. P1 guesses P0's first card is a 2. Right: Ammlu (2) turned up. P1 stops, keeping their new 9 hidden. Now P0 has 3 cards up and 2 hidden, and P1 has 2 up and 4 hidden. P0 is closer to being out, so P0 has to guess carefully.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Three cards each. A helper keeps the numbers in order. Only the number is guessed, and a wrong guess just ends your turn (no penalty). Last to run out of hidden cards wins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Four cards each, with the colour and serial order for equal numbers. A wrong guess turns up your new card.

L3 · age 8 and up

The second player gets an extra card (5 against 4). At 3 or 4 players, deal 4 each and play to the last player with a hidden card.

Solo

Solo, Cipher Breaker: deal 4 cards face down and sort them into a row as usual. Guess a card's number, then turn it up if right. Every wrong guess is 1 miss, and a wrong guess at a card rules that number out for that card. Crack all four with as few misses as you can. Medals: Gold 4 misses or fewer, Silver 5 to 7, Bronze 8 to 10. (Set from a bot run; not tested with people.)

Two players

This is the tested game: two players, the first with 4 cards and the second with 5.

Maths and skills in this game

Logical deduction with ordered information, counting copies (six of each number), and probability: which guess is most likely.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule what you guess, and what orders the row
ColoursRule the tie-break for equal numbers (lower first colour goes left)
Suit pairNot used
Back patternFlavour opponents see only the backs; the backs hide the number
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule the last tie-break for equal numbers and equal colours
NamesFlavour the children in the row
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill (chunk 2): a bot that tracks which numbers are still possible beat a random guesser 97% of the time.

  • Length (chunk 2): two such bots took 15 turns each, about 10 minutes at 12 to 20 seconds a turn. The first player won 56% to 44%, which is why the second player gets an extra card.

  • Solo (my run of 100 games): a bot that samples possible rows and always guesses the most likely number averaged 5.4 misses and 9.4 guesses to crack a row of 4, with quartiles of 4, 5 and 7 misses. The medal lines come from these quartiles.

  • The bot's method: it samples possible hidden rows from the cards it has not seen, keeps only the rows that fit the face-up cards in their places, and guesses the most common number in the most common place. It keeps guessing after a right answer only when that guess is better than 50% likely.

  • Order matters: the row is sorted by number, then by the lower colour number, then by serial. That ordering is what makes position a clue.

  • Tested at 2 players only; 3 and 4 players are an extension and are untested.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. The bot reads probabilities, humans use hunches about hands and body language.

  • Not tested: 3 or 4 players, L1 (3 cards each), or the solo medals.

  • Not tested: the extra card for the second player. The 56 to 44 first-player edge was measured with 4 cards each; the 5th card is the remedy suggested by that result and I did not manage to re-simulate it for this page, so treat it as unconfirmed.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

NUMBER CIPHER. Stand your cards in a row, fronts toward you, lowest number on the left (equal numbers: lower first colour, then lower serial). Opponents see the backs. Turn: DRAW a card and slide it into your row. GUESS the number of one hidden opponent card. Right: it is turned up and you may guess again or stop. Wrong: turn up the card you drew this turn.

Back

WIN. All your cards face up and you are out. 2 players: the second player starts with 5 cards, the first with 4. 3 to 4 players: last with a hidden card wins. LEVELS. L1 three cards, no penalty. L2 four cards. L3 extra card. SOLO: crack a dealt row; see the page.

Cave of Dares

Walk into the cave one room at a time. Friends dare you, hand you gear and share snacks. Get out with courage to spare.

Inspired by Scoundrel by Zach Gage and Kurt Bieg

RecommendedFamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-02
Players
1 (or 2)
Time
L1 10 to 15 min, L2 and L3 15 to 20 min
Age
L1 from 5, L3 from 8
Dice
None at L1 and L2; 1 die at L3 (Suit key)
Pawns
1 (2 for two players)

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Face three of the four cards in every room. Dares cost courage, gear cuts a dare down, snacks give courage back. Reach the end of the cave with courage left. A playable version of this game is on its own page.

What you need

The cardsL1: 36 of the 54, picked blind. L2 and L3: all 54
The Cave cardthe game's own small rule card: a courage track from 0 to 20 and the Who is who key
1 pawnstands on your courage (two players use two pawns)
1 dieL3 only: the suit die, read on the Suit key (Ref 4)

Set up

  • Put the pawn on 20 on the Cave card. That is your courage.

  • Shuffle all the cards face down. This is the cave. L1: take 36 cards from the shuffled pile without looking, and put the other 18 back in the box.

  • Turn up 4 cards from the cave in a row. That is the first room.

  • You have no gear yet. Keep a spot beside the Cave card for it.

  • Who is who (read the animal at the foot of the card; the number is the strength): Dares are Tigers, Peacocks and Cobras (28 cards): lose their number in courage. Gear is Elephants and Monkeys (18 cards): takes its number off a dare. Snacks are Bears (8 cards): gain their number in courage, up to 20.

How to play

  1. Run? (L2 and up). Before you face any card you may run: put all 4 cards at the bottom of the cave, in any order, and turn up 4 new ones. You may not run twice in a row, and not in the last room.

  2. Face 3 of the 4 cards, one at a time, in any order you like. Dare: lose its number in courage, or use your gear and lose only the number minus the gear (never less than 0), then the dare goes in the discard. Gear: take it and lay it beside the Cave card; if you already held gear, the old gear and anything piled on it go in the discard. Snack: gain its number in courage, up to 20; any courage above 20 is lost.

  3. The card you did not face stays where it is. Turn up 3 new cards beside it. That is the next room.

  4. Gear wears out (L2 and up). When you beat a dare with your gear, lay that dare on the gear. From then on the gear works only on dares whose number is the same or lower than the dare on top of the pile. A bigger dare you face with bare hands: lose the full number. You may also choose bare hands on any dare, to keep your gear fresh. A new gear starts with an empty pile. L1: gear never wears out.

  5. Bond strike (L3). If your gear and a dare add up to 9 (7 and 2, 6 and 3, 5 and 4 and so on), the dare costs nothing, and the gear does not wear: do not pile the dare.

  6. Shadow die (L3). At the start of each room roll the die and read it on the Suit key. Any card in that room showing that suit on either medal is in the shadow. A dare in the shadow costs 1 more. A snack in the shadow gives 1 less. Gear is not changed. If you run, roll again for the new room.

How it ends

When the last card of the cave is turned up, that room is the last room: you must face every card in it (no card stays behind, and no running). If your courage is still above 0 when the last card is done, you win, and your score is the courage you have left. If your courage hits 0 at any time you lose; your score is minus the total of every dare still in the cave and the room. Medals for a win: Bronze for finishing, Silver and Gold for courage left (see Solo).

Words in this game

  • Cave the face-down pile.
  • Room the cards turned up for one turn (four, or fewer at the end).
  • Courage your pawn on the track. 20 is the most. 0 and you are out.
  • Pile the dares you beat with your gear, stacked on it. The top dare sets the limit.
  • Bare hands facing a dare without using gear: lose its full number.
  • Bond two numbers that add to 9. Used for the bond strike at L3.

Common questions

  • Does the order I face the three cards matter? Yes, a lot. Take gear first so it can cut the dares. Beat the bigger dares first, because the limit only goes down. Take a snack after you have lost courage, not before, or part of it is lost above 20.

  • Can I choose which card stays behind? Yes. That is the main choice. Usually leave a snack when you are healthy, or a small dare you can take bare-handed later.

  • My gear has limit 4 and a 6 dare comes up. Do I have to run? No. Face it with bare hands and lose 6, or leave it behind as the card that stays.

  • Equal numbers? The same number is allowed: a gear with limit 4 can beat another 4.

  • I took a new gear. What happens to the old one? It and its pile go in the discard. The new gear starts with no limit.

  • Twins? They are two separate cards. Their numbers add to 9 (a bond), but twins have no special rule in this game.

Tips

  • Take gear first. 82% of first rooms hold at least one gear card.

  • Beat the bigger dares first with your gear, because the limit only goes down.

  • Take a snack after you have lost courage, not before, or part of it is lost above 20.

  • Leave behind the biggest dare, or a snack when you are healthy. Leaving the biggest dare behind, plus taking gear first, is all it takes at L1.

  • Run from a bad room (L2 and up), but not twice in a row. Running won 68% against 64% without it for the careful bot.

  • Plan for the last room: 83% of a careful player's losses at L2 happen there, so carry gear that still works and courage to spare into the finale.

Worked example

  1. L3, so the shadow die is in play. The pawn is on 20 and there is no gear yet. Room 1, die shows 2. The cards: Guhan (3) (Guhan, 3, Elephants: gear 3), Gopi (5) (Gopi, 5, Peacocks: dare 5), Kanasu (3) (Kanasu, 3, Tigers: dare 3) and Naresh (3) (Naresh, 3, Bears: snack 3).

  2. Kanasu (3) shows suit 2, so it is in the shadow and her dare costs 4. You take Guhan (3) first: gear 3. Gopi (5) next: 5 minus 3 is 2, courage 18, and Gopi goes on the gear (limit 5). Then Kanasu (3): 4 minus 3 is 1, courage 17, limit 3. Naresh (3) stays behind: a snack is no use at nearly full courage.

  3. Room 2, die shows 3. Naresh stays, plus Gowri (9) (Gowri, 9, Cobras: dare 9, suit 3, shadow: costs 10), Ajay (2) (Ajay, 2, Cobras: dare 2) and Dharsh (7) (Dharsh, 7, Elephants: gear 7).

  4. Your Guhan gear has limit 3, so it cannot beat Gowri. You take Dharsh (7) first: new gear 7, the old gear and its pile are discarded. Ajay (2): 7 plus 2 is 9, a bond strike, so it costs 0 and the gear stays fresh. Gowri (9): 10 minus 7 is 3, courage 14, limit 9. Naresh still stays.

  5. Room 3, die shows 6. Naresh stays again, with Dhruv (6) (Dhruv, 6, Bears: snack 6), Sharada (6) (Sharada, 6, Peacocks: dare 6) and Nakul (4) (Nakul, 4, Tigers: dare 4, suits 3 and 6, so in the shadow: costs 5). Gear 7, limit 9.

  6. Sharada (6): 6 minus 7 is below 0, so it costs 0, limit 6. Nakul (4): 5 minus 7 costs 0, limit 4. Dhruv (6): snack 6, courage 14 to 20. Naresh's snack would give nothing at full courage, so it stays behind once more.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

A short cave of 36 cards. Gear never wears out, and no running. Face 3 cards, leave 1. A helper can read the team out loud: tiger, peacock, cobra, dare; elephant, monkey, gear; bear, snack.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

The whole cave of 54 cards. Gear wears out (the limit), you may run once in a while. Say the name of the friend who dares you.

L3 · age 8 and up

Add the bond strike (gear and dare make 9) and the shadow die (one suit is in shadow each room). Now you plan the order of all three cards, and every roll changes the best plan.

Solo

That is the game: you against the cave. Medals for a win, by courage left: L1 finish, Silver 17 or more, Gold 20. L2 finish, Silver 13 or more, Gold 18 or more. L3 finish, Silver 14 or more, Gold 19 or more. Silver is the middle result of a careful player who wins (L1: the lower quarter mark, because nearly everyone finishes high). Gold is the upper quarter mark.

Two players

The hot card. Two explorers share one cave but have their own courage (two pawns), their own gear and their own pile. Rooms alternate. The first player turns up 4 cards, faces 3 and leaves 1. The card you leave is the hot card: turn it sideways in the middle. It goes to your opponent. Your opponent's room is the hot card plus 3 new cards; they must face the hot card and 2 of the 3 new ones. The third new card is left, turned sideways, and becomes the next hot card for you. No running in two players. When the cave is empty, the cards still in the room are shared out, taking turns facing one card each. If your courage hits 0 you lose at once; otherwise the player with more courage left wins; a tie is shared. The first seat is a little stronger, so play two games and swap who starts.

Maths and skills in this game

Subtraction with a floor of 0 (dare minus gear), adding to a cap (snacks up to 20), counting down a track, comparing numbers to a limit, bonds to 9 at L3, and above all planning: three cards, six orders, and one to leave behind.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule a dare's cost, gear strength, snack size, the limit, the bond strike
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule L3 only: the die names a suit that is in shadow
Back patternNot used
TeamRule the team is the card's job: dare, gear or snack
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour say the name of the friend who dares you or hands you something
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Win rates of the solo game, 3,000 games each (150 for L2 and L3 and 100 for L1 for the lookahead bot). L1: random 36%, plain 75%, careful 91%, planner 92%, lookahead 91%. L2: random 0%, plain 3%, careful 67%, planner 70%, lookahead 95%. L3: random 0%, plain 4%, careful 68%, planner 74%, lookahead 92%.

  • Skill decides this game far more than the shuffle. Even the lookahead bot loses only about 5 caves in 100 at L2 to bad luck.

  • The limit on gear is the game. Without it a careful player wins 95% and a planner 96%: no thinking needed.

  • L3 is as hard as L2: the bond strike helps (careful 74% against 68%) and the shadow die hurts (careful 62%); together they roughly cancel. A planner uses about 3.0 bond strikes a game, a careful player about 2.8.

  • Length: L1 is about 11.5 rooms, L2 and L3 about 17.9 rooms. At 30 to 45 seconds a room that is 6 to 9 minutes for L1 and 12 to 16 for L2 and L3 (an estimate).

  • When a game is lost: 83% of a careful player's losses at L2 happen in the last room and only 1% before room 10. The median score of those losses is minus 21.

  • Medal marks (quartiles of courage left by careful winners): L1 [17, 20, 20], L2 [7, 13, 18], L3 [8, 14, 19]. Two players: the first seat wins 53% to 45% at L2 between equal planners, 53% to 44% at L3.

  • Team roles tried: more snacks makes it far too easy (99% careful with 18 snacks); more dares and less gear makes it harder (50%). The thematic split of 28 dares, 18 gear and 8 snacks was kept.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real children. The careful bot is a guess at a patient adult or a good 8-year-old.

  • Not tested: time per room (30 to 45 seconds is an estimate).

  • Not tested: the two-player hot-card rule with human players.

  • Not tested: other starting courage and cave sizes for L1.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CAVE OF DARES. Solo. Pawn on 20 (courage). Cave face down; turn up a room of 4. L2 up: you may run once (not twice in a row, not in the last room). Face 3 of the 4 in any order, leave 1, turn up 3 new. DARE (Tigers, Peacocks, Cobras): lose its number, or lose number minus gear. GEAR (Elephants, Monkeys): keep one, new one replaces. SNACK (Bears): gain its number up to 20.

Back

L2: gear works on dares at or below the last dare it beat (pile). L3: gear + dare = 9 costs 0, no wear. Die suit is in shadow: dares +1, snacks -1. Last room: face all cards. Win with courage above 0; score = courage left. LEVELS. L1 36 cards, no wear, no run. L2 all 54. L3 bond strike and shadow die.

Poker by Team

Five cards, one draw, one bet. The old betting game, with six teams in place of suits and a hand table ranked by how rare each hand really is in this deck.

Inspired by Five-card draw poker (Chicago Poker, Head-to-Head Poker, Pala)

RecommendedGrown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.6 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-03
Players
2 to 6 (tested at 3 to 5)
Time
15 to 30 min
Age
L1 from 7, L3 from 12
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone antes a point, is dealt five cards, swaps up to three, then one round of betting follows: bet, call or fold. The best hand left takes the pot. After 12 hands the biggest stack wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsfive-card hands. The number, the team and the serial all matter
Pencil and papereach player starts with 30 points; the table keeps one tally sheet
Hand tablethe rank list under How it ends, or the rule card

Set up

  • Each player starts with a stack of 30 points, written on the tally sheet. Nothing else is needed: there are no chips.

  • Pick a first Dealer at random. The Dealer moves one seat left after every hand. The player on the Dealer's left is first to act.

  • Every hand: shuffle all 54 cards, every player puts 1 point into the pot (the ante), and the Dealer deals 5 cards to each player, face down. Look at your own cards only.

  • Keep the rest of the deck face down in the middle. It is the draw pile for this hand.

How to play

  1. Draw. Starting on the Dealer's left, each player may throw away up to 3 cards face down and take the same number from the draw pile. You may keep all five (stand pat).

  2. Bet. Starting on the Dealer's left, each player in turn may bet 2 points or pass. Only the first bet counts: there are no raises. If everyone passes, go straight to the showdown.

  3. Call or fold. Once someone has bet, every other player in turn (continuing round the table back to the bettor) either calls by paying 2 into the pot or folds by putting their cards face down. A player who has fewer than 2 points left must fold.

  4. Showdown. Everyone still in turns their cards face up. The best hand wins the whole pot. Equal hands are impossible once the serial tie-break below is applied.

  5. Pass the Dealer seat left and start the next hand. Play 12 hands.

How it ends

After 12 hands the player with the most points wins. A tie goes to the player who won more showdowns; still tied, the player who holds the highest serial in their last hand. Hand ranks, lowest to highest (ranked by how rare they are in this deck): high card; one pair (51.6% of hands); two pair (10.8%); three of a kind (5.7%); a run of five numbers in a row, such as 3-4-5-6-7 (1.2%); full house, three of one number and two of another (0.7%); four of a kind (0.2%); five cards of one team (0.026%, about 1 hand in 3,800); five of a kind (54 hands in all); a run of five that is also all one team (12 hands in all). Inside one rank, compare the numbers that make the hand (the three or four of a kind first, then the pair, then the rest from high to low; for a run, its top number). If that is still level, the hand holding the highest serial wins.

Words in this game

  • Ante the 1 point every player puts in before cards are dealt.
  • Stand pat keep all five cards and draw none.
  • Team flush five cards that all belong to the same team (all Bears, say). It beats four of a kind.
  • Run five different numbers in a row, from 1-2-3-4-5 up to 5-6-7-8-9.
  • Pot all the points put in this hand. The showdown winner takes it.

Common questions

  • Can I raise? No. One bet of 2, then others call or fold. That keeps the game short and the hands readable.

  • Why does a team flush beat four of a kind? Because it is rarer. There are 6 copies of each number, so four of a kind turns up about once in 490 hands, but a hand of five from one team only once in 3,800. The table is ordered by the real odds.

  • Can five of a kind happen? Yes, but only 54 five-card hands out of 3.1 million. If it happens, enjoy it.

  • What if everybody folds to the bettor? The bettor wins the pot without showing cards.

  • What if I run out of points? You can still play hands: ante what you have, and you may check and see the showdown, but you cannot call a bet unless you have 2. If everyone is out except one player, the game ends.

Tips

  • Keep a pair or a four-card run, and throw the rest. Bots that did this and bet by hand strength won 89% to 94% against random players.

  • Bet when your hand is better than about 6 hands in 10 (any two pair or better) and call with anything better than about 4 in 10 (a decent pair). Folding weak hands is where the points are saved.

  • Do not chase a team flush. Four cards of one team is a thin draw (only the 4 to 6 remaining cards of that team can finish it); a pair is worth more.

  • Bluff rarely. The bots that bluffed about 1 hand in 12 were fine; players who bluff more get called by the stations.

  • Count the number of draws the other players take. Someone who stands pat is either very strong or bluffing; someone who draws three has nothing to start with.

Worked example

  1. 3 players: Smaya's table. Everyone antes 1, so the pot is 3. Hands dealt: Seat 0 holds Idhayan (8), Smaya (8), Arvind (1), Shreya (2), Adhiraa (6). Two 8s make a pair. Seat 1 holds Arvind (8), Bn Sharada (2), Nakul (4), Dhruv (3), Dhruv (6): no pair and no run. Seat 2 holds Anayka (8), Naresh (3), Gopi (4), Pinku (2), Ammlu (7): no pair.

  2. Draw. Seat 0 keeps the two 8s and throws three cards; they draw Rihansh (9), Rihansh (9) and Shreya (7): two 9s and a 7. That is now two pair, 9s and 8s. Seat 1 throws Arvind (8) and Bn Sharada (2) and draws Kanasu (3) and Bharati (4): they now hold 4, 3, 6, 3, 4, which is two pair, 4s and 3s. Seat 2 keeps Anayka (8) and Ammlu (7) and draws Amyra (5), Adheesh (9) and Guhan (3): 8, 7, 5, 9, 3, a high card only.

  3. Bet. Seat 0 (first to act) bets 2, pot 5. Seat 1 calls, pot 7. Seat 2 folds with high card 9.

  4. Showdown. Seat 0 shows 9, 9, 8, 8, 7. Seat 1 shows 4, 4, 3, 3, 6. Both are two pair, so the higher pair decides: 9 beats 4. Seat 0 wins the pot of 7.

  5. Stacks after hand 1: Seat 0 has 30 - 1 - 2 + 7 = 34. Seat 1 has 30 - 1 - 2 = 27. Seat 2 has 30 - 1 = 29. Total 90, as it should be.

  6. A rare one: five cards that all belong to one team are a team flush and beat four of a kind. If one player holds four 6s and a 2 and another holds five Monkeys of mixed numbers, the Monkeys win.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Showdown only (age 7 with a helper). Deal 5 each, no draw, no bets, no points to track. Only three hands count: three of a kind beats a pair, a pair beats nothing. Highest number wins a tie. First to 5 wins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Full draw and one bet of 1 point, with a stack of 15 and 8 hands. Use the full table up to a run. A helper can read the rank list aloud.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: stack of 30, bet of 2, 12 hands, the whole rank table, serial tie-breaks.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about reading other players.

Two players

Works as a duel with the same rules. Two players have not been simulated; the 3 to 5 player numbers are the tested ones.

Maths and skills in this game

Comparing hands, estimating how likely a hand is (probability in plain words), keeping a running total of points, and deciding when a bet is worth its price.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule pairs, triples and runs are made of numbers
ColoursNot used The colour flush (five cards sharing any colour, 1.6% of hands) is an option that has been counted but not played
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule five cards of one team is the team flush, rarer than four of a kind
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks every tie, so no two hands are ever equal
NamesFlavour faces at the table
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill: a bot that draws to keep pairs, four-card flushes and four-card runs and bets by hand strength wins 94%, 91% and 89% against random players at 3, 4, 5 players (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%), and 96%, 90% and 88% against players who always call. Against its own kind it sits at baseline, so luck is shared fairly (simulation, 1,500 games per cell).

  • Hand frequencies, computed exactly over all 3,162,510 five-card hands: high card 29.75%, pair 51.62%, two pair 10.75%, three of a kind 5.73%, run 1.23%, full house 0.68%, four of a kind 0.20%, team flush 0.026% (836 hands), five of a kind 0.0017% (54 hands), team run 0.0004% (12 hands).

  • Why a rare table: with only 54 cards and six copies of each number, pairs are far more common than in a normal deck (more than half of all hands hold one) and four of a kind is 7 times as common as a team flush. Ranking by rarity makes the ladder honest.

  • Length: 12 hands is about 14, 19 and 24 minutes at 3, 4, 5 players (estimate at 8 to 20 seconds a decision).

  • Five cards that share any colour come up in 1.6% of hands, far livelier than the team flush. It is the colour flush the final-cut table says to test.

  • Stakes in the sim: stack 30, ante 1, one fixed bet of 2, bots call when their hand is better than about 45% of hands and bet above about 62%.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people, who read tells and bluff in ways the bots do not.

  • Not tested: two and six players.

  • Not tested: the colour flush as an extra rank.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

POKER BY TEAM. 2 to 6 players. Start with 30 points each. Each hand: everyone antes 1, deal 5 cards. Draw: throw up to 3, take that many. Bet: from the Dealer's left, bet 2 or pass; only one bet, no raises. Others call 2 or fold. Showdown: best hand takes the pot. Dealer moves left. Play 12 hands.

Back

RANKS, low to high: high card, pair, two pair, three of a kind, run of five, full house, four of a kind, five of one TEAM, five of a kind, team run. Ties: compare the numbers that make the hand, then the highest serial. Most points after 12 hands wins; tie: more showdowns won. LEVELS. L1 showdown only. L2 stack 15, bet 1, 8 hands. L3 full game.

Mind games · Tricks and shedding · Fronts

Haggis Hills

Climb the hill by playing sets of one number or runs of three or more, each play beating the last. Empty your hand first, and make the others pay for every card left.

Inspired by Haggis, Gang of Four, Lexio (climbing games)

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-04
Players
3 to 6
Time
15 to 25 min (5 to 10 min a round)
Age
L1 from 7, L3 from 10
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

A climbing game. Lead a set of cards with the same number or a run of three or more numbers; each player must beat it with the same shape and a higher top card, or pass. The first to empty their hand ends the round. Three rounds, fewest cards left wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsdealt out so every player has the same number of cards
Pencil and paperto total cards left after each round

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Deal each player a hand: 13 cards at 3 players, 12 at 4, 10 at 5 and 8 at 6. Put any left over in the box, unseen.

  • Round 1: the player on the Dealer's left leads. Later rounds: the player who went out first in the previous round leads.

  • Sort your hand by number. Keep it hidden.

How to play

  1. Lead. The leader plays any legal combination face up: a set (1 or more cards with the same number) or a run (3 or more cards with consecutive numbers, one card per number).

  2. Beat. The next player must play the same shape and the same number of cards with a higher strength, or pass. Strength is the top number of the play; if the top numbers are equal, the top serial decides (so there are never ties). A pair beats a pair, a run of four beats a run of four, a single beats a single.

  3. Going round the table, each player in turn beats the last play or passes. Passing does not lock you out of the trick: you can play on your next turn if you can beat the latest play.

  4. When all other players have passed in a row after a play, the player who made that play wins the trick: pile the cards aside and they lead the next trick.

  5. The first player to play their last card ends the round.

How it ends

When a player goes out, every other player counts the cards left in their hand: 1 point each. Play 3 rounds and add up the points. The player with the fewest points wins. A tie goes to the player with more rounds won (rounds in which they went out first).

Words in this game

  • Set one or more cards with the same number, played together (a single is a set of 1).
  • Run 3 or more cards with numbers in a row, such as 4-5-6. One card of each number.
  • Strength the top number of a play; equal top numbers are decided by the highest serial.
  • Trick the plays from one lead until everyone else passes.
  • Going out playing your last card.

Common questions

  • Can I play a run of 3 on a run of 4? No. A beat must be the same shape and the same number of cards.

  • Are two cards of the same number a set even if I want them in a run? Yes, you choose each turn. A set uses cards of one number; a run uses different numbers.

  • Can a twin pair or bond count as special? Not in the simulated game. The first design had bonds as bombs and twin pairs as wild; they are listed under Not tested.

  • Do I have to play if I can? No. You may pass even when you could beat the play. Saving a strong set can be wise.

  • What if two top numbers match? The higher serial wins, so one of the two plays is always stronger.

Tips

  • Lead your lowest sets and runs first. The bots that led their longest low set or run needed 24 to 41 decisions a round, against 33 to 65 for random players.

  • Beat with the smallest card that works. Spending a 9 to beat a 3 wastes your power for when it matters.

  • Keep your 8s and 9s for the end unless somebody is close to going out. Passing early with high cards and keeping them is a good plan.

  • Watch the smallest hand. When someone has two or three cards, stop passing and beat everything you can.

  • Break long sets into smaller ones only if you must; sets shed cards faster than singles.

Worked example

  1. 3 players, 13 cards each. Trick 1: Seat 0 leads a pair of 3s: Guhan (3) and Dhruv (3). Top number 3, top serial 10.

  2. Seat 1 beats it with a pair of 5s, Gopi (5) and Archana (5): a pair with a higher number. Seat 2 passes. Seat 0 passes. Everyone else has passed, so Seat 1 wins the trick and leads.

  3. Trick 2: Seat 1 leads a run of three, Nakul (4), Nakul (5), Naresh (6). Top number 6.

  4. Seat 2 beats it with a run of three that tops at 7: Amyra (5), Guhan (6), Shreya (7). A 7 beats a 6.

  5. Seat 0 also has a run of three topping at 7: Avika (5), Dhruv (6), Ammlu (7). The top numbers are equal, so serials decide: Ammlu (7) has serial 14 and Shreya (7) has serial 6, so Seat 0 beats Seat 2. Seats 1 and 2 pass. Seat 0 wins the trick and leads.

  6. End of round: Seat 2 is first out. Seat 0 holds 4 cards and Seat 1 holds 7, so they score 4 and 7. Seat 2 scores 0. Three rounds later, the lowest total wins.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Sets only (age 7 with a helper): no runs, play by number only. First to empty their hand wins the round. Win 2 rounds.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Sets and runs of three, and count cards left. Play 2 rounds.

L3 · age 8 and up

Full game: sets and runs of any length, 3 rounds, fewest total cards left wins. Optionally use Take the Set (below).

Solo

No solo mode: the game is a race against other hands.

Two players

Not tested at 2 players. Try 13 cards each and treat the rest as a draw pile of 28: when you pass, draw one.

Maths and skills in this game

Comparing numbers, spotting runs and sets in a hand, planning the order to play cards, and counting what is left.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule sets and runs are made of numbers
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks every tie between equal tops, so no two plays are equal
NamesFlavour faces in your hand
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill: a bot that leads its longest low set or run and beats with the smallest card that works wins 78%, 68%, 58%, 48% against random players at 3, 4, 5, 6 players (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%, 17%). Against its own kind it sits at baseline.

  • Decisions per round: the bot needs 24, 35, 40, 41 at 3 to 6 players; random players need 33 to 65. That is about 4 to 7 minutes a round at 8 to 20 seconds a decision.

  • Using the serial to break ties between equal numbers removes every tie, which is why top serial is the tie-break.

  • Hand sizes: 13, 12, 10, 8 cards at 3, 4, 5, 6 players, using 39, 48, 50, 48 of the 54 cards.

  • Three rounds with fewest cards left is the one change from the final cut table; it smooths the luck of a single deal (not separately simulated).

  • The bot may pass on a beating play with a high card (8 or 9) when its hand is bigger than 5 cards and nobody is near out, 70% of the time; this saving rule is part of the simulated skill.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: bond pairs as bombs and twin pairs as wild cards, from the first idea. They are not in the simulated game.

  • Not tested: Take the Set (below) and 2 players.

  • Not tested: real people; bots do not bluff by passing.

Variants and options

  • #75 Set Steal Optional Take the Set rule: when you beat a play, you may take the beaten cards into a face-up pile in front of you. At round end each card in that pile cancels one card left in your hand. Untested.

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

HAGGIS HILLS. 3 to 6 players. Deal 13/12/10/8 cards at 3/4/5/6 players. Lead a SET (same number) or a RUN (3+ in a row). Next player beats it with the same shape and size and a higher top number (tie: higher serial) or passes. When all others pass, the last player to play wins the trick and leads. First out ends the round.

Back

SCORING. Others count cards left in hand: 1 point each. Play 3 rounds; fewest points wins. Tie: more rounds won. LEVELS. L1 sets only, 2 rounds. L2 sets and runs of 3, 2 rounds. L3 full game with 3 rounds. OPTION: Take the Set (see page).

Number Letters

You hold one card, draw one, play one. Each number has a power, and the highest card standing wins the round. You will win by remembering what has already gone.

Inspired by Love Letter and Coup d'Etat

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-05
Players
3 to 6
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 8
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Hold one card. On your turn draw a second and play one of the two, using the power of the number you play. Powers guess, peek, compare, shield, redraw and swap. Last player left, or the highest card at the end, wins the round. First to 5 rounds wins.

What you need

25 cards from the deckfor each round: 24 to draw from and 1 set aside face down (the burn card)
Ref card (powers list)the 9 powers, one for each number
Pencil and paperto count round wins

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. For each round take the top 25 and put the rest aside. Take one more card off the top of the 25 and put it face down, unlooked at: the burn card. The other 24 are the draw deck.

  • Deal 1 card to each player, face down. Look at yours and keep it secret.

  • Have a place for the discard pile: a face-up row so everyone can see what has gone.

  • The first player is chosen at random in round 1. In later rounds the winner of the last round goes first.

How to play

  1. On your turn, draw a card from the top of the deck. You now hold two cards. Play one of them face up on the discard pile and do what its number says.

  2. The powers. 1 Guess: name a number from 2 to 9 and a player. If they hold it, they are out. 2 Peek: look at another player's card. 3 Compare: secretly compare your remaining card with another player's. The lower number is out; ties do nothing. 4 Shield: you cannot be chosen by anyone until your next turn. 5 Redraw: choose a player (you may choose yourself). They discard their card and draw a new one; if they discarded a 9, they are out. 6 Swap: swap your card with another player's. 7 No power, but if you hold a 7 and a 5 or 6 you must play the 7. 8 has no power. 9: if you ever discard a 9, you are out.

  3. If all other players are shielded or out, a power that needs a target does nothing (a 5 must then be played on yourself).

  4. A player who is out shows their card (puts it on the discard pile) and takes no more turns.

  5. If the draw deck has run out when you need to draw (for example after a 5), take the burn card instead.

How it ends

A round ends when only one player is left, or when the draw deck is empty at the end of a turn. In the second case the highest card in hand wins. If two or more share the highest number, the one with the highest serial wins. The winner of the round gets a round win. First to 5 round wins wins the game.

Words in this game

  • Burn card a card set aside unseen at the start; adds uncertainty
  • Out a player who has lost the round but still takes part in the next one
  • Discard the face-up pile; its contents are public and are your best clues
  • Shield a protection from the 4 that stops other players choosing you
  • Round one deal, ending when one player stands or the deck is empty

Common questions

  • How many of each number are in the 24 cards? Roughly 2.7 of each; there are six of every number in the whole deck, but a round only uses 25 of the 54 cards.

  • Can I play a 9? Only if you must (when you hold two 9s, say). Playing a 9 knocks you out.

  • Do I have to use a power? Yes. When you play a card its power happens if it can. If no legal target, nothing happens.

  • What does 'must play the 7' mean? With a 7 and a 5 or a 6 in hand you cannot keep the 7; it is played and does nothing, which hides a 5 or 6.

  • What if a Guess names a number I know is gone? Fine. Naming a number nobody holds just wastes the power.

Tips

  • Keep a high card and play a low one. Your hand is your life: a 9 can never be played, an 8 is a safe winner.

  • Track the discards. When all six 9s are visible you know nobody has one; that makes a Guess on 8 much more worthwhile.

  • Peek (2) before you Guess (1). A peeked card is a sure guess next turn.

  • A 5 on yourself is a safe way to improve your hand, but never when you hold a 9.

  • Use a 6 to steal a high card when you hold a low one. A player who just played a Shield cannot be swapped.

  • With a 7, check your other card first. Holding 7 with a 5 or a 6 is a signal the other players can use.

Worked example

  1. 3 players. Seat 0 holds Naresh (6), seat 1 holds Guhan (3), seat 2 holds Smaya (8).

  2. Seat 0 draws Dharsh (2) and plays the 2: Peek at seat 2, and sees the 8. Seat 0 keeps the 6.

  3. Seat 1 draws Shreya (7) and plays the 7 (no power), keeping the 3. Seat 2 draws Amyra (4) and plays the 4: Shield, keeping the 8.

  4. Seat 0 draws Arvind (1) and plays the 1: Guess. Seat 2 is shielded and cannot be chosen. Seat 0 says "Seat 1, you have a 3". Seat 1 does, so seat 1 is out.

  5. Seat 2 draws Gowri (9) and plays the 8 (no power), keeping the 9. Seat 0 draws Nakul (5) and plays the 5 on seat 2: seat 2 must discard the 9, and is out. Seat 0 is the last player standing and wins the round (it took 6 turns).

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Higher or lower (age 8). Only these powers: 1 Guess, 3 Compare, 9 you are out if you discard it. The other numbers have no power. Rounds are very short.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Add 2 Peek, 4 Shield and 5 Redraw. Play first to 3 round wins.

L3 · age 8 and up

All nine powers, including 6 Swap and the 7 rule. First to 5 round wins.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about people holding secret cards.

Two players

Not simulated and not recommended: with 2 players a Guess is a coin flip. Use 3 to 6 players.

Maths and skills in this game

Memory (what has been discarded), probability (how many 8s are left?) and inference (why did the last player play that card?).

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule every number is a power and the strength of a hand
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule breaks ties between equal highest cards
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The bot that guesses the number most likely to remain wins 59%, 49%, 42% and 36% against random players at 3 to 6 players (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%, 17%) and sits at baseline against itself (fair).

  • Rounds are very short: 8, 12, 14 and 15 turns at 3 to 6 players, about 1.5 to 3 minutes.

  • Rounds end with one player left standing 98% and 88% of the time at 3 and 4 players, but at 6 players only 35% (21% when all play well); the rest go to the highest card when the deck runs out.

  • First to 5 round wins is 7 to 9 rounds at 3 players, about 15 to 20 minutes.

  • The sim uses a 24-card deck plus a burn card (25 of 54 cards, with six copies of each number from 1 to 9 in the full deck), the same nine powers as listed, a shield that blocks every target, and a 9 that is out when discarded.

  • The skill edge is smaller than in other bluffing games: 59% at 3 players is the highest. Luck of the deal is part of the fun.

  • Ties for the highest card in hand are common at 6 players; the final cut asked for the serial as the tie-break (not part of the sim, which split the win).

Not tested:

  • Serial as a tie-break; the sim split tied wins.

  • L1 and L2 power sets.

  • The 7 rule against human players. The bot only plays it when it holds a 5 or 6.

  • Two-player games.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

NUMBER LETTERS. 3 to 6 players. Round: take 25 cards, 1 face down aside (burn), 24 to draw. Hold 1 card. Turn: draw 1, play 1 face up and do its power. 1 GUESS a number 2 to 9 (hit = out). 2 PEEK. 3 COMPARE (lower out). 4 SHIELD until your next turn. 5 REDRAW (a discarded 9 is out). 6 SWAP hands. 7 must play if you also hold 5 or 6. 8 no power. 9 out if discarded.

Back

Round ends when one player is left or the deck is empty (highest card wins; ties: higher serial). Winner starts next round. First to 5 round wins. L1: powers 1, 3, 9 only. L2: add 2, 4, 5. L3: all nine. Track the discards.

Liar's Ledger

Everyone wears one card on their forehead. You can see every number except your own, so you bid the total of the whole table and dare the next player to call you a liar.

Inspired by Coyote, Liar's Dice and Bluff, with the card on your forehead

FamilyGrown-upsEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-06
Players
2 to 6
Time
10 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 5
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round every player holds one card on their forehead. Take turns bidding a higher total for all the cards on the table, or call Liar. If the total is at least the bid, the caller loses a life. If not, the bidder does. Last player with lives wins.

What you need

All 54 cardsone card each per round; the number on the card is what counts
Pencil and paperto tally lives (3 each); pawns can stand in as life markers at 2 players

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards and put them face down as the draw deck.

  • Each player starts with 3 lives. Write them on paper (at 5 or 6 players use 2 lives each to keep the game short; this is not yet tested).

  • Choose the first Starter at random. After round 1 the Starter is the player who lost a life in the round before.

  • Each round, every player who still has a life takes one card from the top of the deck and holds it against their forehead, number outward, without looking at it. Everyone else can see it.

How to play

  1. Open. The Starter says a total: a whole number of 1 or more. The total means: the numbers on all the cards in play added together, including your own card that you cannot see.

  2. Raise or call. Going clockwise, each player either raises (says a strictly higher total) or says Liar. There is no limit on raising except that the total must go up.

  3. Reveal. When someone says Liar, everyone takes their card down and the numbers are added up.

  4. Pay. If the real total is equal to or higher than the last bid, the bid was true and the caller loses a life. If the real total is lower than the bid, the bidder loses a life.

  5. Next round. Put the used cards aside. Players take new cards. The player who just lost a life Starts. When the deck is empty, shuffle the used cards and carry on.

  6. A player with no lives left is out and does not hold a card.

How it ends

The game ends when only one player still has a life. That player wins. In simulation a table of bots played about 7, 10, 13 and 17 rounds at 3, 4, 5 and 6 players (3 lives each). There are no ties: only one player can lose a life in a round, so two players never run out together.

Words in this game

  • Total the sum of the numbers on every card in play this round, yours included
  • Bid a total you say aloud; it must be higher than the last bid
  • Call saying Liar. It ends the round.
  • Starter the player who opens the bidding; the last round's loser
  • Visible total the sum of the cards you can see (everyone else's)

Common questions

  • Can I look at my own card? No. If you peek, the round does not count and you lose a life.

  • Does a bid of exactly the real total count as true? Yes. A bid is a claim that the total is at least that number, so equal is true and the caller loses.

  • What if the Starter has a huge visible total? Then a safe opening is the visible total plus 1, because your own card is at least 1. It cannot be false.

  • Can I raise by just 1? Yes. Small raises are often the best way to push a nervous player into a bad call.

  • What if I am the last two players? Play on the same way. With two players the one you call is always the other; the one who bid last when you call is the bidder.

Tips

  • Add up what you can see before you speak. Your safe floor is the visible total plus 1, and your ceiling is the visible total plus 9.

  • Bids at or below the safe floor can never be false. Raising to exactly that number is free: nobody can punish it.

  • Bids above the ceiling (visible plus 9) can never be true. If the bid you face is over your ceiling, call Liar every time.

  • The middle is where the game lives: your own card is about 5 on average, so the visible total plus 5 is the fair bid. Raise a little above it when the next player has to guess, and a little below when you are afraid of being called.

  • Look for twins. If two players hold the two cards of one child, their numbers add to exactly 9, so you can count that pair as 9 without adding.

  • When you are the player after a big bid, remember that the bidder cannot see their own card either; a bid that is high for what you see may be a bluff or may be a lucky guess.

Worked example

  1. 3 lives each, 4 players. Seat 0 holds Naresh (6), seat 1 holds Shreya (2), seat 2 holds Nysha (8) and seat 3 holds Idhayan (1). The real total is 6 + 2 + 8 + 1 = 17. Seat 0 can see 2 + 8 + 1 = 11. Seat 1 sees 15. Seat 2 sees 9. Seat 3 sees 16.

  2. Seat 0 is the Starter and opens with 15 (11 plus 4, a little under the average of 5 for their own card).

  3. Seat 1 sees 15, so any bid of 16 is certain to be true (their own card is at least 1). They raise to 19.

  4. Seat 2 sees 9. For 19 to be true their own card would need to be 10, and the highest card is 9, so 19 is impossible. Seat 2 says Liar.

  5. Everyone looks: 6 + 2 + 8 + 1 = 17, lower than 19, so the bidder loses. Seat 1 goes from 3 lives to 2 and is the next Starter.

  6. Round 2. Cards: Smaya (1), Bharati (4), Dharsh (7), Bharati (5) for seats 0 to 3. Total = 1 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 17. Seat 0 sees Bharati (4) and Bharati (5), the two Bharati cards, and knows they make 9 together. They see 9 + 7 = 16 in all.

  7. Seat 1 (visible 13) opens with 17. Seat 2 sees only 10 and calls Liar. The total is 17, equal to the bid, so the bid was true: Seat 2 loses a life (3 down to 2) and starts round 3.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Count tall cards instead of adding. The bid is how many cards on the table are 5 or higher (including yours). Everything else is the same. Two to four players, one life each is a quick game; use 2 lives for a longer one. A helper may whisper the count of tall cards they see.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Bid the real total, but a helper (or the player on your left) says your visible total aloud, so you do not have to add. Use 3 lives. You still decide how much to add for your own card.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: add up the cards yourself, 3 lives (2 at 5 and 6 players), and the Starter is the player who lost the last round.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about reading other players' faces and voices, so it needs at least two people.

Two players

Works at two. Each round both players hold a card, so you see exactly one number and bid the total. Aim for 3 lives each. It is a pure guess about one hidden card between 1 and 9 and is the shortest version.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding several numbers quickly, estimating an average (the average card is 5) and judging a risk: how likely is it that my one hidden card pushes the total over the bid?

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule every number is part of the total
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour twin pairs on the table help you count
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The bot that works out the odds that the total reaches the bid (from the numbers it can see and the cards not yet seen) wins 62% to 68% against random players. The even-share baselines are 33%, 25%, 20% and 17% at 3 to 6 players.

  • Call thresholds from 0.4 to 0.6 (call when the chance the bid is true falls under that figure) gave the same results, so the exact tuning does not matter.

  • A game takes about 7, 10, 13 and 17 rounds at 3, 4, 5 and 6 players with 3 lives each.

  • Every card is a whole number from 1 to 9 with six copies of each, so one hidden card has mean 5 and a standard deviation of about 2.6. The total of n cards has a standard deviation of about 4.5, 5.2, 5.8 and 6.3 at 3 to 6 players (computed from the card list: variance per card is 80/12).

  • A bid at or below the visible total plus 1 is always true, and a bid above the visible total plus 9 is always false. Those two limits give every player a free raise and a free call.

  • The sim reshuffles the used cards when the draw deck runs out; at 6 players one round takes 6 cards, so a deck of 54 lasts 9 rounds.

  • The sim's starter rule (the loser of the last round starts) is used throughout, so no seat gets a built-in edge.

Not tested:

  • Two lives at 5 to 6 players: suggested to cap the game, but not simulated.

  • The L1 tall-card count and the L2 spoken helper total were not simulated.

  • Real people bluff and read faces; the bots only compute odds.

  • Two-player games were not simulated.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

LIAR'S LEDGER. 2 to 6 players. 3 lives each (2 at 5 or 6 players). Each round everyone holds one card on their forehead, number outward, unseen. Starter bids a total for ALL cards on the table (yours too). Next player raises (higher total) or says LIAR. Total at least the bid: the caller loses a life. Total less than the bid: the bidder loses a life.

Back

The loser of the round starts the next. Out of lives = out. Last player standing wins. L1: bid how many cards are 5 or higher. L2: a helper says your visible total. Tips: visible total plus 1 is always true; visible plus 9 is always false; fair bid = visible plus 5.

Mind games · Bluff and hidden role · Fronts

Coup of Faces

Each team in the deck gives its holder a power. You may claim any power at any time, but anyone can challenge you, and the loser of a challenge gives up a card.

Inspired by Coup

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-07
Players
3 to 6
Time
10 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 8
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Hold two face-down cards. On your turn name an action and claim the team that allows it. Others may challenge or block. A caught liar loses a card; a wrong challenger loses a card. Be the last player with a card.

What you need

18 cards, three of each teamthe Court: 3 Tigers, 3 Elephants, 3 Bears, 3 Monkeys, 3 Peacocks, 3 Cobras. Pick any three of each team and leave the other 36 in the box.
Ref 4 (Team key)to read the team of a card by its animal name
Pencil and paperto keep each player's coins

Set up

  • Make the Court: take any three cards of each of the six teams (18 cards). Shuffle them and put the rest of the box away.

  • Deal 2 cards face down to each player. These are your influence. Look at them and keep them secret. Put the rest of the Court face down as the Court deck.

  • Every player starts with 2 coins. Write them on paper.

  • The youngest player goes first, then clockwise.

How to play

  1. On your turn do one action. Some actions are open to anyone. Others you claim by naming a team: you say "I am the Tiger", for example. You do not have to have the card.

  2. Open actions. Income: take 1 coin. Foreign aid: take 2 coins (a Tiger can block it). Coup: pay 7 coins and choose a player to lose one influence card. You cannot be stopped. If you have 10 or more coins you must Coup.

  3. Team actions (claim the team). Tiger (team 1) Tax: take 3 coins. Elephant (team 2) Steal: take 2 coins from another player. Bear (team 3) Assassinate: pay 3 coins, one player loses an influence card. Monkey (team 4) Exchange: draw 2 cards from the Court deck, keep any of your cards and the new ones to hold 2 or 1 as before, and put the extras back at the bottom. Cobra (team 6) Spy: look at one of another player's influence cards (no coins change).

  4. Blocks. Foreign aid is blocked by anyone claiming Tiger. Steal is blocked by the target claiming Elephant or Monkey. Assassinate is blocked by the target claiming Peacock (team 5). A block is also just a claim.

  5. Challenge. Any player may challenge a team claim, whether it is an action or a block. The claimer shows the card of that team. If they have it, the challenger loses an influence card; the claimer puts the shown card back into the Court deck, shuffles, and draws a new one. If they do not have it, the claimer loses a card and the action fails.

  6. Losing a card. You choose which of your cards to give up and turn it face up, where it stays. Someone with no cards is out. Coins spent on a failed Assassinate are not refunded.

How it ends

The game ends when only one player still has an influence card. That player wins. There are no points and no ties. At 3 players two clever players may circle for a long time; there is no time limit, so agree on one if you wish.

Words in this game

  • Influence the cards you hold face down; losing them all knocks you out
  • Claim saying you have a team's card, true or not
  • Challenge calling a claim a lie; one player is about to lose a card
  • Block stopping another player's action by claiming a team
  • Court the 18 cards the game uses

Common questions

  • Can I claim a team I do not have? Yes. That is the game. If nobody challenges you, the action works.

  • Can I challenge a block? Yes. If you are wrong you lose a card, and the block stands.

  • If I tell the truth and am challenged, do I keep my card? You show it, it goes back in the Court deck, and you draw a replacement, so the challenger learns nothing lasting.

  • Who can challenge? Anyone. If two players speak at once, the one nearest to the claimer's left goes first.

  • What if I have 10 coins and cannot Coup? You must Coup. With fewer than 7 coins you cannot, so you are never in a spot where you must but cannot.

Tips

  • Early on, take Tax or Income and keep your cards. A player with two cards is much stronger than one with a few spare coins.

  • If you hold two cards of one team, challenge anyone who claims it: the Court holds only one more, so a claim from them is a lie 87% of the time (computed below).

  • If you hold one copy of a team, a rival's claim of it is real about 24% of the time. With none in your hand, it is real about 31% of the time. Challenge anything above your comfort level.

  • A claim of Assassinate when you have 3 coins is expensive. Pair it with a Peacock block when you are the target. If you really hold the Peacock, the target is safe.

  • Truthful play beats casual bluffing. In simulation a careful player who bluffs only rarely beats a player who bluffs often.

  • Coup the player who threatens you most: the one with most coins or the one with only one card left.

Worked example

  1. 3 players. Court: three of each team. Seat 0 holds Shreya (2) (Tiger) and Smaya (1) (Bear). Seat 1 holds Anayka (1) (Elephant) and Sharada (3) (Peacock). Seat 2 holds Arvind (1) (Monkey) and Adhiraa (3) (Tiger). Each has 2 coins.

  2. Seat 0 says "Tiger, Tax" (true: Shreya (2)). Nobody challenges. Seat 0 now has 5 coins.

  3. Seat 1 says "Elephant, Steal from seat 0" (true: Anayka (1)). Nobody challenges the claim. Seat 0 blocks by claiming Monkey, which is a bluff.

  4. Seat 1 challenges the block. Seat 0 has no Monkey, so they lose a card and turn Smaya (1) face up. The block fails and the steal goes ahead: seat 0 5 → 3 coins, seat 1 2 → 4 coins.

  5. Seat 2 (2 coins) takes Foreign aid, which would make 4. Seat 0 blocks by claiming Tiger, which is true (Shreya (2)). Seat 2 challenges. Seat 0 shows Shreya (2). The challenger loses a card: seat 2 turns Arvind (1) face up. Seat 0 shuffles Shreya (2) into the Court deck and draws a replacement (this time Kanasu (3), another Tiger). The block stands: seat 2 gets no coins and stays on 2.

  6. Standing: seat 0 has 1 card and 3 coins, seat 1 has 2 cards and 4 coins, seat 2 has 1 card and 2 coins.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Open Court (age 8): play with the cards face up in front of you. Actions can only be taken with the card you show, and nobody challenges. Only Income, Foreign aid, Tax, Steal, Assassinate and Coup. It teaches the powers and the coin counting.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Four teams: use only Tigers, Elephants, Bears and Peacocks (12 cards in the Court). Full claims, challenges and blocks. Exchange and Spy are not available.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: all six teams, with Exchange and Spy. Note: in simulation Exchange and Spy had no effect, so these two powers are untested.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is claims and challenges between people.

Two players

Not recommended and not simulated: with two players a challenge is a coin flip on each claim. Use 3 to 6.

Maths and skills in this game

Reasoning about hidden information (how many cards of a team are left?), simple probability and keeping track of coins.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Against two truthful bots, a bluff-happy bot wins 6%, 1% and 0% at 3, 4 and 5 players. Truthful players win 71%, 69% and 53% against bluffers at 3, 4 and 5. Careful beats naive bluffing.

  • The bluffer still wins 81%, 69%, 58% and 49% against random players at 3 to 6 players (baselines 33%, 25%, 20%, 17%), so there is real skill.

  • Between bluffers a game is short: 10, 13, 16 and 22 turns in total at 3 to 6 players. Between truthful players it is long: 25 to 72 turns (about 18 minutes at the high end).

  • Bluffers: 1.8 to 3.8 bluffs and 3.7 to 8.7 challenges per game. A table of truthful players averages only 0.5 to 0.9 bluffs per game.

  • Mirror matches are fair: in games of identical bots every seat wins within a point or two of the even share (for example 33 / 34 / 33% at 3 players).

  • Computed from the Court (3 copies of each team among 18 cards, so a rival holds 2 of them at most): a rival holds at least one copy of a team 31% of the time when you hold none, 24% when you hold one, and 12.5% when you hold two.

  • Exchange (Monkeys) and Spy (Cobras) had no effect in the simulated build; only the four other teams are really tested.

Not tested:

  • Exchange and Spy: the rules above are written but the sim ignored them.

  • A bonus for a bluff that survives a challenge was suggested in the final cut. It is not included, because an unchallenged bluff cannot be checked by the table.

  • Human bluffing and reading faces. The bots work from card counts only.

  • Games at 2 players.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

COUP OF FACES. 3 to 6 players. Court = 3 cards of each team (18). 2 cards each face down, 2 coins. On your turn do ONE action: Income +1. Foreign aid +2 (Tiger blocks). Coup: pay 7, target loses a card (must at 10 coins). Claim a team: TIGER Tax +3. ELEPHANT Steal 2. BEAR Assassinate (pay 3). MONKEY Exchange. COBRA Spy.

Back

BLOCKS: Tiger blocks aid. Elephant or Monkey blocks steal. Peacock blocks assassinate. CHALLENGE any claim: liar loses a card; if the claimer has the team, the challenger loses a card and the claimer swaps the shown card for a new one. Last player with a card wins. L1: cards face up, no challenges. L2: four teams only.
