Skull Walk

Everyone lays a card face down in a stack. Then you bet how many cards you can turn over without hitting the one suit the die has made dangerous.

Inspired by Skull (Skull and Roses) and Cash n Guns

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-08
Players
3 to 6
Time
10 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 6
Dice
1 die
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Roll the suit die: any card showing that suit is a hazard. Everyone stacks cards face down, then bids how many cards they can flip, their own first. Flip them all safely and score a point. Hit a hazard and you lose a card for good. First to 3 points wins.

What you need

All 54 cardseach player owns 4 cards; the two suits printed on a card decide whether it is a hazard
1 dieread on the Suit key (Ref 4) to name this round's hazard suit
Ref 4 (Suit key)shows which medal each die number means
Pencil and paperto keep points, if you like

Set up

  • Shuffle the 54 cards. Deal 4 cards to each player. These are your walkers. Put the rest of the deck away; it is not used.

  • Each player keeps their 4 cards in a hand. You will take your remaining cards back into your hand at the start of every round.

  • Pick the first Starter at random. After that the Starter is the player who just bid in the last round (see below).

  • Each player needs a place in front of them for a stack of face-down cards.

How to play

  1. Roll. Roll the die and look up the number on the Suit key. That suit is the hazard for this round. A card is a hazard if either of its two suit medals is the hazard suit.

  2. Lay one. Starting with the Starter and going clockwise, each player puts one card from their hand face down in front of them. This is the first card of their stack. You may look at your own stack at any time.

  3. Add or bid. Continuing clockwise, on your turn you do one of two things. Either add another card from your hand face down on top of your own stack, or bid: say a number of cards you will flip (at least 1 and at most the number of cards on the table). Once someone bids, no one adds any more cards.

  4. Raise. After a bid, going clockwise, anyone may raise the number (up to the number of cards on the table) or pass. This continues until everyone has passed in a row. The highest bidder is the Walker.

  5. Flip. The Walker flips cards one by one. They must flip all of their own stack first, starting from the top card (the last one laid). Then they flip cards from other players' stacks, top card first, choosing any stack each time, until they have flipped as many cards as they bid.

  6. Safe or not. If every card flipped is safe, the Walker scores 1 point. If they flip a hazard, they stop at once, put all the flipped cards back, and the Walker loses one card of their choice from their 4. That card is out of the game for good. A player with no cards left is out.

  7. Next round. Everyone takes their cards back, the Walker is the new Starter (if the Walker is out, the next player is), and the die is rolled again.

How it ends

The game ends when a player has 3 points: they win. If all but one player have lost all their cards, the last player with cards wins. Only the Walker can score, so two players can never reach 3 at once. At 4 or 5 players games often end in about 3 rounds because a failed bid takes a card.

Words in this game

  • Hazard a card showing the suit the die named; flipping one ends the Walker's turn
  • Stack your face-down cards, the last one laid on top
  • Walker the player with the highest bid, who has to flip
  • Bid the number of cards the Walker promised to flip

Common questions

  • Why does the Walker flip their own stack first? Because you control your own cards. It makes a big bid only believable if your own stack is clean.

  • Can I put a hazard in my own stack? Yes, but you can only walk if your stack is safe. A hazard on the bottom is a trap for someone else, but if you become the Walker you hit it yourself after the cards above it.

  • Can I bid after someone has already bid? Only by raising. You cannot add cards after the first bid.

  • Can I lie? Everything is hidden. You can say anything; only the bid binds you.

  • What if nobody raises? Then the first bidder is the Walker with their bid.

Tips

  • Roll first, then lay. The hazard is known before any card goes down, so you can lay safe cards and keep the hazard ones in your hand.

  • A hazard card at the bottom of your own stack is safe until you must flip it. Keep it only if you are sure you will not be the Walker.

  • A card is a hazard one time in three on average (two suits out of six), so a random card is safe 2 in 3. Two random flips are both safe 44% of the time and three 30%.

  • Bid your own stack size when your stack is all safe. Every extra card you ask for from another player is a one in three risk.

  • If someone else bids high, raise only if your own stack is safe: you will be flipping it first.

  • Lose a hazard-heavy card first. When you fail a bid, give up the card most likely to be a hazard again, not your best safe card.

Worked example

  1. 3 players, 4 cards each. Hands: seat 0 Amay (1), Smaya (1), Idhayan (1), Dharsh (2); seat 1 Pinku (2), Ammlu (2), Ajay (2), Bn Sharada (2); seat 2 Nysha (1), Anayka (1), Shreya (2), Arvind (1). Seat 0 starts.

  2. Round 1. The die shows 4, the torch suit on the Suit key. Hazards this round: Idhayan (1), Ajay (2), Shreya (2) and Arvind (1) (each shows suit 4). Everyone knows their own hazards and keeps them in hand.

  3. Each lays one card: Amay (1), Pinku (2), Nysha (1). Then each adds a second: Smaya (1), Ammlu (2), Anayka (1). Each stack has two cards: six on the table. Seat 0 bids 3.

  4. Seat 1 raises to 4. Seats 2 and 0 pass. Seat 1 is the Walker. They flip their own stack first: Ammlu (2) (top, safe) then Pinku (2) (safe). They need two more and pick seat 0's top card Smaya (1) (safe) and seat 2's top card Anayka (1) (safe). Four safe flips: seat 1 scores 1 point.

  5. Round 2. Seat 1 starts. The die shows 3, so hazards are every card with suit 3 on it; Nysha (1) has one. Seat 1 lays Bn Sharada (2), seat 2 lays Nysha (1) (a hazard, now at the bottom of their stack), seat 0 lays Dharsh (2). Seat 1 adds Ajay (2). Seat 2 adds Shreya (2) on top of the hazard. Seat 0 bids 4 and nobody raises.

  6. Seat 0 flips their own Dharsh (2) (safe). They then pick seat 2's stack: Shreya (2) on top (safe), then Nysha (1) underneath, which shows suit 3: hazard. Seat 0 fails, stops, and loses one of their 4 cards. They give up Amay (1). Seat 0 now has 3 cards; seat 1 has 1 point. Seat 0 starts round 3.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

The Quick Walk (age 6). No bidding. Everyone lays one card and the die is rolled. Going clockwise each player flips one card from someone else's stack; a safe flip scores 1 point, a hazard scores nothing and ends your turn. First to 3 points wins. No cards are ever lost.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Three cards each instead of four. Full bidding, but a failed Walker just loses their turn instead of a card. First to 2 points wins.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: 4 cards each, a failed Walker loses a card of their choice for good, first to 3 points.

Solo

No solo mode: bluffing and bidding need other people.

Two players

Not simulated at 2 players and not recommended: with two stacks the Walker's choice of whose stack to flip next is trivial. Use 3 or more.

Maths and skills in this game

Estimating a risk of 1 in 3 per card, multiplying that risk over several cards (2/3 × 2/3 × 2/3), and reading what an opponent's bid means.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule a card is a hazard if either of its two suits equals the die number
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • The bot (places safe cards, bids by odds) wins 43% to 46% at 3 and 4 players and 34% at 5, against random opponents. Even shares are 33%, 25% and 20%.

  • First to 3 points takes about 7.8 rounds at 3 players but only about 3 rounds at 4 to 5 players, because a failed bid costs a card and speeds the elimination of walkers.

  • Each card has two different suits out of six, so exactly 2 of 6 = one in three cards is a hazard for a given die roll (computed from the card list). Safe odds: 1 flip 67%, 2 flips 44%, 3 flips 30%, 4 flips 20%.

  • In simulation the Walker's extra flips come from a randomly chosen opponent stack. Real Walkers choose the stack, which should make skilled bids a little safer.

  • The bot treats each unknown card as a 25% hazard when it bids; the true rate is 33%, so the bot is a little bold.

  • Skill edge is modest (43% to 46% against random players) compared with other bluffing games in the set. Luck of the die is part of the fun.

  • Bots lose a random card on a failed bid. A human chooses, so the real game will be a bit faster to settle.

Not tested:

  • Choosing which opponent stack to flip (the bot flips random ones) and choosing which card to lose were not modelled.

  • L1 and L2 were not simulated.

  • Two-player games and games of 6 players were not simulated for length.

  • Eliminated players sitting out is the only rule in this build; the idea of 'ghosts' who stay in play is not included.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

SKULL WALK. 3 to 6 players. Each has 4 cards. Roll the die and use the Suit key: any card with that suit is a HAZARD. Everyone lays 1 card face down. Then in turn: ADD a card to your stack, or BID a number of cards you will flip. Raise or pass round the table. The highest bidder (the Walker) flips their own stack first (top card first), then others' stacks, top card first.

Back

All safe: +1 point. Hit a hazard: stop, lose a card of your choice for good. First to 3 points wins; no cards left = out. L1: no bids, flip one card each, 3 points wins. L2: 3 cards each, no card loss, 2 points. A random card is a hazard 1 time in 3.

Mole in the Camp

Five missions, each needing a total from the cards the team secretly plays. One or two players in the camp are Moles and want the missions to fail.

Inspired by The Resistance, Saboteur and Spyfall

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-09
Players
4 to 6
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
L1 from 7
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each mission, the Leader picks a team. Each team member secretly plays one card; if the numbers reach the target, the mission succeeds. Honest players play their highest card; Moles may play low. First side to three missions wins.

What you need

All 54 cardshands of 6 cards, and role cards taken from the deck
Ref 4 (Team key)to know which of your role cards is a Tiger or a Cobra
Pencil and paperto count successes and failures (or use three cards each)

Set up

  • Make the role cards. 4 players: 3 Tigers and 1 Cobra. 5 players: 3 Tigers and 2 Cobras. 6 players: 4 Tigers and 2 Cobras. Shuffle them and deal one face down to each player. A Cobra is a Mole; a Tiger is an honest camper. Look at your own card in secret.

  • If there are two Moles, everybody closes their eyes. The two Moles open their eyes and look at each other, then close them again. (With one Mole nothing happens, but close eyes anyway so nobody can tell.)

  • Shuffle all the other cards (everything except the role cards). Deal 6 cards to each player. The rest is the draw deck.

  • Choose the first Leader at random. The Leader moves clockwise every mission.

  • Team size for missions 1 to 5 is: 4 players 2, 2, 2, 3, 3; 5 players 2, 3, 2, 3, 3; 6 players 3, 3, 3, 4, 4. A team of 2 needs a total of 12 (use 13 at 4 players), a team of 3 needs 19 (use 20 at 4 players), a team of 4 needs 26 (use 27 at 4 players).

How to play

  1. Pick a team. The Leader chooses the players for this mission. The Leader must include themself. The team size is fixed for the mission number.

  2. Play. Each member of the team secretly plays one card from their hand face down. An honest player must play their highest card. A Mole may play any card; a smart Mole plays their lowest when it matters.

  3. Count. The Leader shuffles the played cards face down, turns them over, adds the numbers and says only Success or Fail. The cards go into a discard pile. Nobody sees which card came from whom.

  4. Draw. Everyone who played draws a card to get back to 6.

  5. Talk. Before the next team is chosen, players may talk freely. A failed mission is never proof: honest teams fail by luck 3% to 8% of the time with standard targets.

  6. The next mission's Leader is the next player clockwise.

How it ends

Missions are played until one side has 3 wins. If 3 missions succeed, the honest players win. If 3 fail, the Moles win. At the end the roles are turned face up.

Words in this game

  • Mole a player whose role card is a Cobra; they want three failed missions
  • Honest a player whose role card is a Tiger; they want three successes
  • Leader the player who picks the team for the mission
  • Target the total the played cards must reach for the mission to succeed
  • Sabotage a Mole playing a low card on purpose

Common questions

  • Must the Leader be on the team? Yes. The Leader always plays a card. This gives the Leader something to say about their own honesty.

  • Can honest players play a low card? No. Honest players always play their highest card; that is how a Mole is spotted.

  • Does a failed mission mean a Mole was on the team? Not always. Bad luck (a mission needing a big total from low hands) can fail with only honest players. Ask who has been on the failed teams.

  • Do Moles have to sabotage? No. A smart Mole sometimes plays high to stay hidden.

  • Do Moles know each other? In the two-Mole games, yes: they look at each other during set-up.

Tips

  • Count how many 9s and 8s are in your hand. Honest players should say whether their hand is strong, because a team needs the totals.

  • As Leader, choose players who were on successful teams. Keep players who were on failures away until you have to use them.

  • As a Mole, sabotage on the missions that decide the game, not the first one. Failed first missions make the table suspicious.

  • Teams of three or four are where one low card is most hidden: with a big target the totals fail by luck anyway.

  • With two Moles, put only one of them on a team. Two Moles together would show up in the totals.

  • If you are honest, ask for the smaller teams early: a team of two needs two high cards, and a single low card is a sure fail.

Worked example

  1. 4 players (one Mole, tight targets). Seat 2 holds the Cobra role card Ajay (2); the other role cards are Tigers Shreya (2), Adhiraa (3) and Kanasu (3). Hands: seat 0 Guhan (6), Dharsh (7), Adhiraa (6), Gowri (9), Shreya (7), Bn Sharada (7); seat 1 Sharada (3), Dhruv (3), Adheesh (9), Kanasu (6), Nysha (8), Arvind (8); seat 2 Dharsh (2), Rihansh (9), Archana (4), Bn Sharada (2), Anayka (1), Smaya (1); seat 3 Amyra (5), Amay (8), Amyra (4), Nakul (5), Archana (5), Rihansh (9).

  2. Mission 1, 2 players, target 13. Seat 0 leads and picks seat 1. Seat 0 plays Gowri (9), seat 1 plays Adheesh (9): total 18. Success. They draw Nakul (4) and Idhayan (1).

  3. Mission 2, 2 players, target 13. Seat 1 leads and picks seat 2. Seat 1 plays Nysha (8). Seat 2 is the Mole and sabotages with Smaya (1): total 9. Fail. Seat 1 and seat 2 draw Bharati (4) and Gopi (4).

  4. Everyone now suspects seats 1 and 2, because they were both on the failed team, and trusts seat 0, who was only on a success.

  5. Mission 3, 2 players, target 13. Seat 2 leads and picks seat 0. The Mole plays Rihansh (9) to look honest, seat 0 plays Dharsh (7): total 16. Success.

  6. Score: honest side 2, Moles 1. One more success and the honest players win; two more failures and the Moles win.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

The Camp Run (age 7). No Mole. Everyone is honest and plays their highest card. Play five missions with the targets for 4 players; the whole camp wins if 3 succeed and loses if 3 fail. Teaches sums.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

One Mole, loose targets (12, 19, 26). Four to five players. Honest players are told the Mole only plays one low card when the Leader chooses a team of 3 or more (no sabotage on teams of 2).

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: set-up per player count, tight targets at 4 players, two Moles at 5 and 6 players, and sabotage on any mission.

Solo

No solo mode: the game is about finding the Mole.

Two players

Not possible: you need at least four people.

Maths and skills in this game

Adding small totals under time pressure, tracking which players were on which team, and reading a group's behaviour.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule the totals decide success
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternNot used
TeamRule Tigers are honest, Cobras are Moles in the role cards
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • With one Mole and standard targets, the honest side wins 78% at 4 players, 96% at 5 and 92% at 6 against a smart Mole, and 89% to 98% against a Mole that sabotages at random. One Mole is too weak.

  • Two Moles with the same missions give the honest side 42% at 5 players and 56% at 6 (standard targets), and 34% at 6 with tighter targets.

  • At 4 players, one Mole with tighter targets (13 / 20 / 27) gives the honest side about 65%.

  • Honest teams fail on bad luck alone 3% to 8% of the time with standard targets (4% to 11% tighter), so no single failure proves a Mole.

  • A bot that picks teams from a running suspicion score adds little against a smart Mole: honest wins 78% against 82% for random teams at 4 players, 96% against 88% at 5 and 92% against 82% at 6. Without table talk there is not much deduction to do.

  • A game is 5 missions or fewer, with 9 to 16 card plays plus talk, around 15 minutes.

  • The 5 player game (two Moles with easier targets) was never simulated. The easier targets suggested here are one lower than standard.

Not tested:

  • 5 players: two Moles with easier targets (11 / 18 / 25) is a guess.

  • Table talk and voting. The bots choose teams from a score but cannot argue.

  • Hiding the played cards (reveal pass or fail only) was the simulated rule; showing the shuffled cards is untested.

  • Role cards from teams (Tiger or Cobra) are a build choice; the sim picked the Mole at random.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

MOLE IN THE CAMP. 4 to 6 players. Role cards: 3 Tigers + 1 Cobra (4p), 3 Tigers + 2 Cobras (5p), 4 Tigers + 2 Cobras (6p). Cobra = Mole. Two Moles see each other. 6 cards each. Missions 1 to 5 (4p: 2,2,2,3,3; 5p: 2,3,2,3,3; 6p: 3,3,3,4,4). Leader picks a team (Leader included); each plays a card face down. Honest = highest card; a Mole may play any.

Back

Shuffle, add up, say only SUCCESS or FAIL. Targets: team of 2 = 12, 3 = 19, 4 = 26 (4 players: 13 / 20 / 27). Refill hands to 6. First side to 3 missions wins. L1: no Mole, play together. L2: one Mole, no sabotage on teams of 2. A fail is not proof: honest teams fail by luck 3 to 8% of the time.

Mind games · Deduction and party and acting · Fronts

Hidden Rule

The Dealer has a secret rule for which card may follow which. You play cards, they say yes or no, and the first player to work out the rule wins the round.

Inspired by Eleusis

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 7 / 10
Game code
MG-10
Players
4 to 7 (one Dealer, 3 to 6 guessers)
Time
20 to 30 min
Age
L1 from 8
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

The Dealer writes a secret rule about how a new card may follow the last card in the line. Everyone else plays cards and the Dealer only says Yes (the card stays) or No (it goes back). Work out the rule and name it before the others.

What you need

All 54 cardsthe line is built from face-up cards, each judged against the one before
Pencil and paperthe Dealer writes the rule; guessers may keep notes
Ref 3 and Ref 4 (Colour key and Team key)to settle colour and team questions quickly

Set up

  • Choose a Dealer for the first round. Every player will be Dealer once.

  • The Dealer thinks of a rule, writes it on a slip of paper face down, and puts it aside. The rule must say whether a new card may follow the last accepted card, using only those two cards. For example: "shares a colour", "same team", "different team", "number up or equal", "alternate odd and even". Any rule is allowed, but it must be decidable from the two cards.

  • The Dealer shuffles the cards and deals 5 cards to each other player.

  • The Dealer turns over the top card of the deck and puts it face up as the start of the line. This card is accepted by default.

  • Put the rest of the cards as the draw deck.

How to play

  1. Starting with the player to the Dealer's left, each player in turn plays one card from their hand, face up, next to the last accepted card.

  2. The Dealer says Yes or No and nothing else. On Yes the card joins the end of the line and becomes the card the next play is judged against. On No the card is taken back out of the line and put in the discard pile.

  3. The player then draws a card from the deck to have 5 again, and the next player takes a turn.

  4. Guess. Instead of playing, a player may say "I know the rule" and state it. The Dealer checks the written slip. A guess is right if it accepts and rejects the same cards as the Dealer's rule would; the Dealer is the judge. If it is right, the round ends and that player scores 2. If wrong, the player misses their next turn.

  5. If nobody guesses the rule after every player has played 6 cards (the cards of the line plus rejections), the round ends and the Dealer reads the rule. The Dealer scores 1 point.

  6. The Dealer scores 1 point if the rule is guessed after at least 4 plays and 0 if it is guessed sooner (too easy).

How it ends

After every player has been Dealer once, the player with the most points wins. Ties: play one more round with the tied players dealing in turn.

Words in this game

  • Line the accepted cards in a row, each following the one before
  • Rule a statement about the last accepted card and a new card
  • Yes / No the only words the Dealer is allowed to say during play
  • Reject a card the rule refuses; it goes back to the discard pile

Common questions

  • Can the rule use more than two cards? No. Keep it to the new card and the last accepted card. It keeps the game short.

  • Can I play the same kind of card over and over? Yes, and it is a good way to test. Repeating the same test twice tells you whether the rule depends on the previous card or not.

  • What makes a good rule? One the Dealer can judge from the two cards in a second or two, that accepts roughly half the cards, and that is not a near-twin of an easier rule.

  • May the Dealer make the rule different for the first card? No. The first card of the line is placed by the Dealer. All later cards must satisfy the rule.

Tips

  • Play a card that would split the rules you are thinking about: for example one that shares a colour but not a team. The answer then eliminates half your ideas at once.

  • Notice what the rejected cards have in common. A single Yes teaches little; a No next to a Yes teaches a lot.

  • As Dealer, a rule that accepts about half the cards (around 50%) is the best: 'alternate odd and even' or 'serial higher'. A rule that accepts 15% (same team) is slow; 85% (different team) is almost always Yes.

  • Beware of look-alike rules. 'Share a colour' and 'share a colour or a team' agree on 93% of card pairs, so test with a card that has the same team but not the colour.

  • Watch the other guessers. If one player starts playing safely, they probably know the rule and are hiding it.

Worked example

  1. Four people: the Dealer and three guessers. The Dealer's rule on the slip is "shares a colour with the last card". The line starts with Nysha (1) (Yellow and Green).

  2. Seat 1 plays Anayka (1) (Green and Purple). It shares Green. Yes. The line is now K04, K06.

  3. Seat 2 plays Smaya (8) (Red and Blue). Shares nothing with K06. No; back it goes. Seat 3 plays Amay (8) (Orange and Yellow). No colour in common with K06. No.

  4. Seat 1 plays Rihansh (9) (Yellow and Purple). Shares Purple with K06. Yes. Seat 2 plays Gopi (4) (Red and Blue): no. Seat 3 plays Smaya (1) (Orange and Purple): shares Purple with K53, Yes.

  5. After six plays, seat 1 guesses: "The new card must share a colour with the last card." The Dealer checks the slip. Right. Seat 1 scores 2, the Dealer scores 1 (the rule took six plays).

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

A short list (age 8). The Dealer chooses from four rules shown to everyone: same team, different team, shares a colour, number up or equal. The guessers know the rule is one of these.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

A list of ten (age 8+): add alternate odd and even, number down, serial higher, shares a suit, bond or same number, sum over 9. The Dealer picks one without saying; guessers may try to name it from the list.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: any rule at all, written on paper by the Dealer. No printed list.

Solo

No solo mode: a Dealer is needed.

Two players

Needs at least one Dealer and 3 guessers. With only a Dealer and one guesser the guessing is too easy.

Maths and skills in this game

Forming and testing hypotheses, logical thinking: a Yes tells you what is allowed, a No tells you what is not, and the next card is a test. This is how scientists work.

Which card elements do the work

NumberFlavour one kind of rule can use it: higher, lower, odd, even, bond
ColoursFlavour a typical rule shares a colour
Suit pairFlavour shares a suit
Back patternNot used
TeamFlavour same team or different team
Letter tileFlavour letter later in the alphabet
SerialFlavour serial higher
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • With a printed menu of 20 rules (shared colour, same team, alternate odd and even, bond or same number, serial higher and so on), a bot that crosses off rules finds the answer in a median of 4 to 6 plays whoever plays: smart plays median 5, 4, 5, 5 at 3 to 6 players; random plays median 6.

  • 5% to 7% of games with smart play, and 2% to 5% with random play, never resolve because some rules look alike: share a colour matches colour-or-team on 93% of card pairs, and different team matches number-and-team-differ on 93%.

  • Rule acceptance on random card pairs runs from 15% (same team) to 85% (different team); most rules sit near 50% (serial higher 50%, alternate odd and even 50%, share a colour 59%).

  • A game is a round of 2 to 5 minutes; each player deals once, so 15 to 25 minutes in all.

  • The fun is a Dealer free to invent any rule, which a printed menu removes. So there is no menu on the rule card: the Dealer states any rule on paper (L3).

  • Other rules with high acceptance, such as 'different team', give long runs of Yes answers and little information: 85% of random pairs are accepted.

Not tested:

  • No real people have played it. Whether a Dealer can invent fair rules is unknown.

  • The scoring (2 for a correct guess, 1 for the Dealer) is not simulated.

  • L1 and L2 lists were not simulated.

  • Rules that depend on more than the last card were not tested.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

HIDDEN RULE. 4 to 7 players (a Dealer + 3 to 6 guessers). The Dealer writes a secret rule on a slip: when may a card follow the last accepted card? It may use only the two cards. 5 cards each; one card starts the line. In turn, play a card next to the last accepted card. The Dealer says only YES (it stays) or NO (it goes back). Draw to 5.

Back

GUESS instead of playing: right = 2 points, wrong = miss a turn. After 6 plays each with no guess, the Dealer scores 1. Dealer also scores 1 if the rule is found after 4+ plays (0 if sooner). Everyone deals once. L1: pick from 4 shown rules. L2: pick from 10. L3: any rule on paper.

Card Quarto

You never choose your own card. You choose the one your opponent has to place, and the first line of four that share anything wins for whoever places it.

Inspired by Quarto

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 8 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-11
Players
2
Time
10 to 15 min (best of three)
Age
L1 from 7
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Lay out a 4 by 4 grid and 16 cards. On your turn you hand your opponent a card to place anywhere. The player who places the card that completes a line of four sharing a colour group, a suit group, a team group or odd or even wins.

What you need

16 cards from the deckshuffle the 54 and take the top 16
Ref 3 and Ref 4 (Colour and Suit keys)to read which half (1 to 3 or 4 to 6) a colour or suit is in
A 4 by 4 spacea grid of 16 squares; the cards just need room to be laid in four rows of four

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards and take the top 16. Spread them face up in a pool at the side of the table where both players can see them. Put the other 38 back in the box.

  • Leave a 4 by 4 square of empty space in the middle: this is the board. Number the rows A to D from the top and columns 1 to 4.

  • The younger player gives the first card.

  • The four groups that count: colour (judge each card by its first colour: 1 to 3 against 4 to 6), suit (first suit: 1 to 3 against 4 to 6), team (team 1 to 3 against 4 to 6, i.e. Tigers, Elephants, Bears against Monkeys, Peacocks, Cobras) and number (odd against even).

How to play

  1. The first player gives any card from the pool to the other player. They must name it clearly.

  2. The other player places that card on any empty square of the board.

  3. If the placed card makes a full line of four (a row, a column, or one of the two long diagonals) in which all four cards are on the same side of at least one group (all low first colours, or all odd, and so on), the placer wins at once.

  4. If not, the placer now gives a card from the pool to the first player, who places it. So the roles swap after every placement.

  5. You always place exactly the card you were given, and you always give a card from the pool, never one of your own choosing from the board.

How it ends

The first player to complete a line wins the game. If all 16 cards are placed and no line wins, it is a draw (in simulation this almost never happens). Play a best of three: the loser of a game gives first in the next.

Words in this game

  • Pool the 16 cards not yet placed
  • Group a two-way split of one card feature: low or high first colour, first suit, team, odd or even
  • Line a row, column or long diagonal of four squares
  • Safe card a card that cannot complete a line wherever it is placed

Common questions

  • Which colour counts? Only the first colour printed on the card. A card with colours 2 and 6 counts as low.

  • Can I look at the groups of a card quickly? Yes: use the keys. A colour or suit in the first half of each key is low, the second half high. Team dice 1 to 3 are low.

  • What if I have no safe card to give? Then you must give a card that lets your opponent win, unless the board is such that no card can win.

  • Does a line of four of the same colour but different teams count? Yes, if all four share one group (they would all be low or all high first colour).

Tips

  • Before you give a card, look at every line that has three cards and an empty square. Check each group on those three cards. If a group is shared, the card that fits is deadly.

  • Count the safe cards in the pool: cards that cannot complete a line wherever they go. The player who has to give when no safe card is left loses. Steer the game so your opponent runs out first.

  • Place a card where it spoils a line. Putting a low card among three high ones makes that line dead for that group.

  • Keep a mental list of which groups each line still allows. Early on, plain groups like odd and even matter most because they are everywhere.

  • If you see that the pool will force your opponent to give you a winning card, play safe and wait.

Worked example

  1. Board after nine placements (rows A to D, columns 1 to 4; name and number): row A: Adhiraa 6, empty, Bn Sharada 2, empty. Row B: Gowri 9, empty, Smaya 1, Kanasu 3. Row C: empty, empty, Dharsh 2, Sharada 6. Row D: empty, Pinku 2, Amay 8, empty.

  2. Seven cards remain in the pool: Nysha (1), Adhiraa (3), Amyra (5), Archana (5), Ajay (7), Anayka (1) and Guhan (3). Every one of them has an odd number.

  3. Row B has three odd cards, Gowri (9), Smaya (1) and Kanasu (3), and one empty square at B2. Any odd card placed there completes the line.

  4. It is Player 2's turn to give, and every card in the pool is odd, so there is no safe card. They give Guhan (3). Player 1 places it at B2: row B reads 9, 3, 1, 3, all odd. Player 1 wins.

  5. Notice the move before: Player 1 gave Adhiraa (6) (6, even). It was the only safe card in the pool of eight (checked by computer), and giving it left Player 2 with seven odd cards and no safe card.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Three in a row (age 7). A 3 by 3 board with 9 cards. Only two groups count: odd or even, and team 1 to 3 against 4 to 6. A line is 3 cards.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

A 4 by 4 board, rows and columns only, with all four groups.

L3 · age 8 and up

The full game: rows, columns and both long diagonals, all four groups, and a best of three.

Solo

No solo mode: it is a duel about what you give your opponent.

Two players

This is a two-player game only.

Maths and skills in this game

Reading several features of a card at once, planning two moves ahead, and counting the safe cards left, which is a first lesson in parity.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule odd or even is one group
ColoursRule the first colour, low or high
Suit pairRule the first suit, low or high
Back patternNot used
TeamRule teams 1 to 3 against 4 to 6
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesFlavour you can read the names in the example
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • As first specified (judging by first colour, first suit, team, and odd or even, with equal values only) the strong bot draws 67% of games against itself; allowing any shared colour still draws 52%, because lines rarely share a colour, suit or team.

  • Using two-way groups instead (colour 1 to 3 against 4 to 6, the same for suit and team, odd against even) gives no draws. The strong bot wins 100% of games against a random player and two strong bots split 50% each. Games last about 11 turns.

  • Re-run for this page: strong bot against random 99% / 1%, strong bot mirror 49% / 51%, random against random 50% / 50%, no draws in any, and an average of 7.7 turns (strong vs random), 11.4 (mirror) and 9.6 (random vs random).

  • Computed from the card list: first colour is 1 to 3 on 43 of 54 cards, first suit on 44 of 54, team die 1 to 3 on 24 of 54, and odd numbers on 30 of 54. The colour and suit groups are lopsided, which makes lines more likely to share a group.

  • A random line of four cards shares at least one two-way group about 75% of the time (200,000 random lines, computed). That is why the game almost always ends before the 16th card.

  • It takes 3 to 6 minutes a game; a best of three is the intended length.

Not tested:

  • Real people: the bots do not talk.

  • The 3 by 3 L1 board was not simulated.

  • The lopsided colour and suit groups may make low-colour lines too common; a better split (for example judging by the colour whose die number is higher) was not tried.

  • Drawing the 16 cards: only a random 16 was tested.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

CARD QUARTO. 2 players. Take 16 cards face up as a pool. Board = 4 by 4 squares. You GIVE your opponent a card; they PLACE it on any empty square; then they give you one. Groups (judge by FIRST colour and FIRST suit): colour 1 to 3 vs 4 to 6; suit 1 to 3 vs 4 to 6; team 1 to 3 vs 4 to 6; number odd vs even.

Back

A line = row, column or long diagonal of 4. The player who places a card completing a line in which all four are on the same side of at least one group WINS. All 16 placed, no line: draw. Best of three; the loser gives first next. L1: 3 by 3 board, odd/even and team groups only. L2: rows and columns only.

Mind games · Pattern and tiles and maths and counting · Fronts

Three Ways

Everyone picks a card in secret, then all cards go down on one shared grid, lowest first. Complete a line of three that matches in number, run or suit, and the points are yours.

Inspired by Thricewise (P. D. Magnus's Decktet game)

FamilyGrown-upsEasyComplexity 1.3 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-12
Players
2 to 5 (best with 2 to 4)
Time
25 to 30 min (two grids of about 14)
Age
L1 from 7, L3 from 10
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Each round you secretly choose a card. All are revealed and placed on a shared 6 by 6 grid, lowest number first. When you complete a line of three squares, it scores the best pattern: same number 6, run 3, shared suit 1.

What you need

All 54 cardsnumbers, suits and serials all matter
Table spacea 6 by 6 grid of cards, about 45 cm square
Pencil and paperfor the score

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. The grid is 6 by 6 squares, empty, in the middle of the table.

  • Deal 4 cards to each player. The rest is the draw pile.

  • Choose a first player. In the second grid, move the first player one seat clockwise.

How to play

  1. Pick. Everyone secretly picks one card from their hand and puts it face down. Reveal together.

  2. Place. Place the cards one at a time, lowest number first. Equal numbers: the lower serial first. The first card of the game goes on any of the four middle squares. Every later card goes on an empty square touching a placed card side to side. If a card has nowhere to go, discard it.

  3. Score each card as you place it (see below), then everyone draws back to 4.

How it ends

Scoring. When you place a card, look at every line of exactly 3 squares, across or down (not diagonal), that is completely filled and includes your new card in any of its three places. Each such line scores its best pattern: Set (all three numbers equal) 6; Run (three consecutive numbers in any order, such as 4, 6, 5) 3; Flush (one suit shared by all three cards; either of a card's two suits counts) 1. The points go to the player who placed the card. The grid ends when it is full, or the draw pile cannot refill every hand to 4 (then the game ends after that round). If the grid fills in the middle of a round, the remaining cards are not played. Play a second grid with a freshly shuffled deck. Add the scores; highest wins. Tie: more sets, else share.

Words in this game

  • Grid a 6 by 6 set of squares in which cards are placed.
  • Set a line of three cards with the same number (6 points).
  • Run a line of three consecutive numbers in any order (3 points).
  • Flush a line of three sharing one suit (1 point).
  • Line exactly three touching squares in a row or column.

Common questions

  • Do diagonals count? No. Counting diagonals made scores jump and skill fall.

  • Can a card complete more than one line? Yes. A card can finish two lines at once, for example one across and one down; each scores its best pattern.

  • What if a line has more than three cards? Only lines of exactly three squares count, so a longer row is scored in overlapping windows of three squares that include the new card.

  • Who places first when numbers are equal? The card with the lower serial.

  • What if the draw pile is short? Finish the round; the game ends after it.

Tips

  • Runs are the most common pattern and are worth three times a flush. Plan runs, and hold on to sets for lucky moments.

  • Place your card where a rival's best line would end, or where it makes a run with a card you hold next.

  • You place in order of strength: a low number gets the best squares but sees fewer open lines.

  • The secret pick is mostly a guess. Think about what the others need, but do not over-think.

  • Do not just play the lowest or highest every time: always lowest, always highest or always blocking each win only 9% against simple players.

Worked example

  1. 3 players. Round 1. Picks: Seat 0 Pinku (2) (number 2), Seat 1 Ajay (2), Seat 2 Nakul (5).

    Pinku (2) and Ajay (2) are both 2s, so Pinku (2) goes first on the lower serial. Seat 0 places Pinku (2) in the middle, row 4 column 4. Seat 1 places Ajay (2) at row 4 column 5. Seat 2 places Nakul (5) at row 4 column 3. 0 points each.

  2. Round 2. Picks: Seat 1 Dharsh (2), Seat 0 Adhiraa (3), Seat 2 Avika (5). The order is K07, K14, K29. Seat 1 places Dharsh (2) at row 4 column 6. Row 4 columns 4 to 6 are Pinku (2), Ajay (2), Dharsh (2) = 2, 2, 2: a set, 6 points. Seat 0 places Adhiraa (3) at row 3 column 6: no full line yet. Seat 2 places Avika (5) at row 5 column 4.

  3. Round 3. Picks: Seat 0 Amay (1), Seat 1 Idhayan (1), Seat 2 Arvind (8). Amay (1) goes before Idhayan (1) on the lower serial.

  4. Seat 0 places Amay (1) at row 5 column 6. Column 6 rows 3 to 5 are Adhiraa (3), Dharsh (2), Amay (1) = 3, 2, 1: a run, 3 points.

  5. Seat 1 places Idhayan (1) at row 2 column 6. Column 6 rows 2 to 4 are Idhayan (1), Adhiraa (3), Dharsh (2) = 1, 3, 2: a run, 3 points. With the set from round 2, Seat 1 has 9.

  6. Seat 2 places Arvind (8) at row 5 column 5. Row 5 columns 4 to 6 are Avika (5), Arvind (8), Amay (1) = 5, 8, 1: no run, but suit 3 is on all three cards, so a flush, 1 point. Scores: Seat 0 has 3, Seat 1 has 9, Seat 2 has 1.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Sets and runs only, on a 4 by 4 grid with 3 cards each (age 7 with a helper). Count 6 for a set and 3 for a run, ignore flushes.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Full scoring on a 5 by 5 grid, one grid.

L3 · age 8 and up

Full game: 6 by 6, two grids, tie-break by sets.

Solo

No solo mode: the secret pick needs other players.

Two players

A good size: the better bot beats a simple one 69% of the time at 2 players.

Maths and skills in this game

Number patterns, runs and sets, probability (guessing what others pick), and spatial thinking.

Which card elements do the work

NumberRule sets and runs; placing order
ColoursNot used
Suit pairRule a flush needs a shared suit; either suit of a card counts
Back patternNot used
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialRule placement tie-break when numbers are equal
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • 6,000 games for fairness and 2,000 or more for skill. A 6 by 6 grid with 4 cards each takes 36 placements: 13.5 minutes at 2 players and 11 at 4.

  • Seats are fair. The better bot beats a simple one 69% of 2-player games, 49% at 3, 35% at 4 and 26% at 5, against 50, 33, 25 and 20% by chance. Skill is real at 2 to 4 and fades at 5.

  • Runs are about half of all points, with sets and flushes a quarter each.

  • The choice of order to place in does not change skill. Always playing the lowest card, always the highest, or always blocking each win only 9% against simple players, so nothing dominates.

  • The secret pick is mostly a guess, which is why the game is played as two grids and 5 players is a luck game.

  • Counting diagonals as lines made scores jump and skill fall.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people, who may read each other's picks.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written.

  • Not tested: more than 5 players.

Variants and options

  • Five Points A second Decktet grid filler (Quincunx) with 60% skill at 2 players and 42% at 4 is not a separate game: it was cut as weaker than this one.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

THREE WAYS. 2 to 5 players, shared 6 by 6 grid. Deal 4 each. Everyone picks a card in secret; reveal together. Place lowest number first (tie: lower serial). First card on a middle square; later cards touch a placed card side to side. Draw back to 4.

Back

SCORE the lines of exactly 3 squares (across or down) that your new card completes: set 6, run of three (any order) 3, one shared suit 1. Two grids. Highest total wins; tie: more sets. LEVELS. L1 4 by 4, sets and runs only. L2 5 by 5. L3 full.

Old Town

Lay down a city one card at a time and put your pawns on it. Every card sits in two districts at once, one for each of its suits, and the player with the most pawns takes the district.

Inspired by Jacynth (P. D. Magnus's Decktet game)

Grown-upsFamilyMediumComplexity 1.4 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 5 / 10
Game code
MG-13
Players
2 to 3
Time
25 to 30 min (two or three cities of about 12)
Age
L1 from 8, L3 from 10
Dice
None
Pawns
3 each at 2 players, 2 each at 3

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Play a card next to the city and put a pawn on any card. A district is a group of touching cards sharing a suit. When the city is full, in each district of 3 or more cards the player with strictly the most pawns scores one point per card.

What you need

All 54 cardsthe city is built from them; only the two suits on each card matter
Pawns3 each at 2 players, 2 each at 3
Table spacea 6 by 6 square of cards at 2 players (5 by 5 at 3)

Set up

  • Shuffle all 54 cards. Each player draws 3 cards.

  • 2 players get 3 pawns each; 3 players get 2 each.

  • The city may not grow beyond 6 by 6 cards for 2 players, or 5 by 5 for 3 players.

  • Pick a first player. In each later city, the first player moves one seat clockwise.

How to play

  1. Play a card. Play one card from your hand next to a card already in the city, touching it side to side. The first card of the city goes anywhere. Draw back to 3.

  2. Place a pawn. If you still have a pawn in your supply, you must place one now on any card in the city. Pawns never move after that. Pawns may share a card.

  3. The city is built this way until it is finished.

How it ends

Districts. A district is a group of cards that touch side to side and all show the same suit (either of their two suits). A card is in two districts at once, one for each of its suits. A pawn on a card counts in both of that card's districts. End of the city. The city is finished when it is full (36 cards, or 25 at 3 players) or the deck cannot refill a hand and no card can be played. In each district of 3 or more cards, the player with strictly the most pawns there controls it and scores 1 point for every card in the district. If players tie, nobody scores. Smaller districts score nothing. The match. Play two cities with 2 players (three with 3 players). Shuffle again for each. Add the points. Highest total wins. Tie: more districts controlled across the match, else share.

Words in this game

  • City the cards laid out edge to edge on the table.
  • District touching cards that all show the same suit.
  • Control having strictly more pawns than anyone else in a district.
  • Supply your pawns not yet placed.
  • Match two cities (three at 3 players).

Common questions

  • Can I keep my pawns back? No. If you still have a pawn, you must place one each turn. Holding pawns back until the end beat early placing 99.8% of the time in testing, so the rule forces early placing.

  • Do pawns ever move? Never. In the first version pawns could move and the last player to act won about 90% of games.

  • What if two players tie in a district? Nobody scores it.

  • Can one card be in two districts? Yes: one for each suit it shows. A pawn on the card counts in both.

  • When does the city end early? When the deck cannot refill a hand and no card can be played, even before the city is full.

Tips

  • Think of every card as two chances to join up. A card that links two small districts of one suit can make a big one.

  • Put pawns on cards that sit in two promising districts: one pawn then helps twice.

  • Watch where the count is level. Your opponent can still win a district by out-placing your pawns.

  • A district of 2 cards scores nothing; do not waste a pawn there unless it will grow.

  • More than half the districts in a city never get a pawn, so ignore the small ones and fight over the largest.

Worked example

  1. 2 players, 3 pawns each, first eight turns. Starting hands: P1 Avika (5) Dhruv (6) Adheesh (9); P2 Amyra (5) Gowri (9) Guhan (6). Suits in brackets below.

  2. P1 plays Adheesh (9) [suits 1, 2] as the first card and places a pawn on it. P2 plays Amyra (5) [3, 4] right of Adheesh (9) and places a pawn on Adheesh (9).

  3. P1 plays Dhruv (6) [3, 5] right of Amyra (5) and places a pawn on Amyra (5). P2 plays Guhan (6) [1, 2] left of Adheesh (9) (they share suits 1 and 2) and places a pawn on Adheesh (9).

  4. P1 plays Avika (5) [3, 6] under Amyra (5) (suit 3 now links Dhruv (6), Amyra (5) and Avika (5)) and places a pawn on Dhruv (6). P2 plays Gowri (9) [2, 3] left of Guhan (6) (suit 2 joins Gowri (9), Guhan (6) and Adheesh (9)) and places a pawn on Amyra (5).

  5. P1 plays Pinku (7) [4, 6] under Avika (5). P1 has no pawn left, so there is no pawn action. P2 plays Ammlu (7) [2, 5] under Adheesh (9). Suit 2 now has Gowri (9), Guhan (6), Adheesh (9) and Ammlu (7). P2 has no pawn left.

  6. If the city ended now: the suit-2 district (4 cards) has 2 P2 pawns (both on Adheesh (9)) against 1 for P1, so P2 scores 4. The suit-3 district (Amyra (5), Dhruv (6), Avika (5): 3 cards) has 2 P1 pawns (Amyra (5), Dhruv (6)) against 1 for P2, so P1 scores 3. Suit 1 (Guhan (6), Adheesh (9)) has only 2 cards and scores nothing. P1 3, P2 4.

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Teach round (age 8 with a helper): districts of 2 cards score too, 1 point per card, and the first city is only 4 by 4.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

One city of 5 by 5 with districts of 3 or more, all other rules the same.

L3 · age 8 and up

Full game: two cities (three at 3 players), 6 by 6, districts of 3 or more.

Solo

No solo mode: area control needs rivals.

Two players

The design size. The second player wins 55% of single cities (59% for the last seat of three), so two cities with the starter moved on make it fair.

Maths and skills in this game

Spatial planning, area control, comparing counts, and planning what a card does in two places.

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • 500 to 2,000 games per cell. In the first version pawns could move at any time and the last player to act won about 90% of games; the rule that pawns never move fixed that.

  • Holding every pawn back until the end beat early placing 99.8% of the time, which is why you must place a pawn each turn once you have one.

  • A city takes 42 turns, about 10 minutes. The second player wins 55% of single cities (59% for the last seat of three), so two cities with the starter moved on make it fair.

  • The better bot beats a simple one 66% of single cities and 74% of two-city matches, and beats a bot that stacks every pawn together 75% of the time.

  • At 3 players, the better bot wins 48% against two simple bots (a fair share would be 33%).

  • Weakness: more than half the districts in a city never get a pawn on them, so this is a light filler, not a deep game.

Front

OLD TOWN. 2 or 3 players. Draw 3. Play a card touching the city (6 by 6 limit), draw to 3. Then place a pawn on any card until all yours are down; pawns never move. A district is touching cards that share a suit. A card is in two districts; its pawn counts in both.

Back

SCORE when the city is full. In each district of 3+ cards, the player with strictly the most pawns scores 1 point per card; a tie scores nothing. Two cities (three at 3 players). Most points wins; tie: more districts. LEVELS. L1 4 by 4, small districts count. L2 one city. L3 full.

Overlap Camp

Build a map out of the backs of the cards. Lay one card over the last to grow one huge patch of a single suit, because only the biggest patch counts, and it counts squared.

Inspired by Honshu, with a pick-and-pass draft as in Sushi Go

FamilyGrown-upsMediumComplexity 1.5 / 5Playability 7 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-14
Players
1 to 4 (best with 2)
Time
10 to 15 min
Age
L1 from 6, L3 from 10
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Everyone drafts cards at the same time and lays them overlapping on a private map, backs only. Only uncovered cells count. For each of the six suits, your biggest group of touching cells is squared and added up.

What you need

All 54 cardsonly the backs are used. Fronts are never read
Table spacea 6 by 6 cell window, about 40 cm square
Pencil and paperto keep the suit scores

Set up

  • Every card back shows 6 suit symbols in 3 rows of 2, with three different suits each twice. A cell is one symbol. Cards can be turned any quarter turn.

  • Shuffle all 54. Deal each player 8 cards (10 for the casual 3 to 4 player version). Look at the backs only.

  • Each player has a private Map in front of them: a place on the table where their cards go.

How to play

  1. Pick and pass. At the same time, every player picks one card from their hand and puts it on their own Map, then passes the rest of their hand to the left. Repeat until hands are empty. Everyone ends with a Map of 8 cards.

  2. Placing a card. The first card goes anywhere. Every later card must (a) cover at least 1 cell of your Map, lined up on whole cells, (b) leave every earlier card with at least one uncovered cell, and (c) keep the whole Map, hidden cards included, inside a 6 by 6 square of cells (7 by 7 in the casual version).

  3. A covered cell shows only the top card's symbol. If no card in your hand can legally be placed, discard one and move on.

How it ends

Scoring. Only uncovered cells count. For each of the six suits, find your biggest group of cells of that suit that touch side to side (not corners). Call its size g. Two players: score g times g for each suit and add up the six. Three or four players: the same, plus a contest bonus: for each suit, the player with the biggest g gets 4 points and second place gets 2 (ties share the points, rounded down). Most points wins. A tie goes to the higher total of g values; still tied, share the win.

Words in this game

  • Map your private area of overlapping cards.
  • Cell one suit symbol on a card back. Each back has 6 cells.
  • Group cells of the same suit joined side to side.
  • g the size of your biggest group in one suit.
  • Covered a cell hidden under another card; it does not count.

Common questions

  • Can a card cover another card completely? No. Every earlier card must keep at least one uncovered cell.

  • Can I turn a card half way? Yes, any quarter turn: 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees.

  • What if I cannot place any card? Discard one card and move on.

  • Do the fronts matter? No. The fronts are never looked at, so do not worry about who sees them.

  • Is passing important? Only a little. The cards you leave are the next player's choice, but the effect is small.

Tips

  • Pick a suit early and build it. Squaring rewards one huge area: a group of 11 scores 121, but two groups of 5 and 6 score 61.

  • The order you play cards matters as much as which cards you choose. You can cover a card's bad cells with the next card.

  • Look for cards whose back already shows two touching cells of your suit; they extend the group without covering it.

  • Do not lay cards in a straight line; the 6 by 6 window fills quickly. Use compact shapes.

  • In 3 and 4 player games, decide which suit the others are not building, and build that one for the 4-point bonus.

Worked example

  1. 2 players. Player 0 builds one big suit 5 area. The list g shows the biggest group for suits 1 to 6, in order. Player 0 starts with Amay (8) (back 5 5 / 2 2 / 1 1), turned 180 degrees, then covers 1 cell of it with Avika (5) (3 6 / 5 6 / 5 3), a quarter turn, below. g = 2, 3, 1, 0, 6, 2.

  2. Next Anayka (1) (4 5 / 1 1 / 4 5), turned 270 degrees. Suit 5 joins into one 8-cell group. g = 2, 3, 1, 1, 8, 0.

  3. Then Ammlu (2) (4 5 / 2 5 / 4 2), a quarter turn on the right edge: g = 2, 2, 1, 1, 10, 0.

  4. Bn Sharada (2) (5 4 / 6 5 / 6 4), a quarter turn on the top-left corner, hides some suit 1 cells but grows suit 5 to 11. Arvind (1) (4 4 / 2 1 / 1 2) follows: g = 2, 1, 1, 2, 11, 1.

  5. The last card is Dhruv (6) (4 3 / 3 5 / 5 4). The final g is 2, 1, 1, 3, 11, 1, so the score is 4 + 1 + 1 + 9 + 121 + 1 = 137.

  6. Player 1's final g was 6, 8, 3, 1, 2, 1: 36 + 64 + 9 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 115. Player 0 wins 137 to 115.

  7. The final Map of Player 0, each digit a suit and the dot empty: 4 4 6 5 2 4 / 4 3 5 4 5 5 / 3 5 5 5 5 . / 5 4 5 3 5 . / . 3 5 1 5 . / . . 4 1 4 .

Level ladder

L1 · age 5

Easy build (age 6 with a helper): hand of 4, one suit chosen at the start, count only that suit's biggest group, no squaring. Most cells wins.

L2 · ages 6 to 7

Hand of 6, square the biggest group of any three suits that you choose at the end, ignore the other three.

L3 · age 8 and up

Full rules: hand of 8, all six suits squared, window 6 by 6, bonus points at 3 or 4 players.

Solo

Solo. Play 8 turns. Each turn, turn up 3 cards from the deck, put one on your Map under the placement rules and discard the other two. Score g times g per suit. Under 150 is a hard day; 180 good; 230 great; 270 or more camp legend (add about 25 to each target with a 7 by 7 window). Percentiles of simulated solo scores in a 6 by 6 window: 5th 151, 25th 181, 50th 204, 75th 231, 90th 255, 95th 272, 99th 286.<br>Quilt Solo (variant). Lay nine cards in three rows of three, backs up, each the way it falls. Roll a die for the flag suit and count the cards that show it; if the count is below four or above six, roll again. You have five moves: turn one card half way round, or swap two cards. Your score is your biggest patch of the flag suit at the end. Medals by count: count 4: Bronze 3, Silver 4, Gold 5; count 5: Bronze 4, Silver 5, Gold 6; count 6: Bronze 6, Silver 7, Gold 8.

Two players

This is the best table size. There is no contest bonus, and the score is the sum of g times g. Quilt Duel (variant): lay nine cards in a block that both players share. Roll two dice, one flag suit each; roll again if they match. Each player has six moves (turn a card or swap two cards) and tracks their best patch of their own suit after each move; highest best patch wins, a tie goes to the second player.

Maths and skills in this game

Spatial reasoning, area and squaring numbers, planning an order of play, and drafting.

Which card elements do the work

NumberNot used
ColoursNot used
Suit pairNot used
Back patternRule the whole game is played on the back pattern: 6 cells, 3 suits twice
TeamNot used
Letter tileNot used
SerialNot used
NamesNot used
ExpressionNot used
PlaceNot used

Stats for nerds

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

  • Skill at 2 players: a simple bot that always takes the best immediate placement beats a random one every game (about 165 points to 28). A cleverer bot beats the simple one 67% of two-player games (300 to 600 games per cell). So there is real skill at two players.

  • At 3 and 4 players the cleverer bot did not beat the simple one (35% at 3 and 23% to 26% at 4, against 33% and 25% by chance), whatever was tried. Those tables are a friendly race.

  • Seats are fair. Placements per card average about 84 mid-draft; allowing only 0 and 180 degree turns halves that to about 36, or require 2 cells of overlap.

  • Longer hands (10 or 12 cards) fix the length but not the skill gap.

  • A rule letting each player once cover a chosen opponent's Map made the two-player game a one-button win for whoever used it, so it was left out.

  • Solo score percentiles in the 6 by 6 window: 5th 151, 25th 181, 50th 204, 75th 231, 90th 255, 95th 272, 99th 286.

  • Quilt Solo: gold is possible in about eight deals of ten with perfect play; a one-step greedy player gets it in just over half.

Not tested:

  • Not tested: real people. Bots do not read what passes to them.

  • Not tested: L1 and L2 as written.

  • Not tested: 3 and 4 players for skill; the game is a race there.

Variants and options

  • Quilt Solo The 3 by 3 flag-suit patch puzzle, with medals, is now this game's solo variant, and Quilt Duel is the two-player variant.

Rule card text

Text for the printed card (63.5 x 88.9 mm). Layout comes later.

Front

OVERLAP CAMP. Backs only. Deal 8 cards each. At the same time, pick one card, put it on your own Map (any quarter turn), pass the rest left. Each new card must cover at least 1 cell, leave every earlier card at least 1 visible cell, and the Map must fit in a 6 by 6 square.

Back

SCORE. For each of the six suits, your biggest group of touching cells (g). 2 players: g x g per suit. 3 to 4 players: also 4 points for the biggest g in each suit, 2 for second. Most points wins. SOLO: 8 turns, turn up 3 cards, keep 1. Under 150 hard day, 180 good, 230 great, 270 legend.

Mind games · Words · Deck-building with words · Fronts

Word Caravan

Every word you spell pays for a bigger caravan, but a caravan that is too heavy never reaches the oasis.

Inspired by Paperback and Hardback (word deck-builders), from memory; the bank-or-buy split is our own.

Grown-upsHardComplexity 2.0 / 5Playability 6 / 10Fun 6 / 10
Game code
MG-15
Players
1 to 4
Time
20 to 25 min
Age
10+
Dice
None
Pawns
None

Times include about 20% for learning the rules and for thinking. The raw simulated lengths are in the stats for nerds.

The whole game in one line

Spell a word from your hand, bank its points, spend some of them on a high card from the market, and watch your deck of letters grow stronger or clumsier.

What you need

24 start cardsAll cards numbered 1 to 4. Each player's starting deck.
30 market cardsAll cards numbered 5 to 9. They form the market deck and the market row.
Pencil and paperOne score sheet. Write each turn's banked points and tick the round.

Set up

  • Sort the deck by the number on the front. Cards numbered 1 to 4 are start cards (24). Cards numbered 5 to 9 are market cards (30).

  • Shuffle the start cards. Deal each player a starting deck, face down: eight cards each at two or three players, six cards each at four players. At two players, put the 8 left over start cards back in the box.

  • Shuffle the market cards into a face-down market deck. Turn five face up in a row beside it. This is the market row.

  • Each player draws seven cards (six at four players, because that is their whole deck). Look at your own fronts only.

  • Decide how many rounds you will play: 14 at two players, 10 at three, 8 at four. Write the round numbers on the paper.

  • The oldest player goes first. Play goes clockwise.

How to play

  1. Spell. Choose three or more cards from your hand and lay them face up in a row to spell a word. Any ordinary dictionary word works. No names. The Q card counts as the two letters Qu. Add up the numbers on the cards you laid. That total is your score for the turn.

  2. No word? Then it is a dud turn. Discard your whole hand, draw a new hand, and your turn is over. You score nothing.

  3. Buy. You may buy one card from the market row whose number is no more than your score. The number is the price. Put the bought card in your discard pile. Fill the gap in the row from the market deck. You may also buy nothing.

  4. Bank. Write down your score minus the price of the card you bought. Those points are yours for good. Points spent on a card are not banked.

  5. Clean up. Put the cards you laid and every card left in your hand into your own discard pile. Draw up to seven cards from your deck. If your deck runs out, shuffle your discard pile to make a new deck and keep drawing. If you still have fewer than seven, play with what you have.

How it ends

The game ends after the last round, when every player has had the same number of turns. The player with the most banked points wins. Tie: the player with the larger deck (all cards owned) wins; if still tied, share the win. If the market deck runs out, the row simply gets shorter.

Words in this game

  • score The sum of the numbers on the cards you laid for your word.
  • bank To write points down for good. Banked points are your final score.
  • market row The five face-up high cards you can buy from.
  • dud turn A turn where you cannot spell a word of three cards or more.
  • discard pile Your own pile of used cards. It becomes your new deck when your deck is empty.

Common questions

  • Can I buy a card and also bank points on the same turn? Yes. You bank whatever is left after paying. A score of 14 that buys a 6 banks 8.

  • Do I have to buy? No. Buying nothing banks the whole score. Late in the game that is usually right.

  • What happens to the cards left in my hand? They go to your discard pile with the cards you laid. You start the next turn with a fresh hand.

  • What if my deck has fewer than seven cards when I draw? Draw what is there, shuffle your discard pile into a new deck, and keep drawing until you hold seven.

  • Can I use the Q card? Yes. It counts as Qu, as one card with its own number. It is only useful in words such as QUIT or QUEEN, so it is a poor buy.

  • Is Y a vowel? No. In this game only A, E, I, O and U are vowels, and nothing in the rules depends on it except your own spelling.

  • Can the same word be played again on a later turn? Yes.

Tips

  • Buy early, bank late. The adaptive bot beat never-buy and always-buy bots 75 to 95%, and the rule is to invest in the first few turns and stop buying and bank everything late in the game.

  • Buy vowels. Smart bots bought 55% vowels while the market holds 40%, and a strong deck is one that can spell with its hand.

  • Skip the Q card. It only helps in words like QUIT, so it is a poor buy.

  • Stay under the price. You bank your score minus the price, so a score of 14 that buys a 6 banks 8. Do not buy a card that costs nearly your whole word.

  • Avoid dud turns. A dud means discarding your whole hand, and at four players duds happen 14% of turns, so keep a vowel in your deck and a word in mind before you draw.

Worked example

Two players, Asha and Ben, first five turns (real seeded run). Asha goes first. Each starts with an eight card deck of low cards and the market row shows high cards. Banked points are tracked as a running total.

  1. Asha holds Gopi [P] Bn Sharada [T] Naresh [A] Dhruv [I] Nakul [A] Ammlu [E] Adhiraa [H]. Asha spells PATH with Gopi [P] Nakul [A] Bn Sharada [T] Adhiraa [H]. The numbers add up to 4+4+2+3 = 13. Asha buys Adheesh (9) for 9 and banks 4. The played cards, the buy and the unplayed cards all go to Asha's discard pile. Banked so far: Asha 4.

  2. Ben holds Shreya [D] Anayka [X] Guhan [J] Archana [K] Kanasu [R] Ajay [L] Nysha [A]. Ben spells DARK with Shreya [D] Nysha [A] Kanasu [R] Archana [K]. The numbers add up to 2+1+3+4 = 10. Ben buys Kanasu (6) for 6 and banks 4. The played cards, the buy and the unplayed cards all go to Ben's discard pile. Banked so far: Ben 4.

  3. Asha holds Avika [H] Adhiraa [H] Naresh [A] Dhruv [I] Ammlu [E] Adheesh [R] Nakul [A]. Asha spells HAIR with Avika [H] Nakul [A] Dhruv [I] Adheesh [R]. The numbers add up to 4+4+3+9 = 20. Asha buys Guhan (6) for 6 and banks 14. The played cards, the buy and the unplayed cards all go to Asha's discard pile. Banked so far: Asha 18.

  4. Ben holds Dharsh [I] Anayka [X] Guhan [J] Shreya [D] Kanasu [R] Kanasu [O] Nysha [A]. Ben spells RADIO with Kanasu [R] Nysha [A] Shreya [D] Dharsh [I] Kanasu [O]. The numbers add up to 3+1+2+2+6 = 14. Ben buys Ajay (7) for 7 and banks 7. The played cards, the buy and the unplayed cards all go to Ben's discard pile. Banked so far: Ben 11.

  5. Asha holds Bn Sharada [T] Gopi [P] Adheesh [R] Ammlu [E] Naresh [A] Adhiraa [H] Nakul [A]. Asha spells APART with Nakul [A] Gopi [P] Naresh [A] Adheesh [R] Bn Sharada [T]. The numbers add up to 4+4+3+9+2 = 22. Asha buys Dhruv (6) for 6 and banks 16. The played cards, the buy and the unplayed cards all go to Asha's discard pile. Banked so far: Asha 34.

Level ladder

L1 · first game

First game: spend freely. Buying costs nothing, so you bank your whole score and still buy a card. Play 8, 6 or 5 rounds (two, three, four players).

L2 · standard

Standard game as written above.

L3 · expert

Expert: words must be four cards or longer, and nothing else changes. Duds become common, so a pair of vowels in the deck matters more.

Solo

Play ten turns alone. After every turn of yours, discard the leftmost card of the market row and fill the gap. Count your banked total. Bronze 110, Silver 140, Gold 160 (from 400 runs of a bot that knows every word in the kids list: its median was 158, so real players should find Gold hard).

Two players

Each player gets an eight card deck and the 8 spare start cards go back in the box. Play 14 rounds. Seat order makes no difference (51 to 49 in 200 games).

Maths and skills in this game

Addition of four and five small numbers. Spelling and word building. Weighing cost against benefit (investing points now for more points later).

Word Caravan

Spell a word of 3+ cards from your hand. Score = sum of numbers. Buy one market card costing no more than your score. Bank score minus price.

Stats for nerds: what the simulations showed

Lengths in this section are raw simulated times, without the learning and thinking allowance.

Simulated Buying and banking is a real choice: the adaptive bot beats never-buy and always-buy bots 75 to 95 percent; no one-line rule matches it.

SettingResult
Setting (kids word list, bots know every word)Result
3 players, 200 games: smart / never buy / always buy the best77.5% / 13.5% / 9.0% wins (even share 33%)
2 players, 200 games: smart vs never buy / always buy / random buys95% / 94% / 97% smart wins
4 players, 150 games: smart / never / always / random buys74% / 13% / 9% / 3% wins (even share 25%)
3 players: smart vs a fixed rule (buy best for first 4 tenths, then bank) vs never buy63% / 27% / 10%
Growth: average word score by turn, 3 smart bots, 600 games11.5 on turn 1, 16.4 on turn 3, 19.5 on turn 10 (no collapse)
Buying: smart bots buy 3.8 cards in ten turns; bought cards by number 5 to 922% / 24% / 20% / 21% / 13%; 55% vowels (market holds 40%)
Seat effect, 3 smart bots, 600 games35.1% / 34.6% / 30.2% (even 33.3%); two players 51% / 49%
Dud turns per turn2p 4%, 3p 5%, 4p 14% (hand seven); with hand six 4p was 18%
Length3p: 30 turns at about 35 seconds is 17 to 20 min; 2p 28 turns, 4p 32 turns
Level 1 (buying is free), 3 players, 150 games: always buy best / never / random73% / 10% / 17%: the obvious plan wins, as a first game should
Level 3 (4+ card words)smart 65% vs never 25% vs always 10%; duds rise to 19%

Not simulated. Real vocabulary and speed (bots find the best word in the kids list instantly, which makes duds rarer and scores higher than a family table will see); table talk; how much waiting feels like downtime when a player hunts for a word; whether people enjoy an engine that takes six turns to show its payoff.

Tuning: dropped the keep-two-cards rule; hand six to seven. The big finding is that the points-or-cards decision is not obvious. Buying the highest card every time is the worst plan tested (about 9% wins at 3 players) because the price eats the points. Never buying is almost as weak. Four players is the weakest count (short 6 card decks, 14% duds); I would call two or three the best. A human will see more duds than the bots do; if the table finds them annoying, allow one free swap of three cards per game.

Tuning log

  • round 1: first draft kept up to two good cards in hand between turns and used a hand of six. The keep rule did not help (the smart bot won 83% with no keeping and 77% with keeping two), so it was cut to save rules. Hand six gave 9.5% dud turns at three players and 18% at four with the kids word list.

  • round 2: hand size six to seven (kids word list, three players). Dud turns fell from 9% to 5%, four-player duds from 18% to 14%, and the buy-smart bot's win share against never-buy and buy-the-best bots rose from 69% to 78%. Kept seven.

  • round 3: not needed. Checked that the three obvious simple plans (never buy, always buy the best card, buy for the first four tenths of the game then bank) all lose clearly to a bot that weighs card number, letter and turns left, so the buy decision is not solved by a one-line rule.

How it differs from games already in the set

  • Pen and Plume: also a market take and spend, but Caravan builds a deck of letters and spells with it.

  • Signal Fire and Wordwalk: single-word races; Caravan is a 20 minute engine game.

Ratings

From memory, close to Paperback (about 1.8). Four short rules but a real planning layer (when to stop buying); teach in about four minutes.

10 minus 1 teach time over three minutes, minus 1 for the score sheet, minus 1 for downtime while others hunt for words, minus 1 for four players (14% duds).

The invest-or-bank choice is the engine and it works; a word that pays for your next buy is satisfying. Weakest part: it is a solitary puzzle on your own hand, interaction is only the shared market, and fast word-finders will outpace slow ones.

Card changes requested: none

Party sheets

Two big-print A4 sheets for the party table: Shared Expedition (Avalanche Pass for a crowd) and Fox in the Camp. Each sheet carries the QR code to this page.

Previews are below.

Shared Expedition

Everyone climbs one path. Shuffle all 54 cards and give the cards to a Guide. Play 5 rounds. Each step the Guide flips a card onto the path. The second card of one animal in a round is a rumble. The third is an avalanche: everyone still on the path scores nothing and the round ends. After each safe card, everyone secretly chooses to stay or leave. Leavers split the total of all the numbers on the path, rounding down, and any leftover stays. Most points after 5 rounds wins.

What the simulation showed

  • Fair across unequal teams: the avalanche depends only on the third card of any one animal, so teams of 8 or 10 cards do not tilt it.
  • Five simulated players, each leaving at a random target. With the third card of an animal as the avalanche, a round lasted a median of 7 cards (middle half 5 to 8), and 75% of rounds ended in an avalanche. With the second card, rounds lasted 4 cards and 97% ended in an avalanche, far too harsh. So the third card is the rule. The high avalanche rate is partly because the simulated players never leave early enough, so real players will usually do better.
  • The rumble warning on the second card was added after the simulation as a teaching cue. It does not change the rules.

Fox in the Camp

Full rules are on the Fox in the Camp page and on game card 7.

3. How the cards are balanced

  • Numbers. Six cards of each number from 1 to 9. Twins add to 9 (1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5). The three double-nine faces (Rihansh, Gowri, Adheesh) are the exception: both of their cards are 9. There is no 5 plus 5 bond.

  • Colours. Each card has two different colours. Every colour appears exactly twice at every number, so 18 times overall. All 15 colour pairs are used 3 or 4 times.

  • Suits. The same structure as colours: every suit exactly twice at each number, two different suits per card, all 15 suit pairs used 3 or 4 times.

  • Uniqueness. No two cards share the same colour pair and suit pair together, so a call of “colour pair plus suit pair” always points to one card.

  • Faces and teams. 27 faces with exactly two cards each. Three teams have four faces (8 cards) and three have five (10 cards). Uneven team sizes were accepted rather than forcing an unnatural split.

  • Letters. English letter frequency, so words can be made. There are 20 vowels, and every team has 3 or 4 of them (Tigers 3, Elephants 3, Bears 3, Monkeys 4, Peacocks 4, Cobras 3). A child’s two cards never share a letter.

  • Serials and backs. Serials 1 to 54 are shuffled, so they are unrelated to the card number or card ID. Each back is a unique pattern of three suits twice over, which makes it public information about the card in someone’s hand.

4. How often two cards match

Across all 1,431 pairs of cards (every pair, counted from the manifest):

Share at least one colour59.1%

Share colour and suit35.8%
Same number9.4%
Numbers add to 910.1%
Same team15.3%

Only 11.8% of pairs share nothing at all on colour, suit, number, team or face. Because colour and suit match so often, the dice choose what to look for, and the card supplies the decision. The rarer matches (the same number, a bond to 9, a twin) are used as the exact, exciting calls.

5. How the dice map onto the cards

The four dice are plain d6s with no symbols. A game says what a die means, and the key cards turn the number into a colour, a suit or a team. The mapping is the same everywhere.

Each colour is on 18 cards, each suit on 18 cards, and a team is on 8 or 10 cards. So a colour die and a suit die are equally fair, and a team die is slightly lopsided by design: Monkeys, Peacocks and Cobras come up on 10 cards, Tigers, Elephants and Bears on 8.

Why this balance matters

Because every number, colour and suit appears evenly, no card is a favourite and no seat has an edge, which is why bots find most games close to fair. Because several attributes overlap in different ways, the same 54 cards support a matching game for a 5-year-old and a betting game for grown-ups without changing anything on the cards.

Visuals and expressions

How the cards look

Each card is a small comic panel: a child dressed as an explorer, a place in Bangalore behind them, and a border that tells you the colours. Every visual decision is there because a game needs it.

The style

The art is ligne claire: flat colour, one even navy outline and simple eyes, with no shading to speak of. The palette is taken from Bangalore itself: sand, khaki, moss, terracotta, teal-grey, leather brown and cream. The portraits are muted a little so the six game colours on the borders stay the loudest thing on the card. They are real children, redrawn from photographs with an AI image tool, and the programme draws every border, number, nine-frame, badge and letter itself, so nothing printed on a card is ever invented by the image tool.
